sample_chunks.authors: Vincenzo Marciano, Xiaoming Zhang, et al.
sample_chunks.category: AI in Medical Diagnosis and Medical Imaging
sample_chunks.text_content:
Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (10/2026)
Retrieval-Augmented Correction for Generalist Medical
Image Segmentation
Vincenzo Marcianò
vincenzo.marciano@eurecom.fr
EURECOM
Sorbonne Université
King’s College London
Xiaoming Zhang
xiaoming.zhang@eurecom.fr
EURECOM
Sorbonne Université
Michela Antonelli
michela.antonelli@kcl.ac.uk
King’s College London
Sébastien Ourselin
sebastien.ourselin@kcl.ac.uk
King’s College London
Maria A. Zuluaga
maria.zuluaga@eurecom.fr
EURECOM
King’s College London
Reviewed on OpenReview: https: // openreview. net/ forum? id= PeDqE0SQRe
Abstract
Automated segmentation is routinely used as the first step in quantitative image-based
clinical workflows, where predicted masks are subsequently reviewed and corrected by human
operators.
Automated correction of the residual structural errors is currently addressed
one anatomy at a time, so the number of trained correctors scales with the number of
segmentation targets.
We present GRACE, a retrieval-augmented refiner that edits an
input mask under context drawn from a shared knowledge base of verified prior cases.
The refiner is trained once on a multi-organ corpus spanning compact organs, cavities,
branching vessels, and tumour lesions. In the held-out dataset-transfer evaluation, three
held-out datasets query a fixed knowledge base built from training data only. A separate
leave-one-anatomy-out experiment tests parameter-free index extension: verified cases of
an unseen solid organ enter the knowledge base, and the refiner stays frozen. A shapeaware retrieval projector ranks the neighbours. This light projection head sits on a frozen
multimodal encoder and maps embedding similarity to the shape agreement of the masks.
Thus, the knowledge base returns cases that the refiner can use as a shape prior. We evaluate
GRACE on 18 public datasets spanning CT, MRI and ultrasound, including three held-out
CT/MRI datasets for held-out dataset transfer, using nine refinement configurations and
seven upstream segmentors that span weak, mid, and strong operating regimes. We report
each change with the DSC of its input mask. On the weak tier, the input DSC is 0.386 and
GRACE adds up to +0.35 DSC. On a strong segmentor, the input DSC is 0.932 and the
mean change is small. Transfer to an imaging modality that is absent from training and
from the index is partial and depends on the anatomy. We present it as an open research
direction.
Our results suggest retrieval-conditioned refinement is a practical alternative
to anatomy-specific correction models. Open-source code and implementation available at
https://github.com/robustml-eurecom/grace.
1

sample_chunks.paper_title: Retrieval-Augmented Correction for Generalist Medical Image Segmentation
sample_chunks.authors: Vincenzo Marciano, Xiaoming Zhang, et al.
sample_chunks.category: AI in Medical Diagnosis and Medical Imaging
sample_chunks.text_content:
Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (10/2026)
1
Introduction
Medical image segmentation has advanced rapidly with deep learning (Isensee et al., 2021; Hatamizadeh
et al., 2022; Ma et al., 2024), becoming the de facto approach for extracting anatomical structures in clinical
workflows. Although widely adopted, state-of-the-art models remain prone to structural errors and artifacts
that require costly manual correction before clinical use (Azad et al., 2023; Galati et al., 2022). These artifacts
typically manifest as over-segmentation, under-segmentation, boundary imprecision, or topological violations.
Challenging cases involve ambiguous boundaries, small structures, or out-of-distribution pathologies that
deviate from the expected normative anatomy (Galati et al., 2022).
Despite these advances in segmentation accuracy, automated correction of segmentation errors remains an
open problem. Unlike segmentation, which predicts pixel-wise labels from image intensities, correction requires reasoning about anatomical plausibility and restoring coherent structures from imperfect predictions.
Despite growing interest in automated segmentation quality control and refinement (Valindria et al., 2017;
Robinson et al., 2018; Audelan & Delingette, 2019; Liu et al., 2019; Robinson et al., 2019; Larrazabal et al.,
2020; Painchaud et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020; Fournel et al., 2021; Lin et al., 2023; Qiu et al., 2023;
Marcianò et al., 2026), the field currently lacks generalisable, fully-automated solutions.
Existing approaches largely fall into two restrictive paradigms. On the one hand, single-anatomy specialists (Larrazabal et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020; Painchaud et al., 2020) learn to encode anatomical shape
priors, which are then used to validate and improve anatomically implausible segmentations. However, while
effective, these approaches require training a dedicated model from scratch for each new organ or imaging
modality. Another set of techniques interprets refinement as a signal restoration problem, where given a
corrupted mask, the goal is to recover the anatomically plausible structure (Yuan et al., 2020; Terris et al.,
2026). While such models demonstrate strong capabilities in generic signal restoration, they do not explicitly
incorporate structured anatomical priors, which are critical for correcting geometric segmentation errors.
We argue that medical segmentation refinement can be naturally formulated as a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) problem (Lewis et al., 2020). Given a corrupted segmentation, a model retrieves anatomically
similar cases from a knowledge base and conditions the refinement process on this retrieved context. In this
way, anatomy-specific information is provided at inference time rather than being encoded into the model
parameters, enabling a single refiner to operate across organs and imaging modalities represented in the
knowledge base. Although retrieval has become a powerful paradigm for knowledge-intensive learning, its
potential for anatomy-agnostic segmentation refinement remains largely unexplored. To this end, we present
GRACE (Generalist Retrieval-Augmented Correction for Segmentation Errors) as a retrieval-conditioned
segmentation-refinement framework (Fig. 1) that separates anatomy-aware retrieval from the refiner representation. The framework itself does not commit to a particular refinement representation: pixel-space
and latent-space refiners are treated as interchangeable instantiations of a common retrieval interface. Our
contributions are, thus, summarised as follows:
• A retrieval-augmented framework for segmentation refinement whose common interface supports both
pixel-space and latent-space refiners. The retrieval step supplies anatomy-specific information at inference
time, allowing a single anatomy-agnostic refiner to generalise across the organs and imaging modalities
represented in the knowledge base. The framework can use a fixed knowledge base or incorporate verified
support cases without retraining the refiner.
• Exemplar-conditioned refinement. The retrieved mask enters the refiner as a spatial channel and gives the
shape prior for the correction. When we set this channel to zero, the refiner loses 40% of its gain at the
most severe preset (Sec. 4.5). A shape-aware retrieval projector on a frozen multimodal encoder selects
the same-class case. Its contribution is smaller, and we report it as a component ablation (Table 5).
• Three complementary instantiations of the proposed framework spanning deterministic pixel-space refinement, deterministic latent refinement, and latent flow matching. We compare all three across the
upstream operating regimes and on the trade-off between accuracy and runtime.
• Extensive validation across 18 public datasets, multiple imaging modalities, seven upstream segmentors,
and nine refinement configurations, including three held-out datasets for held-out dataset transfer and a
leave-one-modality-out study. We also analyse retrieval, knowledge-base scaling, robustness to a wrong

Related Work
Segmentation quality control and refinement.
Segmentation refinement is a distinct problem from
segmentation itself and has been approached along three main lines. The first is classical, hand-designed
post-processing that enforces geometric or topological constraints on the raw prediction: morphological operations and connected-component filtering to remove small false-positive blobs or retain the largest anatomically plausible regions (Isensee et al., 2021; Dulau et al., 2023) and topological penalties ensuring continuous
boundaries (Hu et al., 2019; Li et al., 2025). These methods are fast and interpretable but cannot recover
structure that was never in the raw prediction, and their handcrafted rules do not transfer across anatomies.
The second line replaces handcrafted rules with learned anatomical priors, typically encoded through autoencoders, variational autoencoders, or more recently latent diffusion models (Oktay et al., 2018; Larrazabal
et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020; Painchaud et al., 2020; Galati & Zuluaga, 2021; Marcianò et al., 2026). These
methods learn a manifold of anatomically plausible segmentations that guides refinement. However, as the
manifold is typically learned for a single anatomy, these methods require retraining for each new organ or
imaging modality. Finally, the third line does not consider a dedicated corrector, approaching the problem
via test-time adaptation (TTA) (Karani et al., 2021). Instead, the upstream segmentor is briefly refitted on
each test volume to close a domain gap. TTA improves segmentation performance without producing a corrected mask directly. Therefore, it is complementary to a refiner rather than a substitute for it. GRACE sits
in the refiner slot, replaces the per-anatomy autoencoder with a single retrieval-conditioned refiner trained
once on multi-organ data, and preserves the conservative behaviour of morphological post-processing on
inputs that do not need correction.
Foundation models in medical imaging.
Recent foundation and generalist models have broadened
anatomical coverage through diverse paradigms, including prompt-based segmentation (Ma et al., 2024;
Wang et al., 2025b; Ma et al., 2025; Wong et al., 2024), large-scale supervised learning (Wasserthal et al.,

2023), few-shot segmentation (Butoi et al., 2023), and text-conditioned segmentation (Rokuss et al., 2026).
While these methods demonstrate broad generalisation across anatomies and modalities, they are designed
for forward segmentation prediction rather than post-hoc correction and refinement. RAM (Terris et al.,
2026) extends the foundation-model paradigm to generic inverse imaging problems without task-specific
training, but operates in pixel space and does not explicitly exploit anatomical context for segmentation
correction.
Retrieval-augmented learning in medical imaging.
Retrieval-augmented learning (Lewis et al., 2020)
has recently been explored in medical AI for report generation (Xia et al., 2025; Xiong et al., 2024; Hsu
et al., 2025) and few-shot segmentation from retrieved annotated examples (Ahmed et al., 2026; Zhao et al.,
2025). In these settings, retrieval provides external knowledge to improve prediction or support inference.
In contrast, retrieval for direct segmentation refinement has received little attention.
GRACE retrieves
anatomically similar cases to provide inference-time context for correcting an existing segmentation.
Latent-space exploration in medical imaging.
Compact latent representations have become a standard paradigm for modelling anatomically plausible structures in medical imaging. Early formulations use
variational autoencoders (VAEs) as shape priors, learning latent manifolds of plausible organ shapes for
segmentation refinement and shape reconstruction (Painchaud et al., 2020; Larrazabal et al., 2020; Beetz
et al., 2022). Vector-Quantised VAEs (Razavi et al., 2019) and multi-scale volumetric encoders (Pinaya et al.,
2022; Fernandez et al., 2024) extended this framework to high-resolution 3D image and mask generation.
Latent diffusion models (Rombach et al., 2022) and, more recently, rectified flow models (Lipman et al.,
2023) enable efficient generative sampling directly in these compact latent spaces, making full-volume 3D
synthesis computationally tractable (Guo et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025a; Tang et al., 2025). Conditioning strategies have subsequently evolved from partial-noise editing, such as SDEdit (Meng et al., 2022), to
retrieval-guided generation, where retrieved exemplars provide structural guidance during sampling (Molino
et al., 2026). GRACE builds on this latter paradigm by performing class-filtered, shape-aware retrieval to
guide segmentation refinement, and supports deterministic pixel-space, deterministic latent-space, and latent
flow-based refiners within a unified framework.
3
Method
3.1

knowledge base K of previously verified cases. The framework decomposes this task into three components:

3.2
Anatomy-aware knowledge base
For each verified case, the binary mask is overlaid as a contour on each corresponding slice of the paired
scan, aggregated in a 3D volume as suggested in Sellergren et al. (2025), and the composite is paired with a
structured textual prompt:
You are an expert radiologist.
The highlighted region (red contours) represents:
{class_name}.
Describe its visual characteristics.
The composite is processed by a frozen multimodal encoder P. Unless otherwise stated, we use MedGemma
4B (Sellergren et al., 2025) to obtain raw embeddings ei ∈R2560. The main pipeline maps these embeddings
to 256-dimensional shape-aware vectors using ϕψ (Sec. 3.3); the projected vectors are L2-normalised and
indexed with FAISS (Douze et al., 2026). Raw-space indexing is used only in the corresponding ablations.
FAISS is a similarity-search library.
It keeps the normalised embeddings in a flat inner-product index.
Because the vectors have unit length, the inner-product search returns the cosine nearest neighbours. The
index makes the top-k search fast enough for use at inference. Figure 2 illustrates the resulting embedding
topology via a k-nearest-neighbour connectivity graph and hierarchical clustering, revealing strong intrinsic
modality alignment and an emergent anatomical hierarchy within the embedding space. Extending K with
a verified support case requires only embedding and indexing that case, not retraining the refiner.
Construction protocol.
In the main experiments and the held-out-dataset evaluation, cases enter the
knowledge base only from the training splits listed in Sec. 4.1; validation cases, test cases, and every case
from the three held-out datasets in Sec. 4.3 are excluded. The leave-one-anatomy-out support experiment
(Sec. 4.4) and the optional longitudinal-memory analysis (Appendix G) are explicitly identified extensions of
this fixed-index protocol. Their indexed support cases are disjoint from the corresponding evaluation queries.
Multi-class masks are decomposed into per-class binary instances, and each indexed instance is one entry.
A same-class index is materialised at indexing time, avoiding class filtering over the full database during
inference. No scored evaluation query is indexed as its own retrieval candidate. In the reported configuration,
K contains N=3,913 per-class instances drawn from the training splits of the 15 training datasets (Table 12),
out of the 11,900 non-empty instances of these splits (Appendix F).

3.3
Shape-aware retrieval projector
P denotes the frozen MedGemma encoder only. It maps a pair of composite image and prompt to a raw
2560-dimensional embedding. The L2 normalisation, the projector ϕψ and the FAISS index are separate
stages that operate on the output of P. Cosine similarity on the raw embeddings orders the neighbours
by general multimodal appearance. The refiner uses a same-class mask as a spatial exemplar, so it needs
neighbours with a similar shape. We fit a projector ϕψ : Rd →Rd′ on K so that cosine similarity in the
projected space approximates shape-Dice between the underlying masks:

and scale are removed and only shape is preserved. ϕψ is a 3-layer MLP (hidden width 512, output d′=256)
trained for 20 epochs on uniformly-sampled node pairs from K. The projected vectors are L2-normalised,
so the inner product in Eq. 2 is their cosine similarity. The projector is fitted after the raw knowledge-base
embeddings have been constructed. Its normalised outputs replace the raw vectors as FAISS keys, leaving
the refiner and its training unchanged.
3.4
Refiner interface
The retrieved Yr enters Rθ as a spatial conditioning channel that supplies a shape prior, while the sequence
{erj}k
j=1 provides semantic context through cross-attention, whenever supported by the underlying architecture. This interface is compatible with both supervised feedforward networks trained on pixel-wise labels
and conditional generative models that sample from p(Y | Y ∗, X, Yr, {erj}k
j=1). The refiner may operate
directly in pixel space or in a compact latent space obtained through a mask autoencoder. In the latter case,
the retrieved Yr is projected through the same encoder. The latent refinement interface is independent of
the particular autoencoder architecture; throughout this work, the latent variants use the frozen encoder of
the MAISI VAE (Guo et al., 2025) together with a mask-tuned decoder. Any compatible mask autoencoder
can be substituted without modifying the refinement procedure.
These two factors, the refinement paradigm (deterministic or generative) and the representation (pixel or
latent space), can be combined to instantiate different refinement architectures within the same retrieval
framework. In our work, they give rise to three variants: a deterministic pixel-space network (GRACE-U), a
deterministic latent autoencoder (GRACE-M), and a latent flow-matching model (GRACE-M-D). GRACEU is a 3D U-Net with three input channels: the corrupted mask, the image and the retrieved exemplar. It
gives a foreground logit for each voxel in one forward pass. GRACE-M encodes the corrupted mask and the
exemplar into a 4×243 latent with a frozen encoder. A small module fuses the two latents, and a mask-tuned
decoder gives the refined mask. GRACE-M-D uses the same latent interface but integrates a learned velocity
field with an ODE solver. Thus, several runs on one input give a set of plausible refinements. All three
variants use the same retrieval context. Appendix A gives the full architectures.
3.5
Two-phase training and corruption schedule
Training Rθ directly on corrupted masks produced by one specific upstream segmentor risks injection bias:
the refiner overfits to the failure modes of that segmentor. To prevent this bias, we train the refiner on
synthetic corruptions of the ground-truth masks. A corruption combines morphological erosion and dilation,
elastic boundary deformation, boundary noise, false-positive blobs and axis-aligned slice dropout (Jebril
et al., 2025). Three severity presets (default, mid, strong) define the synthetic-corruption experiments; a
fourth training preset (mixed) samples uniformly across the three severities. Two more presets, very_strong
and extreme, go beyond the range of the training severities. We use them only for evaluation, in the analyses
of Sec. 4.5. Representative synthetic corruptions are shown in Fig. 5.
Training has two phases. Phase 1 trains the refiner, and Phase 2 fits the retrieval projector ϕψ of Sec. 3.3.
In Phase 1, we train the refiner from random initialisation for 100 epochs at 963 resolution. We use AdamW
with a learning rate of 10−4, a cosine schedule, batch size 8, gradient clipping at 1.0 and mixed precision.

input with probability 0.95, so a small fraction of clean inputs keeps the identity behaviour. The exemplar is
set to zero with probability 0.10. Thus, the refiner stays usable when retrieval gives no result, and it cannot
use the exemplar as a shortcut. The corruption changes for each sample and each epoch. In Phase 2, we fit
ϕψ for 20 epochs on pairs of knowledge-base cases (Eq. 2). Phase 2 does not change the refiner.
4
Experiments
4.1
Experimental setup
Datasets.
The training corpus covers 15 public datasets across CT, MRI, and US and contains 3,866
volumes over 38 anatomical structures across the abdomen, thorax, pelvis, brain, and cardiac chambers
(Table 12 in Appendix F). Multi-class labels are converted to per-organ binary instances; for multi-channel
Medical Segmentation Decathlon (MSD) (Antonelli et al., 2022) tasks the T2-weighted modality is used.
Three datasets are excluded from both training and indexing and are used for held-out dataset-transfer evaluation: ProstateX (Armato III et al., 2018) (346 subjects, multiparametric prostate MRI), CHAOS (Kavur
et al., 2021) (40 CT subjects, liver / kidneys / spleen; CHAOS also has MRI scans of these organs, which
Sec. 4.4 uses), and LUMIERE (Suter et al., 2022) (91 GBM patients across 2–20 longitudinal visits each,
599 timepoints).
Metrics.
We report Dice coefficient (DSC, ↑), 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95, ↓), and signed
deltas over the raw upstream prediction. Unless a caption states otherwise, “±” denotes the sample standard
deviation across cases. Figure 3 instead shows variability across anatomy–dataset pairs, and Table 6 reports
runtime variability across repeated runs. HD95 is reported in millimetres for real-segmentor evaluations and
in voxels for synthetic-corruption analyses.
Upstream segmentors.
Seven segmentors span three operating regimes.
Weak: a MONAI (Cardoso
et al., 2022) 3D U-Net trained for 30 epochs on 10% of each organ split (U-Net@30). Mid: MedSAM2 (Ma
et al., 2025) and ScribblePrompt (Wong et al., 2024) used with an oracle bounding box derived from the
ground truth on the highest-coverage axial slice, and SwinUNETR-BTCV (Hatamizadeh et al., 2022). ScribblePrompt and SwinUNETR-BTCV are used for the held-out dataset evaluation (Sec. 4.3). Strong: TotalSegmentator (Wasserthal et al., 2023) in fast mode on CT organs; a MONAI 3D U-Net trained for 150
epochs on the full split (U-Net@150); a MONAI SegResNet trained for 150 epochs on the full split (SegResNet). This split characterises GRACE when the input carries little usable signal as well as when it is close
to correct.
What the refiner is trained on.
We split each dataset case-wise into disjoint training and test parts.
(i) For Table 1 and the synthetic analyses, one refiner trains on the training split, and we evaluate it on the
test split. It sees other cases of the same datasets, but never the evaluated cases. (ii) For Table 2, we apply
the same refiner to three datasets that are absent from training and from the index. (iii) For Table 3 (Block
A), we retrain the refiner from scratch for each held-out anatomy. That anatomy is absent from training
and from the index. At test time, only support cases enter the index, and they are disjoint from the queries.
(iv) Block B of Table 3 applies the same protocol to a full modality. We rebuild the index for each protocol.
Refiner baselines.
Nine refiner variants are compared: (i) no refinement (raw upstream); (ii) morphological (binary closing then binary opening with a 3×3×3 structuring element); (iii) test-time augmentation
(TTAug) with eight views and mean aggregation; (iv) PostDAE (Larrazabal et al., 2020); (v) RAM (Terris
et al., 2026); (vi) a MONAI 3D U-Net refiner without retrieval (U-Net w/o RAG) that takes (Y ∗, X) as
input; (vii) the same U-Net with the retrieved exemplar as a third input channel (GRACE-U); (viii) a latent autoencoder refiner that fuses the exemplar in the latent bottleneck before decoding (GRACE-M); (ix)
the same latent refiner with flow-matching inference (GRACE-M-D), averaged over three ODE seeds. No
baseline receives the target class as input. PostDAE uses the class implicitly, through one model for each
anatomy. This is the strongest form of class conditioning. The morphological, TTAug and RAM baselines
cannot use a label. U-Net w/o RAG receives only (Y ∗, X). GRACE uses the class to select the retrieval

PostDAE.

Thus, it projects each mask onto its learned manifold. On an almost correct input, this projection removes

on volumetric multi-organ data. This is the gap that our work addresses.
Comparison of the variants.
The three variants achieve comparable aggregate performance but differ in
their behaviour on severely degraded inputs. Consistent with Table 1, GRACE-M produces the larger mean
lift on the mid and most of strong tiers, while all three variants have small non-negative mean changes on
the strongest segmentor, TotalSegmentator. Mechanistically, GRACE-U is a single-pass feedforward network
and produces more conservative corrections when little reliable signal is available; GRACE-M refines in a
frozen latent space and can synthesise anatomically plausible completions guided by the retrieved exemplar.
GRACE-M-D stays within 0.01 DSC of GRACE-M and needs about seven times more compute (Table 6).

index extension. The refiner receives no gradient from a, but the index gives it examples of a. The support
cases are disjoint from the evaluation queries. Both variants improve every held-out anatomy, with mean

Contribution of the exemplar.
We set the retrieval channel of the trained model to zero and keep all
other settings. This isolates the part of the gain that the exemplar gives. At the evaluation-only extreme
severity, averaged over all structures, the exemplar gives 40% of the improvement, and the refiner alone
gives the rest. On the four organs of Table 11, the share is from 39% (pancreas) to 62% (kidneys, spleen).
In Appendix E, a mask-only encoder is close to MedGemma. Thus, the contribution comes mainly from
the exemplar and less from the multimodal retrieval space. We therefore describe GRACE as exemplarconditioned refinement. The refiner uses the retrieved exemplar as a shape prior, and retrieval selects it from
the 15 indexed datasets.
Robustness to a wrong class query.
In a fully automatic pipeline, the class label can be wrong. We
keep the trained refiner and compare three query conditions on four organs at four severities. The conditions
are the correct class, a random wrong class and no exemplar (Table 11). At the extreme preset, the input
DSC is from 0.11 to 0.31. The correct class gives the largest gain on every organ. A wrong class gives 0.077
to 0.151 DSC less. On the compact organs (liver, kidneys, spleen), a wrong-class exemplar still recovers 50 to
72% of the correct-class gain over no exemplar. On the pancreas, which is small and variable, a wrong-class
exemplar is slightly worse than no exemplar. Thus, the robustness to a wrong class depends on the shape of
the target. The stabilisation of refinement under extreme class noise is an open question.
4.6
Ablation studies
We quantify the contribution of the main design choices underlying GRACE through a series of controlled
ablation studies. Specifically, we evaluate the shape-aware retrieval projector while keeping the remainder
of the framework unchanged; the choice of retrieval encoder is reported in Appendix E and the comparison
of refinement paradigms in Appendix A.

Within each checkpoint column, the refiner and retrieval protocol are fixed; paired rows for a given encoder

4.7
Qualitative overview
Figure 5 illustrates representative refinements produced by GRACE across CT (Liver, Pancreas, Spleen) and
MRI (Heart LA, Prostate PZ). For each case, one synthetic corruption and three real upstream segmentors
(U-Net@150, MedSAM2, and TotalSegmentator or SegResNet) are shown together with the corresponding
GRACE-U refinement, with DSC and HD95 overlaid. Three visual patterns recur across the five rows: on
the weakest inputs, retrieval provides a strong anatomical prior and recovers organ topology even when the
raw prediction contains no usable structure; on intermediate inputs, refinement sharpens boundaries and
closes local defects; on strong inputs, refinement makes only minimal changes, consistent with the small
deltas of Sec. 4.2.
5
Discussion and Conclusions
Discussion.
A central question motivating this work is whether retrieval-conditioned refinement can generalise beyond anatomy-specific correction models. Our experiments indicate that the greatest benefit of
retrieval arises when the upstream segmentation is unreliable, precisely the regime in which manual correction is most costly in clinical practice (Galati et al., 2022), while already accurate predictions receive only
minimal changes. The retrieved exemplar gives 40% of the gain at the most severe preset. The correct class
already gives a strong shape prior, and the shape-aware projector adds a smaller gain in that class.
When is refinement preferable to a strong segmentor?
We see four settings. (i) No strong segmentor
exists for the target. TotalSegmentator covers CT anatomy, but not cardiac chambers in ultrasound or most
lesion classes. (ii) The upstream is a black box, for example a vendor model without access to weights
or training data. GRACE needs only the output mask. (iii) A new anatomy must be supported without
retraining (Sec. 4.4). (iv) Promptable models receive imperfect prompts. Our MedSAM2 and ScribblePrompt
results use an oracle bounding box. With real prompts, their masks are probably worse and closer to the
range where refinement helps. For this reason, we put them in the mid tier. For strong CT segmentors, we
do not claim an improvement. GRACE keeps good masks almost unchanged on average, but it degrades
some of them (Appendix D).

Limitations.
The effectiveness of retrieval depends on the diversity of the knowledge base: anatomies or
pathological presentations that are not represented in K provide weaker retrieval context, and the refiner
then remains closer to the raw upstream prediction. Verified support cases can be added to K without
updating the refiner, but genuinely novel morphologies may still require retraining. At the high end of input
quality, 3.8% of the cases with an input DSC above 0.8 lose more than 0.05 DSC (Appendix D). A mechanism
that skips refinement for a probably correct input is a logical next step. GRACE-M-D needs about seven
times more compute than GRACE-M, and its results change with the ODE seed. Transfer to a held-out
modality is partial on MRI and fails on ultrasound. The leave-one-anatomy-out setting needs 118 to 302
verified masks of the held-out organ. We present both as open research directions.
Conclusions.
We introduced GRACE, a retrieval-conditioned framework that replaces anatomy-specific
correctors with a single refiner guided by an anatomy-aware knowledge base. Across upstream segmentors
and held-out datasets, it improved unreliable predictions while leaving accurate ones largely unchanged, and
verified support cases extend the knowledge base without a parameter update.

Appendix Overview
Appendix A compares the three refiner paradigms (deterministic pixel-space, deterministic latent autoencoder, and latent flow-matching) as instantiations of the refiner interface. It reports the mechanistic reasoning
behind the empirical ordering in Sec. 4.2, as well as the associated computational costs of each variant. Appendix B reports the architectural ablation of the latent RAG refiner behind the design choices in Sec. 3.4.
Appendix C explains the ultrasound result of the leave-one-modality-out experiment. Appendix D gives the
case-level failure analysis. Appendix E gives the retrieval-encoder comparison and the per-organ class-query
results. Appendix F summarises the dataset scope, per-dataset case and class counts, and the aggregate
number of non-empty binary-mask instances. Finally, Appendix G reports an emergent temporal-memory
property of the retrieval pipeline on the LUMIERE dataset.
A
Refiner paradigms: deterministic, latent autoencoder, latent flow-matching
The refiner interface (Sec. 3.4) admits three concrete instantiations. They are evaluated with the same data,
corruption schedule, and retrieval pipeline, but differ in network architecture, refinement representation (pixel
or latent), training objective, and inference procedure (deterministic forward pass or generative sampling).
The first instantiation, GRACE-U, is a supervised 3D U-Net trained on pixel-wise labels that consumes
the corrupted mask, the image, and the retrieved exemplar as channel-concatenated inputs and returns a
per-voxel foreground logit. It uses one forward pass with no latent codec or sampler. Its single-pass design
makes it the fastest variant and empirically produces the more conservative behaviour described in Sec. 4.2.
Consistent with Table 1, GRACE-M produces the larger mean DSC gains on the mid tier and on two of the
three strong segmentors, whereas GRACE-U leads on the weak tier and on U-Net@150; all three variants
have small non-negative mean changes on the strong tier.
The second instantiation, GRACE-M, moves the refinement into the mask latent space. A frozen encoder
maps the corrupted mask and the retrieved exemplar into a compact 4×243 latent. A small fusion module
(concat, FiLM, or cross-attention) combines the two latents, while a mask-tuned decoder returns the refined
mask. Since the decoded output is drawn from the learned mask manifold, this paradigm can produce a
plausible completion even when the input carries almost no signal. The reported latent variants use a frozen
MAISI encoder together with a decoder fine-tuned on the binary-mask distribution (Appendix B).
The third instantiation, GRACE-M-D, replaces the deterministic latent decode with an ODE integration
of a learned velocity field conditioned on the retrieved exemplar, following flow matching (Lipman et al.,
2023) for latent generative models. Inference becomes stochastic in the choice of initial noise, so a batch of
runs on the same input yields a family of plausible refinements; averaging or selecting among them supports
the sample-level uncertainty estimates that neither deterministic paradigm provides.
On the aggregate
benchmark in Table 6, its 30-step aggregate DSC closely matches the deterministic GRACE-M decode
while inference is roughly seven times slower; its practical value therefore lies in downstream workflows that
consume uncertainty rather than in additional aggregate DSC.
These architectural differences are reflected in the empirical behaviour observed across experiments. Table 1
supports regime-wise comparisons for the three variants: GRACE-M has the larger mean lift on the mid and
most of the strong tiers, while all three variants have small non-negative mean changes on the top performing
model (TotalSegmentator). On the aggregate benchmark of Table 6, averaged over three ODE seeds, the
30-step GRACE-M-D stays within 0.01 DSC of GRACE-M.
Inference runtime and computational cost.
Table 6 reports wall-clock inference time per case and
mean DSC for the three refiner paradigms. Measurements were obtained on a single NVIDIA A100 with
batch size one using ten representative cases (one per MSD organ) from a stratified 10% hold-out. Each
benchmark run covers those ten cases; runtime means and sample standard deviations are computed across
five repeated runs, with GPU synchronisation before each measurement. GRACE-U runs sub-second per case
using one forward pass, and GRACE-M adds a single deterministic latent decode. GRACE-M-D requires
several seconds at the 30-step operating point because of iterative ODE integration (see Table 6). All three

B
Architectural ablations of the latent RAG refiner
The refiner interface of Sec. 3.4 admits several concrete instantiations. This appendix reports the empirical
characterisation that motivates the choices adopted in the main paper. Three design axes are examined in
controlled comparisons: (i) how the retrieved exemplar Yr enters the refiner (fusion module); (ii) whether
inference uses the deterministic GRACE-M decode or the GRACE-M-D flow-matching trajectory; and (iii)
the training loss, exemplar selection, and velocity-network width for GRACE-M-D. Settings outside the axis
under study are held fixed within each comparison. The same fusion-module ablation is repeated on the
pixel-space variant GRACE-U for completeness.
Fusion module for RAG.
Three interfaces for injecting the retrieved exemplar into the refiner are
compared. The concat module stacks the encoded corrupted latent and the encoded exemplar latent along
the channel axis and applies a 1×1×1 convolution with identity initialisation so the refiner recovers the
corrupted-only forward pass at step zero. The FiLM module pools the encoded exemplar over the spatial
dimensions, passes it through a small MLP that emits per-channel scale and shift, and applies them to the
corrupted latent. The cross-attention module is a single-head projected attention layer with the corrupted
latent tokens as queries and the encoded exemplar tokens as keys and values. The pixel-space ablation
applies the corresponding conditioning operations to U-Net feature maps. Table 7 reports refined DSC for
both refiner variants. Concat gives the highest score for each variant and is retained as the default for its
accuracy, parameter economy, and interpretability. Additionally, Table 8 reports controlled combinations of
training changes for GRACE-M-D: the auxiliary Dice loss and the K-NN exemplar each improve the common
baseline, their combination improves it further, and widening the velocity network produces the highest score
at roughly twice the parameter count.
Decoder handling.
All reported latent variants use the frozen MAISI encoder with a decoder fine-tuned
on the binary-mask distribution; no frozen-decoder comparison is included in the reported ablations.
Inference procedure.
On the aggregate benchmark in Table 6, the 30-step flow-matching procedure
reaches 0.810 DSC versus 0.815 for the deterministic GRACE-M latent decode and is about seven times
slower. The deterministic procedure is therefore used for the reported GRACE-M numbers.

LeViT-UNet++: Towards Balanced Fine-Grained Details and Context for Efficient 
Medical Image Segmentation 
#Guoping Xu
1,2, Jinling Zhu
1, Liuyue Li
3 
1Hubei Key Laboratory of Intelligent Robot, School of Computer Science and 
Engineering, Wuhan Institute of Technology, Wuhan, Hubei, 430205, China 
2Key Laboratory of Symbolic Computation and Knowledge Engineering of Ministry 
of Education, Jilin University, Changchun, 130012, China 
3College of Computing and Data Science, Nanyang Technological University, 
Singapore, 639798, Singapore 
#Corresponding Author: xugp@wit.edu.cn 
Abstract 
Efficient medical image segmentation is essential for clinical applications requiring 
rapid and accurate delineation, including surgical navigation, radiation therapy, and realtime image-guided intervention. Despite substantial advances in convolutional neural 
networks and Transformers, achieving high segmentation accuracy with limited 
computational resources remains challenging. In particular, reducing model complexity 
often comes at the expense of fine-grained structural details and effective global context 
modeling, resulting in an unfavorable trade-off between computational efficiency and 
segmentation accuracy. To address this challenge, we propose LeViT-UNet++, an 
efficient encoder–decoder architecture designed to achieve a better balance between 
local detail preservation and global context modeling. Specifically, we introduce a Haar 
Wavelet Multi-Scale Downsampling (HWMD) module that explicitly decomposes feature 
representations into low- and high-frequency components and extracts multi-scale 
structural information to mitigate the loss of fine-grained details during downsampling. 
Furthermore, we develop a depthwise convolution-based decoder that efficiently 
integrates multi-scale global representations from Transformer blocks with local spatial 
features, enabling progressive feature refinement while reducing computational 
overhead. We evaluate LeViT-UNet++ on four medical image segmentation 
benchmarks—Synapse, ACDC, LA2018, and MSD Heart—using both 2D and 3D 
experimental settings. Extensive experiments show that the proposed approach yields 
competitive segmentation accuracy with a compact parameter footprint and fast 
inference speed. On the Synapse dataset, for instance, LeViT-UNet++ attains a DSC of 
76.57% with merely 8.025M parameters and an inference rate of 241.72 FPS, confirming 
its favorable accuracy–efficiency balance. This work demonstrates the effectiveness of 
integrating wavelet-based multi-scale feature extraction and lightweight local–global 
feature fusion for efficient medical segmentation. The source code will be publicly 
available at https://github.com/apple1986/levit_unet_pp. 
Keywords: medical image segmentation, light-weight network, convolution neural 
networks, transformer, wavelet transform, efficient segmentation

sample_chunks.authors: Guoping Xu, Jinling Zhu, et al.
sample_chunks.category: AI in Medical Diagnosis and Medical Imaging
sample_chunks.text_content:
1. Introduction 
Efficient medical image segmentation is essential for clinical applications that require 
rapid and accurate anatomical delineation, including surgical navigation, radiation 
therapy, and real-time image-guided intervention [1]. Over the past decade, encoder–
decoder architectures have become a dominant paradigm for medical image 
segmentation, with representative approaches such as U-Net [2], TransUNet [3] and Swin 
UNETR [4] demonstrating substantial improvements in segmentation accuracy. However, 
the pursuit of increasingly powerful feature representations has often been accompanied 
by growing computational and memory requirements, which can hinder the deployment 
of these models in resource-constrained and latency-sensitive clinical environments. 
Therefore, developing medical image segmentation networks that achieve a favorable 
balance between segmentation accuracy and computational efficiency remains an 
important research challenge, particularly for clinical applications requiring accurate and 
timely delineation under stringent computational constraints. 
Currently, convolutional, and Transformer-based architectures have emerged as the 
mainstream paradigms for medical image segmentation. Convolutional architectures 
primarily exploit local spatial interactions to progressively extract semantic 
representations through hierarchical feature downsampling [5] (see Figure 1 (a)). As the 
spatial resolution decreases, the number of feature channels typically increases, resulting 
in substantial parameter and computational costs in deeper stages. Transformer-based 
architectures offer an alternative mechanism for modeling long-range dependencies 
through token-level self-attention (see Figure 1 (b)). This enables effective global 
contextual modeling but generally introduces substantial computational and memory 
costs, particularly when processing high-resolution medical images [6]. Thus, neither 
purely convolutional nor purely Transformer-based architectures inherently provide an 
optimal solution for simultaneously preserving local structural details, capturing global 
contextual information, and maintaining computational efficiency. 
 
Figure 1. Three categories of segmentation architectures. (a) Pure convolution-based 
methods, represented by U-Net; (b) Pure Transformer-based methods, e.g., SETR [6]; 
(c) Convolution–Transformer hybrid methods, exemplified by LeViT-UNet [7]. Here, C 
denotes convolution-based blocks, and T represents Transformer-based blocks. 
Although the full architecture typically contains more than two such blocks, only two are 
shown for simplicity. 
These observations motivate the exploration of hybrid architectures that exploit the

sample_chunks.paper_title: LeViT-UNet++: Towards Balanced Fine-Grained Details and Context for Medical Image Segmentation
sample_chunks.authors: Guoping Xu, Jinling Zhu, et al.
sample_chunks.category: AI in Medical Diagnosis and Medical Imaging
sample_chunks.text_content:
complementary properties of convolution and Transformer representations. In particular, 
convolutional operations are well suited to capturing local spatial structures and finegrained anatomical boundaries, whereas Transformer-based representations provide 
broader contextual dependencies. An effective and efficient segmentation architecture 
should therefore integrate these complementary representations while minimizing 
redundant computation during feature extraction and decoding. The LeViT-UNet [7] (see 
Figure 1 (c)) represents an early effort to bridge convolutional and Transformer-based 
representations for efficient medical image segmentation. Specifically, it adopts vanilla 
LeViT [8] (a lightweight hybrid convolution–Transformer backbone originally designed for 
image classification) as the encoder and convolution-based blocks as the decoder, 
seeking to achieve a favorable trade-off between segmentation accuracy and 
computational efficiency. Its core design is based on the observation that convolutional 
operations can efficiently extract local spatial representations, while progressive 
downsampling reduces the spatial resolution of feature maps. Transformer blocks can 
subsequently model long-range dependencies on these low-resolution representations 
with substantially lower computational cost than applying global attention at high spatial 
resolutions. This hybrid design therefore provides an efficient means of combining local 
feature extraction with global contextual modeling for medical image segmentation. 
However, LeViT-UNet-like architectures [3, 7, 9] still face two important limitations. 
First, their efficiency-oriented convolutional encoders rely heavily on progressive spatial 
downsampling to reduce computational cost and expand the effective receptive field. 
Although this strategy enables efficient hierarchical feature extraction, conventional 
downsampling operations, such as max pooling and average pooling, inevitably discard 
spatial information [10]. This information loss is particularly problematic for medical 
image segmentation, where accurate delineation often depends on subtle boundary cues, 
thin structures, and small anatomical regions. In particular, high-frequency components 
contain important fine-grained structural information that may be attenuated or lost 
during repeated spatial reduction [11]. Once these details are discarded at early stages, 
subsequent upsampling operations cannot fully reconstruct the original structural 
information. Therefore, an efficient segmentation architecture should not rely solely on 
spatial downsampling for computational reduction, but should also provide an explicit 
mechanism for preserving complementary fine-grained structural information 
throughout the feature extraction process. 
Second, convolution-based decoders suffer from notable computational 
redundancy in feature learning [12, 13]. Within the standard encoder–decoder 
architecture, the decoder gradually fuses features from its previous stage with skipconnected features from the matching encoder layer. Although skip connections help 
restore spatial details, their fusion commonly employs standard convolutions over highdimensional feature maps. This adds a large number of convolutional parameters and 
computation overhead in the decoding branch. Furthermore, concatenated encoder and 
decoder features often contain overlapping, redundant spatial representations, where not 
all signals are essential for faithful feature reconstruction. This motivates a core research 
question: can the decoder maintain the representational capacity of conventional

sample_chunks.paper_title: LeViT-UNet++: Towards Balanced Fine-Grained Details and Context for Medical Image Segmentation
sample_chunks.authors: Guoping Xu, Jinling Zhu, et al.
sample_chunks.category: AI in Medical Diagnosis and Medical Imaging
sample_chunks.text_content:
convolutional feature fusion while drastically cutting its computational redundancy? 
To address these two challenges, we introduce two complementary architectural 
enhancements to preserve fine-grained structural information during encoder 
downsampling and improve computational efficiency in the decoder. First, we propose a 
Haar Wavelet Multi-Scale Downsampling (HWMD) module that combines Haar wavelet 
decomposition with parallel depthwise convolutions of different kernel sizes. Haar 
wavelet decomposition separates feature representations into low- and high-frequency 
components, capturing complementary structural information, while multi-scale 
depthwise convolutions extract spatial patterns across different receptive fields with 
limited additional computational cost. This design helps preserve fine-grained anatomical 
details during downsampling while maintaining efficient feature extraction. 
Furthermore, we develop a Depthwise-based Local and Global feature fusion and 
learning decoder (DLGD) that employs lightweight depthwise convolutional blocks [14] 
to progressively integrate global contextual representations from Transformer blocks with 
local spatial features propagated through encoder skip connections. By enabling efficient 
feature fusion and refinement, the proposed decoder reduces computational overhead 
while integrating complementary local and global representations. Together, HWMD and 
DLGD improve the balance between structural detail preservation, contextual 
representation, and computational efficiency. 
In summary, we introduce LeViT-UNet++, an enhanced version of our previous 
LeViT-UNet [7] that improves both the encoding and decoding processes for efficient 
medical image segmentation. The main contributions of this study are as follows: 
(1) We introduce a Haar Wavelet Multi-scale Downsampling module (HWMD) that 
combines wavelet-based information preservation with parallel depthwise convolutions 
at multiple scales. HWMD retains complementary structural information during spatial 
downsampling while providing multi-scale representations with limited computational 
overhead for the encoder. 
(2) We propose a Depthwise-based Local and Global feature fusion and learning 
decoder (DLGD) that efficiently integrates local spatial features from the convolutional 
encoder with global contextual representations from the Transformer. By leveraging 
lightweight depthwise convolutional blocks for progressive feature fusion and refinement, 
DLGD reduces decoder computational overhead while effectively integrating 
complementary local and global information. 
(3) We develop LeViT-UNet++, a convolution – Transformer hybrid encoder –
decoder framework that integrates HWMD and DLGD to jointly preserve fine-grained 
structural information, capture global contextual representations, and improve 
computational efficiency. 
(4) We conduct extensive experiments on four challenging medical image 
segmentation benchmarks covering both 2D and 3D segmentation scenarios. The results 
demonstrate that LeViT-UNet++ achieves a competitive balance between segmentation 
performance and computational efficiency compared with representative state-of-theart methods.

sample_chunks.paper_title: LeViT-UNet++: Towards Balanced Fine-Grained Details and Context for Medical Image Segmentation
sample_chunks.authors: Guoping Xu, Jinling Zhu, et al.
sample_chunks.category: AI in Medical Diagnosis and Medical Imaging
sample_chunks.text_content:
2. Related Work 
2.1 Downsampling in Image Segmentation 
Downsampling is a fundamental operation in semantic segmentation networks, as it 
progressively reduces spatial resolution to decrease computational cost and enlarge the 
effective receptive field while constructing hierarchical feature representations. 
Conventional segmentation architectures typically employ pooling operations, such as 
max pooling [15] and average pooling [16], for spatial reduction. For example, SegNet 
[15] adopts pooling indices to facilitate efficient feature reconstruction in the decoder. 
Beyond conventional pooling, multi-scale feature aggregation has been widely explored 
to improve the representation of objects with varying spatial scales. PSPNet [17] 
introduces spatial pyramid pooling to aggregate contextual information from multiple 
spatial regions, while DeepLab [18] employs atrous spatial pyramid pooling to capture 
multi-scale contextual representations without further reducing spatial resolution. 
Despite their effectiveness, conventional downsampling operations inevitably 
discard spatial information as the feature resolution decreases. Such information loss can 
affect segmentation performance, particularly for objects with complex boundaries, small 
structures, or fine-grained details. To alleviate this issue, several studies have explored 
information-preserving downsampling strategies [10, 11, 19]. Haar wavelet-based 
downsampling (HWD) [11], for instance, replaces conventional spatial reduction with Haar 
wavelet decomposition to preserve complementary frequency components during 
downsampling. By retaining low- and high-frequency information, wavelet-based 
approaches provide richer representations for subsequent feature extraction while 
maintaining the computational benefits of spatial reduction. 
However, HWD employs standard convolution to process and fuse the decomposed 
frequency components, introducing additional learnable parameters and computational 
overhead compared with conventional pooling operations. Moreover, its feature 
extraction remains based on a fixed convolutional receptive field and does not explicitly 
exploit spatial patterns at multiple scales, which may limit its ability to capture structural 
variations across different object sizes and spatial contexts. These limitations motivate the 
development of a more efficient information-preserving downsampling strategy that can 
simultaneously retain fine-grained structural information and capture multi-scale spatial 
patterns. Hence, we introduce an efficient Haar Wavelet Multi-Scale Downsampling 
module for image segmentation to address these challenges in this study. 
2.2 Architectures for Efficient Neural Networks 
A broad range of strategies has been explored to develop lightweight neural 
architectures, with existing approaches generally falling into two complementary 
categories: efficient building-block design and holistic architectural optimization [20]. The 
former aims to reduce computational complexity at the individual module level, whereas 
the latter seeks to improve efficiency through the design and optimization of the overall 
network topology. 
At the module level, depthwise separable convolution is a fundamental technique

sample_chunks.text_content:
for reducing computational cost. It decomposes a standard convolution into a depthwise 
convolution, which independently processes each input channel, followed by a pointwise 
11 convolution, which facilitates cross-channel information integration. This 
factorization substantially reduces the number of parameters and floating-point 
operations 
(FLOPs),

representations. Representative architectures that exploit this principle include the 
MobileNet series [13, 21, 22] and Xception [14]. In addition, ShuffleNet [23] and 
ShuffleNet V2 [24] combine group convolution with channel shuffling to reduce 
computational redundancy while enabling information exchange across channel groups. 
GhostNet [12] further improves computational efficiency through its Ghost module, which 
generates additional feature maps from a limited set of intrinsic features using 
inexpensive linear transformations, thereby reducing reliance on computationally 
intensive conventional convolutions. Collectively, these approaches demonstrate how 
carefully designed computational primitives can substantially improve the efficiency of 
deep neural networks without fundamentally compromising their representational 
capacity. 
In contrast, holistic architectural optimization targets the overall network structure, 
including the allocation of computational resources across stages, the scaling of network 
depth, width, and input resolution, and the organization of feature extraction pathways. 
EfficientNet [25, 26] systematically investigates the joint scaling of these dimensions 
through compound model scaling, achieving a more balanced trade-off between 
computational cost and representational capacity. Other representative architectures, 
such as BiSeNet [16], DDRNet [27], and LGNet [28], explore complementary two-branch 
strategies for learning and fusing local and contextual information. SegFormer [29], by 
contrast, designs efficient MLP-based decoders to aggregate multi-layer features 
extracted from the encoder. Instead of optimizing individual operations in isolation, these 
approaches emphasize coordinated design of network components and their global 
configurations to attain more favorable efficiency–accuracy trade-offs. 
While these lightweight architectural design principles were originally developed for 
natural image recognition, they have been increasingly adapted to medical image 
segmentation. Typical approaches include embedding efficient modules into existing 
networks or directly adopting lightweight backbones. Nevertheless, medical 
segmentation poses unique challenges: it demands a delicate balance among 
computational efficiency, multi-scale contextual modeling, and the preservation of finegrained anatomical details. Representative architectures, including LeViT-UNet [7], 
MedNeXt [30], Mobile U-ViT [31], explore different strategies for efficient feature 
extraction and contextual modeling. Despite these advances, the design of an effective 
and computationally efficient decoder remains a critical challenge. A well-designed 
decoder must progressively recover spatial details and integrate complementary local 
and global representations across multiple scales, while minimizing the computational 
and memory overhead associated with feature fusion and refinement. This challenge 
becomes even more pronounced in 3D medical image segmentation, where the high 
dimensionality of volumetric features substantially increases computational demands [32].

(2) Frequency-specific multi-scale depthwise convolution 
To extract features at different receptive-field scales while maintaining 
computational efficiency, HWMD applies parallel depthwise convolutions with different 
kernel sizes to the low- and high-frequency components, respectively. Let K = (k₁, k₂, ..., 
kₘ) denote the set of convolutional kernel sizes. The low-frequency representation is 
obtained as follows. 
𝐹𝐿= 𝐶𝑜𝑛𝑐𝑎𝑡(𝑘∈𝐾)𝐷𝑊𝑐𝑜𝑛𝑣(𝑘×𝑘)(𝑋𝐿𝐿) 
(2) 
Here, the Concat denotes concatenation along the channel dimension. This 
operation captures low-frequency contextual patterns over multiple receptive fields. For 
the high-frequency branch, the three directional subbands are first aggregated along the 
channel dimension. 
𝑋𝐻= 𝐶𝑜𝑛𝑐𝑎𝑡(𝑋𝐿𝐻, 𝑋𝐻𝐿, 𝑋𝐻𝐻) 
(3) 
The aggregated high-frequency representation is then processed using the 
corresponding multi-scale depthwise convolutions. 
𝐹𝐻= 𝐶𝑜𝑛𝑐𝑎𝑡(𝑘∈𝐾)𝐷𝑊𝐶𝑜𝑛𝑣(𝑘×𝑘)(𝑋𝐻) 
(4) 
By operating independently on the low- and high-frequency representations, the 
two branches learn complementary features: the low-frequency branch emphasizes 
coarse semantic structures, whereas the high-frequency branch captures fine-grained 
variations and orientation-dependent structural cues. The parallel multi-scale design 
further enables the module to characterize structures of different spatial extents while 
limiting the computational overhead associated with conventional dense convolutions. 
(3) Low–high-frequency feature fusion 
Finally, the extracted low- and high-frequency representations are integrated using 
a pointwise convolution. Specifically, the two branches are concatenated and projected 
into a unified feature representation.

𝑌= 𝑃𝑊𝑐𝑜𝑛𝑣(1×1)(𝐶𝑜𝑛𝑐𝑎𝑡(𝐹𝐿, 𝐹𝐻)) 
(5) 
Here, Y denotes the output feature map with dimensions H/2 W/2 C_out, where 
C_out is the desired output channel dimension. The 1 1 convolution enables channelwise interactions between complementary frequency representations and integrates 
multi-scale contextual information with fine-grained structural details. Consequently, 
HWMD performs spatial downsampling and frequency-aware feature extraction within a 
unified module, providing a computationally efficient alternative to conventional 
downsampling operations that may inadequately preserve fine structural information. 
3.3 Depthwise-based local-and-global feature fusion and learning decoder 
The proposed decoder (DLGD) is designed to efficiently integrate multi-scale global 
contextual representations from the Transformer encoder with local spatial features, 
progressively refining the fused representations to recover fine-grained details for 
accurate segmentation. As illustrated in Figure 2 (b), the decoder consists of three 
principal components: (1) a multi-scale global feature fusion module that aggregates 
hierarchical representations from the Transformer blocks; (2) a local and global feature 
fusion and learning module comprising three depthwise separable convolutional blocks, 
which progressively fuse and refine complementary local and global features while 
maintaining computational efficiency; and (3) a segmentation head that generates the 
final pixel-wise prediction. 
Specifically, the multi-scale global feature fusion module combines hierarchical 
Transformer features to provide contextual guidance at different semantic levels. These 
fused global representations are subsequently integrated with local spatial features 
through the three successive depthwise separable convolutional blocks. By progressively 
refining the fused features, DLGD facilitates the interaction between global semantic 
context and local spatial information, thereby supporting the recovery of fine-grained 
anatomical structures and object boundaries. Furthermore, the use of depthwise 
separable convolutions reduces the computational cost of feature refinement compared 
with conventional convolutional operations, making the decoder more parameterefficient. Overall, DLGD provides a lightweight decoding strategy that balances multiscale contextual integration, local detail recovery, and computational efficiency. 
 
4. Experiments and Results 
4.1 Datasets 
(1). Synapse dataset 
The Synapse Multi-Organ Segmentation (Synapse) dataset contains 30 abdominal 
CT volumes, offering dense voxel-level annotations for eight abdominal organs: aorta 
(Aor), gallbladder (Gal), spleen (Spl), left kidney (LKid), right kidney (RKid), liver (Liv), 
pancreas (Pan), and stomach (Sto). We adopt the data split strategy described in [7], 
where 18 samples are allocated for model training and the other 12 samples are held out 
as the validation set.

(2) ACDC 
The Automated Cardiac Diagnosis Challenge (ACDC) dataset collects cardiac cineMRI sequences captured at end-diastole and end-systole. Every subject is annotated 
manually for three key cardiac structures, namely the left ventricle (LV), myocardium 
(MYO), and right ventricle (RV), to construct pixel-wise ground truth. Consistent with the 
splitting scheme reported in [7], we select 20 subjects (40 volumetric scans) as the test 
set, and utilize the remaining 80 subjects (160 volumes) for network training. 
(3) LA2018 
The Left Atrium Segmentation Challenge (LA2018) dataset [33] comprises 100 
volumetric late gadolinium-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (LGE-MRI) scans, 
each accompanied by a manually delineated segmentation mask of the left atrium (LA). 
In this study, the dataset is randomly partitioned into 70 volumes for training, 10 for 
validation, and 20 for testing. 
(4) MSD Heart 
The Medical Segmentation Decathlon (MSD) Heart dataset (Task02_Heart) [34] 
provides volumetric cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data with segmentation 
annotations for the target cardiac structure. The dataset contains 30 cases, including 20 
cases with ground-truth segmentation labels and 10 cases without publicly available 
labels. In this study, the 20 labeled cases are randomly partitioned into 14 training cases, 
2 validation cases, and 4 testing cases to evaluate the performance of the proposed 
method and competing three-dimensional (3D) segmentation models. 
Table 2 summarizes the four publicly available benchmark datasets used in this study, 
detailing their imaging modalities, target anatomical structures, and respective training, 
validation, and test splits. Different data preparation and evaluation protocols are 
adopted for the 2D- and 3D-based segmentation models. Specifically, for the Synapse 
and ACDC datasets, volumetric scans are decomposed into individual 2D slices for model 
training and inference. In contrast, the original volumetric data from the LA2018 and MSD 
Heart datasets are retained for training and evaluating 3D segmentation models. To 
ensure a consistent volume-level evaluation across different model architectures, the 
slice-wise predictions generated by the 2D models are subsequently reassembled into 
3D volumes in their original spatial order. All segmentation metrics are then computed 
at the volumetric level, providing a unified basis for comparing segmentation 
performance across the evaluated models.

the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) and the 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95), 
following the standard evaluation protocols adopted in previous studies [3, 7]. For the 
LA2018 and MSD Heart datasets, two additional surface-based metrics, namely the 
normalized surface dice (NSD) and average surface distance (ASD), are employed to 
provide a more comprehensive assessment of boundary delineation accuracy. Specifically, 
NSD quantifies the proportion of predicted and reference surface points falling within a 
predefined tolerance, thereby reflecting boundary agreement, whereas ASD measures 
the average distance between the predicted and reference segmentation surfaces, 
characterizing the overall boundary displacement. 
4.2 Implementation details 
In this study, all experiments are implemented using Python 3.10.4 and PyTorch 2.11 
with CUDA 12.8 on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 GPU, running under Ubuntu 24.04.4 
LTS. For all training samples, augmentation strategies including random flipping and 
random rotation are adopted to enhance data diversity. For 2D model training, all input 
images are resized to a spatial resolution of 224 224. All 2D models are optimized with 
the Adam optimizer, using an initial learning rate of 5e-4 and weight decay of 1e-4. 
Cross-entropy loss combined with Dice loss serves as the objective function. The batch 
size is set to 8. We train the model for 350 epochs on the Synapse dataset and 400 epochs 
on the ACDC dataset. Following the strategy adopted in [3, 7], we select the final epoch 
for evaluation on the test set. 
For 3D model training, we use the MONAI framework and adopt the experimental 
configurations of Swin UNETR [4] as a reference for the LA2018 and MSD Heart datasets. 
Specifically, we extend the 2D HWMD and DLGD modules to their 3D counterparts based 
on 3D Haar wavelet transforms and convolutions for the 3D LeViT-UNet++. AdamW is 
used as the optimizer, with an initial learning rate of 0.001 and a weight decay of 1 10⁻⁵. 
The training objective combines cross-entropy loss and Dice loss. The input volume size 
is obtained by randomly cropping 64 64 64 voxel patches centered on target 
regions, and the batch size is set to 4. The models are trained for 200 epochs on LA2018 
and 600 epochs on MSD Heart, respectively. During training, model selection is 
performed based on the mean Dice score on the validation set, and the checkpoint 
achieving the highest validation Dice score is retained for final evaluation on the 
corresponding test set. For methods with multiple publicly available variants, the smallest 
model in terms of parameter count is selected to ensure a consistent comparison of 
model efficiency.

[29] and Swin-UNet [36]; as well as hybrid architectures comprising EfficientViT [37],

4.4 Experiment results under 3D setting 
(1) Results on LA2018 dataset 
To evaluate the performance of LeViT-UNet++, we conduct experiments under the 
3D volume setting by comparing it with a variety of state-of-the-art 3D segmentation 
methods: convolution-based models such as MedNeXt [30], UNet++, nnUNet, V-Net 
[42] and UXNet [43], Transformer-based methods including SegFormer3D and nnFormer 
[44], and hybrid architectures represented by Mobile U-ViT, LeViT-UNet and Swin UNETR. 
As shown in Table 5, the proposed LeViT-UNet++ achieves a competitive DSC of 
84.88%, while maintaining a small parameter footprint of only 8.27 M and a favorable 
inference FPS of 203.52. it reaches the second-lowest ASD (6.32) and a competitive NSD 
(23.22), demonstrating reliable boundary segmentation. MedNeXt-v1 and V-Net obtain 
marginally higher DSC (85.05% and 85.82%), but V-Net has 45.60 M parameters, over five 
times our model’s size. nnUNet runs fastest at 231.99 FPS, but its DSC (82.46%) and 
boundary metrics are inferior. nnFormer has the lowest NSD (14.96), indicating weak 
boundary agreement, and it is computationally expensive (149.46 M params, 21.81 FPS). 
Relative to LeViT-UNet, our method boosts DSC from 81.50% to 84.88% and reduces 
parameters by 75.6%, with improved HD95 and NSD. SegFormer3D achieves a similar DSC 
(84.16%) but poorer ASD and HD95; Mobile U-ViT is lightweight (2.76 M) yet 
underperforms on DSC and boundary metrics. In summary, LeViT-UNet++ strikes a good 
trade-off between segmentation accuracy, boundary quality, parameter cost and 
inference efficiency.

4.5 Ablation study 
We perform ablation experiments to quantify the individual contributions of the 
proposed HWMD and DLGD modules to our LeViT-UNet++. Table 7 presents the 2D

reduction in parameter count while retaining competitive segmentation accuracy.

4.6 Visualization of segmentation results 
In Figures 4 and 5, we qualitatively compare our LeViT‑UNet++ against vanilla 
LeViT‑UNet, Mobile U‑ViT, SegFormer and Swin UNETR. Figure 4 illustrates 2D slice 
overlays for Synapse and ACDC, and Figure 5 provides 3D volume renderings for LA2018

yields segmentation masks with crisp boundaries and faithful anatomical contours: it 
avoids the blurred edges and under‑segmentation observed in vanilla LeViT‑UNet, 
suppresses the spurious fragments prevalent in Mobile U‑ViT, and outperforms 
SegFormer and Swin UNETR, which often produce distorted outlines and incomplete 
structures. In 3D reconstruction, LeViT‑UNet++ preserves the complete topological 
morphology of cardiac structures, while the competing models suffer from surface 
deformation, missing regions and discrete noise. These visual results demonstrate the 
capacity of our method to capture fine anatomical cues in both 2D and 3D segmentation 
scenarios.

5. Discussion 
LeViT-UNet++ was developed to improve the balance between segmentation 
accuracy and computational efficiency by addressing two complementary aspects of 
feature representation: structural information preservation during downsampling and 
computationally efficient feature integration during decoding. Specifically, HWMD 
incorporates Haar wavelet decomposition and frequency-specific multi-scale depthwise 
convolutions to retain complementary low- and high-frequency representations during 
the initial downsampling stage. Meanwhile, DLGD employs depthwise separable 
convolutions to progressively integrate local spatial features and global contextual 
representations while reducing decoder complexity. 
The experimental results across four medical image segmentation benchmarks 
demonstrate the potential of these complementary designs in both 2D and 3D 
segmentation settings. Compared with the original LeViT-UNet, the proposed 
architecture achieves notable improvements on the Synapse and LA2018 datasets while 
substantially reducing the number of model parameters. In particular, the parameter 
reduction is primarily attributed to the lightweight decoder design, whereas HWMD 
contributes to the preservation of complementary structural representations during 
feature extraction. These results suggest that improving architectural efficiency does not 
necessarily require sacrificing the representation of fine-grained structural information. 
Despite these promising results, the proposed architecture has several limitations 
that warrant further investigation. First, although LeViT-UNet++ achieves a favorable 
trade-off between segmentation performance and computational efficiency, its 
performance does not consistently surpass that of state-of-the-art segmentation 
methods, particularly those employing more sophisticated feature representation and 
fusion strategies. This suggests that improving computational efficiency while maintaining 
or further enhancing segmentation accuracy remains a challenging problem. One 
possible contributing factor is the limited adaptability of the current multi-scale feature 
fusion strategy. Specifically, DLGD progressively integrates local and global 
representations through concatenation-based fusion and skip connections. Although this 
strategy is computationally efficient, it may not fully capture the complex dependencies 
and complementary relationships among features at different spatial resolutions. More 
adaptive fusion mechanisms, such as attention-guided feature selection, content-aware 
feature aggregation, or learnable cross-scale interactions, may provide more effective 
ways to exploit complementary local details and global contextual information while 
preserving the lightweight nature of the architecture. Furthermore, knowledge distillation 
represents a promising paradigm for transferring knowledge from heavy, large-scale 
models into lightweight architectures such as our proposed LeViT-UNet++, which helps 
mitigate the requirement for massive annotated training samples in medical image 
segmentation. We hope these explorations will inspire further advances toward compact, 
data-efficient models for routine clinical workflows. 
Second, the evaluation was conducted on a limited number of publicly available 
benchmarks. Although these datasets cover different anatomical structures and imaging 
modalities, further validation on larger, more diverse, and clinically representative 
datasets is required to establish the robustness and generalizability of the proposed

architecture. In addition, its computational efficiency requires systematic evaluation 
across diverse hardware platforms and deployment settings, especially under real-world 
clinical constraints. Furthermore, the current feature fusion strategy mainly relies on 
concatenation and depthwise convolution, which may restrict its capacity to adaptively 
model complex interdependencies among multi-scale features. Accordingly, our future 
work will focus on developing more effective yet computationally economical multi-scale 
feature fusion schemes, extending evaluations to larger clinical datasets, and exploring 
the feasibility of deploying LeViT-UNet++ in resource-limited medical imaging scenarios. 
6. Conclusion 
This study presents LeViT-UNet++, a lightweight convolution–Transformer hybrid 
framework for medical image segmentation, aiming to balance segmentation accuracy 
and computational efficiency. It integrates the Haar Wavelet Multi-Scale Downsampling 
(HWMD) module to preserve fine-grained structural information and the Depthwisebased Local and Global feature fusion and learning Decoder (DLGD) to efficiently 
combine local spatial details with global contextual representations. Extensive 
experiments across four benchmarks (Synapse, ACDC, LA2018, and MSD-Heart) under 
both 2D and 3D settings demonstrate that LeViT-UNet++ delivers competitive 
segmentation performance with substantially reduced model complexity and favorable 
inference speed. These findings highlight the effectiveness of combining wavelet-based 
structural preservation with efficient local–global feature fusion, offering a promising 
solution for medical image segmentation in resource- and latency-constrained 
environments.
