sample_chunks.text_content:
Scribble Once, Segment the Sequence: Bidirectional Temporal Consistency for
Weakly Supervised Segmentation in Echocardiography Sequences
Vincent Li Weixin
University of Oxford
vincent.li@reuben.ox.ac.uk
Chen Jingkun
Northwest Polytechnical University Xi’an
jingkunchen@nwpu.edu.cn
Vicente Grau
University of Oxford
vicente.grau@eng.ox.ac.uk
Abstract
Temporal medical image segmentation relies on pixel-wise
annotations, which are prohibitively expensive for long image sequences. Existing weakly-supervised methods reduce
the annotation burden per frame but still require repeated
annotations across the sequence. Furthermore, sparse supervision can result in temporally unstable representations.
Addressing both challenges requires a model that can leverage strong spatial priors from large-scale pretraining while
minimizing reliance on dense annotations. Frozen 2D vision foundation models provide a promising basis for this
by offering transferable spatial representations with low
trainable parameters. However, their lack of explicit temporal modeling limits their ability to propagate reliable information across anatomical sequences. To address this,
we present a weakly-supervised framework for temporal
segmentation from a single scribble-annotated frame, with
all remaining frames left unlabeled. The framework combines parameter-efficient adaptation of DINOv3 encoders
present in the mean-teacher architecture.
Furthermore,
a set of complementary losses, including a temporal loss
helps generate reliable segmentation priors for the unlabeled frames. This formulation decouples annotation costs
from sequence length while retaining the transferable spatial knowledge of the pretrained encoder.
Extensive experiments on the publicly available CAMUS and CardiacNet datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms
other scribble-supervised methods. These results show that
accurate and temporally consistent segmentation can be
achieved from extremely sparse supervision, substantially
reducing annotation requirements for temporal echocardiographic segmentation and providing a practical framework
for scalable clinical deployment.
1. Introduction
Segmentation of temporal medical sequences is vital in
many clinical applications, as it enables consistent quantification and tracking of anatomical and pathological changes
over time [2, 19, 23]. However, achieving reliable sequence
segmentation remains constrained by the annotation bottleneck. Methods achieving high segmentation performance
conventionally rely on dense pixel-wise annotations for every frame, while obtaining such large-scale annotations in
clinical settings remains a significant challenge [20, 22].
This challenge is particularly pronounced in echocardiography, where speckle noise obscures anatomical boundaries
and adjacent tissues can exhibit similar acoustic properties,
making structures difficult to distinguish without expert interpretation [6, 24]. Consequently, annotation of echocardiographic sequences is both time-consuming and dependent on specialist expertise, with annotation effort increasing with every additional frame in a sequence.
Current methods that reduce annotation requirements
can broadly be divided into two categories.
Semisupervised learning (SSL) combines a small subset of
densely annotated frames with a larger set of unlabeled
frames, as shown in Mean Teacher [21] and Cross Pseudo
Supervision (CPS) [5]. The labeled subset provides direct
supervision through segmentation losses, while the unlabeled subset provides consistency regularization [13] that
encourages reliable and temporally coherent predictions.
Weakly-supervised learning (WSL), in contrast, replaces
dense masks with coarse annotations such as bounding
boxes [8, 9, 15], points [27, 30] or scribbles [1, 3, 4], typically provided on every training frame. These approaches
reduce annotation burden in different ways. SSL reduces
the number of frames requiring dense annotation while
WSL reduces the amount of annotation required per frame.
However, both remain dependent on annotations across the

sequence, so annotation effort continues to increase with sequence length.
To address this limitation, we propose a weaklysupervised framework for segmenting echocardiographic
sequences from a single scribble-annotated frame, with all
remaining frames left unlabeled. The framework consists of
three complementary components that convert sparse spatial supervision into reliable sequence-wide segmentation.
Firstly, a mean-teacher framework generates dense pseudolabels and propagates supervision outward from the annotated frame in a bidirectional manner. Secondly, a frozen
DINOv3-based [18] encoder, adapted to medical images
using Low-rank Adaptations (LoRA) [7] provides transferable spatial representations while restricting adaptation to
a small number of trainable parameters. The representations are fed into a lightweight U-Net-style decoder [16],
keeping trainable parameters low. Thirdly, complementary
spatial and temporal losses enforce consistency across the
sequence while allowing anatomically plausible changes in
cardiac shape.
We evaluate the proposed framework on two publicly
available datasets, Cardiac Acquisitions for Multi-structure
Ultrasound Segmentation (CAMUS) [10] and CardiacNet [25], spanning three different cohorts. Experimental
results demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms existing scribble-supervised baselines in both Dice
and HD95 metrics, while achieving a more favorable balance between precision and recall. These results show that
accurate and spatially well-localized temporal segmentation
can be achieved from only one scribble-annotated frame,
substantially reducing annotation requirements for echocardiographic sequence segmentation. Our key contributions
are summarized as follows:
• We propose a weakly-supervised temporal segmentation
framework for medical imaging sequences based on single slice scribble annotations on the middle frame.
• We demonstrate that a LoRA-adapted foundation model
encoder can improve segmentation performance with significantly fewer parameters compared to state-of-the-art
scribble segmentation methods
• We also propose an anchor-relative bidirectional temporal loss, Ltemp, that can propagate supervision outward
from the anchor frame in both directions while allowing
for drifting so that segmentation masks follow the natural
progression of anatomical structures.
2. Related Work
2.1. Scribble-supervised Segmentation
Scribble-supervised segmentation addresses the problem
of learning dense segmentation masks from sparse pixel
annotations.
Common methods such as partial crossentropy (pCE) compute the supervised loss only over annotated pixels but do not extend supervision to unlabeled
regions. Therefore, existing scribble-supervised methods
extend sparse scribbles through augmentation, consistency
regularization and architectural modifications.
Augmentation-based methods perturb the training samples and enforce consistency between the corresponding
predictions. CutMix [26] constructs a new training sample by combining regions from two images, with the corresponding labels mixed using the same spatial transformation.
This exposes the model to additional combinations of foreground and background regions while preserving the available sparse supervision.
CycleMix [28] extends mixed-sample augmentation with cycle-consistency
constraints, using complementary transformed views to exploit information from both labeled and unlabeled regions.
Together, these strategies encourage predictions to remain
consistent under input perturbations.
Architecture-based approaches instead modify the segmentation framework to better exploit the limited spatial
supervision. ScribFormer [12] combines a convolutional
branch with a transformer branch and a class-activation
branch to integrate local appearance with global contextual information, allowing the network to infer object structure beyond the annotated scribbles. Other methods combine architectural changes with consistency-based training.
HELPNet [29] introduces hierarchical perturbations at multiple spatial granularity and enforces consistency between
the resulting predictions, together with edge-guided refinement to improve boundaries that are not directly specified
by the scribble. Despite different mechanisms, these methods process frames independently and require scribble annotations throughout the sequence, causing annotation cost
to scale with sequence length.
2.2. Vision Foundation Models and ParameterEfficient Adaptation
Large-scale self-supervised pretraining has produced vision backbones with transferable representations that can be
reused across downstream tasks with limited task-specific
supervision [11]. DINOv3 extends this capability through
large-scale self-supervised pretraining, providing spatial
representations that can be transferred to domains where labeled data are scarce. We use a general-purpose DINOv3
rather than an echocardiography-specific foundation model
so that the supervision scheme remains modality-agnostic
rather than tied to a single domain.
Adapting large pretrained backbones to a target medical domain introduces a second challenge. Full fine-tuning
of all backbone parameters increases computational cost
and risk of overfitting [17]. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning
(PEFT) methods instead preserve most of the pretrained
representation while restricting task-specific adaptation to
a small number of parameters.
LoRA introduces train2

3. Methodology
3.1. Overview
As illustrated in Fig. 1, we propose a weakly-supervised
framework for segmenting echocardiographic sequences
from scribble annotations on the anchor frame. The following sections describe each component in detail.
3.2. Segmentation of Echocardiographic Sequences
from a Single Scribble
Let X = {x1, x2, . . . , xT } denote an echocardiographic sequence of T frames. The model predicts a segmentation
mask for every frame with supervision limited to a single
scribble map S defined on the anchor frame xm while all remaining frames are unlabeled. The annotation map contains
both foreground and background scribbles and the scribble
assigns each pixel i of xm one of three values
S(i) =

The framework allows any frame in the sequence to be
selected as the annotated anchor frame. The middle frame
xm provides a natural default by reducing the maximum
propagation distance to approximately T/2 frames. However, keyframes such as end-systole (ES) or end-diastole
(ED) frames may also be selected. Supervision is subsequently propagated bidirectionally from the selected anchor
to the remaining unlabeled frames.
3.3. Parameter-Efficient Encoding and Multi-Scale
Decoding
A frozen DINOv3 encoder is adapted using LoRA on the
query and value projections of three transformer blocks,
introducing 27.6 K trainable parameters corresponding to
0.03% of the 85.7 M while preserving the pretrained representation under sparse supervision. Patch tokens are extracted from the three adapted blocks. Each token corresponds to a 16 × 16 pixel patch so a 512 × 512 input yields
a grid of 32×32 tokens. Since the transformer block applies
no spatial downsampling, all three LoRA block readouts
share this resolution and differ only in semantic depth. They
are resampled to strides 4, 8 and 16, producing 128 × 128,
64 × 64 and 32 × 32 spatial feature maps. A fourth level at
stride 32 is obtained by average pooling the stride-16 map
to 16 × 16, which provides the decoder a coarser representation and a larger effective receptive field.
Each pyramid level is independently projected using a
1 × 1 convolution followed by group normalization and
ReLU. The projected features are then passed to a U-Net
style decoder, beginning at stride-32 level and progressively
upsampled through three stages. At each stage, the upsampled decoder features are concatenated with the corresponding projected feature map from the pyramid. The final decoder output is converted to segmentation logits and bilinearly resized to the original input resolution.
3.4. Dense Supervision from Single Scribbleannotated Frame
3.4.1. Mean Teacher Construction and Scribble Supervision
The framework maintains structurally identical student and
teacher branches. The student is optimized directly through
gradient descent while the teacher parameters are updated
as an exponential moving average (EMA) of the student parameters. Since the DINOv3 backbone is frozen throughout training, its pretrained weights are shared between the
two branches, while the LoRA adapters, feature projections and segmentation decoder are maintained separately
and updated through the corresponding student and teacher
mechanisms.
For each training sequence, the student receives a weakly
augmented view generated using brightness and contrast
perturbations together with additive noise. These transformations modify image appearance while preserving spatial geometry, ensuring pixel-wise alignment between the
student predictions and the supervision generated from the
unaugmented sequence.

xm, which is the only frame containing scribble annotations. We apply pCE exclusively to pixels labeled as foreground and background

4. Experiments and Results
4.1. Datasets
We evaluate our method on two publicly available echocardiography datasets, CAMUS and CardiacNet. All datasets
are divided into training, validation and test sets using a
70:10:20 ratio.
CAMUS contains echocardiographic sequences from 500 patients, from which we use the twochamber (2CH) half-sequence subset. Ground-truth masks
are provided for all frames, so the mask-derived scribble
annotations is on the middle frame of the sequence. Performance is evaluated on three anatomical structures namely
the left-ventricular endocardium (LVendo), left-ventricular
epicardium (LVepi) and left atrium.
CardiacNet comprises two pathology-specific cohorts:
atrial septal defect (ASD) and pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). Segmentation masks are released for only
a subset of the acquired sequences and a small number of
the released files could not be read. We therefore use every
sequence for which a usable annotation exists, giving 135
ASD and 299 PAH sequences. Unlike CAMUS, groundtruth masks are provided for approximately five frames
within each sequence, so the scribble is placed on the middle annotated frame rather than the middle frame of the sequence. Both cohorts are evaluated on four cardiac structures: left ventricle (LV), left atrium (LA), right ventricle
(RV) and right atrium (RA). Across both datasets, training
supervision is restricted to one background and one foreground scribble with all remaining frames unlabeled.
4.2. Implementation Details
All experiments were implemented in PyTorch with Python
3.12 and CUDA 13.2 and conducted on a single NVIDIA
RTX PRO 5000 Blackwell GPU. We use DINOv3 ViTB/16 as the vision foundation model backbone, with rank-3
LoRA adapters applied to the query and value projections
of transformer blocks 3, 6 and 9. Single-channel ultrasound
frames are used across three channels, resized to 512×512,
and normalized using the ImageNet channel-wise mean and
standard deviation.
Models are trained for 40 epochs using AdamW with a
learning rate of 1 × 10−4, weight decay of 1 × 10−4 and
mixed-precision training. The partial cross-entropy, Dice,
temporal consistency and gated-CRF losses are weighted by
1.0, 0.5, 0.1 and 0.1 respectively. The weights of the three
unsupervised objectives are linearly ramped from zero to
their respective values over the first five epochs. The teacher
parameters are updated using an EMA decay of 0.99 and
the connectivity-filtered teacher and student predictions are
mixed using a pixel-wise Bernoulli mask with β = 0.5.

4.3. Baseline and Evaluation Metrics
We compare our method against a U-Net trained with pCE
alone and four scribble-supervised methods: CutMix, CycleMix, ScribFormer and HELPNet. A consistent evaluation protocol is applied across all methods, with performance measured on all frames with available ground-truth
annotations to assess generalization beyond the annotated
frame. We report the Dice similarity coefficient and 95thpercentile Hausdorff distance (HD95), together with precision and recall to further characterize segmentation errors.
Tab. 1 shows that our method achieves the highest
average Dice across all three cohorts, with scores of
0.784, 0.744, and 0.754 on CAMUS, CardiacNet-ASD
and CardiacNet-PAH respectively.
Performance is lowest on the CardiacNet-ASD cohort, where the septal defect disrupts the normal boundary between the atria, increasing ambiguity in chamber delineation. Compared to
consistency-based methods, our method improves over CutMix by 0.097, 0.338, and 0.192 Dice respectively.
The
improvement over dedicated scribble-supervised methods is
larger, particularly on CardiacNet. While ScribFormer and
HELPNet achieve competitive performance on some CAMUS structures, their average Dice remains low on both
CardiacNet cohorts, indicating poor generalization while
our method achieves 0.744 on CardiacNet-ASD and 0.754
on CardiacNet-PAH. Overall, our method achieves the highest Dice on 10 of 11 structures, demonstrating more consistent performance under single-frame scribble supervision.
It also shows that our method achieves the lowest average HD95 across all three cohorts, with 31.25,
41.72, and 28.30 pixels on CAMUS, CardiacNet-ASD, and
CardiacNet-PAH respectively. Consistent with the Dice results, CardiacNet-ASD remains the most challenging cohort, although our method maintains considerably lower
boundary errors across all four structures.
Given the substantial performance gap observed in both
Dice and HD95, we further investigate why existing methods degrade under single-frame supervision. As illustrated
in Figs. 2 to 4, their poor performance is primarily driven
by severe over-segmentation rather than localized boundary
errors, with predictions extending substantially beyond the
target anatomy. This explains the low Dice and high HD95
observed in the quantitative results. To better characterize
this failure mode, we additionally analyze precision and recall in Tab. 2.
Tab. 2 further corroborates this failure mode. The pCE
baseline, CycleMix and ScribFormer consistently exhibit
high recall but extremely low precision, particularly on
the two CardiacNet cohorts.
This pattern shows oversegmentation, where predicted masks cover large regions
of the image, leading to substantial overlap with the ground
truth mask. Thus, recall values are inflated despite poor
localization quality. In contrast, our framework improves
precision while maintaining competitive recall, with precision consistently exceeding recall across all three cohorts.
Overall, the improvements in Dice and HD95 can be attributed primarily to a reduction in false-positive predictions
rather than increased anatomical coverage, consistent with
the qualitative segmentation results.
5. Ablations
All ablation experiments are conducted on the CAMUS
dataset using the LV endocardium. CAMUS is selected as
ground-truth masks are available for every frame so metrics
can be computed on the entire sequence, enabling a more
comprehensive evaluation of temporal segmentation performance. The LV endocardium is used as a representative
structure to systematically isolate the contribution of each
component in the proposed framework. We evaluate the effects of the architectural design, LoRA adaptation, meanteacher framework and individual loss terms.
5.1. Effectiveness of Architecture
We further examine the depth of the feature pyramid by
reducing it from four to three levels, removing the coarsest scale while keeping the frozen DINOv3 encoder and all
other components unchanged. The three-level model decreases Dice from 0.824 to 0.734 on CAMUS and from
0.779 to 0.763 on CardiacNet-PAH. The coarsest level aggregates information over a larger area of the image, allowing the decoder to reason about global shape and spatial
relationships between structures, which cannot be inferred
from local appearance alone. Without this level, the decoder must recover such context from finer scales that look
at smaller areas, so spatially separated regions are processed
largely independently. This is particularly detrimental under scribble supervision, where most pixels and unlabeled
and the network must rely on global shape priors to extend sparse annotations to complete, anatomically plausible
masks.
5.2. Effectiveness of LoRA
Removing the low-rank adapters reduces Dice from 0.824
to 0.784 on CAMUS and from 0.779 to 0.771 on
CardiacNet-PAH. The improvement on CAMUS indicates
that adapting the pretrained DINOv3 features is important
for capturing echocardiographic characteristics such as lowcontrast boundaries and speckle patterns.
5.3. Effectiveness of Mean Teacher Framework
Removing the EMA teacher while retaining all other components reduces Dice from 0.824 to 0.799 on CAMUS
and from 0.779 to 0.772 on CardiacNet-PAH. The consistent reduction across both datasets demonstrates the benefit of maintaining a temporally averaged teacher. Without EMA updates, both branches adapt directly to similar

6. Conclusion and Future Work
We propose a weakly-supervised framework for temporal
echocardiography segmentation using only two scribbles on
an anchor frame. By combining a mean-teacher framework,
a LoRA-adapted DINOv3 encoder and connectivity-filtered
pseudo-labels with spatial and temporal losses, supervision
is propagated across unlabeled sequences. Experiments on
CAMUS and CardiacNet demonstrate consistent improvements over existing scribble-supervised methods in Dice
and HD95 while substantially reducing false-positive predictions. These results show that annotation cost can be decoupled from sequence length without sacrificing reliable
temporal segmentation.

sample_chunks.text_content:
FGCARL: Fisher-Guided Continuously Adaptive Representation
Learning for Medical Image Segmentation
Xiaobing Yua,c,∗, Jin Yangb,∗, Peijie Qiua, Weiwei Maa and Xiaofeng Liuc
aMallinckrodt Institute of Radiology, Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis, St. Louis, 63110, MO, USA
bDepartment of Radiation Oncology, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York, 10029, NY, USA
cDepartments of Radiology and Biomedical Imaging, and Biomedical Informatics and Data Science, Yale University, New Haven, 06519, CT, USA
A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords:
Incremental learning
Domain Adaptation
Medical Image Segmentation
Representation learning
A B S T R A C T
Deep learning (DL) has achieved remarkable success in medical image segmentation by learning
data-driven representations from large-scale annotated datasets. However, medical images are often
collected independently across clinical sites, resulting in substantial domain shifts due to differences
in imaging modalities, acquisition protocols, and intensity distributions. Meanwhile, segmentation
classes may vary across sites due to differences in annotation standards, leading to class shifts.
These evolving domains and class definitions can substantially degrade segmentation performance on
newly encountered data, while sequential adaptation may cause catastrophic forgetting of knowledge
acquired from previously encountered domains and classes. Existing incremental learning methods
for medical image segmentation primarily address either domain shifts or class shifts, with these
two settings largely investigated independently. This separation leaves a critical gap in developing a
unified approach that can simultaneously adapt to evolving domains and newly introduced classes
while retaining previously acquired knowledge. To address this challenge, we propose FisherGuided Continuously Adaptive Representation Learning (FGCARL), a unified framework for
domain- and class-incremental 3D volumetric medical image segmentation. FGCARL comprises
two key components: Mutual Adaptive Instance Representation (MAIR), which adaptively aligns
feature distributions across sequentially encountered domains through bidirectional normalization and
denormalization, and Fisher-Guided Knowledge Retention (FGKR), which selectively preserves
parameters important for previously learned domains and classes through Fisher-guided regularization. We conducted extensive experiments across six cross-institutional segmentation tasks using
diverse segmentation architectures. Experimental results demonstrate that FGCARL consistently
outperformed state-of-the-art continual learning methods, effectively adapting to domain and class
shifts while mitigating catastrophic forgetting and maintaining strong segmentation performance on
both previously learned and newly encountered domains.
1. Introduction
Segmentation of anatomical structures and pathological
regions in medical images plays a critical role in supporting diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment planning. It has
markedly progressed by the development in deep learning
(DL)-based methods [58, 11, 1, 69, 71]. DL models achieve
impressive segmentation performance due to their ability to
capture rich, data-driven features [26, 79, 70, 56]. Typically,
these models are trained on a specific domain to effectively
learn features from domain-specific data. However, when
these models are employed to make zero-shot predictions
on new domains, they fail to capture domain-specific patterns, thus limiting their generalizability and applicability
to unseen datasets or tasks [46, 72]. Moreover, in clinical
practice, DL models are generally developed for specific
tasks. However, clinical datasets are often constructed and
developed incrementally across multiple sites, each using
different imaging modalities and acquisition protocols or
parameters [40, 44, 41, 43]. Additionally, the set of annotated anatomical structures may expand over time as new
lesions or structures of interest are introduced, driven by the
∗Xiaobing Yu and Jin Yang contributed equally to this work and are
co-first authors
xiaofeng.liu@yale.edu (X. Liu)
ORCID(s):
specific goals of the study, clinical needs, or newly available
modalities [52, 38]. Specifically, as illustrated in Figure 1,
a segmentation model was trained to segment enhancing
tumor (ET) from three modalities, including pre-contrast T1
weighted (T1w-pre), post-contrast T1-weighted (T1w-post),
and Fluid-Attenuated Inversion Recovery (FLAIR), in the
UCSF-BMSR dataset [59]. However, the model was subsequently adapted to segment ET and two additional structures,
tumor core (TC) and surrounding non-enhancing FLAIR
hyperintensity (SNFH), with the inclusion of additional T2weighted (T2w) modality in the BraTS-METS 2023 dataset
[50]. This example highlights the challenges posed by domain shifts and incremental annotation in medical image
segmentation.
To enable continual model adaptation to evolving clinical data, incremental learning (IL) frameworks have been
increasingly explored in medical image segmentation. Existing approaches can be broadly categorized into two paradigms:
domain-incremental learning (DIL) and class-incremental
learning (CIL). DIL focuses on adapting segmentation
models to sequentially encountered domains with different
data distributions, such as those arising from changes in
imaging modalities, acquisition protocols, or clinical sites
[74, 19, 3, 42]. In contrast, CIL addresses the sequential
introduction of new anatomical structures or pathological

Although these approaches have advanced continual adaptation for medical image segmentation, several important
challenges remain.
First, existing methods predominantly consider domain and class shifts independently. Most DIL and CIL
approaches are specifically designed for either evolving data
distributions or expanding label spaces, while real-world
clinical deployment may involve both changes simultaneously. For example, a model may be sequentially deployed
across institutions that use different imaging modalities
while also requiring segmentation of newly introduced
anatomical structures or lesion types. Although a few classdomain-incremental learning approaches have been explored in natural image recognition [31, 55], their underlying assumptions and learning mechanisms do not directly
translate to medical image segmentation. In particular, many
natural-image approaches rely on image-level class representations, prototypes, or classification-oriented objectives,
whereas medical image segmentation requires dense voxelwise predictions and preservation of spatially structured
anatomical representations. Consequently, a unified framework specifically designed for simultaneous domain and
class shifts in volumetric medical image segmentation remains underexplored.
Second, rehearsal-based strategies for mitigating catastrophic forgetting raise important challenges in clinical
applications. Rehearsal methods preserve knowledge from
previous tasks by storing and replaying representative samples or exemplars [19]. However, retaining patient imaging
data for continual model training can introduce privacy, security, and data-governance concerns, particularly in multiinstitutional clinical settings where patient data may be
subject to strict access and retention policies [33]. This motivates rehearsal-free approaches that can preserve previously
acquired knowledge without retaining sensitive patient data.
Third, existing adaptation mechanisms may be closely
coupled to specific segmentation architectures and normalization strategies. This issue becomes particularly relevant as modern medical image segmentation increasingly
incorporates diverse architectures, including convolutional
neural networks (CNNs) and vision transformers (ViTs).
For example, ViT-based models commonly employ layer
normalization (LN) [2], which normalizes feature statistics
within individual samples and may not explicitly account for
domain-level distribution differences. Such normalization
can therefore limit the model’s ability to explicitly adapt its
feature representations to substantial domain shifts. More
broadly, architecture-specific adaptation mechanisms may
hinder the development of a general continual learning strategy that can be consistently applied across heterogeneous
segmentation architectures.
These limitations limit the applicability and generalizability of current IL methods on medical image segmentation, and highlight the need for a unified, rehearsal-free, and
architecture-agnostic framework that can simultaneously accommodate evolving domains and class spaces while preserving previously acquired knowledge. Such a framework
is particularly important for clinical scenarios in which
segmentation models must continuously adapt to new institutions, imaging protocols, and anatomical or pathological
targets without access to historical patient data.
To address these limitations, we propose Fisher-Guided
Continuously Adaptive Representation Learning (FGCARL), a unified framework for domain- and class-incremental
learning in 3D volumetric medical image segmentation. FGCARL is designed to simultaneously accommodate evolving imaging domains, including differences in modalities,
acquisition protocols, and institutional distributions, and
expanding or changing segmentation label spaces, without
requiring access to previously observed patient data. The
framework consists of two complementary components:
Mutual Adaptive Instance Representation (MAIR) and
Fisher-Guided Knowledge Retention (FGKR).
The MAIR module addresses the representation-level
challenges arising from domain shifts. It performs bidirectional feature transformation through adaptive normalization and denormalization, enabling the model to establish
consistent feature representations across previously encountered and newly observed domains. Specifically, MAIR normalizes feature representations during the forward propagation to reduce domain-specific distribution discrepancies and subsequently restores domain-relevant statistics
through denormalization during backward propagation, allowing domain-specific information to be adaptively incorporated during optimization. Unlike methods that rely on
storing historical samples or explicitly maintaining domainspecific representations, MAIR performs adaptation directly
in the feature space and therefore does not require retention
of raw patient data. Moreover, its feature-level formulation

sample_chunks.text_content:
FGCARL for Medical Image Segmentation
is decoupled from task-specific output spaces and sequencelength dependencies, facilitating integration with heterogeneous segmentation architectures, including both convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and vision transformers
(ViTs).
The FGKR strategy addresses catastrophic forgetting
during sequential adaptation. Rather than relying on rehearsal of historical exemplars, FGKR estimates the importance of model parameters to previously learned tasks
using Fisher information and selectively constrains updates
to parameters that carry critical historical knowledge. This
parameter-level knowledge retention enables the model to
acquire new domain- and class-specific knowledge while
preserving information accumulated from previous tasks,
without requiring storage or replay of sensitive patient data.
FGCARL therefore provides a unified solution to the
three key challenges in medical image segmentation continual learning: simultaneous domain and class shifts, privacy constraints associated with rehearsal-based learning,
and adaptation across heterogeneous segmentation architectures. Unlike conventional domain-specific normalization approaches [7, 39, 13], MAIR performs bidirectional
statistical adaptation without requiring access to previously
observed datasets. Furthermore, its non-parametric distribution matching formulation does not impose restrictive Gaussian assumptions on medical imaging feature distributions,
allowing it to accommodate complex and potentially nonGaussian representations. By combining representationlevel domain adaptation with Fisher-guided parameter-level
knowledge retention, FGCARL enables continual learning
across domains with different imaging characteristics and
evolving anatomical or pathological label spaces while
mitigating catastrophic forgetting.
Extensive experiments across multiple cross-institutional
segmentation tasks and heterogeneous segmentation architectures demonstrate that FGCARL consistently outperforms state-of-the-art incremental learning methods, validating its effectiveness, robustness, and generalizability for
domain- and class-incremental medical image segmentation.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:
• We propose Fisher-Guided Continuously Adaptive
Representation Learning, a unified framework for
domain- and class-incremental learning in 3D volumetric medical image segmentation. FGCARL simultaneously addresses evolving imaging domains and
segmentation label spaces while supporting adaptation across heterogeneous segmentation architectures.
• We introduce Mutual Adaptive Instance Representation, a feature-level adaptation module that performs bidirectional normalization and denormalization to align feature representations across sequentially encountered domains. MAIR enables effective
adaptation to distribution shifts without requiring access to previously observed patient data and can be
integrated with diverse segmentation architectures.
• We develop Fisher-Guided Knowledge Retention, a
rehearsal-free optimization strategy that uses Fisher
information to selectively preserve parameters critical
to previously learned domains and classes. FGKR
mitigates catastrophic forgetting while allowing the
model to acquire new knowledge during incremental
training without storing historical patient data.
• We conduct extensive cross-institutional domain- and
class-incremental experiments across multiple medical image segmentation tasks and architectures. FGCARL consistently outperforms state-of-the-art incremental learning methods, demonstrating its effectiveness and generalizability across diverse segmentation
settings.
2. Related Works
2.1. Class Incremental Learning
CIL aims to sequentially incorporate newly introduced
classes while preserving the segmentation performance of
previously learned classes. Existing CIL approaches can
be broadly categorized into four main paradigms. First,
replay-based methods retain a subset of historical data or
generate synthetic samples and replay them during incremental training to alleviate catastrophic forgetting [3, 57,
23, 64, 66, 16, 34, 37, 61]. Although effective, storing or
replaying historical medical images and annotations can
introduce substantial privacy, security, and data-governance
concerns in clinical applications. Second, architecture-based
methods dynamically expand model capacity by introducing
task-specific branches, sub-networks, or other architectural
components for newly encountered classes [15, 24, 29, 35,
45, 76]. While these approaches can isolate newly learned
knowledge from previously acquired representations, continual network expansion increases model complexity and
may limit scalability and consistency across incremental
tasks. Third, regularization-based methods constrain updates to parameters or representations that are important
for previously learned classes, thereby preserving historical
knowledge while adapting the model to new classes [8, 28,
30, 42, 53]. However, existing regularization strategies often
rely on parameter-importance estimation or optimization
mechanisms that are closely coupled with specific model
architectures, which can limit their generalizability across
heterogeneous segmentation backbones. Fourth, knowledgedistillation-based methods transfer knowledge from a previously trained model to the incrementally updated model by
encouraging consistency between their predictions or intermediate representations, thereby reducing forgetting of previously learned classes [3, 12, 38, 54, 62, 65, 68, 75]. However, distillation-based approaches typically require maintaining a previous model and designing appropriate distillation objectives to preserve knowledge across changing
label spaces, which can become challenging when newly
introduced classes and previously learned classes have substantially different distributions or semantic relationships.

FGCARL for Medical Image Segmentation
2.2. Domain Incremental Learning
DIL focuses on sequentially adapting models to evolving
data distributions, enabling segmentation models to accommodate changes in imaging modalities, acquisition protocols, and institutional characteristics. Similar to CIL, however, DIL is inherently susceptible to catastrophic forgetting,
as adaptation to a newly encountered domain can overwrite
knowledge acquired from previously observed domains.
Early DIL approaches commonly employed exemplar-based
rehearsal, retaining data from previous domains for joint
training with the current domain [74]. To reduce the dependence on historical data, Li et al. proposed recovering information from previously encountered domains using an auxiliary generative model [33]. However, generating realistic
and sufficiently representative medical images solely from a
trained model remains challenging [73] and may introduce
additional privacy risks if sensitive patient information is
inadvertently encoded or reproduced [77]. More recently,
several studies have explored extending DIL toward more
general continual learning settings. Nevertheless, existing
approaches remain constrained by important assumptions
that limit their applicability to medical image segmentation.
Some methods are primarily developed for natural-image
classification and therefore do not directly accommodate
dense, voxel-wise prediction in 3D medical image segmentation [31, 55]. Other approaches are specifically designed for
conventional convolutional architectures and may not readily
generalize to transformer-based segmentation models [19,
42]. In addition, several methods rely on access to previously
observed data during incremental adaptation [18, 19], which
is undesirable in clinical settings because historical patient
data may be inaccessible across institutions or subject to
strict privacy and data-governance constraints. These limitations become particularly pronounced for high-dimensional,
multimodal 3D medical images, where effective continual
adaptation must preserve rich spatial and semantic representations while accommodating substantial distribution shifts.
Normalization-based approaches have also been explored
for domain adaptation by adjusting feature statistics to
reduce distribution discrepancies across domains [51, 49, 4].
However, conventional instance normalization and related
approaches primarily focus on aligning representations toward the current target domain and do not explicitly preserve domain-specific knowledge acquired from previously
encountered domains. Consequently, directly applying such
approaches to DIL may improve adaptation to the current
domain at the expense of historical knowledge. This motivates a continual representation adaptation mechanism that
can not only adapt feature statistics to newly encountered
domains but also retain and recover knowledge associated
with previously learned domains without requiring access
to historical patient data.

The proposed alignment loss complements the two
stages of MAIR by explicitly constraining the residual
distributional discrepancy between incoming and previously
learned representations. Forward MAIR first suppresses
instance-specific intensity and feature-scale variations in
the incoming domain, thereby providing a more stable
representation for incremental adaptation. Backward MAIR
subsequently restores the statistical characteristics associated with the previously learned domain, helping preserve
historical knowledge while reducing representation drift.
Building upon these two operations, the proposed alignment
loss further regularizes the residual discrepancy between
the incoming and historically aligned representations during

The proposed framework is particularly relevant to medical image segmentation, where domain shifts can arise
from differences in imaging modality, acquisition protocols,
scanner characteristics, and intensity distributions. Importantly, the alignment is performed directly in the learned
embedding space and does not require storing or replaying
historical medical images. Thus, the proposed approach provides an additional mechanism for controlling incremental
representation drift while avoiding direct access to previously collected patient data.
The two alignment components within the framework
play distinct but complementary roles. Higher-order moment
matching characterizes and reduces discrepancies in the
statistical shape of feature distributions without imposing an
explicit parametric distributional assumption, making it suitable for capturing non-Gaussian characteristics of medical
image representations. In contrast, Wasserstein alignment
explicitly regularizes the residual discrepancy between the
incoming and historical embeddings, providing a direct consistency constraint during optimization. These two mechanisms therefore operate at complementary levels: moment
matching focuses on the statistical structure of the feature
distributions, whereas Wasserstein alignment constrains the
overall embedding-level discrepancy.
Overall, the combination of Forward and Backward
MAIR with the two alignment mechanisms establishes a
hierarchical adaptation strategy: forward normalization for
representation stability, backward realignment for historical
knowledge retention, higher-order moment matching for
non-Gaussian distribution alignment, and Wasserstein regularization for explicit embedding consistency. This design
enables the model to simultaneously mitigate instance-level
variation, preserve previously learned statistical characteristics, and constrain residual representation drift during
incremental adaptation.

modified to accommodate new data, resulting in catastrophic
forgetting.

segmentation targets, providing a comprehensive testbed for
evaluating domain- and class-incremental learning.
UCSF-BMSR. The UCSF Brain Metastasis Segmentation and Registration (UCSF-BMSR) dataset contains
560 brain MR scans acquired using three modalities: T1weighted pre-contrast (T1w-pre), T1-weighted post-contrast
(T1w-post), and FLAIR. It provides voxel-wise annotations
for 5,136 brain metastases and supports volumetric segmentation of metastatic lesions [59].
BrainMetShare. BrainMetShare is a multi-institutional
dataset comprising 156 whole-brain MR scans with four
modalities: T1w-pre, T1w-post, T2-weighted (T2w), and
FLAIR. Each scan includes voxel-wise annotations of brain
metastases. Its multi-institutional nature introduces substantial acquisition and distribution variability, making it suitable for evaluating domain-incremental learning [20].
BraTS-METS 2023. The BraTS-METS 2023 dataset
contains 1,303 multi-parametric brain MR scans with T1wpre, T1w-post, T2w, and FLAIR modalities. It provides
voxel-level annotations for three tumor regions: enhancing tumor (ET), tumor core (TC), and surrounding nonenhancing FLAIR hyperintensity (SNFH), providing a challenging setting for class-incremental segmentation [50].
Multi-Center, Multi-Vendor and Multi-Disease Cardiac Segmentation (M&Ms). The M&Ms dataset contains
375 cardiac MR scans acquired from multiple institutions
using four MRI vendors, with 125, 125, 75, and 50 scans
from the respective vendors. Voxel-wise annotations are
provided for the left ventricle (LV), right ventricle (RV), and
left ventricular myocardium (MYO). The multi-center and
multi-vendor characteristics introduce substantial domain
variability for evaluating domain-incremental learning [6].
Beyond the Cranial Vault (BTCV). The BTCV dataset
contains 50 abdominal CT volumes with voxel-wise annotations for 13 anatomical structures. The diversity of target
organs and their anatomical characteristics provides a challenging benchmark for class-incremental segmentation [32].
Liver Tumor Segmentation (LiTS). The LiTS dataset
contains 131 abdominal CT volumes with voxel-wise annotations for the liver and liver tumors. The substantial
variation in tumor size, morphology, and appearance provides an additional challenging benchmark for incremental
segmentation [5].
Collectively, these datasets enable evaluation of FGCARL across heterogeneous MR and CT imaging scenarios, multiple anatomical regions, and diverse segmentation
targets, allowing us to assess its robustness to both domain
and class shifts.
4.2. Implementation details
All experiments were implemented in PyTorch and conducted on a single NVIDIA Tesla A100 PCIe GPU with 40
GB of memory. We employed Swin UNETR as the vision
transformer (ViT)-based backbone and nnU-Net as the convolutional neural network (CNN)-based backbone [21, 26].
Both architectures were evaluated under the same incremental learning settings to assess the architecture-agnostic
capability of FGCARL. The models were optimized using
AdamW with an initial learning rate of 1×10−4 and a weight
decay of 1 × 10−5. We adopted a linear warm-up followed
by cosine annealing learning-rate scheduler, with a warm-up
period of 50 epochs. All models were trained for 300 epochs
with a batch size of 2.
Raw volumetric images were preprocessed to 3D patches
of size 96 × 96 × 96 and standardized using Z-score normalization. During training, patches were augmented using
random flipping, random 90◦rotations, and random intensity
scaling and shifting. Each dataset was divided into training
and test sets at a ratio of 70% ∶30%. Unless otherwise specified, all compared methods used the same data splits, preprocessing procedures, augmentation strategies, and training
settings to ensure a fair comparison.
Segmentation performance was evaluated using the Dice
Similarity Coefficient (DSC), reported as a percentage. For
multi-class segmentation tasks, the DSC was calculated for
each foreground class and then averaged across the target
classes.
4.3. Comparison with state-of-the-art methods
We compared FGCARL with various state-of-the-art
(SOTA) CIL and DIL methods for 3D multi-modal medical image segmentation. The methods include replay-,
regularization-, architectural-, and knowledge-distillationbased approaches, covering both CNN- and ViT-based segmentation architectures. We considered two experimental
stages to separately assess the segmentation capability before incremental adaptation and the ability to simultaneously
accommodate domain and class shifts. In Stage 1, segmentation models were trained independently on the UCSF-BMSR
and BraTS-METS 2023 datasets. These results provided
a reference for the achievable segmentation performance
when no incremental adaptation was implemented. In Stage
2, models were initially trained on UCSF-BMSR to segment
ET using three modalities, including T1w-pre, T1w-post,
and FLAIR, and were subsequently adapted to the BraTSMETS 2023 domain, where they were required to segment
ET, TC, and SNFH using four modalities, including T1wpre, T1w-post, T2w, and FLAIR. Therefore, this setting
simultaneously introduced substantial domain shifts caused
by differences in data distributions and modality configurations and class shifts caused by the introduction of
new segmentation targets. To accommodate the different
numbers of input modalities between the source and target
domains, we additionally constructed a subtraction modality
by computing the difference between T1w-pre and T1w-post
images, thereby maintaining a consistent number of input
channels across the two domains.

domain- and class-incremental setting (Table 1). With Swin
UNETR, FGCARL achieved a mean DSC of 68.28% on

than competing methods. For example, on UCSF-BMSR
after adaptation, CLAMTS and Lifelong-nnUNet achieved
substantially lower performance than FGCARL. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the FGKR strategy in
protecting parameters associated with previously acquired
knowledge and mitigating catastrophic forgetting.
Robustness to simultaneous domain and class shifts.
Conventional CIL methods generally assume that the imaging distribution remains relatively stable and focus primarily
on learning newly introduced classes, whereas DIL methods
primarily address changes in data distributions. In contrast,
the Stage 2 setting requires the model to simultaneously
adapt to a new institution/dataset, different modality configurations, and an expanded label space. Most existing methods exhibited a substantial performance degradation under
this combined shift. FGCARL consistently maintained high
segmentation performance across both previously learned
and newly introduced targets, demonstrating that the proposed combination of MAIR and FGKR provides a unified
mechanism for feature adaptation and knowledge retention.
Qualitative comparison. Figure 4 presents qualitative
comparisons between FGCARL and representative incremental learning methods, including Lifelong-nnUNet and
CFIL, on both the original and incrementally adapted domains. On the UCSF-BMSR samples, which represent the
previously learned domain, FGCARL preserves the overall
morphology and spatial localization of the metastatic lesions after adaptation to BraTS-METS 2023. In contrast,
Lifelong-nnUNet and CFIL exhibit more pronounced prediction errors, including incomplete lesion delineation, spurious predictions, and deviations from the reference boundaries. These observations are consistent with the quantitative results and indicate that FGCARL better preserves
previously acquired segmentation knowledge during incremental adaptation. On BraTS-METS 2023, FGCARL produces segmentation masks that more closely follow the
reference annotations, particularly in delineating the spatial
extent and boundaries of different tumor subregions. The
competing methods exhibit greater segmentation discrepancies, including missing regions and inaccurate predictions
of individual tumor classes. Notably, FGCARL maintains
relatively coherent predictions for ET, TC, and SNFH despite the simultaneous changes in imaging distribution and
label space. Overall, the qualitative results demonstrate that
FGCARL achieves a favorable balance between plasticity,
i.e., learning new domain and class knowledge, and stability,
i.e., retaining previously acquired knowledge.
Overall, the results demonstrate that FGCARL provides a more effective solution for unified domain- and
class-incremental medical image segmentation than existing
SOTA methods. Its consistent performance across both
Swin UNETR and nnU-Net, together with its superior
target-domain adaptation and source-domain knowledge
retention, validates the effectiveness, generalizability, and
architecture-agnostic nature of the proposed framework.
4.4. Ablation Study
4.4.1. The effectiveness of MAIR
We first evaluated the effectiveness of the proposed
MAIR for domain-incremental learning under unaligned
modality settings. We compared MAIR with representative
SOTA DIL methods and several normalization-based approaches, including Batch Renormalization and Continuous
Batch Renormalization. We also compared the incorporation
of MAIR with the only forward MAIR. Experiments were
conducted using both nnU-Net and Swin UNETR, with domain adaptation evaluated in both directions: UCSF-BMSR
→BrainMetShare and BrainMetShare →UCSF-BMSR.
This bidirectional evaluation allows us to assess whether
MAIR provides consistent adaptation benefits across different source-target domain configurations.
Comparison with existing DIL methods. MAIR consistently achieved the strongest performance among the evaluated methods across both segmentation architectures and
adaptation directions (Table 2). With Swin UNETR, the proposed Forward & Backward MAIR achieved DSC scores of
77.32% and 68.27% on UCSF-BMSR and BrainMetShare,
respectively, when adapting from UCSF-BMSR to BrainMetShare. In the reverse adaptation setting, it achieved
81.62% and 62.15% DSC on UCSF-BMSR and BrainMetShare, respectively. These results substantially outperformed existing DIL methods, including Lifelong nnUNet,
UNEG, Mdvit, and CFIL. In particular, for UCSF-BMSR
→BrainMetShare, Forward & Backward MAIR improved
the BrainMetShare DSC from 65.11% achieved by Lifelong
nnUNet to 68.27%, while simultaneously retaining substantially higher performance on the previously learned UCSFBMSR domain (77.32%).
Effect of bidirectional MAIR. The ablation results
demonstrate that the the combination of Forward and Backward components is critical to the effectiveness of MAIR.
For nnU-Net, Forward MAIR alone achieved only 50.13%
DSC on UCSF-BMSR after adaptation from UCSF-BMSR
to BrainMetShare, whereas incorporating both Forward and
Backward MAIR increased the DSC to 72.47%. A similar
improvement was observed for the reverse adaptation direction, where the UCSF-BMSR DSC increased from 77.98%
with Forward MAIR alone to 78.96% with Forward &
Backward MAIR, while the BrainMetShare DSC increased
from 47.99%to 56.27%. These results indicate that forward
normalization alone can facilitate feature adaptation to the
incoming domain but is insufficient to preserve the feature
statistics associated with previously learned domains. The
backward alignment mechanism provides the complementary capability of restoring domain-specific feature characteristics, thereby improving the stability of previously
acquired representations during incremental adaptation.

Overall, these experiments demonstrate that the effectiveness of MAIR arises from the combination of its forward and backward operations rather than from normalization alone. Forward MAIR facilitates the stabilization of
incoming domain representations, while Backward MAIR
restores domain-specific feature characteristics and supports
retention of previously learned representations. Their combination enables robust adaptation in both directions and
across distinct segmentation architectures, providing an effective foundation for domain-incremental medical image
segmentation.
4.4.2. The effectiveness of FGKR
To further evaluate the effectiveness of FGKR under class-incremental learning, we conduct experiments on
BTCV and LiTS using a stage-wise incremental learning
setting, where new classes are introduced sequentially across
domains. All methods achieved identical performance at
Stage 1, providing a consistent starting point for evaluating
their ability to adapt to the subsequent incremental stage
(Table 3).
After introducing the new classes in Stage 2, FGKR
consistently achieved competitive or superior performance
compared with existing class-incremental learning methods. In particular, FGKR combined with Swin UNETR
achieved the best performance on both BTCV and LiTS,
reaching 83.08%and 47.59% DSC, respectively. On BTCV,
this corresponded to a substantial improvement over the
strongest competing baseline, demonstrating the effectiveness of FGKR in preserving and adapting semantic knowledge when new classes are introduced. FGKR also achieved
the best performance on LiTS when paired with either
nnUNet or Swin UNETR, with the latter providing the
strongest overall results.
The consistent improvements across the two datasets
and segmentation architectures demonstrate that the effectiveness of FGKR is not restricted to a particular network or dataset. Notably, the stronger performance obtained
with Swin UNETR suggests that FGKR can effectively
complement different segmentation architectures and facilitate knowledge retention and adaptation during classincremental learning. Overall, these results provide further
evidence that FGKR is robust to sequential class expansion
and domain variation in realistic incremental segmentation
scenarios.
4.5. The analysis on MAIR configurations
We further investigate the effectiveness of MAIR by
incorporating it into two representative segmentation architectures, nnU-Net and Swin UNETR, and evaluating
their performance on UCSF-BMSR, BrainMetShare, and
BraTS-METS 2023. MAIR consistently improves segmentation performance across both architectures, with more
pronounced gains observed for Swin UNETR (Table 4).
For nnU-Net, incorporating MAIR improves performance across all three datasets, and applying MAIR to all
layers consistently outperforms the single-layer configuration. On BraTS-METS 2023, for example, the mean DSC
across TC, SNFH, and ET increases from 61.34% for the
original nnU-Net to 64.14% with all-layer MAIR. These
results demonstrate that MAIR can effectively enhance conventional convolutional segmentation networks and that its
benefits are further strengthened when integrated throughout
the network.

The improvement is more pronounced for Swin UNETR.
The baseline model achieves a mean DSC of 63.15% across
the three BraTS-METS 2023 tumor regions, which increases
to 67.57% with all-layer MAIR. Moreover, the performance
consistently improves as MAIR is incorporated into more
layers, from single-layer to two-layer and finally all-layer
integration. The all-layer configuration achieves the best
performance across the three tumor regions and also obtains
the highest DSC on both UCSF-BMSR and BrainMetShare.
These results suggest that distributing MAIR throughout
the network enables Swin UNETR to better accommodate
variations in data distributions across different datasets.
We further compare MAIR with alternative normalization strategies. Replacing the original normalization with
batch normalization (BN) or instance normalization (IN)
substantially degrades performance, whereas MAIR consistently improves upon the original Swin UNETR. In particular, BN and IN achieve mean DSCs of only 56.02%
and 59.31%, respectively, compared with 67.57% for alllayer MAIR. This comparison indicates that the performance gains are not simply attributable to changing the normalization strategy. Instead, the progressive improvement
from single-layer to all-layer MAIR suggests that integrating
MAIR throughout the network is important for effectively
mitigating distribution shifts and improving segmentation
robustness.
Overall, these results demonstrate that MAIR is compatible with both convolutional and transformer-based segmentation architectures and provides consistent performance
improvements under heterogeneous data distributions. The
superior performance of the all-layer configuration further
supports the effectiveness of applying MAIR across multiple
normalization layers rather than restricting it to a single
layer.
4.6. Generalization of MAIR on 2D medical
images
To further evaluate the generalizability of MAIR beyond the primary experimental setting, we conducted experiments on the M&Ms dataset, which comprised cardiac
MRI data acquired from multiple vendors. MAIR consistently improved segmentation performance across all four
vendors, demonstrating its robustness to vendor-induced domain shifts (Table 5). When combined with nnU-Net, MAIR
outperformed all competing continual domain adaptation
methods across vendors, with particularly notable gains over
the strongest baseline on Vendor C.
We further combined MAIR with Swin UNETR to examine its compatibility with different segmentation backbones. MAIR + Swin UNETR achieved the best performance on three of the four vendors and remained highly
competitive on the remaining vendor. The consistent performance of MAIR with both nnU-Net and Swin UNETR
demonstrate that its effectiveness is not dependent on a specific segmentation architecture. Overall, these results highlight the strong generalization capability of MAIR across
heterogeneous vendors and different backbone architectures
for 2D medical image segmentation.
4.7. Generalization across network architecture
To evaluate the architecture generalization of FGCARL,
we incorporated FGCARL into two representative 3D segmentation architectures, nnU-Net and Swin UNETR, and
evaluated their performance under the UCSF-BMSR →
BraTS-METS 2023 incremental learning setting (Table 6).

FGCARL can be directly integrated into different network
architectures as an adaptive normalization mechanism, without requiring architecture-specific modifications.
FGCARL consistently improved segmentation performance for both architectures. In Stage 1, where the networks
were trained and evaluated within the same domain, incorporating FGCARL improved the baseline performance of both
nnU-Net and Swin UNETR on UCSF-BMSR and BraTSMETS 2023. Notably, the improvement is particularly pronounced for Swin UNETR, indicating that the adaptive
normalization provided by FGCARL can also enhance the
representation learned by transformer-based segmentation
networks even in the absence of domain shifts.
More importantly, FGCARL maintained its effectiveness during continual adaptation from UCSF-BMSR to
BraTS-METS 2023. In Stage 2, FGCARL achieved the highest performance among the evaluated incremental learning
methods on both the source and target domains for both
network architectures. For nnU-Net, FGCARL substantially
improved retention of the previously learned UCSF-BMSR
knowledge while simultaneously achieving the strongest
performance on BraTS-METS 2023. A similar trend was
observed with Swin UNETR, where FGCARL considerably
outperformed the competing incremental learning methods
on both domains. These results demonstrate that the benefits
of FGCARL are not tied to a particular segmentation architecture and that its adaptive normalization and knowledge
retention mechanisms can be effectively combined with both
convolutional and transformer-based networks.
4.8. Parameter sensitivity analysis
We evaluated the sensitivity of segmentation performance, measured by DSC, to the regularization weighting
hyperparameters in the UCSF-BMSR →BraTS-METS 2023
setting. Specifically, we independently varied the weights
of the three regularization components, 𝜆seg, 𝜆dist, and 𝜆FG
(Figure 6 (A)–(C)), respectively.
Overall, the three regularization terms exhibit similar
trends across the evaluated tumor subregions. Increasing
the regularization weight from 𝜆= 0 generally improves
segmentation performance, indicating that each component
contributes to effective continual adaptation and knowledge
retention. Across the evaluated components and tumor subregions, 𝜆= 1.0 provides a favorable balance between
retaining previously learned knowledge and adapting to the
target domain, yielding consistently strong performance on
both the source and target datasets. We therefore set the regularization weight to 𝜆= 1.0 in the remaining experiments.
5. Conclusion
In this work, we presented Fisher-Guided Continuously
Adaptive Representation Learning (FGCARL), a unified
framework for continual 3D medical image segmentation
under evolving domain and class shifts. By integrating Mutual Adaptive Instance Representation (MAIR) for adaptive
domain alignment with Fisher-Guided Knowledge Retention
(FGKR) for selective preservation of previously acquired
knowledge, FGCARL enables continuous adaptation while
mitigating catastrophic forgetting. Extensive experiments
across multiple cross-institutional segmentation tasks and
diverse segmentation architectures demonstrated that FGCARL consistently outperforms existing continual learning
approaches, achieving effective adaptation to newly encountered domains and classes while maintaining knowledge of
previously learned ones. These results highlight the potential
of FGCARL as a unified and generalizable solution for
continual medical image segmentation in dynamic clinical
environments.

sample_chunks.paper_title: Medical Image Segmentation: Foundation Model Adaptation versus Task-Specific Training
sample_chunks.authors: Emre Kutlusan, Yongmin Li
sample_chunks.category: AI in Medical Diagnosis and Medical Imaging
sample_chunks.text_content:
Medical Image Segmentation: Foundation Model Adaptation versus
Task-Specific Training
Emre Kutlusana, Yongmin Lia,∗
aDepartment of Computer Science, Brunel University of London, Uxbridge, UB8 3PH, United Kingdom
Abstract
Foundation models pretrained on large natural-image collections are increasingly adapted for
medical image segmentation, in the expectation that they will replace models trained for each
task. Most comparisons, however, use data from the training distribution and a single taskspecific baseline whose configuration is rarely justified, and therefore provide limited evidence
of performance at new clinical sites. It also remains unclear how much of a foundation model
must be adapted, and what determines this. We adapted a foundation model, DINOv2, with
strategies ranging from tuning only its bias terms to full fine-tuning, and compared it with U-Nets
and ResU-Nets trained from scratch. Experiments covered colonoscopy, breast ultrasound and
dermoscopy, with testing on held-out data from the training source and on independent datasets
from other institutions. The adapted foundation model generalised better on every external
dataset. Within the training distribution, the task-specific models remained competitive when
training data were abundant, and delineated boundaries more precisely, while the foundation
model more often missed small lesions. Only a small fraction of the foundation model required
adaptation, and the capacity needed was determined by the imaging domain rather than by the
adaptation method. A widely used polyp test set was also found to duplicate images from another
benchmark. Foundation-model adaptation is therefore warranted where models must work across
sites, with capacity selected on the target domain.
Keywords:
medical image segmentation, foundation models, parameter-efficient fine-tuning,
cross-dataset generalisation, U-Net, ResU-Net, nnU-Net
1. Introduction
Vision foundation models, pretrained on hundreds of millions of images at a scale no clinical
dataset approaches, have made a question urgent for medical image segmentation. Given a new
dataset and task, is it better to adapt one of these models, or to train a task-specific architecture
from random initialisation as the field has done since U-Net?
The question matters because of where segmentation models are deployed. A model trained
at one hospital is intended for use at others, on images from different scanners, protocols and
patient populations. This distribution shift, rather than in-domain accuracy, is the principal
obstacle to clinical adoption, and it is invisible in the measurement usually reported. Every model
in this study is therefore evaluated under two regimes: in domain, on held-out data from the
training distribution, and out of distribution, on data from institutions that contributed nothing
to training.
The literature comparing the two approaches generally reports that adapted foundation
models win, and three properties of how that comparison is made limit what follows from it. It is
usually conducted within the training distribution, so a property of the evaluation is reported as a
