2.2. Integrity Properties
We consider four relations a write stands in: to its source
and the record it joins, to its owner, to the sequence of states
before it, and to the actions it enables. Asking one question
about each relation defines one property.
Is it supported? Grounded state consistency (GSC):
every accepted fact f ∈zn,t has an unbroken provenance
path to authoritative evidence and violates no declared contradiction rule, unless an explicit unresolved-conflict state
records the violation.
Whose is it? Cross-patient noninterference (CPN): for
patients i ̸= j, changing only untrusted inputs in i’s history
cannot change the canonical state, memory, or action trace
of j, apart from a declared, minimized allow-list of shared
metadata that carries no patient-distinguishing signal.
Does it follow from the history? Longitudinal transition
integrity (LTI): the sequence of admitted states follows a
declared transition relation. What may it trigger? Authorized action integrity (AAI): every action taken on twin
state is permitted by an explicit action policy.
The four properties mirror classical integrity policy.
GSC corresponds to the Clark–Wilson rule that unconstrained inputs are either validated into constrained data
or rejected [10]. LTI corresponds to the Clark–Wilson requirement that transformations move data from one valid
state to another, and AAI to its rules on who may run
which transformation. CPN is noninterference [11] with
patients as the security domains and the allow-list as the
only sanctioned downgrading channel.
The properties do not collapse into one another: individually grounded writes can trace an illegal trajectory (LTI),
a grounded write can land in the wrong record (CPN),
admissible state can drive an unauthorized action (AAI),
and a correctly attributed write can be unsourced (GSC).
We do not claim completeness; we argue coverage against
Clark–Wilson instead. The append-only ledger realizes its
logging rule, while periodic verification of stored data and
separation of duty are not modeled. The set targets the
integrity of persistent state against an attacker who can propose writes. Legality of transitions over time falls under LTI;
interval-aware contradiction rules remain GSC checks on the
current record. Clinical correctness of authoritative evidence
is left to clinical validation, and confidentiality, availability,
and model integrity are out of scope. TWINGUARD-LITE
enforces per-write approximations of GSC and CPN, the
two properties that need no transition relation or action
policy. Because CPN relates two runs, the namespace check
enforces a stronger per-write condition: no write crosses
namespaces outside the allow-list. Under a trusted origin
binding, this approximates CPN for direct writes on the
canonical-state channel, the only channel implemented. Influence routed through shared stores, such as a retrieval
index, needs lineage tracking: the namespace check does
not see it, and only the GSC checks can stop it.
2.3. Threat Model and Trust Assumptions
The adversary seeks a target-state change, cross-patient
influence, or an unauthorized action, and enters through a
prompt, a retrieved document, a memory candidate, or a
tool output. We parameterize capability rather than assume
one universal attacker [12]. The evaluated attacker proposes
candidate writes, may spoof the mutable origin label, and
knows the frozen two-pair contradiction policy (Section 4.1),
but it is nonadaptive at run time. It cannot alter the policy
engine or the true originating namespace, which the benchmark supplies as trusted transport metadata.
Two assumptions bound every result. (i) CPN is evaluated given a correct binding between each write and the
patient it came from. A deployment must obtain that binding
from an authenticated session or a signed, patient-bound
event envelope. Our experiment validates the policy under
this binding but does not show how to establish the binding;
without the binding, CPN inherits the label-spoofing weakness of the provenance check (Section 3). (ii) Evaluation
starts once a poisoned item has become a candidate write.
We model neither index construction nor retrieval ranking,
so we study retrieval-mediated state poisoning rather than
end-to-end retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) poisoning.
3. TWINGUARD-LITE: A Rule-Based Gateway
Candidate writes from all three trust zones go through
the three checks of Fig. 1, described here from top to bottom.
(1) The provenance check (GSC) rejects a medication,
diagnosis, or laboratory candidate whose origin label is not
authoritative. It reads only the label: it builds no provenance
chain and verifies no signature, so it is cheap but spoofable.
Treatment candidates are outside its scope.
(2) The contradiction check (GSC) rejects a medication
candidate that forms a declared conflict pair with a medication already admitted to the same episode; drug names are
matched after normalization. The prototype implements no
unresolved-conflict state, so every match is rejected.
(3) The namespace check (CPN) rejects a candidate
whose true originating namespace, taken from trusted transport metadata, differs from the namespace it claims, unless
its type is on the frozen shared-metadata allow-list.
How the checks combine. Admission is a conjunction: a
write enters canonical state only if all three checks pass, and
any single failure rejects it. The checks are side-effect-free
predicates, so their order decides only which rule the ledger
records as the reason, never whether a write is admitted. We
chose conjunction because each check encodes a hard invariant, not a score; weighted or learned fusion would let strong
evidence on one property buy admission for a violation of
another. Beyond the ablation arms and surface baselines in
Table 1, we have not evaluated other combination rules;

4. Preliminary Evaluation
4.1. Benchmark
Benign trajectories come from the eICU Collaborative
Research Database (eICU-CRD) Demo v2.0.1 [13], the
openly licensed subset of the full eICU-CRD [14]. Namespaces are people, not intensive care unit (ICU) stays: our
500 unit stays resolve to 362 people, and we split by
person, 253 for calibration and 109 (148 ± 7 stays) for
testing, so no person lies on both sides. Times in eICU are
offsets from each unit stay’s own admission. We therefore
rebuild a shared episode clock for each hospital admission
as offset −hospitalAdmitOffset and replay admitted medication state within each episode (424 episodes;
133 in the first seed’s test split). Events cover medications,
diagnoses, laboratory results, and treatments.
The cohort is the 500 smallest patientunitstayid
values among Demo stays with at least 20 extracted events.
This rule is exactly reproducible but not random: stay identifiers are not assigned at random with respect to hospital, and
the event threshold favors data-rich stays. The cohort spans
48 distinct de-identified values in the source hospitalid
field (dataset codes, not a verified count of real sites), so
the results should not be read as generalizing across sites
or acuities. Once missing payloads are removed, 3 stays fall
below 20 usable events (15 at the minimum); we keep them
rather than reselect. Drug names are missing for 6137 of the
16,335 medication rows (38%; 103,821 rows overall); they
are dropped at load, so no medication attack or vocabulary
uses a missing-value marker. However, 559 retained laboratory rows lack a numeric result, and cross-patient copies
of them are still rejected by the namespace check. The
medication table’s coded fields (drugHiclSeqno, GTC)
are not used.
Only the benign stream is observed data; every adversarial write, origin label, and namespace binding is generated by the benchmark. Three attack families are injected
into the test split, giving 29,131 ± 2706 candidates per
seed, 1090 ± 16 of them malicious. Direct/indirect injection has loud (instruction tokens), quiet (a plain fact), and
provenance-spoof (a forged authoritative label) subtypes.
Like the spoofs, retrieval-mediated state poisoning targets
the declared conflict pairs, but it carries a curated origin.
Cross-patient contamination copies an event type and its
exact value from a different person’s real stream. The spoof
attacker is targeted and causal: it reads only earlier records
in the episode it writes to and places a real surface form
of a declared-conflict drug at a strictly later episode time.
The contradiction rule matches each declared drug name as
a whole word anywhere in the payload, because eICU text
often opens with a package quantity (2 ML - DIGOXIN
0.25 MG/ML IJ SOLN). It covers only string-matchable
conflicts and, in this corpus, one of the two declared
pairs: apixaban never appears, so warfarin/apixaban never
fires and every contradiction decision comes from amiodarone/digoxin.
4.2. Defenses and Protocol
The surface baselines are a keyword filter over the
loud-injection generator’s own instruction tokens and an
anomaly detector. The detector scores each write by its percharacter negative log-likelihood under a Laplace-smoothed
fourth-order character Markov model fitted on calibration
text only, and flags scores at least two standard deviations
(2σ) above the mean score of benign calibration writes.
Two choices keep this baseline honest. Text is case-folded
and whitespace-collapsed before scoring, and every injected
medication value is a verbatim corpus string; otherwise
the detector would separate typography, not content. The
structured arms ablate the gateway check by check: provenance only, contradiction only, GSC only (provenance +
contradiction), CPN only (namespace), and TWINGUARDLITE (GSC+CPN). A no-defense arm flags nothing and
gives the attack-success baseline.

baselines are weak for a structural reason. The keyword
filter recalls only 0.16: it catches every loud injection (1.00),
while quiet, spoofed, poisoned, and cross-patient writes
carry no token to match (0.00 on quiet injection, 0.00 on
the provenance spoofs). The anomaly detector recalls 0.24
(F1 = 0.190±0.017). It too sees mainly loud writes (0.84),
falling to 0.19, 0.17, 0.16, and 0.04 on quiet, spoofed,

also flags 0.049 ± 0.006 of the mean 28,041 benign writes
per seed, which rules it out as a standalone admission control. Provenance alone reaches recall 0.599 ± 0.009 with no

origin is authoritative for its source patient. GSC alone
reaches 0.605 ± 0.009 and CPN alone 0.300 ± 0.005. Only
their combination reaches recall 0.905 ± 0.008 (precision
0.991 ± 0.006, F1 = 0.946 ± 0.005) at a 0.033% FPR, or
9.35 ± 5.75 rejected benign writes per seed, and it drives
retrieval-mediated poisoning and, given the trusted binding,
cross-patient contamination to 0% success.
Why the combined row is nearly a sum. The recall
and false-positive count of TWINGUARD-LITE are almost
exactly the sums of the GSC-only and CPN-only values.
This is not because one check is selected per write; every
write must pass all three. The two properties catch nearly
disjoint attacks, sharing only 1 of 19,742 pooled true positives (largely by construction; Section 5), and CPN adds no
false positives.
The contradiction check alone. By itself, the contradiction check reaches only recall 0.028 ± 0.008 (precision
0.764±0.141; 9.40±5.78 false positives per seed), because
it inspects only medication writes that name a declared drug.
Its pooled false positives rise from 187 (GSC only) to 188
because a malicious medication write that the provenance
check would have rejected is admitted and becomes a conflict partner of a later benign write. It is therefore not a
detector in its own right, but it is the only check that can stop
a write with a forged authoritative label. In the full gateway,
145 rejections are logged under it, all provenance spoofs
except 1 cross-patient write that the namespace check also
rejects. It thus stops 144 attacks that no other check stops but
causes all 187 benign rejections, more than it alone prevents;
its worth therefore depends on a better-sourced rule set.
That role matters because the 0% retrieval result reflects
trust-zone enforcement, not robustness to poisoned retrieval:
the provenance check rejects the family’s curated origin

about its origin (authoritative), so that only the contradiction check can still reject those writes. Then 92.9%
of that family is admitted, and TWINGUARD-LITE falls
to recall 0.626 ± 0.010 (F1 = 0.766 ± 0.008), with the
benign stream and its 187 false positives unchanged. The
residual 24% injection success in the main run likewise

episodes with no drug whose declared partner the attacker
could supply—and the check caught 84% of those, or 6.5%
of all spoofs. Contradiction checking is a partial backstop
against spoofing, not a substitute for authenticated ingestion.
With the strictest episode boundary, where no state crosses
a unit stay (500 episodes), the conclusions hold: recall
0.904 ± 0.008, precision 0.993 ± 0.004, injection residual
24%, 7.25 ± 4.25 false positives per seed, and 134 pooled
contradiction true positives.

5. Discussion and Limitations
We discuss the main limits, including those raised in
review, and our view of each.
Strength by construction. The benign data is real, but the
origin labels, namespace bindings, and attacks are generated,
so the structured checks are strong partly by construction.
Likewise, the keyword list is the loud generator’s own, so
its 1.00 loud recall is guaranteed, and neither baseline is
state of the art. The near-disjointness of GSC and CPN
detections also follows from the family construction, and the
injection and retrieval families violate the same provenance
check, so their separate rates report attack provenance, not
independent defenses.
Trusted patient binding. CPN’s 0% cross-patient success
holds given a trusted true-origin binding. Once that binding
exists, detecting a crossing is simple; the hard problem is
establishing the binding through authenticated sessions or
signed, patient-bound event envelopes, and this work does
not solve it. The CPN allow-list is also unvalidated and
unexercised: no evaluated write uses an allow-listed type, so
the CPN numbers are those of a deny-every-crossing rule.
Authenticated provenance. The provenance check reads a
label, and the spoofed-retrieval run shows the consequence:
92.9% of lying retrieval writes are admitted. Authenticated,
origin-bound provenance is therefore central to making the
approach usable, and the label check stands in for it here.
The check also covers only medication, diagnosis, and laboratory writes, so the 12,172 treatment rows (12% of the
corpus) pass it unexamined. No attack exploits this gap:
treatment-type attacks occur only as cross-patient copies,
which the namespace check rejects.
Contradiction coverage. The declared list holds two drug
pairs that we chose as demonstration policy, not drawn from
an interaction authority, guideline, or prespecified protocol. It therefore carries a cherry-picking risk as well as a
coverage limit, and the reported contradiction recall is an
upper bound conditional on the list. Our extraction omits
drugStopOffset, so medication state is cumulative and
a flagged pair may never have been active at the same
time. Even an active pair need not be an error: amiodarone
with digoxin, the pair behind every false positive here, can
be prescribed deliberately with a reduced digoxin dose. A
larger, clinically grounded rule set with medication start and
stop times would make the evaluation more convincing and
reduce such rejections. Until then, flagged writes should be
quarantined for clinician adjudication, with the ledger entry
and rule attached, rather than silently rejected.
End-to-end evaluation. No language model, agent, or
retriever runs here. Starting at the admission boundary
isolates the mechanism: the decision depends only on the
candidate write, its transport metadata, and the admitted
state, though the producing pipeline sets the fields the checks
read, notably the origin label. It does not show how often,
or in what form, real injected or retrieved content becomes a
candidate write. A small end-to-end study, in which an LLM
agent with retrieval produces writes that reach the gateway,
is the most important next experiment. The attacker is also
nonadaptive at run time. Ongoing work adds authenticated
ingestion, a maintained rule set with medication intervals,
LTI and AAI enforcement, adaptive attackers, and patientclustered statistics.
6. Related Work
Agentic prompt-injection benchmarks and defenses [3],
[4], [9], [15], retrieval and memory poisoning [5], [6], and
medical-model poisoning [7] establish the individual attack
surfaces, and adversarial machine learning taxonomies [12]
structure our threat model. At HealthSec’25, Nagaraja and
Bahsi [8] apply goal-driven risk assessment to an LLMpowered healthcare system, including prompt injection and
knowledge-base poisoning, and identify cross-patient context contamination through poor memory isolation as a risk;

CPN addresses the integrity side of that risk for persistent state. At HealthSec’24, Hallajiyan et al. [16] anticipate inference-time false data injection attacks on machinelearning-enabled medical devices. Both study how corrupted
inputs reach clinical systems; we add an enforcement point
for the state they leave behind.
CaMeL [9] stops untrusted data from steering control flow within one execution; TWINGUARD-LITE governs
what an execution may persist across executions. Neither
subsumes the other: a protected run can still commit an
unsourced fact, and CPN quantifies over a second patient’s
history, which no single trace expresses.
7. Conclusion
Attacks that evade surface filters are textually ordinary
but structurally invalid. Enforcing rule-level approximations
of GSC and CPN as auditable admission checks detects
90.5% of the malicious writes here at a 0.033% falsepositive rate. Every admitted attack is a provenance spoof,
calling for authenticated ingestion, and every rejected benign
write comes from the contradiction rule, calling for rules
from a maintained interaction authority. The main practical
takeaway is a workflow for systems that persist patient state:
bind every write to an authenticated source and patient,
check it against declared rules before it persists, log each
decision, and quarantine what the rules flag. As no language
model, agent, or retriever is run, these results validate defined properties under stated trust assumptions, not clinical
readiness.
Ethics and Data
Benign streams derive from the open-access eICU-CRD
Demo v2.0.1 [13], which PhysioNet [17] distributes under
the Open Database License (ODbL) 1.0 without a credentialing agreement; it is a de-identified subset of the full
eICU-CRD [14]. Privacert certified its re-identification risk
as meeting the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) Safe Harbor standard (Certification
no. 1031219-2). The study involves no interaction with
human subjects and no direct identifiers, and we make no
attempt to re-identify anyone; our derived tables remain
under ODbL 1.0 with attribution. All adversarial writes
are benchmark-generated; no real eICU record is labeled
malicious.
Acknowledgments
We are deeply grateful to the three anonymous reviewers
of HealthSec’26 for their careful, generous, and constructive reviews, which substantially improved this paper. They
asked how the integrity properties were chosen and whether
they are complete, how the implemented properties combine,
and what the contradiction check contributes on its own.
They helped us examine the trust assumptions behind the
patient binding and the provenance check, the scope of the
contradiction rules, and the missing end-to-end experiment,
and they showed us how to organize the paper and name
its properties clearly. The paper is clearer and more precise
about its assumptions because of them. We also thank the
HealthSec’26 workshop chair and program committee for
their guidance.

October 14, 2026
PocketTSLM: Deploying an On-Device
Soft-Prompt Time-Series Language Model
for Privacy-Preserving Smartphone
Reasoning
Max Rosenblattl
1, Nikhil Krishnaswamy1, Leon Nissen
1, Manuel Milling
2, Nicolas
Zumarraga4, Ning Wang4, Thomas Kaar
1,3,4, Robert Jakob
3,4, Björn W. Schuller
2,5, Elgar
Fleisch
4,6, Patrick Langer
1,3,4, and Paul Schmiedmayer
1
1Stanford University, USA; 2CHI, Technical University of Munich University Hospital, Germany; 3Aionic Labs,
Switzerland; 4ETH Zurich, Switzerland; 5GLAM, Imperial College London, UK; 6Centre for Digital Health Interventions
(CDHI), University of St. Gallen, Switzerland
Correspondence mrosenbl@stanford.edu · Code github.com/SchmiedmayerLab/PocketTSLM · Code license MIT
Abstract
Consumer phones and wearables increasingly collect physiological time-series data, yet most mobile systems
treat these streams as summaries or text rather than as temporal evidence. This representation is poorly
matched to personal health systems that need to retrieve, route, or summarize sensor evidence while preserving
temporal structure. Cloud-hosted time-series language models avoid smartphone limits, but they repeatedly
move sensitive physiology off the device and add latency and per-query compute cost. Mobile model alternatives
that aggregate time-series data into statistical features or serialize raw samples as text either compress temporal
structure or exhaust the context and memory budgets of small on-device models. We present PocketTSLM, a
mobile-native deployment of OpenTSLM SoftPrompt, the soft-prompt variant of the OpenTSLM time-series
language model. PocketTSLM runs fully on a consumer smartphone by injecting encoded time-series windows
as embeddings instead of tokenizing time series as text. A numerical parity protocol verifies identical greedydecoded token sequences between the Swift port and a Python reference using Apple’s MLX machine-learning
framework. Answers also match the PyTorch reference, although rationale wording can differ. An on-device
context-economics benchmark compares the soft-prompt path with a text-serialized baseline on the same
backbone. In our benchmark format, soft-prompting uses approximately 12× fewer time-series tokens and
reduces prompt-prefill cost. PocketTSLM processes 30-second Sleep-EDF electroencephalography clips for sleep
staging and a 1,000-sample (10 s) 12-lead electrocardiogram clip from ECG-QA. In comparison, text-serialized
baselines exceed the phone’s context or memory budget at longer time-series windows. All inference runs
entirely on the device, with no health data transmitted during inference.
A version of this paper was accepted at the Workshop on Deploying AI in Healthcare (DAIH) at the Conference on
Language Modeling (COLM 2026).

PocketTSLM
1 Introduction
Consumer devices now collect physiological time-series data that were previously limited to clinical or
research environments [1, 2]. Smartwatch irregular-pulse notifications have been evaluated for atrial
fibrillation screening in large cohorts [3], phone-connected systems make electroencephalography
(EEG) acquisition more accessible [4], and passive wearable streams such as heart rate, sleep, and
activity have been used for infectious-disease surveillance, COVID-19 detection, and prospective
health-risk assessment [5–7]. In each case, measurements are captured close to the patient, but the
interpretation delivered to a patient or downstream system is often a label, score, or study endpoint.
Digital biomarker pipelines make this pattern explicit: continuous measurements are translated
into digital endpoints or biomarkers for evaluation and decision support [8]. Those outputs support
screening, monitoring, and study endpoints, but they do not explain the source time-series window itself.
Recent personal-health large language model (LLM) systems interpret wearable-derived sleep, activity,
and fitness data through natural-language coaching or insight generation [9, 10]. Therefore, patientfacing assistants, clinician review tools, and supervised health agents need descriptions grounded in
source time-series windows that can be retrieved, routed, summarized, or used to defer a response
when the evidence is insufficient.
Time-series language models (TSLMs) are designed for this time-series-to-language interface. They couple time-series encoders to language models and generate natural-language descriptions or rationales
from raw physiological time-series data such as electrocardiogram (ECG), EEG, and accelerometry [11, 12]. These outputs give software a text interface to sensor evidence while preserving the
temporal structure in the model input [11]. Time Series Language Models may enable systems that
reason over sensor windows rather than only aggregate features.
Personal-health LLM systems are important reference points, but they do not solve the deployment
problem addressed here: they reason over derived wearable data with large language models rather
than running a time-series-native model on the phone [9, 10]. When interpretation is served remotely,
personal physiological streams or derived sensor evidence must leave the device, making privacy and
secondary-use risks part of the inference pathway [13]. Server-side inference also adds a network
dependency and per-query compute cost. General on-device LLM work identifies limited device
memory as a central inference bottleneck [14]. Medical LLM benchmarks show the same tradeoff: local
inference improves the privacy and cost posture, while memory and efficiency become the limiting
constraints [15]. For physiological time-series data, moving inference onto the phone shifts the system
boundary: raw data can remain local, offline analysis becomes possible, and cloud storage is no longer
required for each query.
The main obstacle is representation rather than model size. Mobile LLM runtimes are built around
token-identifier input and do not expose a path for injecting precomputed embeddings, so a timeseries encoder’s output cannot be fed to the model directly. If the runtime cannot accept encoder
embeddings, the time-series data must be serialized as text. Text serialization reuses an unchanged
language-model interface and can cast time series as next-token prediction [16], but it expands
each sample into multiple vocabulary tokens, formats or rounds numeric values, and spends the
same limited context window needed for instructions and generated text. OpenTSLM soft-prompt
(OpenTSLM-SP) avoids that prompt-level bottleneck by using representation-level fusion: a time-series
encoder projects time-series windows into soft-prompt embeddings that are injected directly into the
LLM’s embedding sequence [11]. That design is better matched to physiological time-series data, but
2

sample_chunks.text_content:
PocketTSLM
it requires embedding-level access to the forward pass and cannot be expressed through token-only
generation interfaces.
We present PocketTSLM, an on-device port of OpenTSLM-SP to MLX-Swift that evaluates whether
the soft-prompt pathway can run on a consumer smartphone without changing the reference model’s
greedy-decoding behavior. The port preserves the encoder-projector-LLM architecture while modifying
the on-device generation path to accept projected time-series embeddings. PocketTSLM is scoped as a
deployment and evaluation of on-device soft-prompt physiological time-series reasoning, not clinical
validation, autonomous medical action, or behavior-change efficacy. We contribute: (1) a method
for migrating soft-prompt TSLMs to MLX-Swift; (2) a numerical parity protocol that compares the
on-device implementation against the reference under greedy decoding; (3) an on-device contexteconomics benchmark comparing soft-prompt encoding with a text-serialized baseline on the same
backbone; and (4) a HealthKit-enabled iPhone demo that runs ECG and EEG reasoning locally without
sending health data off-device.
2 Related Work
Time-series interfaces for language models. Integrating time-series data into LLMs is an active
research area [17], with approaches spanning text serialization, model reprogramming, soft prompting,
and cross-attention fusion [18]. Text serialization preserves the ordinary token interface and has been
used for forecasting and wearable-health prediction [16, 19], but language models often struggle to
reason over numbers presented this way [20]. Since every serialized sample consumes vocabulary
tokens, long time-series windows can spend the same context window needed for instructions and
generated text. Reprogramming methods keep the language-model backbone frozen while aligning
time-series patches or text prototypes to the model input space [21, 22]. These methods show that
representation choice matters, but they primarily target prediction, classification, or forecasting rather
than natural-language rationales grounded in raw time-series data [16, 19, 21, 22]. Representationlevel fusion instead learns a time-series encoder whose embeddings are injected into the model as soft
prompts or cross-attention inputs, preserving free-form generation [23, 24]. OpenTSLM [11] uses this
approach for chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning [25], coupling a time-series encoder to a frozen LLM
through soft prompts and generating rationales for clinical time-series tasks. We port its soft-prompt
variant fully onto a smartphone and quantify the token, memory, and latency cost of soft prompts
against text serialization on the same backbone (§4).
Wearable and physiological time-series language systems. In personal-health and wearable sensing,
recent LLM systems often reason over derived variables, contextual summaries, or tool-generated
features rather than raw physiological time-series windows [10, 19]. SensorLLM and LLaSA align
inertial measurements with language outputs for human activity recognition and sensor question
answering, but they focus on motion sensing rather than physiological ECG or EEG interpretation [26,
27]. ECG-QA provides a benchmark for ECG question answering, and ECG-Chat trains an ECG-language
model for report generation and dialogue [28, 29]. These systems expand time-series language
modeling for health and wearables, but they do not establish whether a soft-prompt physiological
TSLM can run fully on a consumer smartphone.
3

sample_chunks.paper_title: PocketTSLM: Deploying an On-Device Soft-Prompt Time-Series Language Model for Predictive Wearable Health Analytics
sample_chunks.authors: Max Rosenblattl, Nikhil Krishnaswamy, et al.
sample_chunks.category: Healthcare Wearables, IoT and Predictive Analytics
sample_chunks.text_content:
PocketTSLM
Deployment settings for health time-series inference. Most time-series-to-language and wearablehealth language models are developed and evaluated in server-side or offline research settings
[10, 11, 19, 29], so privacy, latency, and per-query cost remain deployment constraints rather than
solved properties of the model. On-device LLM inference is an emerging direction, but it is tightly
constrained by memory and efficiency, including for clinical models [14, 15]. For privacy, federated
learning decentralizes training rather than inference [30], and fog execution keeps inference within
a trusted local network [31]. On-device, ODCSIS [32] runs a small language model on a phone
for human activity recognition, but injects sensors by serializing statistical features into text rather
than encoding the raw time-series data. PocketTSLM therefore targets a remaining deployment
constraint: soft-prompt TSLMs require embedding-level input and enough context headroom for raw
time-series windows, whereas text serialization preserves an unchanged token-level generation path
at the cost measured in §4. Prior work therefore covers time-series-to-language modeling, wearable
and physiological language systems, privacy-preserving inference, and on-device language models,
but not soft-prompt physiological TSLM inference fully on a consumer smartphone.
3 Methods
Reference model and migration strategy. PocketTSLM ports OpenTSLM-SP, the soft-prompt variant
of OpenTSLM, from PyTorch into an iOS/MLX-Swift runtime. The PyTorch reference does not run
in the target environment without reimplementation, as the model depends on framework-specific
modules and a generation path that accepts projected input embeddings. We migrate the model in
two stages: first from PyTorch to Python MLX, then from Python MLX to Swift MLX. This staging
separates framework-level parity from Swift runtime parity and provides a Python MLX reference for
the final port.
Soft-prompt architecture. The architecture receives channel- or lead-wise physiological time-series
windows, including the single-channel EEG (Sleep-EDF sleep staging) and 12-lead ECG (ECG-QA)
inputs evaluated in §4. A raw physiological time series is split by temporal position into fixed-length
patches and fed to a time-series encoder: a CNN patch encoder followed by a Transformer that produces
one embedding per patch (Fig. 1). Patch length, stride, z-normalization, and lead ordering follow the
OpenTSLM reference without modification.
A learned multilayer perceptron (MLP) projector maps the encoder outputs into the input space of a
frozen pre-trained LLM, Llama-3.2-1B in our deployment. The projected embeddings are interleaved
with the embedded text prompt as soft-prompt tokens, meaning continuous vectors are injected directly
into the model’s embedding sequence rather than vocabulary tokens. [11] Different LoRA adapters [33],
each roughly 1% of the model’s parameters, adapt the frozen backbone to the ECG and EEG tasks. The
selected adapter determines the modality-specific mapping used at inference. This representation-level
pathway reduces prompt length, as each time-series patch becomes one embedding, but it requires
the decoder forward pass to accept precomputed embeddings rather than only token identifiers.
Migration implementation. The first migration stage reimplements three OpenTSLM-SP components
in Python MLX: the TransformerCNNEncoder, the MLPProjector, and the interleave logic that inserts
projected time-series embeddings between text-token embeddings before the LLM forward pass. The
4

Figure 1. The OpenTSLM-SP pipeline running fully on-device. Health time-series data are split into
patches and encoded by a convolutional neural network (CNN) patch encoder and transformer (the timeseries encoder), projected into the LLM embedding space, and interleaved with the embedded text prompt.
The combined sequence is decoded by a frozen pre-trained LLM with a low-rank adaptation (LoRA) adapter
into a natural-language model rationale. The entire pipeline executes on the device through the MLX-Swift
runtime on Apple silicon, with no health data leaving the phone. Figure adapted from Langer et al. [11].
trained encoder, projector, and LoRA adapter weights are loaded directly from the original PyTorch
checkpoints and converted to the MLX format. Conversion applies layout transforms where the two
frameworks use different weight conventions, including Conv1d kernel transposition and fused querykey-value (QKV) splitting. The LLM backbone uses Llama-3.2-1B with bfloat16 (bf16) base weights,
matching the adapted checkpoint format.
The second migration stage ports the Python MLX reference module by module to Swift MLX, targeting
Apple’s MLX-Swift framework. Since both stages share MLX operator semantics, discrepancies introduced in the Swift port can be separated from discrepancies introduced during the PyTorch-to-MLX
conversion. MLX-Swift’s high-level generation path could not be used directly, as it accepts token
identifiers rather than precomputed input embeddings. MLX-Swift exposes the lower-level tensor
operations needed to rebuild the pipeline, so we adapted its Llama implementation and forward pass
to accept input embeddings. Since the Swift modules use the same parameter keys as the Python MLX
reference, the encoder and projector weights load from safetensors without further remapping.
Three implementation details affect reproducibility. Several NumPy-style convenience functions available in Python MLX have no direct Swift counterpart and were reconstructed from lower-level MLXArray
operations. MLX’s lazy-evaluation model requires explicit evaluation barriers during the encoderprojector hand-off so intermediate tensors are materialized before generation. Certain operations
dispatch to Metal graphics processing unit (GPU) kernels unavailable in headless continuous integration (CI) environments, so parity tests are pinned to the central processing unit (CPU) backend for
deterministic comparison.
Evaluation data and benchmark protocol. The reported benchmarks use fixed, public, de-identified
research samples from Sleep-EDF [34, 35] and ECG-QA [28]; they do not use prospective HealthKit

sample_chunks.paper_title: PocketTSLM: Deploying an On-Device Soft-Prompt Time-Series Language Model for Predictive Wearable Health Analytics
sample_chunks.authors: Max Rosenblattl, Nikhil Krishnaswamy, et al.
sample_chunks.category: Healthcare Wearables, IoT and Predictive Analytics
sample_chunks.text_content:
PocketTSLM
records from patients. We evaluate two OpenTSLM tasks: single-channel Sleep-EDF sleep staging and
12-lead ECG-QA. Both tasks run with a Llama-3.2-1B backbone, bf16 base weights, and the original
LoRA checkpoints without retraining.
The benchmark has two components. First, a numerical parity protocol compares the Swift MLX port
with the reference implementation under greedy decoding. For each evaluated prompt, the protocol
compares the full greedy-decoded token sequence from the Swift port against the Python MLX and
PyTorch references.
Second, a context-economics benchmark compares two encodings of the same raw time series with
the same backbone and generation loop. Text serialization is the natural baseline for soft prompting
on device: it preserves an unmodified token-level generation interface and is the established method
for feeding raw time series to a language model as tokens [16, 19].
The soft-prompt arm injects representation-level embeddings and produces ⌈𝐿/4⌉temporal tokens per
channel or lead, where 𝐿is the length of the time-series. The text-serialized arm uses OpenTSLM’s
prompt-level format [11], a fixed-precision encoding in the style of LLMTime [16]: each z-normalized
sample is rounded to two decimals, its decimal point dropped, and the result rendered as "012"-style
text fed as vocabulary tokens. For the zero-padded sample format used here, the text arm costs 3
byte-pair encoding (BPE) tokens per raw sample per channel or lead, measured with the backbone
tokenizer. Both arms decode greedily with a maximum of 80 new tokens, so differences in prompt
tokens, time to first token (TTFT), and peak memory are attributable to the input encoding rather
than the decoder policy.
We sweep series length 𝐿and report, per encoding, time-series tokens, full-prompt feasibility, TTFT,
peak memory, and the context-window ceiling. We report TTFT rather than end-to-end latency, as
truncating below the training window can change the generated-token count, while the prefill cost is
directly driven by the input encoding. The theoretical capacity estimates use the backbone’s 8192-token
context window, whereas the measured on-device sweep uses a lower 4,300-token prompt budget to
preserve runtime memory headroom during generation. The two arms share the same LoRA-adapted
backbone. LoRA changes generated content but not prefill cost or memory, so the reported context
economics are unaffected by the adapter choice. All on-device measurements were collected on an
iPhone Air running iOS 26.4.1 with MLX-Swift 0.21.3. The reported TTFT and peak memory values
are means over five repeated sweeps of the same configuration, given as mean ± standard deviation.
TTFT is measured from the start of prompt prefill to the emission of the first generated token. Peak
memory is the high-water mark of MLX’s unified-memory allocator, reset immediately before each arm,
so it covers the resident model weights plus that arm’s prefill activations and KV cache but excludes
allocations made outside the MLX allocator.
App integration. The on-device executable is embedded in a demo iOS app for local physiological
time-series interpretation (Fig. 2). The demo runs the pipeline on bundled evaluation samples, the
same fixed samples used in the benchmark (§4), included in the app bundle, and on request on
the most recent ECG recorded by a paired Apple Watch and read from HealthKit on the device. All
inference runs locally: the encoder, projector, and LLM execute in-process through MLX-Swift, and no
health data leaves the device. Network access is unused during inference; the app makes no outgoing
connections while running the pipeline.

sample_chunks.category: Healthcare Wearables, IoT and Predictive Analytics
sample_chunks.text_content:
PocketTSLM
4 Results
These results are scoped to implementation parity and on-device context economics. They do not test
clinical performance or patient-facing deployment.
The benchmark protocol is defined in §3; the results below report the observed token, latency,
and memory consequences of the two encodings. Prior clinician review of ECG rationales from
the OpenTSLM model family supports the underlying task [11], but the present study only tests the
mobile port and benchmark behavior.
Implementation parity. Four components (encoder, projector, fused encoder-projector pipeline, and
rotary embedding) match the Python MLX reference within a maximum element-wise tolerance of
10−4 and mean 10−5 (10−3 for the rotary embedding), checked on the CPU backend. The tokenizer
reproduces the reference token IDs exactly, and the text-serialization baseline is byte-identical to
the OpenTSLM format. End-to-end, the Python MLX and Swift implementations produce identical
greedy-decoded token sequences. Against the PyTorch reference the decoded answers agree, while
the intervening rationale wording can differ under bf16 arithmetic.
On-device task performance. The parity result above concerns implementation equivalence rather
than task accuracy, so we also measure accuracy directly on device. We pinned the first 20 samples of
the Sleep-EDF CoT test split as a fixed export, so that index 𝑖denotes the same recording in every
implementation, and ran them under greedy decoding through the PyTorch reference, our Python
MLX reference, and the Swift port on the iPhone. All three score 17/20 and agree on every prediction,
including the same three errors with the same incorrect labels, and the on-device prompt length
matched the PyTorch reference at every sample. Agreement on the errors is the stronger signal, since
a port that only approximated the reference would diverge first where the model is least confident;
it anchors the parity claim above to the original PyTorch implementation rather than only to our
intermediate MLX reference. The measured 85% is consistent with the 81.08% Langer et al. [11] report
on the full test split, but 20 samples give a 95% interval of roughly ±16 points, so this corroborates the
deployment rather than estimating accuracy. Soft prompting also does not trade quality for context
economy: on this task the reference reports 69.88 F1 against 9.05 for the same backbone fine-tuned
on a text serialization of the same signal [11]. The compression ratio is fixed rather than tuned: patch
length and stride follow the OpenTSLM reference, as the encoder, projector, and LoRA adapters are
loaded from its checkpoints, so varying it would require retraining all three, which is a change to the
model rather than to its deployment.
Context economics. Soft prompts produce one token per four-sample patch, rounding up partial
patches, compared with 3 BPE tokens per raw sample for text serialization in the benchmark format
(Tables 1, 2; Fig. 3a). This yields an approximately 12× token advantage across evaluated lengths
and both tasks, with rounding to whole patches giving 11.9× at 𝐿=250. Both encodings are charged
per lead, so channel count preserves the per-lead token ratio. A 12-lead ECG window of 𝑁samples
costs 36𝑁text tokens versus 12⌈𝑁/4⌉soft-prompt tokens. Channel count grows the absolute token
saving (12 leads × the per-lead gap). Extrapolated to the backbone’s 8192-token context window, text
supports ∼2,659 single-channel EEG samples (∼53 s of 50 Hz time-series data) but only ∼212 samples
per ECG lead, whereas soft prompts support ∼31,912 and ∼2,553 respectively under the same budget.

In the measured sweep, the lower 4,300-token on-device prompt budget is the practical cutoff used to
preserve runtime memory headroom during generation.
Latency and memory. The token gap dominates on-device cost, and the decisive case is 12-lead ECG.
There, text serialization is infeasible beyond the shortest window. At 𝐿=100 it already needs 4,133
prompt tokens and 4.3 GiB, and every window extension (𝐿≥250, ≥9,533 tokens) is skipped to
avoid an uncatchable operating system (OS) memory termination. Soft prompts run the full evaluated
1,000-sample clip with TTFT ≤11.6 s and peak memory ≤4.2 GiB (Table 2, Fig. 3b). The bf16
backbone weights alone account for about 2.3 GiB of peak memory, and the remainder grows with
prompt length. At truncated lengths the soft-prompt arm’s generated text degenerates, since a window
shorter than the 1,000-sample training clip is out of distribution; the reported token, latency, and
memory costs are unaffected, as they depend on the input encoding rather than on the decoded
content. TTFT and peak memory are means over five repeated sweeps. For EEG, the spread is under
6% of the mean at 𝐿≥1000 but reaches roughly 30% at 𝐿≤500, where short prefills are dominated
by fixed overhead rather than by compute. For ECG, it is 19–27% at every length, driven by a faster
first run. For EEG, the reported thermal state rises from nominal to serious within the first sweep
and remains there. For ECG, it reads nominal at each run start, although the first run is 1.6× faster
than the last. Thermal throttling is a possible explanation for the ECG slowdown, but was not directly
established. The reported means include all five sweeps, including the faster first run, and therefore
describe repeated-run performance rather than an isolated cold start or a verified steady state. We do
not report energy consumption.

5 Limitations and Future Evaluation
The present evaluation establishes implementation parity and on-device context economics. The
OpenTSLM study included clinician review of ECG rationales from its model family [11], and our
numerical parity protocol (§3) confirms identical greedy-decoded token sequences between the Swift
port and the Python MLX reference. Decoded answers also agree with the PyTorch reference, although
rationale wording can differ under bf16 arithmetic. This supports implementation equivalence for
the evaluated prompts, but it does not constitute new clinical validation. The benchmarks use fixed
Sleep-EDF sleep-staging samples [34, 35] and ECG-QA samples [28] rather than prospective HealthKit
data from patients. Consumer wearable time-series data may include sensor noise, lower or variable
resolution, missing data, device-specific preprocessing, and population shift not captured by these
samples. Prospective studies with real-world wearable time-series data, clinical review, institutional
review board (IRB) approval, and predefined safety boundaries are needed before patient-facing or
clinical use.
On-device deployment remains bounded by measured memory and effective prompt budget. We use
Llama-3.2-1B, as it fits the target device while supporting the adapted OpenTSLM-SP pipeline. Larger
backbones were not evaluated and may exceed the memory budget of current smartphones in this
architecture. Quantization and future hardware may increase feasible model and input size, but the
present claim is limited to the 1B backbone, the evaluated device class, and the soft-prompt path
tested here. Tablets such as the iPad Pro may relax the thermal and memory constraints observed on
the phone. The evaluation also covers only the soft-prompt fusion pathway. Cross-attention fusion,
as in Flamingo [18] and OpenTSLM-Flamingo [11], is an alternative embedding-level interface, but
it modifies the decoder’s internal attention layers rather than only the input-embedding sequence
adapted here; porting and benchmarking it on device is left to future work.
Local inference reduces exposure from routine cloud inference, but it does not remove governance
obligations. In the current demo, inference runs on the device and HealthKit data are not transmitted
during inference. Whether Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), General Data
Protection Regulation (GDPR), or other privacy requirements apply depends on the deployment context,
data controller or covered-entity role, consent model, logging, export behavior, and downstream data
flows. The local design also changes monitoring trade-offs. If deployed without central telemetry,
performance surveillance and drift detection would require privacy-preserving reporting, local audit
mechanisms, or supervised clinical review rather than server-side logs. Pre-deployment parity testing
can confirm that the port preserves reference behavior before evaluation, but it is not a substitute for
real-world monitoring.
10

sample_chunks.authors: Max Rosenblattl, Nikhil Krishnaswamy, et al.
sample_chunks.category: Healthcare Wearables, IoT and Predictive Analytics
sample_chunks.text_content:
PocketTSLM
6 Conclusion
PocketTSLM demonstrates that a soft-prompt physiological TSLM can run fully on a consumer smartphone in the evaluated setting. By porting OpenTSLM-SP to MLX-Swift and integrating it into a
HealthKit-enabled demo app, the encoder, projector, and LLM execute locally rather than through
cloud inference. The evaluation compares the Swift MLX port with the reference implementation
under greedy decoding and benchmarks soft prompts against text serialization on fixed Sleep-EDF
[34, 35] and ECG-QA samples [28]. Soft prompts use approximately 12× fewer time-series tokens
than the text-serialized baseline, reducing prompt-prefill cost and allowing longer physiological timeseries windows to fit within the measured on-device budget. These results support PocketTSLM as an
implementation and deployment contribution, not as evidence of clinical performance in new settings.
The main remaining step is a prospective evaluation on real-world wearable time-series data with
predefined review, safety, monitoring, and governance procedures.
Ethics Statement
This study uses public, de-identified research datasets and does not introduce new protected health
information collection. No IRB approval was obtained for this deployment and benchmarking study, as
the reported evaluation did not involve prospective recruitment, participant interaction, intervention,
or collection of identifiable private information.
Acknowledgments
This manuscript was prepared using A Reproducible Workflow for Evidence-Centered Scientific Papers [36].

sample_chunks.paper_title: Wearable Data Profiling for NDN-Based Smart Healthcare: Performance Comparison and Energy Efficiency
sample_chunks.authors: Mohammad R. Shakournia, Nasser Yazdani, et al.
sample_chunks.category: Healthcare Wearables, IoT and Predictive Analytics
sample_chunks.section_heading: Wearable Data Profiling for NDN-Based Smart
sample_chunks.text_content:
Wearable Data Profiling for NDN-Based Smart
Healthcare: Performance Comparison with an IP
Baseline
Mohammad R. Shakournia1, Nasser Yazdani1, and Carlos T. Calafate2
1 Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, University of Tehran,
Tehran, Iran
{shakournia,yazdani}@ut.ac.ir
2 Department of Computer Engineering, Universitat Politècnica de València,
Valencia, Spain
calafate@disca.upv.es
Abstract. Smart healthcare IoT requires low-latency and reliable delivery of patient data, yet IP-based communication remains host-centric
and offers limited support for mobility, caching, and request aggregation. This paper evaluates a smartphone-centric Named Data Networking (NDN) approach in which a patient’s smartphone aggregates sensor
streams and publishes a stable “latest profile” under a consistent name,
enabling effective in-network caching. Using ndnSIM simulations on a
realistic medical IoT topology, we compare NDN and IP under identical traffic and link conditions. Results show that per-sample naming
provides little benefit, but smartphone aggregation with stable naming
allows NDN caching to reduce delay after cache warm-up and achieve
significantly higher delivery ratios under congestion compared to IP.
Keywords: Named Data Network · Smart Healthcare · IoHT · Mobile
Health.
1
Introduction
The growing use of wearable sensors, home medical devices, and mobile health
(mHealth) applications is moving healthcare from occasional, hospital-centered
visits to continuous, patient-centered monitoring. In these systems, body-worn
and ambient sensors measure vital signs and other physiological parameters and
send them, often over short-range and multi-hop wireless links, to a nearby
gateway such as a smartphone, which must then forward the data to healthcare staff with low delay and high reliability [11, 2]. Many smart-hospital and
remote-monitoring platforms already combine IoT, edge, and cloud components
to provide such continuous services [13]. However, most of these platforms are
built on the traditional TCP/IP protocol stack and therefore inherit its known
limits in terms of scalability, mobility support, and efficient, secure data delivery in dense and dynamic IoT environments [8, 3]. Beyond performance concerns,
arXiv:2610.20215v1 [cs.NI] 14 Oct 2026

sample_chunks.authors: Mohammad R. Shakournia, Nasser Yazdani, et al.
sample_chunks.category: Healthcare Wearables, IoT and Predictive Analytics
sample_chunks.text_content:
2
M. R. Shakournia et al.
the underlying networking substrate can also influence how efficiently data and
resources are shared across stakeholders, i.e., whether the network itself can facilitate a form of network-level collective intelligence by enabling reuse and local
sharing of previously retrieved medical information.
The traditional Internet architecture is host-centric: routers forward packets
toward IP addresses that identify endpoints rather than the data itself. This
model is not well suited for data-intensive smart environments and IoT systems, where applications are mainly interested in named content (for example,
the latest ECG of a given patient) instead of a specific server. Recent surveys
on NDN in smart environments and IoT report several limitations of the IP
model in this setting, including complex address management, limited mobility
support, and lack of pervasive in-network caching, which are especially problematic in dense and dynamic IoT healthcare environments. This paper focuses on
smartphone-centric IoT healthcare and demonstrates how NDN can overcome
these challenges in such settings by offloading much of the traffic management to
in-network caches and enabling faster, more efficient data retrieval. In this sense,
repeated clinical queries (e.g., by a physician, a clinic system, or an authorized
service) can benefit from data that the network has already fetched, effectively
turning the network into a shared pool of reusable content. By eliminating the
need for traditional IP-based address resolution and supporting mobility, NDN
proves to be a better fit for healthcare IoT systems where real-time data from
wearable sensors is crucial [8, 12, 1, 3]. These studies argue that simply running
application-layer protocols such as MQTT or CoAP over IP cannot fully solve
these structural problems; instead, the network layer itself must evolve toward
a data-centric design.
Named Data Networking has been proposed as a prominent informationcentric networking (ICN) architecture to address these limitations [14]. In NDN,
applications request content by hierarchical names rather than by host addresses;
routers forward Interest packets according to name prefixes and return Data
packets that can be cached at any hop. This leads to a stateful forwarding plane,
based on Pending Interest Tables (PITs), Forwarding Information Bases (FIBs),
and Content Stores (CSs), which natively supports in-network caching, multipath retrieval, and efficient multicast, while data-centric security is achieved by
cryptographically binding each Data packet to its producer, independent of the
delivery path [14]. As a result, the distributed CS across routers can be viewed
as a continuously updated, network-wide knowledge pool: once data is retrieved,
it becomes locally available for subsequent consumers without requiring them to
know the original producer. Moreover, the cooperative behavior of PIT aggregation and CS hits enables decentralized coordination of data retrieval, allowing
the network as a whole to efficiently satisfy repeated requests without a central
controller. Surveys on NDN for smart environments and on hierarchical naming
for NDN-IoT conclude that these properties align well with the requirements
of smart cities, buildings, and health spaces, but also emphasize open issues in
naming scalability, resource constraints, and security [8, 12].

sample_chunks.authors: Mohammad R. Shakournia, Nasser Yazdani, et al.

sample_chunks.section_heading: Wearable Data Profiling for NDN-Based Smart Healthcare
sample_chunks.text_content:
Wearable Data Profiling for NDN-Based Smart Healthcare
3
Recent work suggests NDN can improve performance and security in healthcare IoT [13, 6, 7, 9], but many studies focus on architecture/security/caching
strategies rather than a clean baseline comparison against IP under matched conditions [3, 8, 12, 1]. This paper isolates the effect of NDN’s caching and request
aggregation in a realistic smartphone-centric healthcare topology and compares
delay and delivery reliability to IP.
This work focuses on an underexplored but highly relevant scenario in healthcare IoT, namely a smartphone-centric system, where the patient’s smartphone
serves as the data aggregation point for multiple wearable sensors, and acts as
the NDN data producer for the patient’s health profile. While the literature
has demonstrated the potential of NDN for healthcare, few studies have explicitly tested NDN in small-scale, smartphone-centric topologies that simulate
real-world, patient-centric monitoring systems. To address this limitation, we
present a comprehensive comparison of NDN and IP in a smartphone-centric
healthcare scenario, evaluating their performance under identical experimental
conditions. Our study demonstrates that NDN can improve real-time data delivery by exploiting data-centric communication and in-network caching while
requiring only minimal modifications to existing infrastructure. Experimental
results further indicate that this architecture reduces communication latency
and better accommodates user mobility, highlighting the potential of NDN as a
practical networking solution for future smart healthcare systems.
The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews background
on NDN and summarizes related work on NDN-based healthcare and smart
environments. Section III presents the proposed system model, including node
roles, naming scheme, and traffic types. Section IV describes the simulation setup
and performance metrics. Section V discusses the numerical results comparing
NDN and IP. Finally, Section VI concludes the paper and outlines directions for
future work.
2
Related Work
Early IP-based BAN/WSN healthcare systems forward sensor data via gateways over TCP/IP (often 6LoWPAN), but the host-centric model offers limited
support for mobility, in-network caching, and data-centric security.[11, 2].
Information-centric networking, and in particular NDN, has been proposed to
better match the data-oriented nature of IoT and smart environments. Amadeo
et al. review ICN for the Internet of Things and argue that name-based access,
in-network caching, and data-centric security can address many of the scalability
and mobility issues that arise under IP [1]. Zhang et al. present the NDN architecture, in which consumers issue Interests for named content and Data packets
can be served from any node that holds a copy, whether the original producer
or an intermediate cache [14]. Recent surveys extend this perspective to smart
environments and NDN-IoT deployments. Islam et al. show that NDN’s hierarchical naming, stateful forwarding, and built-in caching align well with the needs
of smart cities, buildings, and health spaces, but also highlight practical barriers

M. R. Shakournia et al.
such as interoperability with IP and limited testbeds [8]. Shah et al. focus on
hierarchical and hybrid naming schemes for NDN-based IoT, including e-health
scenarios, and discuss how naming choices interact with access control, content
protection, and the resource constraints of IoT devices [12]. Azamuddin et al.
provide a broad overview of NDN architecture, applications, and open research
problems, further motivating its use in emerging IoT and edge-computing settings [3]. On the caching side, Jafari et al. propose ECLAT-LRU, a predictive
caching policy that improves NDN cache performance [10].
On top of this architectural groundwork, several NDN-based frameworks for
healthcare and related IoT domains have been proposed. Wang and Cai introduce SHNIE, a secure healthcare monitoring framework that integrates clustered
IoT devices with an NDN-based edge cloud [13]. SHNIE uses hash-based ciphertext names, encryption, and signatures to protect medical data and exploits
request aggregation and in-network caching to reduce communication latency
and message cost compared with an IP-based smart hospital system. Dudeja et
al. design an NDN-based data communication framework for IoT–edge ecosystems in which edge nodes act as cluster heads and assign priorities to periodic sensor data; these priorities are then mapped to different caching strategies
(e.g., Leave-Copy-Everywhere versus Leave-Copy-Down) in the NDN core [6].
In a follow-up work, they propose a secure and pervasive NDN communication framework for connected healthcare that supports both consumer-initiated
and producer-initiated data dissemination and evaluate its performance under
various network conditions [7]. Demir and Manap implement a Named Data
Networking of Things (NDNoT) stack on the Contiki-NG operating system and
demonstrate the feasibility of NDN-based medical data retrieval on constrained
IoT devices using Cooja simulations [5]. Islam et al. outline an NDN-aided edge–
cloud architecture for continuous smart healthcare, where NDN is used at the
edge and an NDN edge gateway bridges local NDN domains to IP-based cloud
services such as AWS IoT [9].
These efforts collectively illustrate the potential benefits of NDN in healthcare and IoT-edge settings, including improved content delivery efficiency, flexible data dissemination patterns, and stronger data-centric security. However,
most existing works either focus on security mechanisms and naming schemes,
on architectural integration with edge and cloud platforms, or on NDN-only
performance tuning. SHNIE does include an analytical and simulation-based
comparison with an IP smart-hospital baseline, but its design centers on a relatively complex edge-cloud security framework rather than on a minimal end-toend communication model [13]. Other proposals evaluate NDN-based healthcare
or IoT frameworks in isolation, without constructing a matching IP reference
system over the same topology and traffic patterns [6, 7, 5, 9]. Despite recent
advances, controlled side-by-side comparisons between NDN and IP under identical experimental conditions remain limited, particularly in smartphone-centric
medical IoT scenarios where the patient’s smartphone serves as both the edge
device and the primary data producer. In such environments, remote caregivers
retrieve up-to-date patient information directly by name, making it possible to

sample_chunks.text_content:
Wearable Data Profiling for NDN-Based Smart Healthcare
5
evaluate the practical benefits and limitations of NDN relative to conventional
IP networking.
3
System Model and Proposed Architecture
We study the use of NDN in a smart healthcare system where patients are
equipped with wearable IoT sensors. Our goal is to evaluate whether NDN can
provide communication performance comparable to, or better than, a traditional
IP-based solution when delivering medical data from patients to remote caregivers. In addition to end-to-end performance, we are interested in whether
NDN’s data-centric mechanisms enable efficient reuse of previously retrieved
health information across multiple authorized stakeholders, effectively leveraging the network as a shared substrate for data access.
3.1
Overall Scenario and Node Types
We consider a hospital or clinic scenario in which each patient is continuously
monitored by a set of body-worn sensors. These sensors periodically generate
physiological measurements such as heart rate, SpO2, and blood pressure. A
patient’s smartphone acts as a local gateway and edge device that collects sensor
data and makes it available to remote caregivers.
In our evaluation, we model six patients, each with one smartphone. The
smartphones and caregivers are interconnected by a fixed multi-hop network.
On the caregiver side, we consider six monitoring consumers representing clinics,
physicians, or hospital monitoring stations. This multi-consumer setting naturally captures repeated access to the same patient state from different monitoring points, which is precisely where in-network caching can provide network-wide
reuse by serving subsequent requests from nearby nodes. Between smartphones
and consumers, the network includes nine routers (e.g., access routers and intermediate/core routers), resulting in a 21-node topology. The same topology, node
roles, and traffic patterns are used in both NDN and IP scenarios (Section IV
will detail link capacities, propagation delays, and traffic parameters).
The medical traffic of interest consists primarily of periodic monitoring flows
(vital signs) and time-critical updates (e.g., alarms or abrupt changes). We focus
on end-to-end delay and packet loss as the main performance metrics; all security
mechanisms (encryption, signatures) are abstracted away and not modeled in the
simulations.
3.2
Baseline NDN Design: Direct Sensor-to-Consumer
Communication
As an initial baseline, we consider a straightforward NDN design in which each
body-worn sensor acts as an NDN data producer. Every new measurement generated by the sensor (e.g., once per second, once per minute, or at any other

configured sampling interval) is published as a distinct NDN Data packet with
a unique name that encodes the generation time. In this model, clinics, doctors,
or hospital servers act as NDN consumers and retrieve samples directly from
the sensors by issuing Interests for these time-stamped names over a multi-hop
topology, similar to IP-based body area network designs where sensors forward
data to a sink or gateway [11, 2]. For such time-critical flows, where each sample
is unique and must be delivered as soon as it is produced, in-network caching and
request aggregation offer little benefit, because each measurement is requested
exactly once and is not reused by other consumers. As a result, this baseline
intentionally represents a setting where the network cannot exploit reuse across
stakeholders, since there is no shared, repeatedly requested content to retain in
the forwarding plane.
To better isolate this effect, we also conduct a micro-benchmark in a minimal topology consisting of a single producer (modeling a body-worn sensor), one
intermediate router, and a single consumer. In this setup, the producer generates 1000 distinct packets, each carrying a unique name (or, in the IP case, a
unique sequence identifier), and we transmit the same 1000 packets over both
an IP and an NDN stack under identical link settings, measuring the end-to-end
request–response delay. Since all packets are strictly non-reusable, this experiment intentionally removes the main performance advantages of NDN, namely
in-network caching and request aggregation. Intermediate NDN routers still perform per-packet lookups in CS and PIT, in addition to FIB lookups, whereas
the IP baseline only maintains a routing table and forwards packets without
per-request state. In our ns-3/ndnSIM implementation, the additional CS/PIT
processing overhead is modeled at a logical level and therefore manifests as only
a small difference in simulated delay; however, in a real implementation with
non-negligible lookup and memory costs, this overhead can become more pronounced and may make NDN slower than a stateless IP forwarder under purely
time-critical, non-cacheable traffic. The numerical results of this sanity-check
experiment, summarized in Table 1, confirm that under these conditions NDN
does not provide a delay advantage over IP.
3.3
Proposed Smartphone-Centric NDN Architecture
To enable NDN to exploit its strengths in this setting, we propose a smartphonecentric architecture in which the patient’s smartphone acts as an edge device and
the primary NDN data producer.
Body-Worn Sensors and Smartphone Edge Device In the proposed architecture, each patient wears multiple body-mounted sensors that measure physiological parameters such as heart rate, SpO2, and blood pressure. These sensors
communicate wirelessly with the patient’s smartphone, which acts as a local
edge device and data aggregator. In line with current commercial practice, we
assume that body-worn sensors use Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) to connect to
the smartphone, which plays the role of the BLE central device and periodically

many consumer-grade wearable healthcare and fitness devices (e.g., chest straps,
smartwatches, and glucose monitors) deliver physiological data to mobile phones
in real deployments.
In our system model, the details of the BLE link (pairing, GATT services,
etc.) are abstracted into a single logical low-power link from the sensor set to
the smartphone. We focus on the end-to-end delivery of aggregated medical data
from the smartphone to remote caregivers over either NDN or IP.
NDN Naming and Personal Health Profile The smartphone continuously
aggregates the incoming sensor readings into a personal health profile that is
updated whenever new data arrive. Instead of publishing every raw sample as a
separate NDN object, the smartphone exposes a single named NDN Data object
that always represents the latest state of the patient’s vital signs. For a patient
with identifier patientID, the current profile may be published under a stable

The smartphone therefore acts as the sole NDN producer for this profile, while
clinics, doctors, and hospital servers act as NDN consumers that issue Interests
for this name whenever they need the most recent health status.
Because all monitoring systems use the same content name to retrieve the
patient’s latest profile, intermediate NDN routers and edge nodes can cache the
Data packet and satisfy subsequent Interests from nearby caches. This is particularly relevant for smart-healthcare monitoring, where multiple monitoring points
(e.g., ward dashboards, nurse stations, physician terminals) repeatedly request
the same patient’s current status. In this way, the distributed caches collectively
act as a shared pool of recently retrieved patient profiles, enabling consumers
to obtain the closest available copy without needing to target a particular host.
In our evaluation (Section IV), we consider several such monitoring consumers
that periodically retrieve the profile of each patient; once a profile is fetched the
first time, subsequent requests can be served from caches, and NDN’s in-network
caching begins to provide a clear benefit.
3.4
Consistency and Freshness Semantics
A key requirement in this architecture is that caregivers must receive up-todate information. NDN provides built-in mechanisms to express freshness requirements. Each Data packet includes a FreshnessPeriod indicating how long
cached copies should be considered valid, and consumers may set the MustBeFresh
selector in their Interests to request only fresh Data.
In our design, we align the FreshnessPeriod of the health-profile Data with
the sensor update period. As a result, cached copies of the profile automatically
expire in routers roughly when new data are produced, and Interests marked as
MustBeFresh are forwarded toward the smartphone if cached content has become
stale. This ensures that doctors and monitoring systems obtain a consistent
and up-to-date view of the patient’s vital signs while still benefiting from innetwork caching between updates. Put differently, freshness semantics help keep
the shared cached pool reliable by preventing stale profiles from being served
beyond their validity window.
A high-level representation of the proposed architecture is shown in Fig. 2.
Wearable sensors attached to each patient send data to the patient’s smartphone,
which acts as an edge device and NDN producer. A set of intermediate routers
connects the smartphones to multiple monitoring consumers (clinics, doctors,
and hospital servers). NDN runs from the edge devices to the consumers, using
hierarchical names and in-network caching, while the specific low-power protocol
between sensors and the smartphone is abstracted away in the system model.
3.5
IP Reference Architecture
For a fair comparison, we also construct an IP reference architecture that uses the
same physical topology, node roles, and traffic patterns as the NDN architecture.

In the IP baseline, each patient’s smartphone still collects sensor data via BLE
and maintains an internal health profile, but communication with caregivers
follows the conventional host-centric model.
Specifically, the smartphone transmits monitoring data to caregiver nodes
using UDP over IP. Intermediate routers maintain IP routing tables and forward packets based on destination IP addresses. There is no in-network content
caching in the network: routers do not store application-layer data, and each
monitoring request must be served by the smartphone or a backend server every
time. Consequently, the network does not accumulate reusable content state on
the path, and repeated monitoring requests cannot benefit from previously retrieved data at intermediate nodes. No NDN-specific state (such as PIT or CS) is
present. This IP baseline allows us to quantify the impact of NDN’s name-based
forwarding and in-network caching on end-to-end delay and packet loss under
identical network and traffic conditions.
4
Simulation Setup and Metrics
We compare the proposed smartphone-centric NDN architecture with an IP
baseline in ns-3, using the standard Internet stack for IP and ndnSIM for NDN.
Both scenarios share the same physical topology, node roles, and traffic patterns;
only the network layer (IP vs. NDN with name-based forwarding and caching)
differs.
4.1
Topology and Traffic Overview
We use the 21-node topology from Section III: six monitoring consumers, six
patient-side producer/server nodes (smartphones), and nine routers connected
through a constrained core. All consumer–producer traffic traverses the same
core bottleneck, enabling controlled congestion and loss experiments.
Each consumer is associated with one patient. In IP, consumers send UDP
traffic to the corresponding patient-side server; in NDN, they issue Interests to
the corresponding producer. Applications run over the same time interval in both
cases, and packet/payload sizes are matched for fairness. Table 2 summarizes the
main simulation parameters.
Unless otherwise stated, NDN uses ndnSIM’s MulticastStrategy; we also
tested BestRoute. In this static, tree-like topology, both yield nearly identical
RTT and delivery ratio, indicating that the observed gains mainly come from
in-network caching rather than path diversity.
4.2
Metrics
We use two primary performance metrics:
– Round-trip delay (RTT): Both IP and NDN follow a request–response
model. In IP, RTT is measured from sending a probe packet to receiving its

We compare end-to-end performance of IP and NDN under (i) sensor-level, persample naming and (ii) a smartphone-centric, profile-based naming model that
enables in-network caching.

time-critical traffic with non-reusable samples, exposing every measurement as

Based on this observation, the main experiments use a profile-based model:
the smartphone aggregates sensor readings into a continuously updated personal health profile and publishes it under a stable name (e.g., /HospitalID/
patientID/vital/latest). As summarized in Table 2, repeated queries for the
same patient map to the same name and can benefit from in-network caching.
5.2
Short-Term Cache Warm-Up Behavior
Figure 3 shows a 10-packet rolling mean RTT over the first 2500 packets. In both
loss and no-loss runs, NDN exhibits a short initial RTT spike corresponding to
cache warm-up, when early Interests traverse the full multi-hop path to the
smartphone.
After a few requests, the profile Data are cached near the monitoring stations,
and subsequent Interests are satisfied locally, causing NDN RTT to drop quickly
to a low, nearly constant value. IP shows no such warm-up effect: RTT stays
roughly constant without loss, but grows and oscillates under congestion. These
results confirm that NDN gains here are driven by caching profiles close to
consumers.
5.3
Delay Under Packet Loss
To induce congestion and loss, core links are set to 200 kbps, making the core
the dominant bottleneck and causing frequent queue drops. As shown in the
upper plots of Figs. 3 and 4, IP exhibits unstable RTT with pronounced oscillations and values often exceeding 103 ms, due to repeated queue overflows and
retransmissions in the request–response exchange.
