VII. CONCLUSIONS AND FUTURE WORK 
In this research, our focus was specifically on improving 
healthcare services for diabetes prediction through the 
development of an Edge-based Smart Healthcare System, 
named SmartEdge, that utilizes deep learning and IoT for the 
automated prediction of diabetes. SmartEdge improves 
healthcare delivery by offering edge services that adeptly 
handle data from diverse IoT devices, enhancing patient data 
management. By incorporating deep learning within edge 
computing devices SmartEdge has been applied successfully 
to real-world heart disease analysis. Unlike previous efforts 
that lacked the use of deep learning and thus suffered from 
inadequate prediction accuracy, our approach enables the 
embedding of complex machine learning networks within 
edge computing frameworks. We achieved this through 
innovative communication and model distribution strategies, 
such as ensembling, ensuring high precision with minimal 
latency. The efficacy of SmartEdge was demonstrated through 
validation against real patient data, employing the FogBus 
framework within an edge computing environment, and 
evaluating the system's performance across several metrics 
including power consumption, network response time, 
latency, and accuracy. 
Looking ahead, we aim to evolve SmartEdge by 
integrating cost-effective execution strategies that consider 
various Quality of Service (QoS) attributes and edge-cloud 
cost dynamics. Although SmartEdge currently operates on 
file-based input data, future iterations will seek direct sensor 
data integration to enhance user interaction. Additionally, we 
plan to refine the model training approach, which presently 
involves independent training at each worker node followed 
by an ensemble of models through bagging. By exploring 
more sophisticated ensemble techniques, we anticipate further 
enhancements in prediction accuracy. Moreover, we intend to 
expand the robustness and versatility of the proposed 
architecture to support a wider range of edge computing 
applications beyond healthcare, including agriculture, weather 
forecasting, traffic management, and smart city initiatives.

sample_chunks.text_content:
Abstract — Incorporating cloud technology with Internet of 
Medical Things for ubiquitous healthcare has seen many 
successful applications in the last decade with the advent of 
machine learning and deep learning techniques. One of these 
applications, namely voice-based pathology, has yet to receive 
notable attention from academia and industry. Applying voice 
analysis to early detection of chronic diseases holds much 
promise to improve health outcomes and quality of life of 
patients. In this paper, we propose a novel application of acoustic 
machine 
learning 
based 
triaging 
into 
commoditised 
conversational virtual assistant systems to pre-screen for onset 
of diabetes. Specifically, we evaluate a novel triaging system 
which extracts acoustic features from the voices of n=24 older 
adults when they converse with a virtual assistant and predict 
the incidence of Diabetes Mellitus (Type 2) or not. Our triaging 
system achieved hit-rates of 70% and 60% for male and female 
older adult subjects, respectively. Our proposed triaging uses 7 
non-identifiable voice-based features and can operate within 
resource-constrained embedded systems running voice-based 
virtual assistants. This application demonstrates the feasibility 
of applying voice-based pathology analysis to improve health 
outcomes of older adults within the home environment by early 
detection of chronic conditions like diabetes. 
 
Keywords — Diabetes Mellitus, T2D Pre-Screening, Voice 
Pathology, Voice Analysis, Digital Biomarkers, Conversational AI, 
Virtual Assistants, Triaging, Geriatrics, Monica, MiiCare, 
MiiHealth 
I. INTRODUCTION 
Several medical conditions have been shown to affect the 
voice due to changes that either occur in the speaker’s speech 
organs or in the brain. These changes in voice could 
theoretically be analysed to learn specific acoustic patterns, 
and generalised across populations, irrespective of languages 
spoken. There have been prior publications in the clinical 
literature over the past decade examining voice patterns in 
different neurological and psychological conditions like 
Stress [1], Autism [2], Dysphonia [3], Parkinson’s Disease 
[4], Alzheimer’s Disease [5], COVID19 [6], etc. Of note, a 
“digital biomarker” is a characteristic objectively measured 
by a digital device or captured by a digital algorithm that is 
evaluated as an indicator of normal biological processes, 
pathogenic processes or pharmacologic response to 
therapeutic treatments. A voice-based digital biomarker in 
this regard, converts human speech audio input into an 
evaluation of subject’s speech generation capabilities. Voicebased (vocal) digital biomarkers are alluring and well-suited 
features for predictive algorithms like that in machine 
learning and deep learning as they are non-invasive, 
instantaneous and cost-effective to use and easy to scale 
across large populations. There is a pressing need for 
innovative solutions in medicine to better understand 
diseases, improve health outcomes, and alleviate the growing 
constraints of health care budgets. However, the application 
of vocal biomarkers has been largely limited to the 
neurological diseases [7], per our review of clinical literature. 
In contrast, the use of vocal biomarkers remains scarce. 
We noted that almost all of the existing works using voice 
biomarkers to predict for pathologies use audio data collected 
in controlled acoustic scenes [3, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13] with little 
to no ambient noise and presence of overlapping acoustic 
events. The authors of [12] collected speech data by having 
the participants say pre-written words to reduce influence of 
language during the analysis. The data-capture primarily 
happened several times within a well-defined data collection 
period. We were unable to find relevant literature where voice 
biomarkers were collected continuously to showcase changes 
over periods longer than a few weeks [10, 13, 14] or days [8, 
12, 13]. Such methodologies for voice biomarkers are 
restrictive by design and do not lend into ease of integration 
within existing care pathways in real-world deployments. 
Similarly, accessibility by vulnerable demographics like older 
adults and those with high social deprivation [15], 
disadvantageous social determinants of health [16] (SDOH) 
and individuals with cognitive challenges, further influence 
their feasibility. It is precisely this challenge that drives our 
motivation to develop a new approach to collect voice 
biomarkers in a more sustainable manner. Our goal is to 
enable data-capture through widely accepted Assistive 
Technologies (AT) that already rely on voice-based 
conversations for engagement and care delivery, ensuring 
seamless integration into existing systems of care. 
 Conversation-based AT fall within the domain of 
“telehealth” which promises the advantage of enabling 
patients to self-care by delivering supportive care, guidance 
and necessary health literacy, remotely [17, 18, 19]. The 
COVID19 pandemic gave strong impetus [17] to the rise of 
telehealth tools and saw rapid adoption of programmable 
conversational agents [18] and virtual assistants [19] like 
chatbots and voice-based assistants. Since 2020, there has 
been several published literature reviews demonstrating [17, 
18, 19] that virtual assistants and chatbots can be used to assist 
in clinical workflows, deliver health programs, personalise 
support at scale with low costs. 
In this paper, we investigate the feasibility of using a 
commercially available conversational virtual assistant 
product to capture speech audio from community-dwelling 
older adults, with the aim of extracting voice biomarkers that 
strongly correlate with a diagnosis of type 2 diabetes mellitus 
and predicting the same for the individual. We also envision 
our approach as a “triaging toolkit” that can be adapted to 
predict other conditions [1, 2, 3, 4] affecting the voice, such

sample_chunks.text_content:
as high stress, mental disorders, neurodegenerative conditions 
and non-communicable diseases [8, 10, 12]. However, these 
applications are beyond the scope of this study. We 
summarise the contributions of this work as follows: 
1. Using virtual assistants to perform voice-based 
triaging for type 2 diabetes, one of the most prevalent 
[20] medical conditions across the world. 
2. Developing a “triaging toolkit” suited for embedded 
system applications to comply with data-protection 
and user-privacy regulations like GDPR and HIPPA. 
3. Improving triaging robustness in voice biomarker 
extraction in noisy polyphonic environment of the 
home environment. 
We have organised the paper as follows: In Section II, we 
present the current state-of-the-art of voice biomarkers, its 
extraction from voice-based sources, diagnostic relationships 
drawn between these biomarkers and type 2 diabetes, and 
underpinnings of virtual assistants in personalised care 
coaching and delivery. In Section III, we explain our approach 
leveraging Monica, a voice-based conversational health 
assistant developed by MiiCare [21]. In Section IV, we lay 
out the results of our method applied to a cohort of older 
adults where Monica had already been deployed to support 
daily chronic management. 
II. BACKGROUND 
A. Voice Disorders 
Voice and speech production involves the coordinated 
functioning of multiple organ systems. Airflow generated by 
release of pressure from the lungs passes through the vocal 
folds in the larynx, causing them to vibrate which produces 
sound. The articulation of this sound forms speech. [22]. This 
functional dependency between several biological structures 
makes the voice vulnerable to being affected by diverse 
conditions. 
Anomalies in vocal quality, such as pitch, volume,, 
resonance and duration, that are unexpected for individuals 
regardless of their gender and age, are indicative of voice 
disorders. There is no globally accepted nomenclature for 
voice disorders. The authors of [22] list structural, 
inflammatory, traumatic, systemic, aerodigestive, psychiatric 
and psychological, neurological and functional voice 
disorders as major categories in this subfield. Medical 
specialists (like a Speech Therapist) can diagnose voice 
disorders through several in-person examinations and tests. 
The current approach relies on clinical examinations 
consisting of interviews, perceptual voice evaluation, patientreported outcomes, laryngoscopy, aerodynamic assessment, 
voice profiles, acoustic spectral analysis, and laryngeal 
electromyography [22], which is time consuming, resource 
expensive and generates high economic burden. Appraising 
the vocal biomarkers gathered by a clinician is what 
ultimately leads to a formal diagnosis of a disorder. Prescreening at source, for instance, within the home 
environment of the patient, not only reduces the overall cost 
of diagnosis, but also the workload on the healthcare system 
by prioritising the undiagnosed who are at higher risk. 
B. Blood Glucose and Voice 
Diabetes mellitus is a chronic metabolic disorder 
characterized by the impaired regulation of blood glucose. It 
is broadly categorized into two types: type 1 diabetes, which 
results from inadequate production of insulin by pancreas, and 
type 2 diabetes, which is caused by reduced cellular 
sensitivity to insulin. Type 2 diabetes accounts for the vast 
majority of diabetes cases, comprising approximately 90-95% 
of all diagnosed cases, while type 1 diabetes represents a 
smaller proportion. 
Authors of studies like [23, 24, 25, 26] make the following 
claims as to how voice is affected by blood glucose: 
1. Glucose related changes in voice can be perceived. For 
example, the authors of [23] and [24] found that people 
who know a diabetic subject well can hear when they 
are hypoglycaemic, i.e. the blood glucose level drops 
below the normal physiological range. 
2. Fluctuations in blood glucose levels can alter the 
elastic properties of the biological tissues in the larynx 
and the vocal cords, leading to changes in the spectral 
properties of the voice in individuals with diabetes. 
The authors of [25] and [26] put forward this idea in 
compliance with Hooke’s law of physics. 
3. Hypoglycaemia is often accompanied [27] by feelings 
of anxiety, causing people to speak faster and with 
greater urgency, whereas hyperglycaemia (higher 
levels of blood glucose over normal baseline) is often 
accompanied by fatigue or lethargy causing speech 
patterns to be slow or slurred. 
Although no supporting references was found in these 
publications, our review found that these association between 
glucose levels and change s in speech patterns is plausible and 
supported by physiological principles. Subjective claims like 
detecting abnormal glucose levels from changes in voice has 
been reported since 1990s [28] and the similarity of symptoms 
in anxiety and hypoglycaemia [29]. Literature using Hooke’s 
law or changes in elasticity of the larynx and vocal cords to 
explain changes in voice is sparse. The earliest work detected 
by the authors of [25] on this argument provided experimental 
evidence that increase in blood glucose levels reduce 
elasticity in the muscles of the aforementioned organs. 
Authors of [8, 10, 11, 12] recently investigated this hypothesis 
and found that glucose levels and the fundamental frequency 
(F0) [30] of the voice had significant positive correlation per 
subject. They also reported that this effect was observed 
across subjects even when grouped by their diagnosis of nondiabetic, pre-diabetic, and type 2 diabetes). 
C. Current State of Voice-based Virtual Assistants 
Intelligent conversational agents and virtual assistants 
proved [17] their potential to benefit over-burdened 
healthcare systems and provide personalised care to patients 
within the comfort of their own homes during the COVID19 
pandemic through their versatility, accessibility, scalability 
for naturalistic communications with them. Arguably, the 
popularity of consumer facing virtual assistants may have 
started with the launch of Apple Siri in 2011. After Amazon 
introduced Alexa and Echo devices in 2014, the technology 
around automatic speech recognition, text-to-speech and

sample_chunks.text_content:
speech-to-text, natural language processing methods, and 
conversational AI has been continuously improving as the 
number of users has been increasing [17, 18]. Recently, with 
the introduction of GPT models [31], Large Language Models 
(LLM) [32] have taken over this field as the state-of-art for 
any conversational virtual assistant technology due to its 
ability 
to 
conduct 
extremely 
realistic 
human-like 
conversations in real time. Virtual assistants have been 
adopted [17] by healthcare institutions for applications such 
as healthcare literacy, to respond to health information, tips 
and guidelines requested by users, health news, updates about 
hospital operations, first aid guidance, and medical 
communications. The convenience of natural conversation 
and hands-free interaction through digital devices has the 
potential to improve the effectiveness of health information 
delivery and communication. 
D. Current State of Predictive Analysis of Diabetes 
The traditional diagnostic methods for diabetes, while 
effective, often diagnose diabetes after significant metabolic 
disruption has occurred. Therefore, there is a growing 
emphasis on developing earlier dictation technologies to 
prevent complications an implement timely therapeutic 
intervention. Advances in machine learning provide several 
promising avenues for early detection. The authors of [33] 
proposed stacking-based ensemble classification methods, 
which integrate outputs from various algorithms to improve 
predictive accuracy, to predict type 2 diabetes. This approach 
has been applied using the publicly available PIMA Indian 
diabetes dataset to predict the onset of Type 2 diabetes within 
a 5-year interval [34]. The authors of [35] presented a soft 
computing-based diabetes prediction that uses the PIMA 
Indian dataset alongside breast cancer datasets for evaluation 
purposes. Both publications rely on traditional machine 
learning algorithms like SVM, Decision Tree, RBF SVM, 
Logistic Regression and Naïve Bayes. The authors of [35] 
were able to achieve a cross-validated accuracy of 79%. The 
authors of [36] used the learnings from the work of [35] and 
applied the algorithms on a dataset of 529 individuals from a 
hospital in Bangladesh through questionnaires. Their 
experimental results show that Random forests tend to 
outperform compared to other algorithms. A review of 
machine learning and statistical learning methods in 
publications produced between 2010 – 2020 [37] indicates 
that the Random Forest algorithm consistently outperforms 
other machine learning mild, including those based on neural 
network, particularly when applied to various tabular datasets. 
All of these works use demographic and patient health data to 
predict the subject’s risk of diabetes. 
Recently, there has been renewed interest in predicting 
whether a subject’s blood glucose levels are high or low by 
analysing their voice audio. The authors of [8] positions 
speech audio as a “biomarker sensor” by applying machine 
learning classification. They achieved a 𝑓(1) score of 0.88 in 
a leave-one-out cross-validated dataset of 70 audio samples 
per subject with 49 participants in total. The authors of [10] 
investigated whether voice analysis can be used as a prescreening tool for type 2 diabetes by examining the difference 
in voice recordings between individuals with diabetes and 
individuals without diabetes. They found significant 
differences, both in the entire dataset and in age-matched and 
BMI-matched samples and their predictive models achieved 
𝑓(1) scores of 0.75 for women and 0.7 for men separately. 
Both works [8, 10] found that frequency-based voice features 
like pitch, jitter, shimmer, etc. show high predictive power 
and collected data samples via a smartphone-based voice 
recorder. 
III. METHODOLOGY 
Our method focuses on collecting voice biomarkers from 
regular everyday engagements between a voice based virtual 
assistant and patients who are primarily community-dwelling 
older adults, living alone. In this section, we present the endto-end pipeline we developed for data collection and 
application of a machine-learning based classifier in a triaging 
system for the continuous screening of the onset of type 2 
diabetes. 
A. Research Motivations 
The works of [8, 10, 12, 33-37] have shown that it is 
feasible to use machine learning algorithms to analyse voice 
features and classify them to belong to someone with diabetes 
or not. Applications of such models in real world clinical 
practice has however been challenged [38] regarding 
reliability and utility of its predictions. The existing works 
focus on individual sample classification performance but fails 
to demonstrate how such models can be used for early 
intervention where its utility is maximised. These works rely 
exclusively on discrete collection of feature samples and is not 
clear how they can integrate within the daily routine of older 
adults who may not be comfortable using smartphones or 
similar data-collection devices. Our motivation behind this 
paper was to develop a triaging system instead of a simple 
classifier, which can be: 
1. seamlessly integrated with voice-based virtual 
assistants which do not require digital literacy to use. 
2. used alongside assistive technology in clinical and 
social care pathways like virtual wards [39], hospitalat-home [40], and discharge-to-assess [41] 
3. used to prioritise those who are at high risk to avoid 
adding unnecessary burden on healthcare systems 
4. flag at first signs of onset, to intervene early improve 
patient outcomes. 
B. System Design 
To support our motivation, we put forward the following 
conceptual design of our triaging system in Figure 1 below. 
 
Figure 1 Conceptual Flowchart of Our Proposed Triaging System 
The system has 4 steps in implementation: 
 
1. Voice Capture: A home hub which hosts the virtual 
assistant is deployed in the home of an older adult 
patient who needs support and long-term care 
monitoring. The assistant interacts with the patient

every day and collects their responses as voice 
recordings. 
2. Biomarker Extraction: The home hub runs a 
program that analyse the voice recordings and extract 
relevant acoustic and vocal features required to 
ascertain risk. The program only sends nonidentifiable features to the cloud in accordance with 
user privacy regulations like GDPR and HIPPA. 
3. Diagnostic Claim Generation: A machine learning 
model is trained and accepts specific voice features to 
output the probability that these features are similar to 
those on the trained dataset of features from people at 
risk. The model generates probability values 
accordingly, for all feature sets captured every day and 
averages them to give a confidence percentage or 
score for the older adult is at risk. 
4. Intervention Thresholding: The daily confidence 
scores are then monitored over a period of time. 
Medical expertise will advise how long the data will 
need to monitored and what confidence threshold 
criteria will need to be met before the patient will be 
deemed to be at risk and require a formal intervention 
from the healthcare system. 
 
In this paper, we focus only on the first 3 steps, and we 
discuss the method we followed to train a machine learning 
model and use it to generate confidence scores for tracking 
onset of diabetes. The last step pertaining to threshold 
confidence scores for intervention is out of scope of this paper 
and will be covered in a future publication. 
C. Sourcing a Voice-based Virtual Assistant 
The first step in our triaging system required a virtual 
assistant technology. We needed a voice-based conversational 
assistant which would not only help us to collect speech voice 
samples but also provide value to the older adult subjects. The 
works of [42, 43] have noted that older adults are more likely 
to adopt new digital technology as part of their daily life if it 
actively supplements their regular needs. 
We sourced Monica (abbreviated for “MiiCare’s Ondemand Neural Intelligence Care Assistant”), a new voicebased conversational virtual assistant from MiiCare [21], 
marketed as a virtual companion and health coach for older 
adults who live alone and have chronic management needs. 
Monica is housed within the MiiCube, a small cube-shaped 
device that serves as a home hub controlling a wireless remote 
patient monitoring ecosystem within the home environment. 
The MiiCube uses a ARM4 processer coupled with a 2microphone setup from Seed Studio’s ReSpeaker Pi Hat [44] 
enclosed in a cubical box enclosure as shown in Figure 2. The 
microphones are located immediately beneath the top grill to 
ensure it is capturing the acoustic scene and all acoustic events 
including the patients’ speech responses without exposing the 
computing unit. 
 
 
Figure 1 The MiiCube recording device from MiiCare 
To comply with user privacy regulations, the device does 
not background record audio. It captures the audio recording 
of the patient’s responses only when either Monica or the 
patient initiates a conversation. In this study, we record the 
patient’s response at each turn of the conversation and for a 
maximum of 10s, to minimise unnecessary recording. The 
speech audio is sampled at 16 KHz 16-bits in PCM WAV 
format and immediately processed within the MiiCube to 
return a response. Monica uses Azure OpenAI [45]’s GPT 
inference to provide human-like natural conversational 
experience for the older adult subjects as well as to provide 
personalised content in the form of reminders and behavioural 
prompts to support self-care and condition management. 
D. Voice Biomarker Extraction 
As part of this research study, we modified the MiiCube to 
run a Python-based script alongside its main system program. 
This Python script accepts a copy of the speech recording data 
captured by the MiiCube system program and extracts voice 
biomarkers. The reasoning behind running the voice 
biomarker extraction step at the point of collection instead of 
in the cloud is to comply with ethics review and ensure highest 
levels of user privacy and data leak protection. This 
implementation demonstrates regulatory compliance by 
design, for privacy-sensitive applications like in clinical trials 
and even the commercial mass market. 
The MiiCube’s compute environment runs Python 3.7.3, 
which can only support 32-bit operating systems. The authors 
of [8, 10, 11, 12] had used Python modules like Librosa [46], 
praat-parselmouth [47] and disvoice [48] to process voice 
audio files and extract voice biomarkers. Librosa cannot be 
used in 32-bit compute environments, therefore we used 
scipy.utils [49] instead to load the voice audio recordings and 
praat-parselmouth to extract the acoustic features as they were 
supported by our compute environment. 
We extracted 7 acoustic features from the voice recordings 
using praat-parselmouth. Some of these acoustic features have 
already been demonstrated to have strong correlation with 
blood glucose levels in the works of [8, 10, 11, 12, 23, 24, 25, 
26]. We list these features in Table 1 below.

E. Data Collection 
To collect the acoustic features from the MiiCubes, we 
built an API endpoint connected with a noSQL database on 
Azure Cloud. The API endpoint was written using Python and 
FastAPI [53] to accept 1x7 floating-point row vectors along 
with the subject identifier and MiiCube device identifier. This 
API accepted each feature vector and stored them in an Azure 
Cosmos DB in an unstructured JSON Collection. This step is 
unique to our setup, as far as we are aware, and can be replaced 
with any suitable data collection and storage suitable with 
voice assistant devices. Storing the data using this way made 
it easy for us to add or remove subjects to the research in a 
staggered fashion without worrying about the data collection. 
MiiCare received consent from n=50 older adult MiiCube 
users living in the UK to be part of this study. Our python 
script, written to extract the 7 acoustic features, was remotely 
installed in these MiiCubes. We let the script run continuously 
for 30 days across these 50 MiiCubes for the entire duration of 
October 2024. All these users shared the following 
similarities: 
1. The subject lives alone and can self-care. 
2. The subject resides in the UK and speaks English as 
their main language. 
3. The subject takes one or more medications as part of 
their daily chronic management needs. 
4. The subject had consented to have Monica be proactive in its engagement approach to collect more 
voice recordings from them. 
We set the system to collect 6 voice recordings over 3 
separate days, i.e. 2 recordings per day at least. We have noted 
that it is possible for a subject to have several conversations 
with Monica and thereby collect more than 2 recordings in a 
single day. The acoustic features in these recordings is 
influenced by the varying blood glucose levels throughout the 
day due to factors like meal timings, physical activity, stress 
levels, etc. and this holds for diabetic as well as non-diabetic 
subjects. We do not want our triage to be impacted by this and 
by setting a minimum data collection duration of 3 days, we 
minimise the influence of temporary blood glucose 
fluctuations on the triage’s performance to track onset of 
diabetes. There was no attempt undertaken to introduce any 
strict daily routine because we wanted to demonstrate 
feasibility of the method in real-world applications where the 
subjects are not expected to change their daily routine to 
accommodate the assistive technology. 
Monica was setup to support the older adult users with their 
daily chronic management needs. This included daily 
reminders for timely medication and fluid intake. In addition 
to this, Monica was programmed to initiate engagement with 
the user at home when they are idle. Users were free to chat 
with Monica whenever they wanted. The setup is similar to 
real world deployments of smart home assistants and virtual 
agents like Alexa, Siri and Google Home when used in 
healthcare applications [17, 54]. 
F. Dataset 
After 30 days, we took stock of all the features collected 
for each subject from our cloud database and applied our 
sampling threshold of 2 recordings every day. We found that 
n=24/50 MiiCube users had enough data to satisfy this 
threshold. The reasons for the remaining 26 MiiCubes failing 
to collect enough data was attributed to poor internet 
connectivity as those patients lived in rural areas. We 
summarise the feature samples collected for each user in Table 
II below. In total, we had data from n=17 male users (11 with 
diabetes and 6 without diabetes) and n=7 female users (3 with 
diabetes and 4 without diabetes).

G. Preprocessing Voice Biomarkers 
Since the voice features captured were all continuous 
floating-point numbers, preprocessing them requires careful 
feature scaling which should have clinical underpinnings. We 
enlisted with the following considerations as part of the 
scaling process: 
 
1. The authors of [50] defined normative ranges for 
articulation rate for human speakers across a variety 
of languages. English speakers have an articulation 
rate of 6.19 syllables per second on average across the 
globe. We defined the scaling as a percentage ratio of 
how fast the observed rate is relative to this average. 
In formulaic terms, if the articulation rate is 𝑎𝑟, then 
the scaling rule is 𝑎𝑟!"#$%& = 
#' )*.,-
*.,- 
2. The authors of [50] establishes the normative range 
of speaking in English speakers at different paces for 
different settings. We used the rate of 150 words per 
minute (WPM) as the upper bound for casual 
everyday conversation and applied the scaling rule 
for speaking rate 𝑠𝑟!"#$%& as s𝑟/150.

H. Training the Machine Learning model 
Taking inspiration from the work of [10], we adopted the 
leave-one-out (LOO) approach to train and cross-validate the 
performance of the machine learning model for ex-situ 
samples for a subject whose features the model hasn’t been 
trained on. The LOO approach was applied separately for the 
male and female subjects. 
The works of [8, 10, 11, 12, 23, 24, 25, 26] has used 
various shallow machine learning algorithms like SVM [55], 
Logistic Regression [56], KNN [56], Decision Trees [56] and 
Random Forests [56]. The authors of [37] have even claimed 
the shallow algorithms are superior to neural network based 
deep learning approaches as they demonstrate similar 
predictive power at lower computational complexity and 
resource needs. The authors of [10] concur with this 
observation and added that neural networks overfit on such 
datasets as these are sparse in nature with only a few hundred 
samples that could be collected per patient in real life 
deployments. We agreed with this analysis and therefore we 
only focused on evaluating the set of algorithms and choosing 
the best performing model using our acoustic features. 
We describe the exact steps followed for evaluation as 
follows: 
1. Choose 1 subject identifier 𝐼𝐷4=$&=>0 from among the 
subjects available. 
2. Separate the feature samples for 𝐼𝐷4=$&=>0 from the 
other subject identifiers 𝐼𝐷=04%'!. 
3. Train the machine learning model 𝑀 on the feature 
dataset for 𝐼𝐷=04%'!. Please note that the label for each 
feature set will be 1 if the subject has diabetes and 0 
if they do not. 
4. Once the training is complete, apply 𝑀 on the feature 
set for 𝐼𝐷4=$&=>0 and extract the probability values 
{𝑝,} for label=1 only. We want to focus on how likely 
the model thinks each feature set from 𝐼𝐷4=$&=>0 has 
similar characteristics to that of features of subjects in 
𝐼𝐷=04%'! who had label=1 (with diabetes). 
5. 𝜇({𝑝1}) gives us an averaged probability score that 
𝑀 thinks the features of 𝐼𝐷4=$&=>0 is like those with 
diabetes. Please note that the feature set must be 
collected over a period of several days when this step 
is executed in a real-life inference application (3 days 
as a minimum as explained already in Subsection E). 
This will give assurance that factors affecting blood 
glucose levels is controlled for in the generation of 
the average probability score for diabetes within that 
period of time. 
6. We now apply a decision framework to determine 
whether we make the claim 𝐶 that subject 𝐼𝐷4=$&=>0 
has diabetic symptoms using 𝜇({𝑝1}). We reason that 
(a) if 𝜇({𝑝1}) > 0.6, then it is highly probable that the 
subject is diabetic and should be flagged for 
intervention (𝐶= 1); (b) If 𝜇({𝑝1}) < 0.4, then the 
subject is less probable to be diabetic and therefore 
currently at low risk for the same (𝐶= 0); (c) If 0.4 
<= 𝜇({𝑝1}) <= 0.6, then we are not confident enough 
at this stage to make a diagnostic claim about the 
subject (𝐶= −1). 
7. We repeat Steps 1 – 6 for all subjects available for a 
either gender separately and tabulate the following 
information: 𝐼𝐷4=$&=>0, 𝜇({𝑝1}), claim made using 
our decision framework 𝐶, and lastly whether 𝐶 
matches the ground truth diagnostic label for 
𝐼𝐷4=$&=>0 (1 if has diabetes and 0 otherwise). 
Tracking the number of claims for 𝐶= 1 over time will show 
the probability of onset of diabetes in undiagnosed subjects 
when the triage is applied to real-life. Determining the 
threshold of positive claims needed and the number of days to

We make the following observations: 
1. For n=17 male subjects, Tree based models Random 
Forests (RF) and Decision Tree (DT) showed the 
highest diagnostic hit rate at 70% with 7 correct claims 
out of 10 total claims made against each of them. 
2. For n=7 female subjects, Decision Tree (DT) had the 
highest diagnostic hit rate at 60% with 3 correct claims 
out of 5 total claims made against each of them. 
3. Algorithms favoured by the authors of [10], notably 
Logistic Regression (LR), SVM and Naïve Gaussian 
Bayes (GNB) came second to the tree-based models 
for both genders. The authors explained that tree-based 
models are not suitable in such cases as they are likely 
to overfit. But we observe that for both genders, these 
algorithms had a lower ratio (around 1:1) of the 
number of correct diagnostic claims against incorrect 
ones compared to that for tree-based models using our 
LOO approach (almost ~2:1). 
V. CONCLUSION 
This paper introduces a novel approach to leveraging 
shallow machine learning algorithms for voice pathology, 
specifically in how they can be used as a triaging tool to 
identify individuals at risk who would benefit from timely 
intervention. We also demonstrate the suitability of this 
method as an alternative to the constrained discrete noncontinuous and intermittent data-capture methodologies using 
smartphone apps. The results presented provides reasonable 
validation as to how this innovative triaging system can be 
used alongside pre-existing commercial voice-based virtual 
assistants. 
Many of these virtual assistants are now being adopted by 
healthcare institutions in telehealth and digital health 
supported pathways to improve patient experience, health 
outcomes and reduce pressure on the healthcare system. By 
embedding our triaging system in mainstream channels and 
solutions, we believe that the roll out, adoption and 
distribution of our system will be easier. Principally, we 
evaluated our concept and showed how it can be used as a 
continuous pre-diagnostic tool for older adult patients at home 
who may be undiagnosed or are pre-diabetic, without 
inconveniencing their daily life. 
For our next work, we will evaluate the triaging system with 
a larger user cohort to study its generalisability and efficacy 
across co-existing medical conditions, age groups, and with 
alternative acoustic features like cepstral peak prominence. 
We foresee consecutive future works focusing on extending 
this voice-based triaging system for other medical conditions 
which can be managed better with early intervention like 
onset of cognitive decline, hypertension and respiratory tract 
infections.

Abstract. Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in highrisks decision-making systems across domains such as healthcare, finance,
and the judicial system. As reliance on predictive models grows, so does
the demand for Explainable AI (XAI) to ensure transparency, trust, and
interpretability. However, existing XAI approaches often fail to present
explanations in a format accessible to domain experts, limiting their practical utility. Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently emerged as a
bridge between complex models and end-users, offering natural language
explanations. Yet, their use introduces new risks, including hallucinated
outputs and lack of source traceability. To address these challenges, we
propose a Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS) that not only combines standard predictive models with XAI techniques but also incorporates a Retrieval-Augmented Generation module as an interactive enhancer. This module grounds explanations in verified medical knowledge,
reformulates technical outputs into a human-like format, and enables
users—such as clinicians—to actively query the system. By fostering an
interactive, human-in-the-loop environment, our approach empowers domain experts to explore model decisions, contextualize explanations, and
build trust in AI-assisted diagnostics. The study concludes with preliminary experiments validating the proposed methodology.

L. Mannocci et al.
1
Introduction
Artificial Intelligence (AI) has rapidly evolved to become a crucial component
in decision-making systems across various fields, including healthcare [42], finance [7], law enforcement [38], and the judicial system [34]. The increasing
reliance on predictive models in these domains necessitates the development of
methods to explain their outputs, a requirement that has led to the emergence of
Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) [20, 16]. XAI aims to make AI models
more interpretable, transparent, and trustworthy, ensuring that domain experts
and end-users can understand and assess the rationale behind automated decisions [10, 31]. The need for trust and transparency in AI decision-making has also
been recognized at the regulatory level. The European Union’s AI Act [37], one
of the first comprehensive legal frameworks for AI, emphasizes the importance of
explainability, particularly for high-risk AI applications. The AI Act mandates
that AI systems used in critical sectors provide clear, understandable, and verifiable explanations to ensure accountability and fairness. This regulatory push
further underscores the necessity of effective XAI techniques that can meet both
ethical and legal standards while supporting domain experts in making informed
decisions.
Many high-risk applications depend on predictive models that significantly
impact human lives. In healthcare, AI-driven diagnostic systems assist doctors
in detecting diseases, recommending treatments, and predicting patient outcomes [42]. In the judicial system, predictive models inform parole decisions
and risk assessments [34]. Despite their effectiveness, these models often operate
as black boxes, making it difficult for domain experts to verify their outputs and
detect potential biases. Without proper interpretability, decision-makers may
struggle to trust AI-driven recommendations, leading to ethical, legal, and social
concerns. Indeed, these explanations might be difficult to interpret, particularly
for professionals outside the field of computer science, such as doctors, lawyers, or
policymakers. The challenge lies in presenting these explanations in a way that
aligns with the expertise and expectations of the end-users [9]. For example,
rule-based explainability methods may generate decision rules with numerical
thresholds that do not align with conventional domain knowledge. In medical
applications, an AI model might define a risk threshold for blood pressure or
glucose levels that deviates from commonly accepted medical guidelines, creating confusion among clinicians. Without proper contextualization, such outputs
can diminish trust in the AI system rather than enhancing its credibility. Moreover, existing XAI methods often fail to present explanations in a format that is
intuitive and easily digestible for domain experts. This limitation has led to the
integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) as interfaces for explainability,
offering a more natural and human-like explanations for AI predictions [3].
LLMs have been increasingly employed as mediators between complex AI
models and domain experts, translating complex mathematical justifications into
human-like explanations. By reformatting and simplifying the outputs of XAI
techniques, LLMs can substantially enhance the interpretability of AI-driven decisions [3]. In a healthcare setting, for instance, an LLM can transform a technical

3
explanation of a machine learning model’s prediction into a structured summary
that aligns with a physician’s diagnostic workflow [23, 30]. More recently, LLMs
have been leveraged not only to translate explanations into natural language but
also to enrich them with contextual information drawn from their pre-trained
knowledge [36]. However, this approach introduces an additional layer of complexity and potential risk. LLMs are known to occasionally produce inaccurate
or misleading outputs, a phenomenon referred to as hallucinations [24]. Furthermore, these models typically do not provide access to the underlying sources
that support their responses, limiting transparency and traceability [27].
One promising approach to mitigating LLM hallucinations in XAI is the use
of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) [26]. RAG enhances LLM-generated
explanations by grounding them in an external, domain-specific knowledge base.
Instead of relying solely on the LLM’s pre-trained knowledge, RAG retrieves relevant information from a curated database to provide more accurate and reliable
explanations. In the context of XAI, RAG can address two critical challenges.
First, it reduces the risk of hallucinations by ensuring that explanations are based
on verified sources rather than probabilistic text generation. Second, it allows for
the integration of domain-specific knowledge, ensuring that explanations adhere
to established medical, legal, or financial guidelines. By leveraging RAG, AIgenerated explanations can be aligned more closely with experts’ expectations,
thereby increasing trust and usability in real-world applications.
In this work, we present, to the best of our knowledge, the first Clinical
Decision Support System (CDSS) that integrates standard predictive models
with XAI techniques and RAG-enhanced explanations. The proposed system
consists of three key components:
1. Predictive Model: A standard classifier, such as a neural network or a random
forest, that generates predictions based on patient data;
2. Explainer: An explanation method that provides insights into the model’s
decision-making process through feature importance-based explanations (e.g.,
LIME [39] and SHAP [28]), decision rules (e.g., LORE [19]) or exemplars and
counter-exemplars [18];
3. RAG-Based enhancer module: A module built on RAG that enhances explanations by grounding them in reliable medical knowledge, mitigating
hallucinations, and transforming traditional explanations into more humanreadable, context-aware formats. It also serves as an interactive tool, allowing
end users to ask specific questions and explore the patient’s clinical profile
in relation to the model’s predictions and explanations.
By combining standard classifiers with RAG-based explanations grounded in
verified medical sources, our system enhances the trustworthiness and domain
relevance of AI-driven medical decisions. This approach addresses key limitations of conventional XAI by providing interpretable, reliable insights tailored
to healthcare professionals. The study concludes with preliminary experiments
validating the proposed methodology.

L. Mannocci et al.
2
Related Works
AI is transforming modern society, largely due to the rise of complex Machine
Learning (ML) models with strong predictive capabilities. However, these models—such as deep neural networks and ensemble methods—are often considered
black boxes due to their lack of transparency [31, 20]. This opacity makes it difficult to identify biases in training data or explain decisions, which is especially
concerning in high-stakes domains like healthcare, finance, and criminal justice.
As Rudin argues [40], the lack of interpretability hinders trust, accountability,
and real-world deployment of AI systems in regulated settings. At the same
time, Large Language Models (LLMs) have opened new possibilities for generating intuitive, accessible explanations. Their ability to bridge technical and
non-technical understanding supports the development of more human-centric,
fair, and transparent AI systems.
We focus next on two key areas: post-hoc explanations, which analyze model
behavior after predictions are made, and human-centered explanations, which
adapt to user needs to improve interpretability.
2.1
Post-hoc explanations
In the context of post-hoc explanation methods for black-box models applied to
tabular data, both local and global approaches have been extensively studied and
benchmarked [5]. Local explanation methods aim to interpret individual predictions by approximating the model’s behavior in the vicinity of a specific instance.
One of the most widely known techniques in this category is LIME, which builds
a simple surrogate model—usually linear—on a locally perturbed dataset to estimate the contribution of each feature [39]. Although popular, LIME suffers
from instability due to its random neighborhood generation strategy. A more
theoretically grounded alternative is SHAP, which relies on Shapley values from
cooperative game theory to assign each feature an importance score based on
its marginal contribution across all possible feature combinations [28]. SHAP
ensures consistency and local accuracy, making it a robust choice for feature attribution. Another relevant method is LORE, which employs genetic algorithms
to generate a neighborhood and extracts interpretable decision rules, offering
both factual and counterfactual explanations [19]. Other approaches provide
local explanations which are based on exemplars or better counter-exemplars,
which enable a counterfactual reasoning that in some sense produce suggestions
to users on what is possible to change for obtaining a different decision from the
machine learning model [18].
On the other hand, global explanation methods focus on understanding the
model’s logic over the entire input space. RuleFit combines decision rules extracted from tree ensembles with linear models to produce sparse, interpretable
explanations of model behavior. Building upon this idea, SkopeRules uses ensemble techniques to extract a set of high-precision rules that summarize the
model’s decision boundaries [14]. More recently, Setzu et al. [41] proposed GLocalX, which aggregates local explanations to form a coherent global understand-

ing of the model, effectively bridging the gap between local interpretability and
global insight. These methods, differing in their assumptions and strategies, collectively contribute to the growing toolbox of post-hoc XAI techniques tailored
for tabular data.
2.2
Human-centered explanations
Both post-hoc and intrinsic XAI methods have advanced model interpretability,
yet a key challenge remains: ensuring explanations are truly comprehensible to
end users. Human-centered XAI addresses this by aligning explanations with
user needs through participatory design methods such as interviews and user
studies [2, 12, 11]. This approach emphasizes contextualized explanations that
integrate seamlessly into user workflows and are validated through real-world
testing [25, 45].
Recent work explores how LLMs can enhance explanation quality by generating adaptive, narrative-style outputs that combine predictions with counterfactuals [29, 23]. For example, x-[plAIn] [30] uses a customized LLM to generate
concise, audience-specific summaries of XAI methods. Narrative explanations are
also being explored across data types, including tabular data[6, 48], graphs [17,
35], and images [44].
Initially framed as a data-to-text task, LLM-generated narratives have evolved
to incorporate broader knowledge, adding context and reasoning beyond simple
summaries [29]. A recent pilot study found users preferred such narratives over
SHAP plots across several metrics [48]. This approach aligns with the concept of
self-explanations, where models articulate reasoning to aid understanding [22].
However, it also introduces risks like adversarial helpfulness, where convincing
but incorrect explanations may mislead users [1]. RAG helps mitigate this by
grounding outputs in trusted sources, improving factual accuracy and transparency [15]. Similarly, Park et al. [36] combine LLMs with knowledge graphs
to generate structured, domain-specific explanations that are both clinically accurate and contextually rich.
3
Method
In light of the growing need for human-centered explanations and the impressive capabilities of LLMs to generate human-like responses, challenges arise,
particularly when LLMs produce convincing yet incorrect answers or exhibit
hallucinations. These issues can compromise the reliability of explanations and
erode user trust. To address these concerns, we propose leveraging RAG, a system that combines the generative power of LLMs with the reliability of external,
grounded, and reliable sources. By integrating RAG, we ensure that the explanations are not only contextually rich and human-readable but also rooted in
verifiable information, thereby enhancing both accuracy and transparency in the
model’s outputs. Figure 1 illustrates the approach proposed in this work, which

3.2
Enhancer
The enhancer module, based on RAG, is designed to support three distinct tasks:
context explanation, classifier and XAI, and question & answer. Each component
in the pipeline operates independently and could, in principle, be implemented
using LLM instead of a RAG-based approach. However, rather than relying
solely on the LLM’s pre-trained knowledge, RAG retrieves relevant information
from a curated medical database to generate more accurate, contextualized, and
reliable explanations.
In the following we described in detail the three potential enhancer’s tasks:
Context explanation. This task enriches an existing explanation by converting the explanation into a human-like format and integrating context from the
RAG’s specialized corpus. This task takes as input the feature vector xi, the
prediction ˜yi made by the classifier, and the initial explanation ei generated
by the local explainer, and provides an enhanced explanation ee

the corpus and transforming it into a more human-comprehensible format. The
resulting output, ee

more detailed understanding of the model’s decision-making process, grounded
in both the prediction and the context of the input data;
Classifier and XAI. In this task, the RAG serves as both a classifier and an
explanation generator. Formally, the task can be defined as: R : X →(Y r, Er),
where the RAG is provided with the input feature vector xi and performs a
classification along with an explanation supporting the prediction. The output
consists of the predicted label yr

the system, allowing users to request interactive explanations. It is performed
at the end of the pipeline, once the user has received the initial results from
the entire decision support system. In this task, a question q is provided as
input along with the entire system’s information. The output a is the answer
to the question, which may take various forms depending on the nature of q.
This task allows the user to query the system for additional information coming
from the specialized corpus of the RAG, clarification, or deeper insights into the
model’s predictions and explanations, providing an interactive and dynamic way
to explore and understand the decision-making process of the AI model.
3.3
Selector
The final component of the proposed method is the selector, serves as a filtering
and governance layer for the information presented to the user. It receives as

4
Experiments and results
In this section, we show some preliminary results of a specific instantiation of
our methodology.
4.1
Dataset and experimental setting
We evaluate our proposed method using the Pima Indians Diabetes Database [43],
a publicly available dataset3 originally provided by the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases. The goal is to diagnostically predict
the presence of diabetes in a patient based on a set of clinical attributes. Prior
to training, the dataset is standardized using a standard scaler, and we applied
random oversampling to balance the class distribution by increasing the number of instances in the minority class, i.e., patients diagnosed with diabetes.
As black-box model, we employed a Random Forest classifier trained on an
80/20 train-test split, using a grid search and 3-fold cross-validation to optimize
the hyperparameters. For local explanations, we use LIME [39], which provides
feature importance scores for each prediction. The enhancer module builds on
the MedRAG framework4, introduced by [46], leveraging the StatPearls corpus
for clinical decision support and the MedCPT retriever tailored for biomedical
content. The LLM used for generation is Mixtral5. Finally, the selector filters
the enhancer’s output, returning the RAG-based explanation er
i only when the
enhancer’s prediction yr
i matches the black-box prediction ˜yi, ensuring that explanations are only provided when there is consistency across models.

4.2
Preliminary results
In this work, we present a preliminary evaluation of the proposed methodology
to highlight the importance of integrating both a predictive model and the RAG
module within the same system. To this end, we compare the predictive performance of the Random Forest (RF) classifier and the MedRAG model on the
Pima Indians Diabetes dataset. The results are reported in Table 1. Given the
imbalanced nature of the dataset, with 65% of the records indicating no diabetes,
the f1-score serves as the primary evaluation metric, alongside the recall for the
“yes" class. This focus is driven by the importance of identifying as many diabetic cases as possible, even at the cost of some false positives. In this context,
the Random Forest model outperforms MedRAG, particularly in the detection
of diabetes cases, where it achieves an f1-score of 0.66 compared to MedRAG’s
0.58. Furthermore, 82% of the time, both models agree on the prediction, which
is the condition required for the selector to output the enhancer’s explanation
er. Figure 2 further breaks down this agreement, showing that the majority of
instances where the models agree, they are correct. The second most frequent

highlighting the greater reliability of the former in making accurate predictions.
5
Discussion and conclusions
Our results show that the traditional Random Forest model outperformed the
RAG-based system, supporting its continued use in our CDSS. Nonetheless,
the strong agreement between the two models suggests that RAG-generated
explanations can complement traditional ones, enhancing interpretability and
user trust.
These preliminary findings, though promising, are limited by the small dataset,
largely due to the computational cost of RAG. Expanding experiments to other
clinical datasets and black-box models will help validate the system’s generalizability. Future work should also explore: i) the impact to use a LLM tailored
to medical domain instead of a generalist LLM, and ii) how factors like model
confidence and explanation alignment affect the CDSS’s reliability.
Privacy remains a major concern, particularly when integrating LLMs and
RAG in healthcare [33, 32]. Explanations often require access to sensitive clinical
data, and using closed-source LLMs risks violating patient confidentiality and
regulations like GDPR [47, 8]. Addressing these challenges will require privacypreserving techniques such as local inference, federated learning [21, 13], and
unlearning methods [4].
In summary, we propose a hybrid XAI approach that combines traditional
models with generative enhancers to support interpretable, human-aligned AI
in clinical contexts. While further validation is needed, this work takes a step
toward more transparent and responsible decision support systems.

You are a helpful medical expert. Your task is to classify a patient as having diabetes or not

Operation-aware Multimodal Clinical Decision Support System
for ICU Discharge Risk Assessment
Guoqing Zhang,1 Rafik Hadfi,1 Takayuki Ito1
1Graduate School of Informatics, Kyoto University, Kyoto, Japan
zhang.guoqing.27t@st.kyoto-u.ac.jp, rafik.hadfi@i.kyoto-u.ac.jp, ito@i.kyoto-u.ac.jp
Abstract
Unplanned 30-day intensive care unit (ICU) readmission following hospital discharge is a major benchmark for evaluating healthcare quality and patient safety in modern critical
care medicine. Most existing predictive approaches assume
that readmission risk is determined solely by a patient’s individual pathophysiological state, ignoring the institution’s
resource capacity and operational context (Hospital Operational Context). In clinical practice, discharge decisions are
frequently dynamic trade-offs made by intensivists balancing patient medical stability against ward bed turnover pressures. To address this gap, we design an Operation-aware
Multimodal Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS) for
ICU discharge risk assessment. On the one hand, the system unites multi-agent collaborative extraction with selfevolving retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to eliminate
formatting-template noise across lengthy progress notes. On
the other hand, it constructs departmental workload indicators (icu_speedup_los) alongside admission flow characteristics, unifying continuous vital signs, hierarchical sparse
medical codes (ICD/DRG), and discharge summary semantics. Addressing the extreme class imbalance (∼10.5% readmission incidence) and the challenge of alarm fatigue, the
system implements data normalization, class reweighting optimization, and an F1 decision-threshold calibration pipeline.
In 20 independent multi-seed runs conducted on a cohort of
20,000 ICU stays from MIMIC-III, empirical findings show
that: a single-modality baseline depending exclusively on vital
signs possesses limited predictive capacity under real-world
class imbalance (PR-AUC of only 0.1387 ± 0.0086); directly concatenating raw text embeddings causes performance
degradation in decision tree models (XGBoost and LightGBM PR-AUC drop to 0.3893 and 0.4030, respectively);
whereas an end-to-end multimodal fine-tuning architecture
(Transformer E2E FineTune) utilizing layer-wise parameter
freezing and differential learning rates successfully reverses
text negative transfer, achieving the overall highest AUROC
of 0.8288±0.0110, PR-AUC of 0.4373±0.0310, and a competitive F1-Score of 0.4757±0.0196. Mechanistic attribution
analyses also confirm that operational indicators supply independent risk signals, establishing an engineering foundation
for deploying high-utility clinical decision support tools in
bedside hospital wards.
Code
—
https://github.com/KuoChing-cmd/
ClinicalNoteAgent/

Intelligence (www.aaai.org). All rights reserved.
S1
Introduction
In intensive care clinical decision-making, identifying vulnerable patients at risk of latent deterioration and avoiding
premature step-down to general wards are core imperatives of
critical care medicine. Patients experiencing unplanned ICU
readmission within 30 days of discharge undergo substantially prolonged hospital stays and face elevated in-hospital
mortality (Klinge et al. 2020; Barbieri et al. 2020; Sheetrit,
Brief, and Elisha 2023). While recent multicenter investigations confirm the promise of machine learning for postdischarge surveillance (Lim et al. 2025), existing clinical
early warning systems commonly encounter barriers during
ward deployment due to alarm fatigue: in low-prevalence
locales where readmissions occur in only ∼10% of cases,
typical models optimized for high AUROC tend to trigger
substantial false-positive alarms, prompting clinicians to turn
off the alert systems. To construct an actionable Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS), one must preserve screening
sensitivity while substantially improving precision, thereby
driving PR-AUC and F1 scores toward clinically acceptable
operating points.
Although electronic health record (EHR) repositories such
as MIMIC-III (Johnson et al. 2016) have advanced machine learning in critical care—spanning deep temporal focus (Madinei, Keyvanpour, and Shojaedini 2024), graphical
EHR representations (Choi et al. 2020), and recent readmission benchmarks (Fathy, Emeriaud, and Cheriet 2025)—
state-of-the-art predictive models still encounter two fundamental deployment bottlenecks. First, they exhibit a neglect
of hospital operational context. Standard models conceptualize patients as closed physiological entities, presuming that
deterioration following transfer stems entirely from built-in
disease progression. In clinical practice, however, ICU discharge is fundamentally a resource deployment and scheduling process carried out under institutional bed constraints
(Kim et al. 2015; Wagner et al. 2013; Long and Mathews
2018). Intensivists must routinely weigh incomplete physiological recovery against acute bed demands driven by emergency department (ED) boarding or post-operative transfers.
Patient transfer frequency before ICU admission, ED boarding durations, and ward acceleration driven by bed saturation
directly mirror operational workflow strain and care coordination friction; yet, customary doctrines remain entirely
agnostic to this systemic background. Second, models suffer

sample_chunks.text_content:
from data disparity and text template noise. Intensive care
records span high-frequency temporal streams, sparse diagnostic codes, and lengthy unstructured progress notes. While
recent studies explore medical text via knowledge graphs
(Lu, Nguyen, and Dou 2021) or multimodal architectures
for readmission prediction (Helmy et al. 2025; Datta et al.
2025), clinical free-text is often lengthy, laden with jargon,
and burdened by copy-pasted administrative templates. Directly feeding unadapted high-dimensional text embeddings
fails to yield meaningful gains and instead introduces severe
feature interference (negative transfer) with strong baselines
such as gradient-boosted decision trees.
To resolve these problems, we reframe ICU discharge
evaluation as an operationally aware multimodal decisionsupport task and develop a CDSS architecture that encompasses self-evolving textual distillation and deep cross-modal
correlation. The core contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:
• Operation-aware Decision Framework: Overcoming randomized timestamp offsets in MIMIC-III, we introduce unit-benchmarked turnover deviation indicators
(icu_speedup_los) and care flow complexity features, eliminating the subjective assumption that outcomes depend solely on physiological status.
• Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Text Distillation: We formulate a 7-domain specialist agent collaborative division
of labor paired with a reflective evolutionary experience
repository, accumulating 3,085 rules across 5,000 patient samples. Combined with FAISS vector retrieval for
structured information distillation, we propose a layerwise, frozen, end-to-end fine-tuning scheme that systematically mitigates interference from template noise in clinical notes.
• Thorough Testing under Low-Prevalence Conditions:
Across a cohort of 20,000 ICU stays, we conduct 20 independent randomized multi-seed runs (Seeds 42–61),
exposing the weakness of single-modality physiological
prediction (PR-AUC of only 0.1387) and verifying the
robustness of the end-to-end fine-tuning architecture in
achieving global optimality (AUROC 0.8288, PR-AUC
0.4373, F1 0.4757).
• Interpretability & Clinical Utility Analysis: Through integrated gradients (Sundararajan, Taly, and Yan 2017),
we systematically explain the mechanistic contributions
of separate physiological channels, pivotal time-based attention windows, and operational flow variables in 30-day
readmission forecasting.
S2
Clinical Workflow and Problem
Formulation
S2.1
Clinical Prediction Task and Endpoint
Definition
The prediction target is unplanned ICU readmission within
30 days following discharge (30-Day Readmission). In light
of complex intra-hospital patient trajectories, endpoint labels
yi ∈{0, 1} follow strict clinical mutually exclusive criteria:
• Cross-admission readmission: The patient undergoes a
separate hospital admission and enters an ICU within
30 days post-discharge (same SUBJECT_ID, distinct
HADM_ID).
• Within-admission readmission: During the same hospitalization episode, the patient is transferred out of the
ICU, deteriorates, and is subsequently readmitted back to
the ICU (multiple ICU stays under the same HADM_ID,
where the subsequent admission timestamp postdates
the preceding transfer timestamp, i.e., INTIMEk+1 >
OUTTIMEk).
• Mortality Mutual-Exclusion: Patients who suffer inhospital mortality (HOSPITAL_EXPIRE_FLAG = 1)
have their readmission risk strictly calibrated to 0, eliminating logical contradictions.
S2.2
Multimodal Clinical Data Streams and
Domain Alignment
For each ICU stay event i ∈{1, . . . , N} (experimental cohort N = 20, 000), the input is structured as a heterogeneous
quadruple:
Xi =
 
Xseq
i
, xstat
i
, xcode
i
, xtext
i
 
(S1)
First, for high-frequency dynamic physiological sequences
(Xseq
i
∈R48×8), the system captures 8 core physiological
signs during the initial 48 hours following ICU admission:
Heart Rate (HR), Respiratory Rate (RR), Oxygen Saturation (SpO2), Systolic Blood Pressure (SBP), Diastolic Blood
Pressure (DBP), Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP), Temperature (Temp), and Blood Glucose (Glucose). Blood pressure
measurements explicitly distinguish invasive arterial pressure from non-invasive cuff pressure; when both coexist, the
invasive arterial line—the gold standard in critical care—is
preferred. Time series are resampled into 1-hour regularized
bins, with missing steps forward-filled.
Second, structured demographic and operational indicators (xstat
i
∈R15) capture baseline patient context and care
delivery friction across three facets: (i) Baseline & Surgical
covariates include age, gender, marital status, ethnicity, insurance, admission source/type, first ICU unit, surgical procedure count, surgery binary indicator, and log-transformed
surgery-to-ICU entry gap ln(1 + ∆tsurg). (ii) Transfer Patterns track the number of ward transfers prior to ICU admission (pre_icu_transfers) along with log-transformed
emergency department wait time ln(1+tED). (iii) Ward Pressure & Turnover Deviation: addressing the obstacle where
randomized absolutetimestamps inMIMIC-III precludeconcurrent bed occupancy observation across patients, we formulate a stay deviation metric aligned with historical unit
benchmarks (e.g., MICU, SICU) along with stay duration
features:
icu_speedup_los = LOSunit −LOSactual
log_icu_los = ln(1 + LOShours)
(S2)
Specifically, under a zero-leakage cutoff, the feature is strictly
computed at the exact moment of the step-down transfer
order, sharing the same temporal cross-section with discharge notes and precluding future information leakage. Crucially, contrary to the naive assumption that shorter stays

merely reflect milder acuity (which would yield lower readmission rates), empirical attribution reveals that positive
icu_speedup_los (early turnover) significantly correlates with higher readmission risk (20.1% continuous IG attribution). This refutes indication confounding and confirms
that the metric captures external operational bed-turnover
pressure and premature discharge before complete physiological stabilization.
Third, hierarchically decoupled sparse medical codes
(xcode
i
) capture hierarchical EHR coding structures (Choi
et al. 2020). Primary ICD diagnoses and primary DRG codes
select the Top-128 categories, mapped into categorical indices feeding a learnable continuous embedding layer (128
dimensions). Secondary diagnoses (Top-32), surgical procedures (Top-64), and prescribed medications (Top-64) are
encoded into multi-hot sparse vectors, projected through embedding weight matrices, mean-pooled across active entries,
and concatenated into compact representations.
Fourth, unformatted clinical progress representations
(xtext
i
) incorporate free-text clinical progress notes. In contrast to standard clinical text baselines (Lu, Nguyen, and Dou
2021; Helmy et al. 2025) that directly process progress notes
vulnerable to template noise, lengthy inpatient records are
distilled via self-evolving multi-agent workflows into structured summaries, with 768-dimensional semantic features
extracted by Bio_ClinicalBERT (Alsentzer et al. 2019).
S3
Operation-aware CDSS Architecture
S3.1
Unstructured Text Mining: Multi-Agent
Self-Evolving RAG Mechanism
Orchestrated multi-agent architectures sustain diagnostic fidelity under complex clinical workloads compared to monolithic models (Klang et al. 2026). To overcome verbosity
and repetitive administrative boilerplate in clinical progress
notes, the system establishes a self-evolving multi-agent distillation pipeline across five coordinated stages: (i) Hierarchical Specialist Collaboration: Clinical text is segmented
across 7 specialized clinical domains (Nursing, Radiology,
ICU Care, ECG, Attending Physician, Discharge Summary,
and Echocardiography), where independent domain agents
extract acute warning signals. (ii) Meta-Agent Synthesis: A
supervisory Meta-Agent aggregates domain summaries, synthesizing a structured JSON report containing a prioritized
vital factor roster and composite risk score. (iii) Reflective Evolution Loop: When predictions diverge from clinical ground truth during training, a Reflection Agent audits causal failure points, extracting physician-vetted heuristic rules into a knowledge base (3,085 rules); correctly
classified trajectories are cataloged as gold-standard exemplars (1,899 cases). (iv) Lightweight RAG Retrieval: Guided
by all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings and a FAISS index, the pipeline dynamically retrieves the Top-5 relevant heuristic rules and Top-1 exemplar case per admission as few-shot in-context demonstrations. (v) Feature Embedding & Projection: Distilled summaries are encoded
by Bio_ClinicalBERT into 768-dimensional contextual
vectors and projected to a d-dimensional embedding Enote
aligned with temporal representations.
S3.2
Cross-Modal Network Architecture and
Deep Fusion Schemes
The framework investigates three architectural paradigms.
First, we evaluate tree-based baselines: XGBoost (Chen and
Guestrin 2016) and LightGBM (Ke et al. 2017) fitted on
physically concatenated vectors combining temporal statistical aggregations, static covariates, multi-hot codes, and 768dimensional text embeddings (Chen et al. 2025). Second,
we construct sequential late fusion (LSTM Late Fusion):
a 4-layer bi-directional LSTM with self-attentive temporal
pooling encodes physiological sequences, concatenated at
the classification tier with static, code, and text representations projected via independent MLP branches. Third, we
formulate parallel multi-branch extraction and late fusion.
Dynamic physiological sequences are encoded via a deep
Transformer encoder (Vaswani et al. 2017) into Zcls; static
operational indicators and medical codes are mapped via independent MLPs into dense vectors Eops and Ecode. These
representations are concatenated with text embedding Enote
to form Zfused = [Zcls ∥Eops ∥Ecode ∥Enote] ∈R2d+64,
feeding a 2-layer MLP head for joint risk estimation. To prevent representational collapse during end-to-end training, the
initial 8 layers of Bio_ClinicalBERT are frozen, leaving deeper layers (Layers 9–12) active; BERT parameters
receive a 0.1× scaled learning rate (lr * 0.1) with gradient checkpointing enabled.
S3.3
Training Optimization and Leak-Free
Validation Protocols
To ensure leak-free evaluation under severe class imbalance (∼10.5% prevalence) and achieve stable multimodal convergence, we institute four disciplined methodological
safeguards:
(i)
Zero-Leakage
Normalization:
StandardScaler parameters are fitted strictly on training splits; validation and testing cohorts inherit these statistics without re-estimation, precluding distribution leakage.
(ii) Dynamic Cost-Sensitive Loss: To counter minority-class
sparsity, a weighted binary cross-entropy loss deploys dynamic inverse class ratio weighting derived strictly from
the training split: wpos = Nneg/Npos ≈8.97. (iii) Cosine
Scheduling & Rollback: A CosineAnnealingLR schedule regulates learning rate decay, paired with early stopping (patience=15) on validation loss; upon termination,
model parameters rollback to the checkpoint achieving the
minimal validation loss. (iv) Decision Threshold Calibration: On validation splits, exhaustive grid search (step size
0.01) determines the optimal decision cutoff t∗maximizing
the F1-Score, replacing the uncalibrated default 0.5 threshold
for final test evaluation.
S4
Experimental Evaluation and Validation
S4.1
Evaluation Protocol and Cohort Setup
Experiments are run across 20,000 ICU stay records from
the MIMIC-III database. The cohort is partitioned into training (14,000 stays), validation (2,000 stays), and test splits
(4,000 stays) in a 7:1:2 ratio, with positive readmission prevalence ranging from 10.5% to 11.4%. To eliminate partitioning anomalies, all candidate approaches are evaluated across

S4.2
Comprehensive Performance Comparison
and Paradigm Defense
Table S1 summarizes the evaluation measures across 15
model configurations evaluated at their optimal F1 decision
thresholds across 20 randomized runs. Three core empirical insights emerge. First, we observe text negative transfer in shallow concatenation. Directly appending unadapted
768-d text embeddings into decision trees (XGBoost/LightGBM) triggers notable performance decline. Inpatient notes
are saturated with administrative templates and boilerplate
shorthand; high-dimensional embeddings diffuse greedy tree
node splitting, diluting compact, high-SNR physiological
and operational signals. Second, results demonstrate the
strength of structured baselines and multimodal reframing.
Purely structured LSTM Base establishes a solid benchmark (F1 = 0.4798), demonstrating the fitting efficiency of
recurrent cells over 48-hour dynamics along with discrete
codes. The multimodal goal is therefore not to surpass structured models trivially, but to resolve a harder clinical challenge: safely incorporating high-value text semantics without
suffering negative transfer (as observed in Transformer EarlyFusion, which degrades under raw text noise). Third, we
achieve a reversal of negative transfer via end-to-end finetuning. With layer-wise parameter freezing (Layers 9–12 active) and differential learning rates, Transformer E2E
FineTune is the sole architecture reversing text negative
transfer into positive gains, securing global peaks in both
AUROC (0.8288) and PR-AUC (0.4373). Paired hypothesis tests across 20 matched random seeds confirm that the
AUROC gain of end-to-end fine-tuning over static early fusion is highly statistically significant (mean AUROC 0.8288
vs. 0.8177; Paired t-test t = 4.89, p < 0.001; Wilcoxon
p < 0.001). This provides strong empirical evidence that
end-to-end backpropagation prevents the text representation
from being overshadowed by dense temporal dynamics, enabling the language model to better align textual risk cues
with structured physiological trajectories.
