S4.4
Modal Ablation and Vitals Collapse
Feature ablation displays strong asymmetries across modalities. Relying exclusively on 48-hour vital signs (LSTM
Base (Only Vitals)) precipitates catastrophic collapse: AUROC plummets to 0.6232 and PR-AUC crashes
to 0.1387 (only marginally above the ∼10.5% prevalence
baseline), yielding an F1 of only 0.2213. This demonstrates the inherent insufficiency of unimodal physiological
surveillance: immediate vitals capture transient acute acuity,
whereas chronic comorbidities and systemic operational friction primarily govern 30-day outcomes. Conversely, static demographics and coding alone (Only Static & Codes)
sustain an AUROC of 0.8227 and PR-AUC of 0.4294
(|∆prob| = 0.1437), establishing patient baseline and operational pressures as basic priors, with dynamic vitals
(|∆prob| = 0.1014) providing acute trajectory corrections.
S5
Mechanistic Attribution and Case Study
S5.1
Multimodal Attribution: Channels,
Dynamics, and Operations
Integrated Gradients (IG) and attention analyses uncover collaborative mechanisms throughout modalities (Figure S2).
First, regarding vital sign dynamics, Heart Rate (32.0%) and
Temperature (22.2%) account for over half of physiological IG attribution, reflecting cardiovascular reserve compensation and occult infection as primary discharge stability determinants. Blood glucose (13.7%), SBP (12.5%), and
SpO2 (10.3%) supply secondary warnings against unmitigated glycemic swings and tissue hypoperfusion. Second,
with respect to time-based attention focus, attention concentrates heavily on initial admission (t ∈[0, 2] h, Hour 0
weight = 0.0806), showing that initial resuscitation difficulty
strongly anchors downstream readmission risk. Across the
48h trajectory, intermediate monitoring (12–36h, 42.3%)
and acute admission (0–12h, 37.9%) dominate reasoning,
while pre-discharge attention declines (36–48h, 19.7%), indicating that the model assesses stabilization effort rather
than superficial pre-discharge calm. Third, empirical findings establish the primacy of operational friction. Pre-ICU
transfer frequency (pre_icu_transfers) accounts for
28.2% of static ablation and 50.9% of continuous feature IG
attribution, dominating all covariates. Ward turnover pressure (icu_speedup_los) contributes 9.6% of ablation
and 20.1% of continuous IG, proving that bed-saturationdriven premature discharge elevates hidden deterioration
risks, alongside surgical count (surg_count) and gap.
S5.2
Typical Clinical Case Vignette
A 68-year-old patient admitted with respiratory failure
achieved stable vitals after 48 hours in the ICU (normal BP and HR). Conventional heuristics mirroring vitalsonly logic would categorize the patient as fully ready
for discharge. However, our CDSS detected that before
ICU admission, the patient spent over 16 hours boarding
in the emergency department and underwent two intrahospital transfers (pre_icu_transfers elevated); furthermore, the patient’s unit was under extreme bed strain
(icu_speedup_los notably positive). Synthesizing multimodal evidence, the CDSS triggered an elevated-risk alert
for handoff friction and metabolic instability, prompting the
intensivist to extend observation by 24 hours and recheck
blood gases, successfully avoiding premature discharge and
subsequent readmission.
S6
Conclusion
Synthesizing system development and 20 experimental runs,
we highlight four engineering lessons for actual clinical AI
adoption. First, we recognize the limits of vitals-only monitoring: the catastrophic failure of Only Vitals (F1 =
0.2213) proves that immediate telemetry reflects transient
acuity rather than medium-term prognosis, mandating holistic cross-modal modeling. Second, mitigating text template
noise is critical; because inpatient records are heavily contaminated with administrative boilerplate, layer-wise parameter freezing and differential learning rates are required to
avoid text negative transfer. Third, operational context acts
as an endogenous risk: pre-ICU transfer friction and turnover

A
Cohort Selection and Flow Diagram
S1.1
Study Population and Cohort Derivation
Protocol
This study derives its analytical cohort from the MIMICIII v1.4 (Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care III)
database (Johnson et al. 2016), which comprises comprehensive clinical records from all intensive care admissions
at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (N = 61, 532 ICU
stays across 46, 520 unique patients).
In contrast to conventional benchmark studies that apply
post-hoc demographic exclusions (e.g., arbitrarily dropping
pediatric/neonatal admissions or short stays), our study retains all real-world ICU care units (including MICU, CSRU,
CCU, SICU, TSICU, and NICU) to preserve clinical generalizability. The end-to-end cohort derivation protocol is
illustrated in Figure S3.
S1.2
Clinical Endpoint (Ground Truth) Definition
The primary target outcome is 30-Day Unplanned ICU
Readmission. In critical care environments, patients frequently transfer between emergency departments, surgical
suites, and step-down units. A positive binary ground truth
label (Y = 1) is rigorously assigned if either of the following
conditions holds:
1. Cross-Admission Readmission (Condition A): The
identical patient (indexed by ‘SUBJECT_ID‘) is discharged from the hospital and subsequently readmitted to
an ICU under a distinct hospital admission (‘HADM_ID‘),
where timestamps satisfy:
INTIMEnext > OUTTIMEcurrent
∧
INTIMEnext ≤OUTTIMEcurrent + 30 days
(S3)
2. Within-Admission
Bounce-Back
(Condition
B):
Within the same hospital encounter (‘HADM_ID‘), the
patient is transferred out of the ICU to a general or stepdown ward, acutely deteriorates, and is readmitted to an
ICU (INTIME > OUTTIME).
Competing Risk Censoring: In-hospital mortality represents a terminal competing risk that precludes future postdischarge readmission. Patients who expired during their hospital stay (HOSPITAL_EXPIRE_FLAG = 1) are censored
with Y = 0. In our final cohort of N = 20, 000 stays, exactly 2, 000 patients (10.00%) experienced 30-day readmission, yielding a natural class imbalance ratio of 1 : 9. During
training, this imbalance is calibrated via an inverse positive
loss weight wpos = Nneg/Npos ≈8.97.
B
MIMIC-III Data Distribution and Baseline
Characteristics
Table S2 details the baseline clinical, demographic, operational, and physiological characteristics across the entire
cohort (N = 20, 000), stratified by 30-day ICU readmission
status (Y = 1 vs. Y = 0). Continuous variables are reported
as Mean ± SD (Median) with hypothesis testing via twosided Mann-Whitney U tests, while categorical variables are
reported as N (%) with Pearson’s χ2 test of independence.
C
Multi-Agent Clinical Prompt
Specifications
The distillation framework deploys a coordinated 3-tier hierarchical agent structure built on Llama-3.1 (via Ollama
local inference). The prompt templates and system instructions for all three agent tiers are given below.
S3.1

Clinical Domain
Risk Task
Rule Specification
Cardiovascular
Readmission
[Readmission Rule]: In post-CABG or post-valve surgery patients, the emergence of new-onset atrial
fibrillation with rapid ventricular response represents an acute readmission hazard even if pharmacological or
electrical cardioversion achieved transient sinus rhythm.
Cardiovascular
Mortality
[Mortality Rule]: In acute myocardial infarction complicated by cardiogenic shock, persistent requirement
for two or more concurrent vasoactive infusions (e.g., Norepinephrine + Epinephrine) indicates extreme inhospital mortality regardless of baseline LVEF.
Respiratory
Readmission
[Readmission Rule]: If a patient was extubated within 24 hours prior to ICU discharge but presents
residual tachypnea (RR > 24) or requires escalating high-flow nasal cannula/BiPAP requirements, assign an
elevated readmission risk.
Respiratory
Mortality
[Mortality Rule]: If a patient treated for acute respiratory distress exhibits documented bilateral radiographic clearance and stable oxygenation on minimal supplemental oxygen (FiO2 < 35%), do not score high
mortality risk solely based on initial intubation status.
Neurology
Mortality
[Mortality Rule]: When physical examination satisfies brain death criteria or presents profound hypoxicischemic encephalopathy with absent brainstem reflexes, assign maximum mortality risk regardless of hemodynamic stability.
Neurology
Readmission
[Readmission Rule]: Residual delirium, agitation, or confusion without acute focal neurological deficits
increases nursing care friction but does not warrant elevated ICU readmission risk unless complicated by imminent
airway compromise.
Infectious / Sepsis
Readmission
[Readmission Rule]: Septic patients completing antibiotic therapy with normalized WBC/procalcitonin
but persistent unexplained fever spikes must not be discharged without negative repeat blood cultures; elevate
readmission risk.
Renal / Fluids
Readmission
[Readmission Rule]: Acute kidney injury resolving with spontaneous diuresis can only be designated as
low readmission risk if serum creatinine has stabilized or trended downward for at least 48 consecutive hours
prior to transfer.
Discharge Flow
Readmission
[Readmission Rule]: An elevated ICU readmission risk should be downgraded if pending laboratory
abnormalities have been formally documented as clinically resolved and stable prior to signing final ward transfer
orders.
Goals of Care
Readmission
[Readmission Rule]: Do not predict elevated ICU readmission risk if remaining clinical complexity is
driven by transitions to palliative comfort care, family DNR/DNI execution, or hospice placement rather than
acute organ failure.

sample_chunks.text_content:
RADIOLOGY GUIDELINE-DERIVED DECISION GRAPH FOR
EFFICIENT CLINICAL DECISION SUPPORT
Xuewen Zhou, Zhen Chen†
Department of Data Science and Artificial Intelligence, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University
ABSTRACT
Radiological risk stratification and management planning are
essential downstream tasks in medical imaging. Automating
these tasks is challenging because clinical guideline criteria are distributed across prose, tables, and cross-referenced
definitions.
We present Guideline-derived Decision Graph
(GDGraph), a framework that decouples guideline compilation from case evaluation. During compilation, a large language model partitions guidelines into section-based chunks,
extracts local decision subgraphs with linked definitions,
and aggregates related branches into an executable decision
graph. During inference, a fast System One model answers
localized clinical questions while deterministic traversal resolves Boolean logic, turning opaque single-pass predictions
into a traceable decision path without task-specific training.
Across 347 cases spanning renal cyst, adnexal mass,
and thyroid nodule guidelines, GDGraph improves System
One accuracy from 57.3% to 90.8%, outperforming retrievalaugmented GPT-4o (80.1%) and graph-guided GPT-4o with
chain-of-thought (82.7%) at substantially lower latency and
cost. The source code will be available.
Index Terms— Clinical guidelines, decision graphs, radiological decision support, System One models
1. INTRODUCTION
Risk stratification and management planning are essential
downstream tasks in medical imaging that connect radiological findings to clinical care [1]. Clinical guidelines standardize these decisions across tasks such as renal cyst management [2], adnexal mass assessment [3], and thyroid nodule
stratification [4], where final recommendations follow from
explicit, discrete decision criteria. Automating these tasks
therefore requires systematically following the interdependent decision steps specified in each guideline, progressing
from case-specific findings through successive criteria to a
final category or recommendation.
Pretrained language models can process free-text clinical reports and imaging findings directly through prompting
without task-specific training [5, 6], yet have been shown to
frequently deviate from established diagnostic guidelines [7].
†Corresponding author.
Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting helps these models with
multi-step clinical problems by eliciting reasoning steps in
text before a conclusion [8]. In guideline-based risk stratification and management, clinical criteria and conditional rules
also provide a structured basis for decomposing the overall
task into a series of localized decisions, such as verifying a
specific imaging feature or comparing a measurement against
a threshold. System One models such as Jev [9] offer a suitable interface for these localized decisions by directly scoring discrete candidate options without generating intermediate text . Thus, the primary challenge is to organize these local
judgments into an explicit decision process that preserves the
guideline’s conditional dependencies and yields a traceable
outcome for high-stakes decisions [10].
Existing clinical frameworks incorporate guideline knowledge in different ways. For a given patient case, retrievalaugmented generation (RAG) systems [11] such as accGPT
[12] retrieve relevant medical passages for the language
model to interpret during response generation. CPGPrompt
[13] converts segmented guideline text into decision trees
for stepwise evaluation, with its reported workflow relying
on manual selection of relevant text sections and manual
validation of the generated trees. Such decision structures
could harness the capabilities and efficiency of System One
language models to support practical applications in clinical decision-making.
However, automatic construction of
these structures from raw guideline documents remains challenging because it requires integrating tabulated criteria and
thresholds with terminology definitions and exception rules
distributed across the document.
To address this, we present Guideline-derived Decision
Graph (GDGraph), an automated framework that compiles
raw clinical guidelines into executable decision graphs for
fast, traceable System One inference (Fig. 1).
By decoupling offline LLM-based guideline structuring from online
deterministic traversal, GDGraph reduces multi-step classification to localized node-level judgments while recording an
explicit decision trace. Across 347 radiology cases spanning
three guidelines, GDGraph raises System One accuracy from
57.3% to 90.8%, outperforming unstructured RAG (80.1%)
and graph-guided GPT-4o with CoT (82.7%) at substantially
lower latency and cost. These results suggest the practical
value of GDGraph for clinical decision support.

2. METHODOLOGY
2.1. Overview
Fig. 1 illustrates the proposed Guideline-derived Decision
Graph (GDGraph) framework, which decouples offline guideline compilation from online case evaluation. In the offline
stage (Fig. 1(a); Algorithm 1), given a clinical practice guideline D containing narrative text, figures, and tables, an LLMbased pipeline partitions D into m section-based chunks
{Ci}m
i=1, extracts local subgraphs {Gi}m
i=1 grounded in a
global definition memory M via Term Frequency–Inverse
Document Frequency (TF-IDF) retrieval [14, 15], and aggregates related branches across sections into a unified decision
graph G = (S, A, E, Y).
In the online stage (Fig. 1(b)),
given the imaging findings of a clinical case X, a fast System One model answers localized questions at active nodes
using attached definitions, while deterministic traversal resolves Boolean transitions along the selected path to reach a
traceable category or management decision.
2.2. Guideline-derived Decision Graph
Graph Representation. The decision graph G = (S, A, E, Y)
comprises clinical states S (clinical contexts or intermediate
conclusions, with entry states S0 ⊂S), atomic conditions
A, directed transition rules E, and candidate outcomes Y (diagnostic categories or management actions). Each state and
outcome carries a clinical label, a source-derived definition,
and supporting text spans from D. Each atomic condition
a ∈A represents a single traceable criterion, written as
a = (τa, κa, Da), where τa specifies the clinical feature and
its anatomical or temporal scope (e.g., lesion diameter), κa
denotes the comparison operator and value (e.g., < 10 cm or
presence/absence), and Da links to the corresponding definitions in M. Deterministic templates render each a and its
referenced definitions Da into a self-contained question for
model evaluation.
Directed rules e ∈E take the form e = (se, ϕe, Te, πe)
and connect source states to targets through Boolean combinations of atomic conditions. Here, se ∈S is the prerequisite
state, ϕe is a logical expression over A using standard operators (∧, ∨, ¬, and AtLeastk), Te ⊆S ∪Y denotes the target
states or outcomes, and πe indicates whether the rule directly
determines, supports, or rules out Te. For instance, requiring both imaging pattern P and diameter below 10 cm for the
same lesion is formulated as ϕe = aP ∧a<10.
Section-Based Chunking and Local Subgraph Generation. We split D by document sections into chunks C =
{C1, . . . , Cm} while keeping tables and footnotes intact. An
LLM scans all chunks to build a global definition memory M
of clinical terms, aliases, and definitions. For each chunk Ci,
we retrieve relevant definitions di ⊂M via TF-IDF similarity while keeping explicitly cited definitions, and prompt the
LLM to extract states Si, atomic conditions Ai, and rules Ei
into a local subgraph Gi. Named imaging patterns are kept
as single conditions linked to M, additional criteria such as
numerical thresholds are separated into individual conditions,
and negative findings are denoted by logical negation (¬).
Cross-Branch Aggregation. To connect related rules across
sections, local subgraphs {Gi}m
i=1 are merged into a unified
graph G. Guided by TF-IDF similarity, an LLM groups subgraphs sharing clinical features or exceptions into potentially
overlapping sets B = {B1, . . . , BL}, processed sequentially
on the latest graph. Within each group Bl, the LLM uses the
source text and definitions dl to merge nodes that share identical clinical meaning and judgment criteria, while keeping

2.3. Graph-Guided Selection
Prior to evaluation, an LLM maps source-supported conclusions in S ∪Y, including intermediate states and terminal outcomes, to the target task’s standardized answer options, as illustrated in Fig. 1(b). During online inference, traversal starts
at S0. At each active state, the System One model answers the
questions of outgoing atomic conditions based on the reported
imaging findings and attached definitions Da, while program
logic evaluates ϕe to advance along satisfied branches. The
final prediction is derived from the task-relevant conclusions
reached during traversal, with the clinical case interpreted
against static option definitions.
The traversal log records
each evaluated question and its answer, preserving the traversed edges as a traceable decision path.
3. EXPERIMENTS
3.1. Experimental Setup
Dataset and Tasks. We evaluate GDGraph on 347 text-based
radiology cases curated from PMC-Patients-V2 [16] and
PubMed Central case reports across three clinical guidelines
(Table 1). Cases were screened for guideline-relevant imaging findings and clinical context. Reference labels were taken
from explicit source labels or derived by applying guideline
criteria to the reported findings. Case descriptions were reformulated using GPT-6.1-sol to remove explicit diagnostic
labels and reduce the risk of answer leakage. CUA evaluates

Implementation and Baselines. Decision graphs are constructed offline using GPT-6-Luna with low reasoning effort,
processing extracted text alongside PDF page images to preserve table structures and footnotes. For online evaluation,
we use the System One model Jev (v1.13.0) [9] and GPT4o across six settings: (1) baselines without retrieval or GDGraph (Direct Jev, Direct GPT-4o, and GPT-4o CoT), which
receive only the clinical case, candidate options, and option
definitions; (2) retrieval-augmented generation (RAG+GPT4o CoT), where GPT-4o generates three search queries per
case and MedCPT [17] retrieves the top-K (K = 5) guideline
chunks per query for CoT reasoning; and (3) graph-guided inference (GDGraph+Jev and GDGraph+GPT-4o CoT), which

Evaluation Metrics. For graph quality (Table 2), we manually verify node precision (proportion of atomic conditions
with source-supported questions and definitions) and rule precision (proportion of extracted transition rules supported by
the source guideline).
For decision performance and efficiency, we report case accuracy (Acc.), weighted F1 (WF1),
and Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) [18], alongside
mean online API time and cost per case.
3.2. Graph Fidelity and Comparison with Retrieval
In the source-based review (Table 2), the constructed graphs

3.3. System One Performance and Inference Efficiency
We next evaluate whether pairing GDGraph with the System
One model Jev improves decision accuracy (Table 3) and
compare its online inference efficiency against the GPT-4o
baselines (Fig. 2). Given only the case content, the candidate
options, and their definitions (Direct Jev), Jev reaches 57.3%
overall accuracy (35.0% on K-TIRADS). When the same
cases are evaluated using GDGraph (GDGraph+Jev), performance improves across all three tasks, reaching 90.8% overall
accuracy and achieving the highest Acc., WF1, and MCC in
each guideline. Additionally, GDGraph+Jev achieves higher
accuracy than both GDGraph+GPT-4o CoT (82.7%) and
RAG+GPT-4o CoT (80.1%), while requiring 0.79–1.62 s per
case in online API time (vs. 6.16–7.15 s for RAG+GPT-4o
CoT and 17.10–34.97 s for GDGraph+GPT-4o CoT) and
0.56–1.07 × 10−3 USD per case in API cost (Fig. 2). These
results indicate that organizing guidelines into localized node
judgments and explicit rules enables the System One model
to resolve multi-condition criteria with low online inference
latency and cost.
3.4. Error Analysis
Among the remaining errors, we identify two recurring patterns that highlight the main limitations of GDGraph-guided
inference. In 11 K-TIRADS cases, “ill-defined margins” or
“irregular shape” were interpreted as “irregular margins,” activating a higher-risk branch because node definitions did not
explicitly contrast these terms. In three O-RADS cases, errors arose when mapping qualitative vascularity descriptions
(e.g., moderate flow) to node-level criteria. These observations highlight the importance of normalizing radiological descriptions and aligning imaging concepts with model representations across varied reports.
4. CONCLUSION
We proposed GDGraph, a framework that converts radiology
guidelines into executable decision graphs for risk stratification and management planning. During compilation, an LLM
constructs the graph through section-based chunking, local
subgraph extraction, and cross-branch aggregation. During
inference, the System One model answers localized questions
along the graph, yielding a traceable decision path. Experiments on three guidelines show that GDGraph+Jev achieves
higher accuracy than CoT-based GPT-4o baselines at lower
latency and cost, indicating its practical value for auditable
clinical decision support.

DocTalk: Enhancing Medical Knowledge Retrieval via Fine-tuned Large 
Language Models with Chain-of-Thought Reasoning for Robust Clinical 
Decision Support 
Asad Gohar, Md Ariful Islam Mozumder, Moon-Il Joo, Hee-Cheol Kim 
Institute of Digital Anti-Aging HealthCare, Inje University, Gimhae 50834, Republic of 
Korea; 
Corresponding Author: heeki@inje.ac.kr 
 
Abstract:- 
Objective: The rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs) in healthcare has opened new possibilities 
for AI-assisted clinical decision-making; however, safe and effective deployment remains challenging becasue of 
hallucination and domain misalignment. This study introduces DocTalk, a doctor-assistive question-answering 
(QA) system designed to generate concise, chart-grounded responses from de-identified discharge summaries. 
Methods: We developed a high-fidelity data generation pipeline that produces 500 clinically relevant QA pairs 
through sentence-level decomposition, chain-of-thought-guided question formulation, and expert review. Six 
open-source LLMs, including three general-purpose and three biomedical models, were evaluated before and after 
parameter-efficient instruction tuning using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA). The framework integrates prompt 
engineering, in-context learning, and medically aligned evaluation to support factual and interpretable responses. 
Results: On DocTalk-QA, instruction tuning produced consistent improvements across lexical, semantic, and 
clinical fidelity metrics. The best-performing tuned model, Llama-3-Med42-8B, achieved ROUGE-L=0.40, 
BERTScore-F1=0.76, and UMLS-F1=0.49. To examine external generalization beyond the DocTalk-QA dataset, 
the two best-performing models, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Llama-3-Med42-8B, were evaluated on PubMedQA 
before and after instruction tuning. Accuracy improved from 0.931 to 0.977 for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and from 
0.935 to 0.943 for Llama-3-Med42-8B. 
Conclusion: DocTalk was deployed as a secure web-based platform for interactive EHR querying. These findings 
suggest that clinically grounded instruction tuning can improve medical QA performance and support practical 
clinical decision support. 
Keywords: DocTalk, Chain-of-thought, Clinical decision support, Large language model, Prompt engineering, 
In-context learning 
1. Introduction 
In recent era, a significant shift towards digital systems for managing medical systems has been observed. The 
electronic health records (EHRs) are most important, which have information of patient’s medical history, 
including diagnosis, medications, procedures, laboratory test results, and follow-up plans [1]. However, there are 
vast amount of unstructured medical data, posing challenges for efficient information extraction and using it for 
the right purpose. These types of documents are generated using complex language, which is difficult to 
understand for the patients. Therefore, this problem can be solved by generative artificial intelligence (AI) 
techniques, particularly large language models (LLMs), by automatic retrieval of structured clinical information 
from unstructured medical reports [2-5]. Recent LLMs have made substantial advancements in medicine,

demonstrating admirable performance in answering medical questions [6-8]. 
The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in healthcare has transformed personal healthcare, enabling 
advancements in diagnostic accuracy [9], treatment personalization [10], [11], and patient management [12-15]. 
At the core of this transformation are LLMs, which show exceptional abilities in understanding and generating 
human-like text. Recently, in healthcare sector, it has become more capable at a growing range of language tasks, 
which inherently constitute a powerful tool that expands equitable to medical knowledge [16]. 
LLMs are getting much better across a diverse spectrum of linguistic tasks, and they inherently represent medical 
information more accessible to everyone. Because of this, people are getting interested in using AI tools based on 
LLMs in different medical tasks. Such applications encompass diagnosis assistance, the automation of 
administrative functions, and even helping healthcare professionals take notes. Furthermore, before we can use 
LLMs in real medical situations, these models need to be checked to make sure they are correct, fair, and safe for 
patients [17-19]. Nevertheless, prior to the development of LLMs for real medical situations, models designated 
for healthcare integration must unequivocally demonstrate accuracy, impartiality, and patient safety. A 
foundational step in the successful evolution of healthcare-specific LLMs necessitates their rigorous evaluation 
against established medical benchmarks. This evaluation process requires the assessment of performance on 
multiple-choice questions from an extensive array of sources to determine their accuracy on various tasks and 
medical topics [20-22]. Much of the existing research has focused on enhancing LLM-based question-answering 
(QA) capabilities, which are pivotal for delivering timely and accurate responses to patient inquiries. Datasets and 
benchmarks such as MedQA [23, 24], emrQA [25], MedMCQA [26], PubMedQA [27], and the MMLU [28] have 
been developed to evaluate the QA abilities of LLMs in healthcare. 
There are several research studies primarily focused on clinical QA. Systems designed to summarize information 
for patients, like discharge instructions or brief hospital summaries, are easy for the public to understand. However, 
they are not effective at answering the detailed questions clinicians require, potentially causing important 
information to be missed [27]. Moreover, QA systems tested with exam-style questions often use multiple-choice 
answers or assess explanation quality. These tests typically do not mimic real EHR environments and are often 
limited to a few medical fields [29]. LLMs for clinical use, trained with specific instructions, perform well on 
general medical tasks. However, they may encounter difficulties with out-of-distribution (OOD) clinical notes that 
vary across institutions or templating formats, and must meet strict safety and bias standards [30]. Nevertheless, 
in recent studies, LLMs evaluated on medical benchmarks showed significant improvement in performance after 
instruction-tuning or fine-tuning based on few-shot and chain-of-thought (CoT) strategic prompting techniques 
[31-33]. The models are trained using these techniques to better understand instruction like humans, and produce 
truthful reasoning in a step-by-step thinking process [34-36]. Therefore, performance optimization of pretrained 
LLMs can achieve state-of-the-art (SOTA) results on medical QA benchmarks with some specific fine-tuning 
techniques. 
In this study, we present the DocTalk prompting platform, a doctor-assistive QA system that is directly based on 
actual and de-identified discharge and EHR documentation. We processed the clinical-oriented data by splitting 
the notes into atomic sentences, writing doctor-style questions with a brief CoT prompt. To carry out this analysis, 
we used six LLMs (i.e., 3 general and 3 biomedical) for evaluation, and each of them is adapted with low-rank

adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning technique [37]. DocTalk aims to relieve the burden on physicians, improve 
accuracy, and able to scale to non-homogeneous real-world environments by decreasing the amount of time 
clinicians spend searching charts, standardizing the quality of answers, and basing the results on existing clinical 
ontologies. The proposed clinical-assistive QA system can return concise and chart-grounded answers from real 
discharge/EHR notes, optimized for clinical decision support. 
2. Related Works 
The application of LLMs in healthcare has rapidly emerged as a central component in modern healthcare AI 
systems, particularly for clinical QA, information retrieval, and decision support [38-40]. Prior research in this 
area can be broadly categorized into five streams: 1) general LLM applications in healthcare, 2) clinical QA over 
EHR narratives, 3) instruction-tuned medical LLMs, 4) prompting and parameter-efficient adaptation strategies, 
and 5) biomedical QA benchmarks and foundation models. 
 
2.1. LLMs in Healthcare 
Recently, it has been analyzed that LLMs can generate coherent, context-aware, and clinical-style text, making 
them attractive for healthcare applications. Early studies like GPT-4 and its successors showed strong performance 
across diverse medical reasoning tasks, including diagnosis-related questions, treatment planning, and clinical 
documentation, exceeding human-level performance on standardized benchmarks [41]. However, subsequent 
analysis revealed important limitations, including skewed memorization effects, factual inconsistency, and 
vulnerability to distributional shifts in clinical data [42]. To address these challenges, researchers have explored 
domain-specific pretraining on EHRs. Models trained directly on longitudinal clinical data have demonstrated 
improved contextual understanding of patient histories and procedural timelines compared to general-purpose 
LLMs [43]. Despite these advances, deploying LLMs in real-world clinical settings remains difficult due to safety 
concerns, interpretability requirements, and the highly heterogeneous nature of EHR documentation across 
institutions. 
 
2.2. Clinical Question Answering over EHR Narratives 
Clinical QA over EHR narratives differs fundamentally from exam-style or patient-facing QA tasks. Early datasets 
such as emrQA introduced large-scale question-answer pairs derived from electronic medical records, enabling 
research on extracting answers from unstructured clinical notes [44]. Traditional sequence models, including 
LSTM-based architectures, were initially applied to these tasks but struggled with long-context reasoning and 
document-level coherence [45]. In [46], they mentioned that recent approaches have focused on retrievalaugmented and experience-based QA systems, which influence past patient records to answer discharge-related 
questions. Moreover, many existing QA systems prioritize patient discharge summarization rather than clinicianoriented decision support, potentially omitting nuanced medical details required by healthcare professionals. 
 
2.3. Instruction-Tuned Clinical LLM 
In medical tasks, instruction-tuning has emerged as a powerful strategy for adapting LLMs. Models like Med-

PaLM demonstrated that targeted instruction fine-tuning can significantly enhance medical reasoning, diagnostic 
accuracy, and explanation quality [47]. The following work showed that LLMs encode substantial latent clinical 
knowledge even before fine-tuning, which can be unlocked through carefully designed instructions and domainspecific supervision [35]. More recent medical LLMs, such as LlamaCare and other healthcare-specialized 
variants, have explored large-scale instruction tuning for medical knowledge sharing and clinician assistance [48]. 
Although these models perform well on curated benchmarks, they often rely on exam-style data and may not 
generalize better to real-world EHR narratives. 
 
2.4. Prompting Strategies and Parameter-Efficient Adaptation 
Prompting-based technique, which offers an alternative to fine-tuning by guiding model behavior through 
structured inputs. In LLMs, CoT prompting has been shown to produce step-by-step reasoning, improving 
performance on complex tasks, including medical QA [49]. Self-consistency and multi-sample reasoning further 
enhance reliability by aggregating multiple reasoning paths [50]. Concurrently, parameter-efficient fine-tuning 
techniques such as Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) enable efficient specialization of large models by updating only 
a small subset of parameters [51, 52]. Therefore, these techniques significantly reduce computational overhead 
while preserving model performance. 
 
2.5. LLMs in Biomedical Question Answering 
Biomedical QA benchmarks have played a crucial role in evaluating language understanding and reasoning in 
medical contexts. Foundational models, such as BERT, GPT, and T5, established transfer learning paradigms that 
were later extended to biomedical text through domain-adaptive pretraining [53-55]. Large open-source models, 
including OPT, BLOOM, PaLM, and LLaMA, further expanded the scale and accessibility of foundation models 
for biomedical research [56-59]. Recently, the researchers focused on generalist biomedical AI systems capable 
of reasoning across clinical, molecular, and literature-based tasks [60]. Models such as BioMistral have shown 
improved performance on biomedical language tasks through targeted pretraining on medical corpora [61]. 
In contrast to prior research works, our study bridges the gap between benchmark-driven biomedical QA and realworld clinical decision support. By constructing a clinician-verified QA dataset directly from de-identified EHR 
discharge summaries and integrating CoT reasoning with parameter-efficient instruction tuning, our proposed 
system, DocTalk-QA, explicitly targets the needs of healthcare professionals. Unlike exam-style QA or patientoriented summarization systems, our approach emphasizes concise, chart-grounded answers that preserve clinical 
accuracy and interpretability. 
3. Materials and Methods 
The overall workflow of the proposed DocTalk framework is illustrated in Figure 1. The framework consists of 
five major components: construction of the DocTalk-QA dataset from de-identified discharge/EHR notes, unified 
prompting and hallucination-mitigation strategies, LoRA-based instruction tuning of general-purpose and 
biomedical LLMs, internal and external evaluation using DocTalk-QA and PubMedQA, and final deployment 
through a secure DocTalk web platform. This design enables the system to generate concise, chart-grounded 
answers while supporting both in-domain clinical QA evaluation and out-of-domain biomedical benchmark

Figure 1: Overall workflow of the DocTalk doctor-assistive question-answering framework. 
3.1. Datasets and Tasks 
In this study, two different datasets were utilized for the development and evaluation of our DocTalk QA system. 
MIMIC-IV [62], which is a publicly available de-identified electronic health record (EHR) dataset compiled by 
the Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (BIDMC) in Boston, in collaboration with the Massachusetts Institute 
of Technology (MIT) laboratory for computational physiology. PubMedQA [63] is a biomedical QA dataset that 
is to answer research questions by reasoning over the corresponding abstract as context. We used PubMedQA as 
an external benchmark to test the generalization of our model on biomedical research questioning tasks. This 
allowed us to compare model performance across different document types and reasoning settings. 
3.2. Data Pre-processing and Tokenization 
All the raw discharge summaries downloaded from the MIMIC-IV database were pre-processed to ensure textual 
consistency, clinical accuracy, and removal of irrelevant artifacts. The workflow of data pre-processing consists 
of format standardization, artifact removal, and medical term normalization, which can be expressed as:

The raw text was standardized to correct irregular text structures, restore line breaks between sections, and unify 
inconsistent spacing. After standardizing the raw text, irrelevant metadata were eliminated to retain only the 
clinically meaningful text required for QA generation. Finally, we applied the normalization technique to maintain 
consistency of medical terminology across the dataset. 
Furthermore, tokenization was performed on the normalized data to convert it into tokens using a biomedicalspecific tokenizer. We removed rare or noisy words based on a frequency threshold to ensure that only clinical 
terms were retained. The resulting vocabulary 𝑉 was defined as: 
 𝑉= {𝑡𝑜𝑘𝑒𝑛|𝑡𝑜𝑘𝑒𝑛∈𝑚𝑒𝑑𝑖𝑐𝑎𝑙𝑐𝑜𝑟𝑝𝑢𝑠, 𝑓𝑟𝑒𝑞𝑢𝑒𝑛𝑐𝑦(𝑡𝑜𝑘𝑒𝑛) ≥𝑡ℎ𝑟𝑒𝑠ℎ𝑜𝑙𝑑} (2) 
In addition, special tokens such as <unk>, <pad>, and <eos> were added to manage unknown words and sequence 
boundaries. This tokenization process prepared the text for model training while preserving the medical meaning 
of important terms and improving computational efficiency. 
3.3. DocTalk-QA Dataset from MIMIC-IV 
We constructed a high-quality clinician-style QA dataset using the pre-processed text generated from discharge 
summaries of the MIMIC-IV database. A representative discharge summary and CoT prompting technique is 
shown in Figure 2, illustrating the type of rich narrative content used for question generation. To create the dataset, 
we followed a multiple-step, CoT-assisted prompting pipeline (Figure 3), designed to enforce stepwise clinical 
reasoning during both question generation and answer formulation. Each discharge summary was first segmented 
into semantically coherent sentences to maintain contextual integrity. We used Meta’s Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct 
model for this task. This particular model was selected based on its linguistic adherence to clinical phrasing and 
section conventions in discharge notes, its independence of instruction on schema-constrained outputs, and its 
ability to handle context (i.e., capability of 128K tokens). Compared to traditional sentence splitters such as NLTK, 
the LLM-based method demonstrated higher accuracy, especially in handling irregular formatting and 
placeholders introduced during anonymization. To ensure integrity, the LLM was instructed to preserve original 
sentence structures, and outputs were string-matched against the source for verification. Then, using prompt 
engineering, the model generated clinically relevant questions aligned with the reasoning style of healthcare 
professionals. 
The QA pairs covered six major clinical categories, which include diagnosis (17.8%), medications (18.6%), 
procedures and tests (20.4%), treatment and hospital course (21.9%), symptoms and complications (16.3%), and 
post-discharge care and follow-up (5.0%). To ensure reliability and clinical safety, each QA pair was reviewed by 
a licensed medical expert. They were assessed for clinical correctness, answer completeness, safety (i.e., absence 
of misleading or potentially harmful information), and alignment with real-world clinician information needs. 
Moreover, we applied ICD-10 coding checks for diagnostic accuracy and UMLS-based validation to confirm 
biomedical concept grounding. This quality assurance process produced a curated set of 500 high-quality QA pairs, 
each pair embeds traceable CoT reasoning steps, facilitating interpretability and structured evaluation. The final 
dataset was formatted in JSON/JSONL, with each entry structured as a triplet (question, context, answer), ready 
for model training and inference tasks.

3.4. Dataset Overview 
In total, 500 QA pairs were developed using the CoT-assisted pipeline, each grounded in real-world clinical 
documents and refined through expert verification. PubMedQA was not used for dataset creation or training; it 
was reserved solely as an external benchmark to evaluate generalization on both patient-focused and literaturebased clinical reasoning tasks. Figure 4 shows the examples of the resulting QA pairs generated from the MIMICIV dataset. 
Figure 4: Example of QA pairs in the DocTalk-QA dataset. 
3.5. Pretrained LLMs and Optimization 
We employed six different open-source models to verify the efficacy of the strategic prompting and CoT reasoning 
on the DocTalk-QA and PubMedQA datasets. These enable us to examine domain-specific reasoning capabilities 
under consistent tuning conditions. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Llama-3-8B-Instruct, and Mistral are general-purpose 
LLMs [64,65], whereas Llama3-Med42-8B, Meditron, and BioMistral are biomedical-specialized BioLLMs 
[23,66,67]. These models were subsequently fine-tuned using LoRA [68,69], a parameter-efficient fine-tuning 
method for efficient instruction-tuning in the medical domain. This method allowed us to quickly test various 
architectures by efficiently specializing large models for medical QA without requiring the entire parameter space. 
Each model is a causal Transformer with multi-head self-attention and gated MLPs. 
We applied LoRA to all six models with the following settings: Rank (r) = 16, Alpha = 32, Dropout = 0.05, and 
Target Modules = q_proj, k_proj, v_proj, o_proj, gate_proj, up_proj, and down_proj. This ensures that clinical 
knowledge can be effectively incorporated into each model during instruction-tuning without requiring a complete 
fine-tuning of all parameters. To optimize the model, the learning rate was set to 2e-4 with a cosine decay schedule 
and a 3% warm-up to stabilize early-stage updates. A gradient accumulation of 8 was employed to simulate a 
higher batch size while preserving hardware efficiency, and the number of epochs was set to 10. To maximize the 
memory use on GPU resources, gradient checkpointing was combined with mixed precision (fp16 and bf16). The 
computation formula for LoRA can be expressed as:

3.6. Few-Shot and Chain-of-Thought Strategic Prompting 
Strategic prompting is essential to enhance the reasoning quality of LLMs and avoid hallucination by grounding 
decisions in evidence from the text. In this study, we employed strategic prompting approaches that combine CoT 
and Few-Shot techniques. These approaches present the model with examples having reasoning chains along with 
input and outputs, which guide the LLM to solve the given problem in a step-by-step manner. Our workflow is 
structured into two stages: constructing a strategy-based clinical dataset using CoT and performing model training 
using Few-Shot prompting. 
Stage 1: In the first stage, we used CoT prompting strategy to generate reasoning-aware QA pairs from preprocessed discharge summaries, shown in Figure 5 (a). This approach guided the model to simulate clinical 
reasoning processes, linking patients history, investigations, treatments, and outcomes, to produce interpretable 
and logically structured answers. The CoT design improved transparency, interpretability, and diagnostic 
consistency during dataset construction. 
Stage 2: In the second stage, a few-shot (k=2) was employed for model training to improve generalization across 
unseen clinical questions. Two concise exemplars were provided before each test item, each comprising a 
discharge summary excerpt (about 4,000-6,000 tokens), a clinician-style question, and a short, chart-grounded 
answer, shown in Figure 5 (b). Examples were sampled only from the training split, ensuring no overlap with 
development or test sets. To maintain the diversity, exemplars were chosen to reflect key clinical question types, 
which include “final diagnosis”, “dated procedures”, “medication changes with dose, route, frequency, and 
rationale”, “complications”, “microbiology findings with corresponding therapies”, and “discharge disposition or 
follow-up care”.

3.7. Evaluation Settings 
To evaluate the models during training and testing, we used LoRA-Supervised Fine-Tuning (LSFT) masked-loss 
strategy, with focus only on answer tokens. The loss function is defined as: 
 𝐿𝑆𝐹𝑇= −∑𝑙𝑜𝑔 𝑝(𝑦𝑖|𝑦<𝑖, 𝑥𝑐𝑙𝑖𝑛𝑖𝑐𝑎𝑙)
𝑖

where 𝑦 represents the sequence of answer tokens, 𝑦<𝑖 denotes the preceding token, and 𝑥𝑐𝑙𝑖𝑛𝑖𝑐𝑎𝑙 indicates 
the clinical input context. 
To evaluate the accuracy scores of the model, we used ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, ROUGE-L, and BERTScore-F1 
performance metrics to measure the textual overlap (how closely the generated answers matched the reference 
answer) [70,71]. ROUGE-1 measures unigram (word-level) overlap between prediction and reference, ROUGE2 measures biggram (two-word sequence) overlap, capturing short-range fluency, ROUGE-L measures the longest 
common subsequence (LCS) between prediction and reference, reflecting sentence-level structure, and 
BERTScore-F1 computes semantic similarity using contextual embeddings from a pre-trained BERT model, 
scoring how meaningfully the generated answer aligns with the reference. While UMLS-F1 is used to measure 
the clinical accuracy beyond the surface text similarity. These domain-specific metrics ensure that the model’s 
outputs are not only textually fluent but also clinically valid and semantically aligned with real-world medical 
knowledge. UMLS-F1 evaluates concept-level correctness by comparing predicted and reference clinical entities 
mapped to Concept Unique Identifiers (CUIs) in the Unified Medical Language System. 
4. Experimental Results 
4.1. Pretrained Model Evaluation on DocTalk-QA 
In this section, we have evaluated six widely used LLMs on the DocTalk-QA dataset to create a baseline before 
any task-specific tuning. As shown in Table 2, the comparative analysis of six different models before instruction-

We can observe two clear patterns from Table 2: first, among pretrained models, semantic similarity scores remain 
moderate (BERTScore-F1=0.66-0.69), which shows that answers are generally well-formed but not deeply 
grounded in the clinical context, and second, all baseline models did not perform well in terms of clinical fidelity 
(UMLS-F1=0.11-0.23). Therefore, these baselines require task-specific supervision, even though they can 
generate concise and coherent outputs. 
4.2. Instruction-Tuned Model Performance on DocTalk-QA 
In this section, we first fine-tuned all six LLMs using the LoRA-based instruction-tuning configuration and then 
evaluated the tuned models on the DocTalk-QA dataset, shown in Table 3. After fine-tuning, the models produced 
substantial improvements across all metrics, especially in clinical correctness scores, demonstrating the 
effectiveness of DocTalk’s structured supervision. In terms of lexical overlap, semantic similarity, and clinical 
grounding, the performance consistently increased across all models. The promising overall performance was 
achieved by bio-LLM (Llama-3-Med42-8B), which improved ROUGE-L from 0.21 to 0.40, BERTScore-F1 from 
0.67 to 0.76, and UMLS-F1 from 0.21 to 0.49. Moreover, comparable gains for general-LLMs were observed, 
+0.16 ROUGE-L, +0.06 BERTScore, and +0.24 UMLS-F1 for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and +0.17 ROUGE-L, 
+0.07 BERTScore, and +0.26 UMLS-F1 for Llama-3-8B-Instruct. At the same time, other bio-LLMs, such as 
Meditron-3-8B and BioMistral-7B, also improved considerably in ROUGE-L (+0.17 to 0.23) and UMLS-F1 
(+0.25 to 0.30). The average scores of the finetuned models improved by 0.18 for ROUGE-L, 0.09 for BERTScore, 
and 0.26 for UMLS-F1, demonstrating that the domain adaptation enhances clinical correctness more than lexical 
similarity.

4.3. Performance Evaluation on PubMedQA 
To assess whether the DocTalk instruction-tuning strategy generalizes beyond discharge-summary question 
answering, we further evaluated two representative models on the external PubMedQA benchmark. The models 
were selected based on their performance on DocTalk-QA: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, which achieved the strongest 
pretrained baseline performance, and Llama-3-Med42-8B, which achieved the best overall results after instruction 
tuning. To examine the effect of DocTalk-based adaptation, both models were evaluated on PubMedQA before 
and after instruction tuning. PubMedQA requires reasoning over biomedical research abstracts and includes 
Yes/No/Maybe answers, making it a significantly different challenge from DocTalk’s answer-only clinical format. 
Although the full benchmark includes Yes/No/Maybe responses, the confusion-matrix analysis presented here 
focuses on the binary Yes/No classification setting. The evaluation set is markedly imbalanced: [N_yes] "Yes" and 
[N_no] "No" instances (92.8% positive). A majority-class predictor that always outputs "Yes" therefore attains 
0.928 accuracy, which limits the informativeness of raw accuracy on this benchmark. We accordingly adopt the 
Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) as the primary discrimination metric, since it accounts for performance 
across both classes, and report accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 as secondary measures. Figure 6 illustrates the 
confusion matrices for the four evaluation conditions: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct baseline, Llama-3-Med42-8B 
baseline, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct instruction-tuned, and Llama-3-Med42-8B instruction-tuned. Table 4 
summarizes the corresponding classification results. 
The baseline models yielded comparable results on PubMedQA (accuracy = 0.931 for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct 
0.935 for Llama-3-Med42-8B). Both models were improved after DocTalk-based instruction tuning, but with 
dramatically different magnitude of improvement. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct showed the largest gain, improving the 
accuracy from 0.931 to 0.977, recall from 0.930 to 0.983, F1-score from 0.962 to 0.987, and MCC from 0.661 to 
0.839. This suggests that discrimination and class-balanced predictive reliability have achieved a significant 
improvement. The instruction-tuned Llama-3-Med42-8B also had an increase in performance compared to 
baseline, with accuracy increasing from 0.935 to 0.943, F1-score from 0.964 to 0.968, and MCC from 0.675 to 
0.707. Although the gain was more modest than that of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, the result confirms that DocTalkbased instruction tuning does not only improve performance on the in-domain DocTalk-QA task, but can also 
transfer positively to biomedical abstract-level reasoning.

5. Discussion 
In this study, to demonstrate the real-world applicability of our instruction-tuned biomedical QA system, we 
developed a fully functional web-based platform, DocTalk, enabling clinicians and researchers to interact with 
large language models directly using electronic health records (EHRs). The system supports secure login, patient 
report selection, and natural-language questioning, simulating real clinical workflows (Supplementary 
Information, Figure S1). Unlike most prior research that relies on simulated datasets or benchmark QA pairs 
separated from practical clinical use [22, 72-74], our work takes a grounded, data-centric approach by curating 
questions directly from authentic clinical narratives. Our methodology ensures high reliability of the original chart 
content and reflects realistic physician information needs. We contributed in three major areas. First, we 
introduced a rigorous dataset construction pipeline that generates QA pairs from atomic sentence-level 
decomposition with concise CoT prompting, followed by manual quality assurance. This careful design directly 
addresses weaknesses in existing datasets, such as BioASQ, that often lack clinical relevance, structure, or factual 
precision [73]. Second, we proposed and implemented a unified prompting strategy incorporating systemgrounding, few-shot in-context examples, and answer-only supervision, fine-tuned via LoRA. This resulted in 
significant improvements across both textual and clinical metrics. Specifically, our instruction-tuned Llama-3Med42-8B achieved performance that outstripped a strong baseline, especially on clinically meaningful measures 
like UMLS-F1. Compared with evaluation strategies that rely mainly on surface-level text similarity, our inclusion 
of clinically grounded metrics provides a more medically meaningful assessment of QA quality. Unlike models 
such as BioGPT [74] or Med-PaLM [35], which prioritize large-scale pretraining or multi-choice reasoning, 
DocTalk is optimized for generating short, precise, and chart-grounded answers, crucial for real-time clinical use. 
Third, we demonstrated that our approach is feasible in real-time settings with limited resources. The use of 
parameter-efficient tuning (LoRA) is more scalable, and our instruction tuning method is concise enough to be 
clinically relevant and suitable for point-of-care integration. Previous approaches typically focus on benchmark

sample_chunks.text_content:
scores or exam-style QA in a practical manner [35], while our pipeline focuses on interpretability, brevity, and 
chart fidelity, which are all important for real-world clinical decision support systems. 
The external PubMedQA evaluation provides further insight into the generalization capacity of the DocTalk 
instruction-tuning strategy. Both selected models achieved higher performance after instruction tuning, 
demonstrating that supervision derived from clinician-oriented discharge-summary QA can transfer beyond the 
original DocTalk-QA task. The improvement was particularly substantial for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, whose 
accuracy increased from 0.931 to 0.977, accompanied by clear gains in recall, F1-score, and MCC. Llama-3Med42-8B also improved after tuning, although by a smaller margin. These findings suggest that DocTalk-based 
adaptation strengthens biomedical reasoning in a model-dependent manner rather than producing uniform gains 
across architectures. At the same time, the results show that the best-performing model on the in-domain DocTalkQA dataset is not necessarily the best-performing model on the external PubMedQA benchmark. This distinction 
is important for clinical AI development, as strong performance on curated clinical QA should be complemented 
by cross-benchmark validation to assess whether the learned knowledge transfers effectively to broader 
biomedical reasoning tasks. 
However, our work has some limitations. First, the QA pairs used for training and evaluation originally stemmed 
mainly from discharge summaries coming from a single healthcare organization. This raises concerns about the 
generalizability of our model across different hospital systems, clinical subspecialties, and documentation styles. 
Furthermore, although our instruction-tuned model shows lower hallucinations and better factual fidelity, it makes 
errors in some complex scenarios combining multiple comorbidities or sophisticated clinical reasoning. One 
disadvantage is the model’s exclusive emphasis on single-turn question answering. Second, real-world clinical 
conversations are multi-turn, which can lead to challenges of contextual recall, follow-up queries, and reasoning 
from temporally scattered information. Adding multi-hop and dialog-based reasoning capabilities presents a 
critical avenue for future enhancements. Third, there is the fact that the existing framework is based exclusively 
on English for development and evaluation. Due to the linguistic variation within the world’s healthcare systems, 
future studies should examine cross-lingual adaptation and performance in non-English clinical data corpora. 
While out-of-distribution generalization was partially addressed, the nature of the dynamic biomedical knowledge 
requires continual refinement and validation in order to ensure further long-term robustness and relevance. 
Future iterations will focus on extending the DocTalk platform by providing advanced use cases, for example, 
summarizing patient data, generating diagnostic recommendations, or tracking temporal reports. Moving on to 
safe and effective deployment with real-world implementations, we will also need feedback from medical 
professionals and undertake prospective clinical trials at scale. 
6. Conclusion 
We present DocTalk, a clinically grounded, instruction-tuned QA system with the aim of improving chart 
comprehension and helping physicians in real-world EHR review workflows. Our methodology balances 
efficiency with medical relevance by generating high-fidelity QA pairs from de-identified discharge summaries 
and fine-tuning open-source LLMs via a lightweight LoRA-based framework. Specifically, our models, such as 
Llama-3-Med42-8B, outperform others not only on text-based metrics but also on clinically aligned metrics.

Assessment on the external PubMedQA benchmark further showed that DocTalk-based instruction tuning can 
improve biomedical reasoning beyond the original clinical QA setting, although the magnitude of transfer varies 
across model architectures. More broadly, we have also deployed our QA system as part of a web platform, a 
platform that also allows interactive clinician engagement, resulting in a system that has proven real-world useful 
and accessible. Our contributions, ranging from data generation, instruction tuning, innovation for evaluation, and 
deployment, provide a scalable solution for embedding LLMs in healthcare applications.

sample_chunks.authors: Simon A. Lee, Jiahang Sha, et al.

sample_chunks.text_content:
MedJev: Evaluating Zero-Shot System-One
Decision Making in Medicine
Simon A. Lee1, Jiahang Sha1, Moonseong Jeong1, Yunbei Pan1 and Jeffrey N. Chiang1,2
1UCLA Computational Medicine, 2UCLA Neurosurgery
System-One decision models such as Jev answer structured questions about a given state, including
option selection and probability estimation, in a single forward pass without generating text. Their speed,
low computational cost, and ability to produce calibrated probabilities make them promising for clinical
decision support. We investigate the zero-shot performance of MedJev, an open System-One model that
runs locally on a laptop, across ten medical benchmarks. Four benchmarks assess medical knowledge
and diagnosis (MedQA, USMLE, NEJM, and DiagnosisArena), while six evaluate patient-level decisions
using cohorts from MIMIC-IV (In-Hospital Mortality, Length of Stay > 7 Days, 30-Day Readmission, and
ED Admission at 2 h) and MIMIC-IV-ED (ED Triage Admission and ED Triage Disposition). We compare
MedJev against zero-shot LLM baselines, including Qwen3.5-9B, MedGemma-1.5-4B, Gemma-3-4B,
Qwen3.5-2B, and Pythia-2.8B. We also compare against published results for GPT-3.5, GPT-4, GPT-4o,
and o1 on the same benchmarks, as well as XGBoost and TF-IDF models. In the zero-shot setting, MedJev
achieves accuracies of 72.5% on MedQA, 75.4% on USMLE, and 80.1% on NEJM, with well-calibrated
confidence estimates (ECE 0.028–0.063). Its accuracy is within 2–4 percentage points of published
zero-shot GPT-4 results on MedQA and USMLE (74.7% and 78.9%, respectively) and substantially
exceeds that of GPT-3.5 (44.6% and 50.8%). On patient-level tasks, MedJev achieves an AUROC of 0.926
for In-Hospital Mortality, matching or exceeding supervised models (XGBoost 0.902), and performs
comparably on 30-Day Readmission. However, it underperforms supervised models on operational
outcomes such as ED Triage Admission (0.745 vs. 0.809). Moreover, its patient-level probability
estimates do not account for local outcome prevalence (In-Hospital Mortality ECE 0.286). To address
this limitation, we introduce a lightweight, two-parameter recalibration method that adapts predicted
probabilities to local patient populations using 50–200 labeled examples, reducing the In-Hospital
Mortality ECE to 0.007. These findings highlight the potential of open System-One models as a new
baseline for medical AI, offering a competitive zero-shot alternative to general-purpose LLMs and
EHR-specific predictive models. We release our code and evaluation harness to support future research.
Github: https://github.com/Simonlee711/MedJev
HuggingFace: https://huggingface.co/Simonlee711/MedJev
1. Introduction
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly evaluated on medical tasks, including clinical question
answering, diagnosis, and patient outcome prediction [1]. Most evaluations use generative models
that produce textual answers, which are subsequently parsed into decisions. However, many medical
prediction tasks require a structured output rather than a generated response. For example, predicting
in-hospital mortality requires estimating the probability of death given the information available at a
particular point in a patient’s hospitalization, while emergency department triage requires selecting
among possible dispositions. These tasks can be expressed as decisions over a fixed set of outcomes,
making them suitable for models that directly estimate probabilities without generating text.
System-One models provide an alternative to generative inference for such tasks. Inspired by the

sample_chunks.authors: Simon A. Lee, Jiahang Sha, et al.
sample_chunks.category: AI-Based Clinical Decision Support Systems
sample_chunks.text_content:
MedJev: Evaluating Zero-Shot System-One Decision Making in Medicine
distinction between fast and deliberative reasoning [2], System-One models directly answer structured
questions about a given state in a single forward pass. Jev [3] implements this approach through
typed requests that pair an input state, represented as text or JSON, with questions specifying
the desired output. A CHOICE request returns a probability distribution over candidate answers,
while a NOUL request estimates the probability of a binary outcome. Unlike conventional generative
evaluation, which relies on decoding and parsing model responses, this interface produces structured
probabilities directly. It therefore provides a common representation for evaluating multiple-choice
medical questions and patient-level predictions from electronic health records (EHRs).
Despite this interface, the applicability of System-One models to medical decision tasks remains
unclear. Previous evaluations of Jev have demonstrated competitive zero-shot performance across
general-purpose benchmarks [4], but medical knowledge, diagnostic reasoning, and EHR-based
prediction present different challenges. Medical knowledge benchmarks require selecting correct
answers from clinical vignettes that mimic differential diagnosis, whereas patient-level prediction
requires interpreting heterogeneous longitudinal records and estimating outcomes whose prevalence
may vary across clinical populations. Furthermore, a model that accurately ranks patients by risk
does not necessarily produce probabilities that reflect observed outcome frequencies. Evaluating
System-One models in medicine therefore requires examining both their predictive performance and
probability calibration across different task types.
In this work, we study how an open System-One model can be incorporated into a medical evaluation
pipeline. We release MedJev which builds on OpenJev [5] and run a suite of evaluations. Our
evaluation represents each benchmark as a Jev request consisting of an input state and a typed
question. Medical question-answering and diagnosis benchmarks are formulated as CHOICE requests,
while patient-level outcomes are primarily formulated as NOUL requests. For EHR-based tasks,
we construct patient states using only information available at a predefined prediction time. This
formulation allows the same inference interface to be applied across medical knowledge questions,
longitudinal patient records, and emergency department triage data.
We evaluate MedJev on ten medical benchmarks (expanding on the work of [6]) spanning medical
knowledge, differential diagnosis, and patient-specific prediction. These include MedQA [7], USMLE
[7], NEJM Case Challenges, and DiagnosisArena [8], together with six outcomes derived from MIMICIV [9] and MIMIC-IV-ED [9]. To assess the effect of System-One training, we compare MedJev against
its underlying language model and other open-weight LLMs using identical prompts and probability
readouts. We additionally consider published results from frontier LLMs and train supervised XGBoost
and TF-IDF baselines for EHR specific tasks. Beyond predictive accuracy and discrimination, we
evaluate probability calibration and examine whether lightweight post-hoc recalibration can adapt
zero-shot predictions to local outcome prevalence. We also vary the number of labeled examples
available to supervised models to characterize when task-specific training becomes preferable to
zero-shot inference.
Our results show that System-One models can serve as competitive zero-shot predictors across several
medical tasks, although their effectiveness depends on the prediction target. MedJev achieves strong
performance on medical knowledge benchmarks and competitive risk discrimination for outcomes
such as in-hospital mortality, while supervised models perform better on operational outcomes
such as emergency department admission. Although its confidence estimates are well calibrated on
medical question-answering benchmarks, its patient-level probabilities require adjustment to local
outcome frequencies. A lightweight recalibration procedure using a small number of labeled examples
substantially reduces this error without changing patient risk rankings. These findings illustrate how
System-One models can be evaluated within a unified medical prediction pipeline and clarify the role
of zero-shot inference, local calibration, and supervised learning in clinical prediction settings.

sample_chunks.text_content:
MedJev: Evaluating Zero-Shot System-One Decision Making in Medicine
2. Related Work
System-One decision models.
Most language models perform decision-making tasks through
autoregressive generation, producing textual responses that must be interpreted or parsed to recover
a final prediction. System-One decision models instead formulate inference as a direct mapping from
an observed state and a structured question to a probability distribution over possible outcomes. Jev
[3] implements this paradigm through three typed primitives: Choice, which returns a distribution
over a finite set of alternatives; Noul, which estimates the probability of a binary outcome; and
Score, which represents judgments on an ordinal scale. These primitives allow classification,
probability estimation, and ordinal assessment to share a common inference interface without
requiring autoregressive decoding. Deußer et. al, [4] systematically evaluate Jev in the zero-shot
setting across 37 public datasets, comparing its predictive performance and computational efficiency
against open-weight LLMs evaluated using exact option probabilities. Their results establish the
feasibility of System-One inference for general-purpose classification and decision tasks. However,
their evaluation includes only one biomedical dataset, PubMedQA [10], and does not examine patientlevel prediction from EHRs. More recently, OpenJev [5] provides an open-weight implementation
of the Jev interface by fine-tuning Qwen3.5-9B [11]. OpenJev obtains structured predictions from
the probability distribution over option-letter tokens, followed by temperature calibration. Our study
extends prior System-One evaluations to medical knowledge, diagnosis, and longitudinal patient
prediction, while examining both zero-shot predictive performance and the reliability of the resulting
probabilities.
Medical question answering and diagnosis.
Medical question answering has become a standard
approach for evaluating the clinical knowledge and reasoning capabilities of language models [12–16].
MedQA [17] evaluates medical reasoning using multiple-choice questions derived from professional
medical examinations, including the United States Medical Licensing Examination (USMLE). MedMCQA [18] provides a large collection of multiple-choice questions spanning medical subjects, while
PubMedQA [10] evaluates biomedical question answering using research abstracts. These benchmarks
have been widely used to measure the medical knowledge encoded in pretrained and instructiontuned language models. Work on medical LLMs, including Med-PaLM [1], demonstrates that large
generative models can achieve strong performance on medical examination questions, motivating
their use as reference models for medical AI evaluation. However, performance on examination-style
questions does not necessarily characterize a model’s ability to interpret complex clinical presentations
or make patient-specific predictions.
Diagnostic benchmarks address this limitation by evaluating models on clinical cases rather than
isolated knowledge questions. DiagnosisArena [8] constructs diagnostic tasks from published case
reports, requiring models to distinguish among candidate diagnoses using clinical histories, examinations, and investigation findings. [19] investigate the diagnostic performance of GPT-3.5 and GPT-4
on clinical vignettes using different reasoning prompts and clinician-graded open-ended responses.
These studies predominantly evaluate generative models through textual answers, often allowing
reasoning or explanation before a final diagnosis. In contrast, our evaluation formulates medical
knowledge and diagnostic tasks as structured multiple-choice decisions, enabling direct probabilitybased comparisons among System-One models and conventional LLMs. Because multiple-choice and
open-ended diagnosis differ in difficulty, previously reported generative results are treated as external
reference points rather than strictly equivalent evaluations.
Clinical prediction from electronic health records.
Clinical prediction from multimodal clinical
data [20–27] and EHRs [28–30] differs from medical question answering because models must
3

sample_chunks.authors: Simon A. Lee, Jiahang Sha, et al.
sample_chunks.category: AI-Based Clinical Decision Support Systems
sample_chunks.text_content:
MedJev: Evaluating Zero-Shot System-One Decision Making in Medicine
reason over heterogeneous patient information collected across time. Established prediction tasks
include in-hospital mortality, length of stay, and hospital readmission, which have been widely studied
using critical care datasets such as MIMIC [31–34]. These tasks require predictions at clinically
meaningful decision times, making the availability and temporal ordering of patient information
important aspects of benchmark construction. The Medical Event Data Standard (MEDS) [35–37]
provides a standardized representation of longitudinal patient records as timestamped clinical events,
facilitating the development and evaluation of models across EHR-derived tasks [28, 29, 38, 39].
Emergency department prediction presents a related but distinct setting in which decisions must
be made using information available early in the patient encounter. [40] study hospital admission
prediction at emergency department triage using routinely collected patient characteristics, vital
signs, and chief complaints. Gradient-boosted trees and other supervised tabular models provide
strong baselines for such structured clinical prediction tasks. Language models offer an alternative by
representing patient records as text and applying pretrained language understanding capabilities
to the resulting sequences. [41] investigate this approach using serialized emergency department
records, while EHRSHOT [42] introduces a framework for evaluating foundation models on EHR
prediction tasks under limited-label settings. These studies motivate the evaluation of pretrained
models on patient-level outcomes, but their settings generally involve either supervised adaptation,
learned patient representations, or conventional language-model inference. We instead examine
whether a System-One model can directly estimate clinical outcome probabilities from serialized EHR
states without task-specific training.
Language models for structured data and probability calibration.
Applying language models to
structured clinical records is closely related to research on language-based representations of tabular
data [41, 43–45]. TabLLM [46] demonstrates that serializing tabular features into natural-language
descriptions enables pretrained language models to perform classification with relatively few labeled
examples. This approach is particularly relevant when task-specific training data are scarce, although
conventional supervised methods often become more competitive as the number of labeled examples
increases. [47] further demonstrate the strong performance of tree-based methods on typical tabular
prediction tasks, motivating their inclusion as supervised baselines. For clinical prediction, this
comparison is important because pretrained models may provide useful predictions without local
labels, whereas models trained directly on EHR data can learn relationships specific to the target
population and outcome.
Beyond discrimination and accuracy, clinical prediction requires an assessment of probability calibration. A model may correctly rank patients by risk while systematically overestimating or underestimating the frequency of an outcome. This distinction is particularly important when a model is
evaluated zero-shot on a patient population whose outcome prevalence differs from the distributions
encountered during pretraining. Post-hoc calibration methods provide a lightweight mechanism for
correcting predicted probabilities without retraining the underlying model. Platt scaling [48] learns a
logistic transformation of model scores, while temperature scaling [49] adjusts the sharpness of a
predicted probability distribution. These approaches preserve binary risk rankings or multiclass predicted labels, respectively, while modifying the reported confidence. In our evaluation, we distinguish
the zero-shot predictive capabilities of System-One models from the calibration of their probabilities
on local patient populations. We investigate whether a small number of labeled examples is sufficient
for post-hoc recalibration and compare this adaptation strategy against supervised models trained
under the same label budgets.
4

3. Methodology
We evaluate MedJev across ten medical benchmarks using a common pipeline that converts each task
into a structured decision request. The pipeline consists of constructing an input state, specifying a
question and its possible outcomes, obtaining a probability distribution from the model, and evaluating
the prediction against the ground-truth outcome. All models are evaluated on the same test examples,
with additional comparisons against supervised baselines and locally recalibrated predictions.

outcome. This interface supports both medical multiple-choice questions and patient-level predictions
without requiring autoregressive answer generation.

throughout the evaluation. Each request is rendered as a prompt containing the state, question

DiagnosisArena [8] contains 915 publicly available case reports with four candidate diagnoses. NEJM
[19] contains 512 diagnostic vignettes originally evaluated using open-ended responses from GPT-3.5
and GPT-4.
