from the original open-ended evaluation, published GPT results are used only as external references.
Longitudinal EHR prediction.
We construct four patient-level benchmarks using MIMIC-IV [31]
represented in the Medical Event Data Standard (MEDS) [37]. The tasks are In-Hospital Mortality,
Length of Stay > 7 Days, 30-Day Readmission, and ED Admission at 2 h. Each task is defined by an
outcome and a fixed prediction time 𝑡∗.
In-Hospital Mortality and Length of Stay > 7 Days are predicted 24 h after hospital admission among
adult patients who remain hospitalized at that time. 30-Day Readmission is predicted at discharge,
and ED Admission at 2 h is predicted two hours after emergency department arrival. For each
prediction, the model receives only events within (𝑡∗−365 d, 𝑡∗]. The available events are serialized
into a compact JSON state containing patient demographics, clinical history, care units, laboratory
measurements, and medications when available.
We exclude information that would not be available at the specified prediction time. In particular,
discharge-stamped diagnoses and diagnosis-related groups are excluded from the 24 h prediction
tasks. For ED Admission at 2 h, we additionally remove admission-only demographic fields, ED and
admission bookkeeping codes beginning 24 h before arrival, and nonlaboratory events recorded after
ED arrival. These restrictions prevent outcome-related information from entering the input state.
Emergency department triage.
We construct two additional benchmarks from MIMIC-IV-ED [50]:
ED Triage Admission and ED Triage Disposition. Both are evaluated at the time of triage using
information available at that point in the encounter. The input state includes age, sex, race, arrival
transport, triage vital signs, pain score, Emergency Severity Index acuity, chief complaint, and
emergency department visits within the preceding year. Subsequent medications, vital signs, diagnoses,
and medication reconciliation records are excluded.
ED Triage Admission is a binary Noul task predicting whether the visit results in hospital admission.
ED Triage Disposition is a six-option Choice task predicting discharge home, admission, transfer,
departure before completion, death, or another disposition. Figure 1 provides an example of the
serialized input and corresponding question.
Dataset preparation.
The longitudinal benchmarks use a MEDS-Transforms extract [51] of MIMICIV v2.2 containing 299,712 patients distributed across five training shards, one tuning shard, and
one held-out shard. Training examples are drawn from the training shards and test examples from
the held-out shard. MIMIC-IV-ED v2.2 contains 425,087 emergency department stays. We retain
adult patients with a corresponding MEDS birth record and assign each patient to the MEDS split
associated with their subject_id. This ensures patient-disjoint training and test partitions across
the EHR benchmarks.

We compare zero-shot MedJev with conventional language models, previously reported frontier-model
results, and supervised models trained on local EHR labels.

We evaluate Qwen3.5-9B [11], the base model from which OpenJev
was fine-tuned, to assess the effect of System-One training. Qwen3.5-2B provides a smaller model

on DiagnosisArena [8]. These models are not re-evaluated in our pipeline. Differences in prompting,
answer format, and benchmark subsets preclude paired statistical comparisons. In particular, the
published DiagnosisArena results use 1,113 cases, whereas our evaluation uses the 915 publicly
available cases.
Supervised EHR baselines.
We evaluate XGBoost [56] and TF-IDF with logistic regression as
supervised baselines for the six patient-level tasks. For longitudinal MEDS records, XGBoost uses
bag-of-codes features, including event counts and last observed values. For emergency department
triage, it uses structured triage features and chief-complaint tokens, following established tabular
approaches [40]. TF-IDF with logistic regression operates directly on the serialized patient state.
Both supervised models are trained using locally labeled examples from the corresponding training
partitions. XGBoost tree depth, column subsampling, minimum child weight, and number of trees are
selected by five-fold cross-validation. TF-IDF 𝑛-gram ranges and logistic regression regularization
are selected using the same procedure. The selected models are refitted using all available training
examples. We evaluate supervised performance with up to 1,000 labeled examples per task.
3.4. Calibration and Evaluation Protocol
We evaluate MedJev in the zero-shot setting without task-specific training or local labels. To examine
the calibration of patient-level probabilities, we additionally consider post-hoc recalibration using
labeled examples from the corresponding training partitions. For binary Noul tasks, we apply Platt
scaling [48] to the predicted logits. For multiclass Choice tasks, we apply temperature scaling [49]
to the predicted distributions. These transformations use at most two fitted parameters and do not
update the underlying language model. For medical knowledge benchmarks, a shared temperature is
fitted using MedQA training questions. For patient-level tasks, recalibration is fitted separately for
each outcome using local labels.
All models are evaluated on identical test examples. Models requiring labeled data, including
supervised baselines and post-hoc recalibration, use the same patient-disjoint training partitions.
Model selection and calibration fitting do not use test labels. We additionally vary the available label
budget from 25 to 1,000 examples to compare the label efficiency of supervised learning and post-hoc
recalibration.
For Choice tasks, we report top-1 accuracy and expected calibration error (ECE) computed from
the probability assigned to the predicted class using 15 equal-width bins [49]. For binary Noul
tasks, we report the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), area under
the precision-recall curve (AUPRC), ECE, and Brier score. We compute 95% percentile bootstrap
confidence intervals over test examples [57]. Differences between MedJev and directly evaluated
baselines are assessed using paired bootstrap resampling of the same test examples.
Implementation.
All language models are evaluated locally using 8-bit MLX builds [58] on an
Apple silicon laptop with 48 GB of unified memory. Our inference engine uses the frozen OpenJev
helper and replaces only the underlying model client. We verify that local inference reproduces the
outputs of the MedJev HTTP server on a verification sample, with a maximum absolute probability
difference of zero. MedJev requires approximately 0.5 s for a MedQA question and 2 s for a serialized
MEDS state. All EHR processing and model inference are performed locally, without transmitting
patient records to external services.

4. Results
Tables 2 and 3 summarize the performance of all models across the ten benchmarks. Table 4 reports
paired differences relative to zero-shot MedJev. We examine performance on medical knowledge and
diagnosis, patient-level prediction, probability calibration, and the effect of local training data.
4.1. Medical Knowledge and Diagnosis
MedJev achieves zero-shot accuracies of 72.5% on MedQA (95% CI 69.8–75.3), 75.4% on USMLE
(73.0–77.6), 80.1% on NEJM (76.6–83.4), and 55.5% on DiagnosisArena (52.5–58.8). These results
exceed the corresponding chance accuracies of 20–25% across all four benchmarks (fig. 2).
We first compare MedJev with Qwen3.5-9B, its underlying language model. Under identical prompts
and probability readouts, Qwen3.5-9B performs -3.9 and -4.6 percentage points below MedJev
on MedQA and USMLE, respectively, with paired confidence intervals of -6.3 to -1.4 and -6.8 to
-2.4. The differences on NEJM (-3.1) and DiagnosisArena (-1.1) are smaller and not statistically
significant. These comparisons indicate that System-One training improves performance on the
medical examination benchmarks, although the improvement is not consistent across all diagnostic
tasks.

improve performance over its base model.
4.3. Probability Calibration
We evaluate whether the probabilities produced by MedJev correspond to observed outcome frequencies. Figures 4 and 5 present expected calibration error and calibration curves across the benchmarks.
MedJev is well calibrated on medical knowledge benchmarks, with ECE values of 0.039 on MedQA,
0.028 on USMLE, and 0.063 on NEJM. In contrast, its zero-shot probabilities are poorly calibrated on
patient-level outcomes. For In-Hospital Mortality, the mean predicted probability is 0.312, compared
with an observed mortality rate of 2.6%, resulting in an ECE of 0.286. The corresponding ECE values
are 0.191 for Length of Stay > 7 Days, 0.272 for 30-Day Readmission, and 0.147 for ED Triage
Admission. These results indicate that good risk discrimination does not necessarily imply calibrated
outcome probabilities in the zero-shot setting.
We apply post-hoc recalibration using labeled examples from the corresponding training partitions.
Recalibration reduces ECE to 0.007 on In-Hospital Mortality, 0.027 on Length of Stay > 7 Days, 0.024
on 30-Day Readmission, and 0.041 on ED Triage Admission. These values are comparable to those
obtained by XGBoost, which achieves ECE values of 0.014, 0.059, 0.046, and 0.042 on the same tasks.
Recalibration changes the probability estimates without changing the reported AUROC.

The number of labels required for supervised models to match zero-shot MedJev varies across tasks.
XGBoost reaches comparable AUROC with approximately 100 labels on ED Admission at 2 h and 200
labels on ED Triage Admission. TF-IDF requires approximately 200 labels to match MedJev on Length

1,000 labels. For In-Hospital Mortality, neither supervised baseline matches the zero-shot AUROC of
MedJev within the evaluated label budgets.
These results indicate that the relative benefit of zero-shot prediction depends on the task and the
availability of local labels. Recalibration requires fewer labels than supervised training to improve
probability estimates, while supervised models can provide better discrimination for some outcomes
when sufficient labeled examples are available.
4.5. Selective Prediction
We evaluate selective prediction by ranking examples according to the probability assigned to the
predicted class and measuring accuracy at different coverage levels. This analysis examines whether
model confidence can identify predictions that are more likely to be correct.

5. Discussion
Our results show that System-One models can perform medical decision tasks without autoregressive
generation. MedJev achieves competitive performance on medical knowledge and diagnosis benchmarks and provides useful discrimination for several patient-level outcomes. However, its performance
varies across clinical tasks, and its zero-shot probability estimates do not consistently reflect local
outcome frequencies. These findings suggest that System-One models can serve as zero-shot baselines
for medical prediction, with local recalibration or supervised training required depending on the task.
Zero-shot predictive performance.
MedJev achieves strong accuracy and calibration on medical
knowledge benchmarks using a single forward pass. Its performance on MedQA and USMLE is within
a few percentage points of published zero-shot GPT-4 results and substantially exceeds reported
GPT-3.5 accuracy. On DiagnosisArena, MedJev outperforms the reported GPT-4o result but remains
below o1. These comparisons are limited by differences in evaluation protocols, particularly for
benchmarks originally evaluated using open-ended responses. Nevertheless, the results demonstrate
that structured probability estimation can provide competitive performance on medical questionanswering tasks without generating textual answers.

On patient-level prediction, MedJev achieves an AUROC of 0.926 for In-Hospital Mortality, comparable
to supervised models trained on labeled examples. Performance is also comparable to supervised
baselines on 30-Day Readmission. In contrast, supervised models perform better on ED admission
and length-of-stay prediction. These differences may reflect the extent to which outcomes depend on
patient characteristics and local clinical practices. Mortality is closely associated with clinical severity,
whereas admission and discharge decisions are also influenced by institutional policies, resource
availability, and care processes. Consequently, the relative performance of zero-shot and supervised
models depends on the prediction target.
Comparisons with Qwen3.5-9B further indicate that System-One training contributes to predictive
performance. MedJev improves accuracy on MedQA and USMLE and discrimination on In-Hospital
Mortality and Length of Stay > 7 Days under the same prompting and readout procedure. It also
produces better-calibrated probabilities than its base model across several benchmarks. However, these
improvements are not consistent across all tasks, as Qwen3.5-9B performs better on ED admission
prediction. System-One training therefore improves performance on selected medical tasks but does
not uniformly outperform the underlying language model.
Probability calibration and local adaptation.
Although MedJev produces well-calibrated confidence estimates on medical knowledge benchmarks, its patient-level predictions exhibit substantial
calibration error. In particular, the model overestimates the probability of in-hospital mortality relative
to the observed event rate. This distinction is important because discrimination measures whether a
model correctly ranks patients by risk, whereas calibration measures whether predicted probabilities
correspond to observed outcome frequencies. A model can achieve high AUROC while producing
probabilities that are unsuitable for direct interpretation as patient risk.
Post-hoc recalibration substantially reduces this error without retraining MedJev. Using Platt scaling
fitted on local labeled examples, we obtain calibration performance comparable to supervised baselines
while preserving the original risk ranking. The label-efficiency experiments show that 50–200 labeled
examples can substantially improve calibration across patient-level tasks. In comparison, supervised
models generally require more labeled examples to match the discrimination of zero-shot MedJev,
although this varies by outcome. Calibration parameters fitted on one medical knowledge benchmark

the target task and population.
These results support separating zero-shot prediction from local probability calibration in the evaluation pipeline. The System-One model provides an initial prediction without task-specific training,
while a small labeled dataset can be used to adjust the probability estimates to the local population.
However, recalibration does not improve discrimination and cannot address limitations in the underlying risk ranking. For tasks where supervised models achieve higher AUROC, additional local
training remains beneficial.
Implications for medical evaluation.
The structured request interface allows medical knowledge
questions and patient-level prediction tasks to be evaluated using the same inference procedure. Each
task is represented by an input state, a question, and a set of possible outcomes, and the model
returns probabilities that can be evaluated for accuracy, discrimination, and calibration. This removes
the need to generate and parse textual responses and allows direct comparisons with other language
models using the same probability readout.
The results also indicate that evaluation of System-One models should consider both zero-shot
performance and the effect of local adaptation. Zero-shot evaluation measures predictive performance
without task-specific labels, while recalibration measures whether the predicted probabilities can
be adjusted using limited local data. Supervised baselines provide a reference for the performance
achievable through task-specific training. Considering these settings together helps determine when a
System-One model provides a useful alternative to conventional predictive models. The local inference
setup further allows these evaluations to be conducted without transmitting patient records to external
model services.
Limitations.
Several limitations should be considered when interpreting these results. First, the
number of positive outcomes is small for some tasks. In-Hospital Mortality contains only 2.6% deaths
in the test set, resulting in wide confidence intervals for AUROC. Second, we evaluate a single prompt
and serialization format for each task. The questions, input representations, and event limits are fixed
rather than optimized, although prior work has shown that serialization choices can affect languagemodel performance on structured data [46]. Third, the NEJM benchmark was originally evaluated
using open-ended diagnoses, whereas our evaluation uses multiple-choice questions. Published GPT
results therefore provide contextual references rather than directly comparable estimates.
The medical knowledge benchmarks also have potential overlap with model pretraining data. MedQA
and USMLE share question stems, and MedQA has been publicly available since 2020. We cannot
exclude the possibility that some evaluation questions appeared during pretraining. For the EHR
benchmarks, the MEDS extract does not provide a complete ICU item dictionary. We identify bedside
measurements using standard MIMIC-IV item identifiers, but omit other chart events that cannot be
reliably interpreted. Finally, MIMIC-IV and MIMIC-IV-ED originate from a single academic medical
center. The results may not generalize to institutions with different patient populations, clinical
practices, or outcome prevalence. Evaluation on additional clinical datasets is needed to assess
generalizability.
Data use and ethics.
MIMIC-IV and MIMIC-IV-ED were accessed under the PhysioNet credentialed
data use agreement. All data processing and model inference were performed locally, with the model
server restricted to the loopback interface. No individual-level patient records are included in this
paper, and calibration parameters fitted on credentialed data are not publicly released. The evaluated

Appendix
A. Question Formats
All benchmarks are represented as Jev requests consisting of a state and a typed question. Choice
questions return a probability distribution over candidate answers, while Noul questions return the
probability of a binary outcome. Table 1 summarizes the questions used for each benchmark.
Benchmark
Type
Question or outcome
MedQA, USMLE, NEJM
Choice
Which option correctly answers the question? Five options for
MedQA and NEJM, four for USMLE.
DiagnosisArena
Choice
Which option is the most likely final diagnosis for the patient
described in the state? Four candidate diagnoses.
In-Hospital Mortality
Noul
Will this patient die before being discharged from the current
hospital admission?
Length of Stay > 7 Days
Noul
Will the current hospital stay last longer than 7 days in total?
30-Day Readmission
Noul
Will the patient be admitted again within 30 days after this
discharge?
ED Admission at 2 h
Noul
Based on the information available 2 hours after arrival, will
this ED visit end in admission to the hospital?
ED Triage Admission
Noul
Based on the information available at triage, will this visit end
with the patient admitted to the hospital?
ED Triage Disposition
Choice
What will the disposition of this ED visit be? Options: home,
admitted, transfer, left before completion, expired, or other.
Supplementary Table 1 | Question formats used across the ten medical benchmarks.
Prompt construction.
Each question is rendered as a prompt containing the serialized state, question
instructions, and candidate options. For Choice questions, the options are assigned single-token
letter labels. The prompt follows the format below.
State:
<state JSON>
Question:
<instructions>
Options:
[A] <option 1>: <description>
[B] <option 2>: <description>
...
Answer with the letter of the best option only.
For Noul questions, the candidate outcomes correspond to true and false, with optional descriptions
specifying each outcome. MedJev reads the option-token probabilities at the first answer position
and applies the transformations in eqs. (1) and (2) to obtain the final probability distribution.

C. Supervised references
Hyperparameters chosen by five-fold cross-validation on the training examples. XGBoost: learning
rate 0.05, subsampling 0.8, a grid over depth {2, 3, 5}, minimum child weight {1, 5} and column
subsampling {0.3, 0.7}, with the number of trees set by early stopping inside each fold. TF-IDF: word
𝑛-grams {(1, 1), (1, 2)}, 50k features, sublinear term frequency, ℓ2 strength 𝐶∈{0.01, 0.1, 1, 10}. For
ED Triage Disposition, classes with fewer than 10 training stays (e.g. expired) are merged into “other”
during training.
D. Reproducibility
Everything is produced by the scripts in src/scripts/: prepare_data.py (Jev requests and training sets), extract_jev.py and run_variants_gpu.sh (zero-shot answers for every language
model; MLX), train_probes.py (recalibration), run_baselines.py (supervised references),
label_efficiency.py (label budgets, from cached outputs), evaluate.py (scores and metrics),
make_paper_assets.py (tables and every number in this paper) and make_figures.py (figures).
Every model output is cached on disk, keyed by the exact request.

sample_chunks.text_content:
Decisions by Discrimination: Differential Evidence for Medical Reasoning
Yunpeng Xiao1, Yuzhang Xie1, Junhao Huang1, Carl Yang1, Xiao Hu2, Kai Shu1
1Department of Computer Science, Emory University,
2Nell Hodgson Woodruff School of Nursing, Emory University
{yunpeng.xiao, yuzhang.xie, junhao.huang,
j.carlyang, xiao.hu, kai.shu}@emory.edu
Abstract
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly studied for clinical decision support,
and medical question answering provides a
testbed for evaluating this capability. In particular, medical multiple-choice questions (MCQs)
reflect a core challenge in clinical decisionmaking: plausible options often share overlapping evidence, while only a few decisive
factors distinguish the correct option from incorrect ones. However, existing retrieval-based
and reasoning-oriented methods mainly focus
on supplying broadly relevant knowledge or
eliciting reasoning paths, rather than identifying the compact differential evidence that
separates confusing alternatives. In this work,
we present a retrieval-grounded differential evidence framework for medical MCQs. Our
method extracts option-specific pieces of differential evidence and organizes them into concise evidence prompts for answer selection.
This design better aligns external knowledge
with differential reasoning while reducing irrelevant context. Experiments show consistent
accuracy gains across multiple datasets and
target LLMs. Ablation studies further show
that our framework outperforms both directly
using retrieved evidence chunks and closedsource LLM-generated general hints, and that
its improvements are not solely explained by
answer-proximal guidance, but are consistent
with differential evidence serving as a compact
aid for reasoning over competing alternatives.
Our findings also offer insights for medical reasoning and other decision-making settings with
multiple possible choices.
1
Introduction
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly
explored as clinical assistants, powering systems
for triage, diagnosis support, and patient education
(Singhal et al., 2023, 2025; Wu et al., 2024). However, even medically tuned LLMs remain prone to
unsafe reasoning behaviors. A common challenge
in clinical reasoning is that many candidate diagnoses or treatment decisions share a large core of
overlapping facts, while differing only in a small
number of critical discriminatory factors (Bowen,
2006; Cook and Décary, 2020). If a model fails
to identify and reason over these few distinguishing facts, then even access to abundant relevant
knowledge may still lead to misdiagnosis or other
incorrect clinical decisions.
In medical multiple-choice questions (medical
MCQs), this challenge is especially well exposed,
making them a natural benchmark for studying differential clinical reasoning. In real clinical practice,
competing diagnoses or treatment options often
share substantial overlapping evidence, with only a
few decisive factors determining the correct choice.
Medical MCQs capture this structure naturally: several answer options may each align with part of the
vignette, but only one is supported by the discriminative evidence that resolves the case. This makes
the benchmark useful for evaluating whether models can identify clinically meaningful differences
among plausible hypotheses, rather than relying on
broadly relevant but non-discriminative facts.
However,
existing
methods
are
still
not
well aligned with this requirement.
Retrievalaugmented generation (RAG) has become a common strategy for medical QA, supplementing
LLMs with external knowledge from structured
resources such as knowledge graphs and unstructured corpora such as textbooks. Current medical
RAG pipelines are primarily designed to retrieve
generally relevant evidence, not the small set of
discriminative facts that separates plausible answer
options. As a result, they often return a broad supportive context while failing to surface the evidence
needed to resolve near-miss alternatives. Figure 1
presents a concrete example in which two clinically
similar diseases share multiple symptoms, while
only a small number of distinctive symptoms determine the final diagnosis.

We therefore propose a retrieval-grounded differential evidence framework for medical MCQs.
Instead of appending broad supporting context, our
method extracts anchor cues, retrieves cue–option
co-occurrence passages from textbooks, and distills them into compact option-specific evidence
for answer selection. This design reduces retrieved
context length by about 85% while improving accuracy across benchmarks.
Our main contributions are:
• We formulate differential evidence as an evidence organization problem, emphasizing
option-discriminative evidence rather than
broadly relevant knowledge.
• We propose a four-stage framework that extracts anchor cues, retrieves cue–option cooccurrence evidence, and distills it into compact option-specific evidence for answer selection.
• Experiments on three medical MCQ benchmarks show consistent gains across multiple
LLMs. Ablation studies with raw retrieved
text, general hints, and evidence-only settings
suggest that the gains come from differential
evidence rather than more text or general answer cues.
2
Related Work
2.1
Medical QA and Retrieval-Augmented
Generation (RAG)
Large-scale medical QA benchmarks, such as
MedQA (Jin et al., 2021), MedXpertQA (Zuo
et al., 2025), and MedBullets (Chen et al., 2025),
have become important testbeds for evaluating finegrained clinical reasoning in LLMs. In particular,
multiple-choice medical QA provides a constrained
decision-making setting in which several candidate
options may all appear clinically plausible at first
glance. This makes such benchmarks especially
useful for assessing whether models can assist in
real-world clinical decision making (Chen et al.,
2025; Wei et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2025b).
Many medical QA tasks, especially MedQAstyle problems, require reasoning beyond the information explicitly stated in the question stem,
thus models often need to draw on background
medical knowledge, including disease mechanisms,
diagnostic criteria, treatment indications, and contraindications (Liévin et al., 2024; Lucas et al.,
2024; Bhasuran et al., 2025). Since this knowledge is broad, evolving, and difficult to capture reliably through parametric memory alone,
retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over external medical knowledge bases has emerged as
a natural solution (Yang et al., 2025b). By retrieving evidence from curated resources such as
clinical guidelines, biomedical ontologies, textbooks, and knowledge graphs, medical RAG systems can ground answer selection in explicit evidence rather than latent memorization (Amugongo
et al., 2025; Ke et al., 2025; Song et al., 2025).
Recent work has explored this direction through
methods such as MIRAGE (Xiong et al., 2024a),
K-Comp (Cho and Lee, 2025), MKRAG (Shi
et al., 2025), MedRAG (Zhao et al., 2025), BriefContext (Zhang et al., 2025a), RAG2(Sohn et al.,
2025), KGARevion (Su et al., 2024), and SelfBioRAG (Jeong et al., 2024). In addition to traditional text-based RAG, recent studies have explored KG-guided retrieval and reasoning frameworks, such as Dr.Knows (Gao et al., 2025),
MedIKAL (Jia et al., 2025), KERAP (Xie et al.,
2025), KG4Diagnosis (Zuo et al., 2024), and
KGARevion (Su et al., 2024), which leverage
knowledge graphs to facilitate answer generation,
diagnostic reasoning, and evidence retrieval.
Although retrieved external evidence can im-

prove factual grounding, conventional retrieval generally prioritizes overall semantic relevance to the
question, often returning broad background knowledge that may support multiple candidate options
simultaneously (Amugongo et al., 2025; Liu et al.,
2025c; Xiong et al., 2024b). However, for medical multiple-choice reasoning, the key challenge is
often not general relevance but discriminative utility: the retrieved evidence should help the model
determine why one option is more appropriate than
other clinically plausible alternatives under the specific case context (Chen et al., 2023; Singh and
Shrivastava, 2025; Alhazmi et al., 2024). These
observations make differential evidence especially
well-suited for medical QA.
2.2
Option Discrimination and Evidence
Selection in Multiple-Choice Reasoning
Existing work has increasingly suggested that the
main challenge in multiple-choice reasoning is not
merely identifying generally relevant knowledge,
but distinguishing among candidate options that
may all appear partially plausible.
Early work
on multi-choice reading comprehension emphasized joint interactions among the passage, question, and candidate answers, rather than questiononly matching (Wang et al., 2018). Recent studies
further show that LLMs are sensitive to candidateoption structure: some methods model elimination over options (Ma and Du, 2023), while others find that predictions can vary under answerorder permutations, indicating unstable discrimination among alternatives (Pezeshkpour and Hruschka, 2024). Related analyses also show that
benchmarks often contain several plausible candidates, and that models may select the least incorrect option rather than one that is distinctly correct
(Wang et al., 2025a; Palta et al., 2024). This issue is especially salient in medical MCQs, where
options often share overlapping clinical facts and
differ only in a few decisive mechanisms, contraindications, or management roles. In parallel,
retrieval-based methods have incorporated answer
options into retrieval or knowledge selection, such
as question-aware knowledge graph prompting and
answer-conditioned support retrieval (Zhang et al.,
2025b; Liu et al., 2025b). However, these methods
mainly improve option-aware knowledge access,
while compact differential evidence for optionlevel comparison remains underexplored. Unlike
prior option-aware retrieval methods that primarily
improve access to option-related knowledge, our
focus is on organizing knowledge into differential
evidence that clearly distinguishing between the
various options.
3
Methods
In this section, we will introduce the proposed
differential evidence reasoning method for clinical decision-making, especially in multiple-choice
questions. Figure 2 shows the framework of our
proposed method, which consists of four stages:
anchor cue extraction, cue-option co-occurrence
retrieval, differential evidence generation, and
evidence-based inference. The first three stages
form the differential evidence construction pipeline,
while the fourth stage uses the generated evidence
for final answer prediction.
3.1
Definition of Differential Evidence
Given a multiple-choice question with candidate
options
O = {o1, o2, . . . , om},
we define differential evidence for an option oi as
external evidence that supports oi more strongly
than competing options under the current case context. In other words, differential evidence is not
merely relevant knowledge, but knowledge with
discriminative utility for separating clinically plausible alternatives.
Formally, if s(e, o) denotes the degree to which
an evidence item e supports option o, then ideal
differential evidence for oi would satisfy
s(e, oi) > s(e, ok),
∀k ̸= i,
or more generally provide substantially stronger
support for oi than for the strongest competing
option.
In practice, explicit support scoring is difficult
because raw textbook passages are often long, redundant, and only indirectly aligned with optionlevel distinctions. We therefore approximate differential evidence through a retrieval-and-distillation
pipeline. The following subsections describe the
first three stages of the framework for differential
evidence construction, while the fourth stage performs evidence-based inference.
3.2
Definition of Atomic Facts and Anchor
Cues
In medical multiple-choice questions, one data sample typically consists of the parts: the background
context C, the explicit question Q and the options

Figure 2: The framework of our proposed method.
O. Since the key clinical evidence is usually conveyed in the background description, we decompose C into a set of atomic facts, following the
intuition of fine-grained factual decomposition in
fact-checking (Min et al., 2023):
C = {f1, f2, . . . , fn},
where each fi denotes a minimal clinical fact, such
as a symptom, laboratory finding, medical history
element, or treatment detail.
However, atomic decomposition alone is insufficient, as the fact set may still contain substantial
redundancy and many facts that are only weakly
relevant to the question Q and final decision. We
therefore define anchor cue, which is to distill the
original fact set into a compact set of highly salient
cues. Formally, we select a subset of atomic facts,
A = {a1, a2, . . . , ai} ⊆C,
i ≪n,
where A denotes the set of anchor cues.
This step can be understood as a general content
distillation problem in text understanding: from
a larger collection of fine-grained facts, we aim
to retain only those that best preserve the core semantics and decision-critical information of the
scenario. This step is not intended for full clinical
reasoning or direct answer prediction, but to distill
the scenario into a few salient anchor cues, similar to focused reading comprehension over clinical
text. For example, the context mentions that the
patient developed tinnitus while the question asks
Which medication caused this phenomenon, then
"tinnitus" serves as the anchor cue for this specific
question.
3.3
Textbook Knowledge Retrieval through
Anchor Cue–Option Co-occurrence
Similar to traditional RAG, we also need to leverage external knowledge to enhance the performance of the target model in medical scenarios.
However, as noted in Section 2, current knowledge graphs are not yet sufficient to distinguish the
subtle nuances between options and generate discriminative evidence; therefore, we identify chunks
in textbooks that exhibit co-occurrence between anchor cues and the options as our preliminary source
of external knowledge.
Specifically, by leveraging the powerful semantic understanding capabilities of external LLMs,
we first input the context C and the question Q into
these models to extract anchor cues
A = {a1, a2, . . . , ai},
and normalize these cues and generate their common variants (e.g., singular/plural forms, abbreviations, etc.). Similarly, we input the options O into
the external LLMs, subjecting them to the same
normalization process and generating their common variants
On = {o1, o2, . . . , oj}.

This strict input separation reduces the risk that
external LLMs act as implicit solvers of the task.
Instead, their role is limited to localized semantic
normalization and variant generation, rather than
answer inference over the full MCQ instance.
Next, we use the textbook provided in the
MedQA dataset (Jin et al., 2021) to identify cooccurring chunks
pij = Co-occurr(ai, oj).
A chunk is considered co-occurring if it contains
at least one normalized variant of an anchor cue
and one normalized variant of an option concept.
In this work, to control prompt length and reduce
redundant evidence, we extract only one chunk
for each anchor cue-option pair. Specifically, we
extract a maximum of |A| × |O| paragraphs. More
details are shown in appendix.
3.4
Textbook-Constrained Differential
Evidence Generation
Compared with knowledge graphs, textbook knowledge provides substantially richer semantic content.
However, it is often fragmented, redundant, and
not explicitly organized around option-level distinctions, which makes it difficult to directly obtain discriminative evidence for specific answer
choices. In addition, textbook retrieval may still
miss relevant information due to limited coverage
or retrieval failures. To address this, we use external LLMs to generate option-discriminative evidence while treating retrieved textbook knowledge
as a constraint on the generation process. Formally, we generate the set of differential evidence
D = {dA, dB, ...} where dA denotes the evidence
specific to Option A, as follows:
D = ExternalLLM(A, Q, O, P).
Here, A is the set of anchor cues, O is the set of
original options, P = S pij is the set of retrieved
external knowledge, and Q is the question. Each do
is generated as a short, option-specific, conditionoriented statement capturing the conditions that
most clearly distinguish option from competing
alternatives. When retrieved evidence is missing
for a given option, the LLM is allowed to provide
limited supplementation from internal knowledge.
3.5
Differential Evidence Quality Control
Because external LLMs may have been pretrained
on overlapping medical QA data, we introduce several safeguards to reduce answer leakage and bias.
First, during anchor cue extraction and normalization, the external LLM only sees the context and
question C, Q without the options O; during option extraction and normalization, it only sees the
options O without the context and question C, Q;
during differential evidence generation, it only sees
the anchor cues, questions, options A, Q, O without context C. As a result, the external model never
has access to the full MCQ instance at any stage.
Second, the system prompt explicitly instructs the
model to prioritize retrieved textbook evidence and
only supplement missing details when retrieval
is insufficient. Finally, for differential evidence
generation with external LLMs, we use carefully
designed prompts to encourage the production of
option-discriminative evidence while preserving as
much neutrality as possible.
3.6
Differential Evidence-Based Inference
Upon obtaining the differential evidence set, the
target LLMs—typically distinct from the external
LLM used in the preceding step—infer the answers
to the medical MCQs using the following method:
Answer = TargetLLM(C, Q, O, D).
Here, C is the clinical context, Q is the question,
O is the set of original options, and D is the generated differential evidence. The target LLM takes
these components as input and produces the final
answer.
4
Experiments
In this section, we will introduce the dataset used in
the experiments, the LLMs employed to generate
anchor cues and evidence (External LLMs), and
the LLMs used for testing (Target LLMs). We then
answer the following research questions:
• RQ1:
Can differential evidence improve
model performance?
• RQ2: Does differential evidence provide benefits beyond generic auxiliary evidence?
• RQ3: Does differential evidence genuinely
support reasoning, or does it risk improving
performance by providing answer-proximal
guidance?

4.1
Datasets and Models
Datasets. We evaluate our method on MedQA
(Jin et al., 2021), MedXpertQA-Text (Zuo et al.,
2025), and MedBullets (Chen et al., 2025) because
together they provide a strong testbed for scenariogrounded, option-discriminative medical reasoning.
By contrast, some medical QA benchmarks, such
as PubMedQA (Jin et al., 2019) and MedMCQA
(Pal et al., 2022), generally feature shorter question
stems and are more oriented toward knowledgecentric medical question answering. Therefore,
they are less suitable for evaluating the scenariogrounded differential reasoning targeted in this
work.
External LLMs. Motivated by RAG2 (Sohn
et al., 2025), we view the external LLM as a differential evidence generator. Its quality mainly affects the generated evidence, which then influences
downstream reasoning. We tested several closedsource LLMs, including Claude-family models,
and selected GPT-5 mini (Singh et al., 2026) as
the evidence generator because it offered the best
overall trade-off among evidence quality, instruction following, cost, and API stability. To improve
reproducibility and assess dependence on closedsource models, we also tested open-source models.
Among them, DeepSeek-V3.2 (Liu et al., 2025a)
produced the most reliable differential evidence in
our experiments. We therefore report an additional
ablation using DeepSeek-V3.2 as the evidence generator.
Target LLMs. We evaluate our method on a series of open-source LLMs. These include Llama 3
(Grattafiori et al., 2024), Mistral (Mistral AI, 2025),
Gemma (Gemma Team et al., 2025) and Qwen 3
(Yang et al., 2025a). All experiments are conducted
through Amazon Bedrock under a unified inference
setup, using deterministic decoding. More details
are shown in appendix.
4.2
Performance of Differential Evidence
(RQ1)
We use four settings for the experiments: Baseline,
CoT, Differential Evidence and CoT + Differential Evidence . Baseline directly predicts the
answer from the original context, question, and
options. CoT uses the same input with an additional zero-shot chain-of-thought instruction. Differential Evidence further augments the input with
our generated option-specific differential evidence.
CoT + Differential Evidence setting simultaneously utilize CoT and differential evidence.
As shown in Table 1, the CoT + Differential
Evidence setting achieves better performance than
both Baseline and CoT across all five models. Notably, using Differential Evidence alone already
achieves performance close to CoT in many settings, indicating that the generated evidence itself
provides useful external knowledge and optiondiscriminative information.
We further examine whether the improvement is
tied to a single proprietary generator by replacing
GPT-5 mini with DeepSeek-V3.2 as the evidence
generator. Table 2 shows that DeepSeek-generated
evidence improves all five target models, increasing the average MedQA accuracy from 63.38% to
69.09%. While GPT-5 mini remains stronger on
average, the consistent gains from DeepSeek-V3.2
indicate that the benefits of differential evidence
are not exclusive to one generator, though generator
quality still affects the magnitude of improvement.

4.3
Benefits Beyond Generic Retrieved
Evidence and Generic Hints (RQ2)
To examine whether the gains of differential evidence go beyond simply adding more external text,
we compare two CoT-based settings: CoT + Text,
which directly appends the retrieved co-occurrence
paragraphs to the input, and CoT + Differential
Evidence, which instead provides the model with
compact option-specific differential evidence distilled from those retrieved materials.
As shown in Table 3, directly using the retrieved
co-occurrence text does not reliably improve performance. In many cases, CoT + Text even performs
worse than the CoT baseline, especially on MedQA
and MedBullets. By contrast, CoT + Differential
Evidence consistently yields positive gains over
CoT across all three datasets. This contrast suggests that the benefit does not come from merely
exposing the model to more retrieved content, but
from organizing external knowledge into a concise
and discriminative form that is more aligned with
multiple-choice decision making.
We further compare the output length of the two
methods using word count. As shown in Table 4,
differential evidence is substantially more compact
than directly concatenated retrieved text across all
three datasets. For example, on MedQA the average length decreases from 677.3 words for cooccurrence text to 108.5 words for differential evidence, with similar reductions on MedBullets and
MedXpertQA-Text. This suggests that the gain
of our framework comes not from adding more retrieved content, but from organizing external knowledge into a shorter and more discriminative form.
Moreover, the substantial number of non-empty cooccurrence retrievals suggests that our method is
supported by sufficient retrieved paragraphs, rather
than depending purely on the external LLM to fabricate evidence.
These findings indicate that generic retrieved text
can be too long, noisy, or weakly structured to effectively support reasoning, and may even distract
the model from the decisive clues in the question.
This observation is also consistent with prior studies reporting that directly concatenating retrieved
medical text often provides limited benefit and can
sometimes degrade performance due to irrelevant
or diffuse context (Kim et al., 2025). In comparison, differential evidence appears to make better
use of external knowledge by highlighting the most
distinguishing facts for separating competing options, rather than requiring the model to infer these
distinctions from raw retrieved paragraphs on its
own.
To test whether the gains come merely from
adding LLM-generated auxiliary medical text, we
construct a general-hint baseline using the same
GPT-5 mini generator. This baseline is conditioned
on the same anchor cues, question, and answer
options, but it does not use retrieved textbook cooccurrence chunks and is not instructed to identify
option-discriminative conditions. Instead, it asks
the generator to produce general option-level medical background notes.
As shown in Table 5, general hints provide only
a modest average improvement over the base setting, increasing MedQA accuracy from 63.38% to
64.71%. In contrast, differential evidence improves
the average accuracy to 71.31%. This gap suggests
that the benefit of our method is not simply due
to appending additional LLM-generated text, but
comes from organized differential evidence.
4.4
Reasoning Support or Answer-Proximal
Guidance? (RQ3)
We further investigate whether differential evidence
improves performance by genuinely supporting reasoning, or by introducing answer-proximal guidance (e.g., the evidence includes a sentence like
“The answer is ...”). To this end, we evaluate four
input settings on three datasets: only options (Only
O), only evidence (Only E), context + question +
options (C+Q+O), and context + question + options + evidence (C+Q+O+E).
Among these settings, C+Q+O serves as
the standard baseline, while C+Q+O+E tests
whether differential evidence provides additional
value beyond the original question input. The Only
O and Only E settings are included to analyze how
much predictive signal is contained in the options

We emphasize that differential evidence is expected to be answer-relevant; otherwise it would
not be useful evidence. The goal of this analysis
is therefore not to show that evidence contains no
predictive signal, but to test whether it collapses
into an answer shortcut.
5
Discussion and Conclusion
We present a differential evidence framework for
medical multiple-choice question answering. Experiments across three medical QA benchmarks
and multiple target models show that differential
evidence consistently improves direct answering
and further complements chain-of-thought prompting. Comparisons with general hints and retrieved
chunks suggest that the gains are not merely due
to adding extra generated text, but depend on the
quality and organization of the evidence. Leakageoriented analyses further indicate that differential
evidence is informative but does not function as a
standalone answer channel. Although our experiments focus on medical MCQs, the underlying
idea may apply more broadly to decision-making
settings where candidate hypotheses, plans, or actions are explicitly provided or can be enumerated,
and where a small number of discriminative facts
determine the final choice.

context+question+options (C+Q+O), and context+question+options+evidence (C+Q+O+E). Differential evidence
alone provides useful signal, but yields the strongest gains when combined with the original question context and
candidate options.
Limitations
Our study still has some limitations. First, our
framework depends on the quality of the external evidence generator.
Although GPT-5 mini
and DeepSeek-V3.2 produce useful differential evidence in our experiments, weaker generators may
produce overly generic, overly short, or answerproximal statements, reducing downstream gains.
In addition, while our prompts and leakage analyses aim to prevent the evidence from directly revealing the answer, subtle answer-proximal cues may
still occur, particularly in management and contraindication questions. Finally, our experiments
are limited to medical multiple-choice benchmarks
with explicit candidate options, and extending the
framework to open-ended or real-world decision
settings will require additional validation.
Ethical Considerations
This work evaluates evidence-based answering on
medical multiple-choice benchmarks. Benchmark
accuracy does not establish clinical safety or effectiveness. Generated evidence, including supplementation from a model’s internal knowledge,
may be incomplete, inaccurate, or biased. These
outputs should not be used as patient-specific medical advice or as a substitute for qualified clinical
judgment; clinical use would require independent
expert review and validation.
We used GPT-5 for limited drafting and language
editing assistance during manuscript preparation.
All technical content, experimental design, analysis, and final wording were reviewed and verified
by the authors, who take full responsibility for the
final paper.

A
Additional Detailed Results for RQ3
We report the full RQ3 results on all three
datasets in Appendix Table 6. We observe that
on MedXpert-Text, the evidence-only setting is relatively strong and for some models is comparable
to, or slightly better than, C+Q+O. A possible
reason is that the overall baseline performance on
this dataset is low, suggesting that the task is difficult for the tested models under the standard input.
In such cases, even a small amount of compact
external signal may lead to a noticeable gain. However, C+Q+O+E still yields the strongest overall
results, indicating that differential evidence is most
effective when combined with the original context.
B
Co-occurrence Retrieval Details
For external knowledge retrieval, we use the textbook corpus provided together with the MedQA
dataset (Jin et al., 2021). Besides the question data,
MedQA also releases reference textbooks that have
already been segmented into chunks, and we directly perform co-occurrence retrieval over these
pre-defined chunks. Since some chunks are overly
long, we additionally cap the length of each retrieved chunk at 400 words. When multiple chunks
satisfy the co-occurrence criterion for the same
anchor cue-option pair, we keep only the first retrieved chunk.
We also explored several retrieval variants, including BM25-based retrieval strategies for identifying anchor-option co-occurrence paragraphs. In
pilot experiments, these variants produced similar
downstream trends. Since retrieval in our framework mainly serves as a grounding constraint for
evidence distillation rather than as the final answerselection mechanism, we use a simple and reproducible retrieval strategy in the main experiments.
C
Implementation Details
We use a unified inference setup for all target models. For direct answer generation, we set max new
tokens =16; for CoT-based settings, we set max new
tokens =512 to allow sufficient space for intermediate reasoning. For decoding, we use temperature
=0.0 and top p=1.0 across all experiments.

Normalization
SYSTEM
You are an extractor for USMLE/MedQA-style
question stems.
USER

question stems.

- "Question": the full question stem
Task:
Identify:
1) `question`: the actual question being
asked, usually the final sentence
2) `entities`: up to 3 medical entities
extracted only from the context/background
part
Rules:
1) Use only the input stem.
2) Do not infer from answer choices.
3) Do not hallucinate image findings.
4) Do not output the context itself.
5) Extract entities only from the context,
not from the final question sentence.
6) Return at most 3 entities, choosing the
most answer-relevant ones.

D.3
Differential Evidence Generation
SYSTEM
You are a medical differential-evidence
generator for multiple-choice question
distillation.
USER
Input includes:
1. the original question,
2. anchor facts extracted from the clinical
background,
3. the answer options,
4. co-occurrence paragraphs between anchor
facts and options.
Task: For each option, generate one short
differential-evidence string that identifies
the option's most distinctive clinical
decision role in the setting of the
question.
Definition of differential evidence:
Differential evidence is a short,
option-specific clinical cue that places the
option on the most relevant decision axis
for this question, such as treatment role,
timing, mechanism, contraindication,
adverse-effect relevance, management
category, or typical use setting. It should
help distinguish the option conceptually
from competing options, but it must not read
like an answer explanation or a statement
about whether the option fits the case.
Guidelines:
- Use the original question only to infer
the general decision setting and the likely
clinical management axis.
- Do not restate or reconstruct the full
case.
- Use co-occurrence paragraphs as grounding
constraints when available.
- If no co-occurrence paragraph is
available, use internal medical knowledge
conservatively and keep it consistent with
the question setting.
- Prefer the option's most distinctive
decision role over generic drug summaries,
broad mechanism descriptions, or
nonessential side effects.
- For medications, prioritize therapeutic
role, management timing, treatment category,
or clinically important risk over general
pharmacology unless pharmacology is itself
the key distinguishing cue.
- Keep the evidence concise and focused.
- Write one sentence whenever possible.
Restrictions:
- Do not solve the question.
- Do not say or imply which option is
correct, incorrect, preferred, excluded, or
should be selected.
- Do not rank options.
- Do not copy the source text verbatim.
- Do not output reasoning steps, bullet
points, or extra commentary.
- Do not explain why the option matches or
fails to match the current case.
- Do not directly justify the statement
using the patient, vignette, described
findings, or anchor facts.
- Do not distinguish the option by saying
what it is not used for, not part of, or
less appropriate than.
- Avoid negative contrast constructions such
as: "rather than ...", "instead of ...",
"not part of ...", "not used for ...", "less
appropriate", "ruled out".
- Express the evidence as a positive
description of the option's own clinical
decision role.
- Avoid generic textbook descriptions that
are not useful for distinguishing the option
on the question's decision axis.
Output format:
Return only a JSON object mapping each
option label to its differential-evidence
string.
Each string should be a standalone concise
sentence.
[paste question, anchor cues, options and
co-occurrence paragraphs]
D.4
Answering with Differential Evidence
SYSTEM
You are taking a medical multiple-choice
exam.
USER
Use the question, options, and differential
evidence to choose the single best answer.
Differential evidence refers to the most
distinguishing evidence for each option,
that is, the evidence most useful for
separating that option from the competing
options.
Use the differential evidence as a set of
discriminative clues, and then look back to
the question context to identify the facts

evidence_passages.heading: ABSTRACT
evidence_passages.text:
ABSTRACT 
Digital twins are virtual replicas of physical entities and are poised to transform personalized medicine 
through the real-time simulation and prediction of human physiology. Translating this paradigm from 
engineering to biomedicine requires overcoming profound challenges, including anatomical variability, 
multi-scale biological processes, and the integration of multi-physics phenomena. This survey 
systematically reviews methodologies for building digital twins of human organs, structured around a 
pipeline decoupled into anatomical twinning (capturing patient-speciﬁc geometry and structure) and 
functional twinning (simulating multi-scale physiology from cellular to organ-level function). We 
categorize approaches both by organ-speciﬁc properties and by technical paradigm, with particular 
emphasis on multi-scale and multi-physics integration. A key focus is the role of artiﬁcial intelligence 
(AI), especially physics-informed AI, in enhancing model ﬁdelity, scalability, and personalization. 
Furthermore, we discuss the critical challenges of clinical validation and translational pathways. This 
study not only charts a roadmap for overcoming current bottlenecks in single-organ twins but also 
outlines the promising, albeit ambitious, future of interconnected multi-organ digital twins for wholebody precision healthcare. 
 
1. Introduction 
Digital twins are now widely seen as a transformative force in healthcare, promising to revolutionize 
personalized medicine by enabling real-time monitoring, predictive diagnostics, and optimized treatment 
strategies1,2. However, the transition from a promising concept to clinically viable tools remain a formidable 
challenge. This challenge requires moving beyond two dominant paradigms: conventional computational 
modeling, which often personalizes anatomy but relies on static, literature-derived functional parameters3, 
and general-purpose AI, such as foundation models, which have garnered signiﬁcant attention for broad 
pattern recognition but often prioritize generality over the deep personalization and interpretability essential 
for clinical trust4-7. The digital twin paradigm proposes a distinct, complementary solution. It is a technology 
fundamentally oriented toward building a patient-speciﬁc, data-assimilating, and dynamically evolving virtual 
replica. This is achieved by continually integrating individual clinical data with well-established mathematical 
and physical models, such as the Navier-Stokes equations for hemodynamics8 or the Monodomain/Bidomain 
models for cardiac electrophysiology9. By grounding predictions in known biophysical principles, the digital 
twin framework aims to deliver inherently personalized, interpretable, and actionable insights, directly 
addressing the limitations of purely data-driven or static modeling approaches10,11. 
 
Constructing such high-ﬁdelity, organ-speciﬁc digital twins confronts the immense complexity of human 
physiology. Unlike their industrial counterparts, which operate in controlled environments, biological digital 
twins must account for intrinsic patient variability, multi-scale interactions (from molecules to whole-organ 
function), and the integration of sparse, noisy, or incomplete clinical data15-18. This complexity reveals 
limitations in both foundational modeling approaches. While physics-based models provide essential 
mechanistic insight and interpretability, they often struggle with computational cost and incomplete biological 
knowledge. Purely data-driven AI models, conversely, may fail under data-scarce conditions and lack the 
interpretability required for clinical adoption19. To bridge this divide, hybrid approaches that synergistically

Digital Twin (DT) technology is revolutionizing healthcare by enabling real-time
monitoring, predictive analytics, and highly personalized medical care. As a key
innovation of Industry 4.0, DTs integrate advanced tools like artiﬁcial intelligence
(AI), the Internet of Things (IoT), and machine learning (ML) to create dynamic,
data-driven replicas of patients. These digital replicas allow simulations of disease
progression, optimize diagnostics, and personalize treatment plans based on
individual genetic and lifestyle proﬁles. This review explores the evolution,
architecture, and enabling technologies of DTs, focusing on their transformative
applications in personalized medicine (PM). While the integration of DTs offers
immense potential to improve outcomes and efﬁciency in healthcare, challenges
such as data privacy, system interoperability, and ethical concerns must be
addressed. The paper concludes by highlighting future directions, where AI,
cloud computing, and blockchain are expected to play a pivotal role in
overcoming these limitations and advancing precision medicine.

capabilities in predictive diagnostics, personalized treatment, workﬂow optimization, and

simulations and informed decision-making (2). In healthcare, DTs create virtual models of
individual patients by combining their health data, medical history, lifestyle, and genetic
information, helping doctors to foresee how diseases will progress, improve treatment
methods, and tailor care to each patient (3). The integration of DTs with AI, the IoT, and

1
Digital-Twins for Cardiovascular Health: Landscape Scenario
With the advent of data-driven models and AI methodologies, the construction of virtual models
of physical and engineering systems, previously based on computational mechanics, has ascended
to unprecedented levels of complexity. Not only data-driven modeling enables the use of virtual
descriptions of complex systems in a wider range of fields (biology, sociology, urban development,
etc.), but the interaction between the physical and the virtual systems is brought to a much more
sophisticated paradigm that takes the name of “digital twins” (DTs). The following definition is
provided in [88]:
A digital twin is a set of virtual information constructs that mimics the structure,
context, and behavior of a natural, engineered, or social system (or system of systems),
is dynamically updated with data from its physical twin, has a predictive capability,
and informs decisions that realize value.
The bidirectional interaction between the
virtual and the physical is central to the digital twin.
Beyond the predictive nature of virtual models, the (bidirectional) integration of data and
conceptualizations opens up a wealth of perspectives.
The virtual twin is not only a tool for
understanding the physical system and designing a better one, but also a “continuous-in-time”
decision-making support. One of the most promising and impactful fields where DTs are expected
to make a difference is medicine, as demonstrated by the abundant literature in the field [35, 110,
109]. In particular, cardiovascular diseases are of interest for at least two different reasons: (i)
they are still the most lethal diseases in the Western world [20]; (ii) mathematical modeling of the
cardiovascular system has an exceptional level of maturity and depth (see, e.g., [39, 114, 101, 99]).
Although the perspectives of DTs for understanding and curing cardiovascular diseases are
enormous [14, 24, 23, 110, 35], many aspects remain challenging for several reasons. In particular,
as noted in [110], mathematical models are well developed and advanced, yet they lack a rigorous
personalization. To be more precise, the cardiovascular apparatus features a hierarchy of components, which correspond to different physical scales. This hierarchy goes from the molecular level
(critical for understanding the electrophysiology of the heart), to the cellular level, the tissue level,
and the organ level, up to the systemic level. The interplay of these different scales has been a
challenge for applied mathematicians for decades, and led to the introduction of specific numerical methods, see, e.g., [38, 121, 102, 91]. On the other hand, the data collection and usage pose
significant challenges, both from the technological and the methodological point of view. In cardiovascular medicine, there are different types of data collected at different frequencies and, thus,
the “dynamical update” advocated by the definition of DT has different implementations. We may
have data from (i) wearable technologies, e.g., smart rings or smart watches, with measurements
almost continuous in time, (ii)
portable technologies, e.g., pressure measurement devices, with
daily (or more frequent) measurements, like home sphygmomanometers; (iii) noninvasive devices,
e.g., ultrasound (US), that can be collected rather frequently in principle, and finally, (iv) invasive
systems, e.g., computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), which can be
collected only sporadically. In general, the quality of the data is inversely proportional to their
frequency. The heterogeneity of the data and their frequency of collection are critical aspects to
address, as well as the intrinsic “multiscale-in-time” nature of many cardiovascular diseases, where
the time scale of a heart beat (order of seconds) impacts the development of the pathology over
weeks or months.
All these aspects challenge applied mathematicians and urge us to extend the concept of “mathematics for clinics” to unexplored territories. Currently, some of the most important keywords of
this process are: (i) personalization and (ii) synthesis. They concern the bidirectionality of the DT
system, being central both at the input (how do the data make a general model patient-specific?)
and at the output (how do the results of the model propagate to the patient?) of the virtual twin.
The concept of “personalization” may sound more in the realm of engineering than of mathematics,
as it is antithetical to the abstraction of a mathematical model, and of providing proofs of concept
at a general level. However, in our opinion, these steps (personalization and synthesis) present a
formidable number of challenges for the combination of deterministic and stochastic components,
and deductive and inductive reasoning. Only the best mathematical tools can provide trustworthy
answers to such challenges.

Abstract
Automated segmentation is routinely used as the first step in quantitative image-based
clinical workflows, where predicted masks are subsequently reviewed and corrected by human
operators.
Automated correction of the residual structural errors is currently addressed
one anatomy at a time, so the number of trained correctors scales with the number of
segmentation targets.
We present GRACE, a retrieval-augmented refiner that edits an
input mask under context drawn from a shared knowledge base of verified prior cases.
The refiner is trained once on a multi-organ corpus spanning compact organs, cavities,
branching vessels, and tumour lesions. In the held-out dataset-transfer evaluation, three
held-out datasets query a fixed knowledge base built from training data only. A separate
leave-one-anatomy-out experiment tests parameter-free index extension: verified cases of
an unseen solid organ enter the knowledge base, and the refiner stays frozen. A shapeaware retrieval projector ranks the neighbours. This light projection head sits on a frozen
multimodal encoder and maps embedding similarity to the shape agreement of the masks.
Thus, the knowledge base returns cases that the refiner can use as a shape prior. We evaluate
GRACE on 18 public datasets spanning CT, MRI and ultrasound, including three held-out
CT/MRI datasets for held-out dataset transfer, using nine refinement configurations and
seven upstream segmentors that span weak, mid, and strong operating regimes. We report
each change with the DSC of its input mask. On the weak tier, the input DSC is 0.386 and
GRACE adds up to +0.35 DSC. On a strong segmentor, the input DSC is 0.932 and the
mean change is small. Transfer to an imaging modality that is absent from training and
from the index is partial and depends on the anatomy. We present it as an open research
direction.
Our results suggest retrieval-conditioned refinement is a practical alternative
to anatomy-specific correction models. Open-source code and implementation available at
https://github.com/robustml-eurecom/grace.

evidence_passages.paper_title: DocTalk: Enhancing Medical Knowledge Retrieval via Fine-tuned Large Language Models for CDSS
evidence_passages.authors: Asad Gohar, Md Ariful Islam Mozumder, et al.
evidence_passages.heading: Abstract:-
evidence_passages.text:
DocTalk: Enhancing Medical Knowledge Retrieval via Fine-tuned Large 
Language Models with Chain-of-Thought Reasoning for Robust Clinical 
Decision Support 
Asad Gohar, Md Ariful Islam Mozumder, Moon-Il Joo, Hee-Cheol Kim 
Institute of Digital Anti-Aging HealthCare, Inje University, Gimhae 50834, Republic of 
Korea; 
Corresponding Author: heeki@inje.ac.kr 
 
Abstract:- 
Objective: The rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs) in healthcare has opened new possibilities 
for AI-assisted clinical decision-making; however, safe and effective deployment remains challenging becasue of 
hallucination and domain misalignment. This study introduces DocTalk, a doctor-assistive question-answering 
(QA) system designed to generate concise, chart-grounded responses from de-identified discharge summaries. 
Methods: We developed a high-fidelity data generation pipeline that produces 500 clinically relevant QA pairs 
through sentence-level decomposition, chain-of-thought-guided question formulation, and expert review. Six 
open-source LLMs, including three general-purpose and three biomedical models, were evaluated before and after 
parameter-efficient instruction tuning using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA). The framework integrates prompt 
engineering, in-context learning, and medically aligned evaluation to support factual and interpretable responses. 
Results: On DocTalk-QA, instruction tuning produced consistent improvements across lexical, semantic, and 
clinical fidelity metrics. The best-performing tuned model, Llama-3-Med42-8B, achieved ROUGE-L=0.40, 
BERTScore-F1=0.76, and UMLS-F1=0.49. To examine external generalization beyond the DocTalk-QA dataset, 
the two best-performing models, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Llama-3-Med42-8B, were evaluated on PubMedQA 
before and after instruction tuning. Accuracy improved from 0.931 to 0.977 for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and from 
0.935 to 0.943 for Llama-3-Med42-8B. 
Conclusion: DocTalk was deployed as a secure web-based platform for interactive EHR querying. These findings 
suggest that clinically grounded instruction tuning can improve medical QA performance and support practical 
clinical decision support. 
Keywords: DocTalk, Chain-of-thought, Clinical decision support, Large language model, Prompt engineering, 
In-context learning 
1. Introduction 
In recent era, a significant shift towards digital systems for managing medical systems has been observed. The 
electronic health records (EHRs) are most important, which have information of patient’s medical history, 
including diagnosis, medications, procedures, laboratory test results, and follow-up plans [1]. However, there are 
vast amount of unstructured medical data, posing challenges for efficient information extraction and using it for 
the right purpose. These types of documents are generated using complex language, which is difficult to 
understand for the patients. Therefore, this problem can be solved by generative artificial intelligence (AI) 
techniques, particularly large language models (LLMs), by automatic retrieval of structured clinical information 
from unstructured medical reports [2-5]. Recent LLMs have made substantial advancements in medicine,

While these methods demonstrate broad generalisation across anatomies and modalities, they are designed
for forward segmentation prediction rather than post-hoc correction and refinement. RAM (Terris et al.,
2026) extends the foundation-model paradigm to generic inverse imaging problems without task-specific
training, but operates in pixel space and does not explicitly exploit anatomical context for segmentation
correction.
Retrieval-augmented learning in medical imaging.
Retrieval-augmented learning (Lewis et al., 2020)
has recently been explored in medical AI for report generation (Xia et al., 2025; Xiong et al., 2024; Hsu
et al., 2025) and few-shot segmentation from retrieved annotated examples (Ahmed et al., 2026; Zhao et al.,
2025). In these settings, retrieval provides external knowledge to improve prediction or support inference.
In contrast, retrieval for direct segmentation refinement has received little attention.
GRACE retrieves
anatomically similar cases to provide inference-time context for correcting an existing segmentation.
Latent-space exploration in medical imaging.
Compact latent representations have become a standard paradigm for modelling anatomically plausible structures in medical imaging. Early formulations use
variational autoencoders (VAEs) as shape priors, learning latent manifolds of plausible organ shapes for
segmentation refinement and shape reconstruction (Painchaud et al., 2020; Larrazabal et al., 2020; Beetz
et al., 2022). Vector-Quantised VAEs (Razavi et al., 2019) and multi-scale volumetric encoders (Pinaya et al.,
2022; Fernandez et al., 2024) extended this framework to high-resolution 3D image and mask generation.
Latent diffusion models (Rombach et al., 2022) and, more recently, rectified flow models (Lipman et al.,
2023) enable efficient generative sampling directly in these compact latent spaces, making full-volume 3D
synthesis computationally tractable (Guo et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025a; Tang et al., 2025). Conditioning strategies have subsequently evolved from partial-noise editing, such as SDEdit (Meng et al., 2022), to
retrieval-guided generation, where retrieved exemplars provide structural guidance during sampling (Molino
et al., 2026). GRACE builds on this latter paradigm by performing class-filtered, shape-aware retrieval to
guide segmentation refinement, and supports deterministic pixel-space, deterministic latent-space, and latent
flow-based refiners within a unified framework.

evidence_passages.paper_title: RAG-Enhanced LLMs for Interactive Explainability in Clinical Decision Support Systems
evidence_passages.authors: Lorenzo Mannocci, Francesca Naretto, et al.
evidence_passages.heading: RAG-Enhanced LLMs for Interactive Explainability in CDSS
evidence_passages.text:
RAG-Enhanced LLMs for Interactive Explainability in CDSS
3
explanation of a machine learning model’s prediction into a structured summary
that aligns with a physician’s diagnostic workflow [23, 30]. More recently, LLMs
have been leveraged not only to translate explanations into natural language but
also to enrich them with contextual information drawn from their pre-trained
knowledge [36]. However, this approach introduces an additional layer of complexity and potential risk. LLMs are known to occasionally produce inaccurate
or misleading outputs, a phenomenon referred to as hallucinations [24]. Furthermore, these models typically do not provide access to the underlying sources
that support their responses, limiting transparency and traceability [27].
One promising approach to mitigating LLM hallucinations in XAI is the use
of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) [26]. RAG enhances LLM-generated
explanations by grounding them in an external, domain-specific knowledge base.
Instead of relying solely on the LLM’s pre-trained knowledge, RAG retrieves relevant information from a curated database to provide more accurate and reliable
explanations. In the context of XAI, RAG can address two critical challenges.
First, it reduces the risk of hallucinations by ensuring that explanations are based
on verified sources rather than probabilistic text generation. Second, it allows for
the integration of domain-specific knowledge, ensuring that explanations adhere
to established medical, legal, or financial guidelines. By leveraging RAG, AIgenerated explanations can be aligned more closely with experts’ expectations,
thereby increasing trust and usability in real-world applications.
In this work, we present, to the best of our knowledge, the first Clinical
Decision Support System (CDSS) that integrates standard predictive models
with XAI techniques and RAG-enhanced explanations. The proposed system
consists of three key components:
1. Predictive Model: A standard classifier, such as a neural network or a random
forest, that generates predictions based on patient data;
2. Explainer: An explanation method that provides insights into the model’s
decision-making process through feature importance-based explanations (e.g.,
LIME [39] and SHAP [28]), decision rules (e.g., LORE [19]) or exemplars and
counter-exemplars [18];
3. RAG-Based enhancer module: A module built on RAG that enhances explanations by grounding them in reliable medical knowledge, mitigating
hallucinations, and transforming traditional explanations into more humanreadable, context-aware formats. It also serves as an interactive tool, allowing
end users to ask specific questions and explore the patient’s clinical profile
in relation to the model’s predictions and explanations.
By combining standard classifiers with RAG-based explanations grounded in
verified medical sources, our system enhances the trustworthiness and domain
relevance of AI-driven medical decisions. This approach addresses key limitations of conventional XAI by providing interpretable, reliable insights tailored
to healthcare professionals. The study concludes with preliminary experiments
validating the proposed methodology.
