LeViT-UNet++: Towards Balanced Fine-Grained Details and Context for Efficient 
Medical Image Segmentation 
#Guoping Xu
1,2, Jinling Zhu
1, Liuyue Li
3 
1Hubei Key Laboratory of Intelligent Robot, School of Computer Science and 
Engineering, Wuhan Institute of Technology, Wuhan, Hubei, 430205, China 
2Key Laboratory of Symbolic Computation and Knowledge Engineering of Ministry 
of Education, Jilin University, Changchun, 130012, China 
3College of Computing and Data Science, Nanyang Technological University, 
Singapore, 639798, Singapore 
#Corresponding Author: xugp@wit.edu.cn 
Abstract 
Efficient medical image segmentation is essential for clinical applications requiring 
rapid and accurate delineation, including surgical navigation, radiation therapy, and realtime image-guided intervention. Despite substantial advances in convolutional neural 
networks and Transformers, achieving high segmentation accuracy with limited 
computational resources remains challenging. In particular, reducing model complexity 
often comes at the expense of fine-grained structural details and effective global context 
modeling, resulting in an unfavorable trade-off between computational efficiency and 
segmentation accuracy. To address this challenge, we propose LeViT-UNet++, an 
efficient encoder–decoder architecture designed to achieve a better balance between 
local detail preservation and global context modeling. Specifically, we introduce a Haar 
Wavelet Multi-Scale Downsampling (HWMD) module that explicitly decomposes feature 
representations into low- and high-frequency components and extracts multi-scale 
structural information to mitigate the loss of fine-grained details during downsampling. 
Furthermore, we develop a depthwise convolution-based decoder that efficiently 
integrates multi-scale global representations from Transformer blocks with local spatial 
features, enabling progressive feature refinement while reducing computational 
overhead. We evaluate LeViT-UNet++ on four medical image segmentation 
benchmarks—Synapse, ACDC, LA2018, and MSD Heart—using both 2D and 3D 
experimental settings. Extensive experiments show that the proposed approach yields 
competitive segmentation accuracy with a compact parameter footprint and fast 
inference speed. On the Synapse dataset, for instance, LeViT-UNet++ attains a DSC of 
76.57% with merely 8.025M parameters and an inference rate of 241.72 FPS, confirming 
its favorable accuracy–efficiency balance. This work demonstrates the effectiveness of 
integrating wavelet-based multi-scale feature extraction and lightweight local–global 
feature fusion for efficient medical segmentation. The source code will be publicly 
available at https://github.com/apple1986/levit_unet_pp. 
Keywords: medical image segmentation, light-weight network, convolution neural 
networks, transformer, wavelet transform, efficient segmentation

evidence_passages.authors: Guoping Xu, Jinling Zhu, et al.
evidence_passages.heading: 5. Discussion
evidence_passages.text:
5. Discussion 
LeViT-UNet++ was developed to improve the balance between segmentation 
accuracy and computational efficiency by addressing two complementary aspects of 
feature representation: structural information preservation during downsampling and 
computationally efficient feature integration during decoding. Specifically, HWMD 
incorporates Haar wavelet decomposition and frequency-specific multi-scale depthwise 
convolutions to retain complementary low- and high-frequency representations during 
the initial downsampling stage. Meanwhile, DLGD employs depthwise separable 
convolutions to progressively integrate local spatial features and global contextual 
representations while reducing decoder complexity. 
The experimental results across four medical image segmentation benchmarks 
demonstrate the potential of these complementary designs in both 2D and 3D 
segmentation settings. Compared with the original LeViT-UNet, the proposed 
architecture achieves notable improvements on the Synapse and LA2018 datasets while 
substantially reducing the number of model parameters. In particular, the parameter 
reduction is primarily attributed to the lightweight decoder design, whereas HWMD 
contributes to the preservation of complementary structural representations during 
feature extraction. These results suggest that improving architectural efficiency does not 
necessarily require sacrificing the representation of fine-grained structural information. 
Despite these promising results, the proposed architecture has several limitations 
that warrant further investigation. First, although LeViT-UNet++ achieves a favorable 
trade-off between segmentation performance and computational efficiency, its 
performance does not consistently surpass that of state-of-the-art segmentation 
methods, particularly those employing more sophisticated feature representation and 
fusion strategies. This suggests that improving computational efficiency while maintaining 
or further enhancing segmentation accuracy remains a challenging problem. One 
possible contributing factor is the limited adaptability of the current multi-scale feature 
fusion strategy. Specifically, DLGD progressively integrates local and global 
representations through concatenation-based fusion and skip connections. Although this 
strategy is computationally efficient, it may not fully capture the complex dependencies 
and complementary relationships among features at different spatial resolutions. More 
adaptive fusion mechanisms, such as attention-guided feature selection, content-aware 
feature aggregation, or learnable cross-scale interactions, may provide more effective 
ways to exploit complementary local details and global contextual information while 
preserving the lightweight nature of the architecture. Furthermore, knowledge distillation 
represents a promising paradigm for transferring knowledge from heavy, large-scale 
models into lightweight architectures such as our proposed LeViT-UNet++, which helps 
mitigate the requirement for massive annotated training samples in medical image 
segmentation. We hope these explorations will inspire further advances toward compact, 
data-efficient models for routine clinical workflows. 
Second, the evaluation was conducted on a limited number of publicly available 
benchmarks. Although these datasets cover different anatomical structures and imaging 
modalities, further validation on larger, more diverse, and clinically representative 
datasets is required to establish the robustness and generalizability of the proposed

architecture. In addition, its computational efficiency requires systematic evaluation 
across diverse hardware platforms and deployment settings, especially under real-world 
clinical constraints. Furthermore, the current feature fusion strategy mainly relies on 
concatenation and depthwise convolution, which may restrict its capacity to adaptively 
model complex interdependencies among multi-scale features. Accordingly, our future 
work will focus on developing more effective yet computationally economical multi-scale 
feature fusion schemes, extending evaluations to larger clinical datasets, and exploring 
the feasibility of deploying LeViT-UNet++ in resource-limited medical imaging scenarios. 
6. Conclusion 
This study presents LeViT-UNet++, a lightweight convolution–Transformer hybrid 
framework for medical image segmentation, aiming to balance segmentation accuracy 
and computational efficiency. It integrates the Haar Wavelet Multi-Scale Downsampling 
(HWMD) module to preserve fine-grained structural information and the Depthwisebased Local and Global feature fusion and learning Decoder (DLGD) to efficiently 
combine local spatial details with global contextual representations. Extensive 
experiments across four benchmarks (Synapse, ACDC, LA2018, and MSD-Heart) under 
both 2D and 3D settings demonstrate that LeViT-UNet++ delivers competitive 
segmentation performance with substantially reduced model complexity and favorable 
inference speed. These findings highlight the effectiveness of combining wavelet-based 
structural preservation with efficient local–global feature fusion, offering a promising 
solution for medical image segmentation in resource- and latency-constrained 
environments.

evidence_passages.authors: Guoping Xu, Jinling Zhu, et al.
evidence_passages.heading: Main Body
evidence_passages.text:
complementary properties of convolution and Transformer representations. In particular, 
convolutional operations are well suited to capturing local spatial structures and finegrained anatomical boundaries, whereas Transformer-based representations provide 
broader contextual dependencies. An effective and efficient segmentation architecture 
should therefore integrate these complementary representations while minimizing 
redundant computation during feature extraction and decoding. The LeViT-UNet [7] (see 
Figure 1 (c)) represents an early effort to bridge convolutional and Transformer-based 
representations for efficient medical image segmentation. Specifically, it adopts vanilla 
LeViT [8] (a lightweight hybrid convolution–Transformer backbone originally designed for 
image classification) as the encoder and convolution-based blocks as the decoder, 
seeking to achieve a favorable trade-off between segmentation accuracy and 
computational efficiency. Its core design is based on the observation that convolutional 
operations can efficiently extract local spatial representations, while progressive 
downsampling reduces the spatial resolution of feature maps. Transformer blocks can 
subsequently model long-range dependencies on these low-resolution representations 
with substantially lower computational cost than applying global attention at high spatial 
resolutions. This hybrid design therefore provides an efficient means of combining local 
feature extraction with global contextual modeling for medical image segmentation. 
However, LeViT-UNet-like architectures [3, 7, 9] still face two important limitations. 
First, their efficiency-oriented convolutional encoders rely heavily on progressive spatial 
downsampling to reduce computational cost and expand the effective receptive field. 
Although this strategy enables efficient hierarchical feature extraction, conventional 
downsampling operations, such as max pooling and average pooling, inevitably discard 
spatial information [10]. This information loss is particularly problematic for medical 
image segmentation, where accurate delineation often depends on subtle boundary cues, 
thin structures, and small anatomical regions. In particular, high-frequency components 
contain important fine-grained structural information that may be attenuated or lost 
during repeated spatial reduction [11]. Once these details are discarded at early stages, 
subsequent upsampling operations cannot fully reconstruct the original structural 
information. Therefore, an efficient segmentation architecture should not rely solely on 
spatial downsampling for computational reduction, but should also provide an explicit 
mechanism for preserving complementary fine-grained structural information 
throughout the feature extraction process. 
Second, convolution-based decoders suffer from notable computational 
redundancy in feature learning [12, 13]. Within the standard encoder–decoder 
architecture, the decoder gradually fuses features from its previous stage with skipconnected features from the matching encoder layer. Although skip connections help 
restore spatial details, their fusion commonly employs standard convolutions over highdimensional feature maps. This adds a large number of convolutional parameters and 
computation overhead in the decoding branch. Furthermore, concatenated encoder and 
decoder features often contain overlapping, redundant spatial representations, where not 
all signals are essential for faithful feature reconstruction. This motivates a core research 
question: can the decoder maintain the representational capacity of conventional

evidence_passages.paper_title: LeViT-UNet++: Towards Balanced Fine-Grained Details and Context for Medical Image Segmentation
evidence_passages.authors: Guoping Xu, Jinling Zhu, et al.
evidence_passages.heading: Main Body
evidence_passages.text:
convolutional feature fusion while drastically cutting its computational redundancy? 
To address these two challenges, we introduce two complementary architectural 
enhancements to preserve fine-grained structural information during encoder 
downsampling and improve computational efficiency in the decoder. First, we propose a 
Haar Wavelet Multi-Scale Downsampling (HWMD) module that combines Haar wavelet 
decomposition with parallel depthwise convolutions of different kernel sizes. Haar 
wavelet decomposition separates feature representations into low- and high-frequency 
components, capturing complementary structural information, while multi-scale 
depthwise convolutions extract spatial patterns across different receptive fields with 
limited additional computational cost. This design helps preserve fine-grained anatomical 
details during downsampling while maintaining efficient feature extraction. 
Furthermore, we develop a Depthwise-based Local and Global feature fusion and 
learning decoder (DLGD) that employs lightweight depthwise convolutional blocks [14] 
to progressively integrate global contextual representations from Transformer blocks with 
local spatial features propagated through encoder skip connections. By enabling efficient 
feature fusion and refinement, the proposed decoder reduces computational overhead 
while integrating complementary local and global representations. Together, HWMD and 
DLGD improve the balance between structural detail preservation, contextual 
representation, and computational efficiency. 
In summary, we introduce LeViT-UNet++, an enhanced version of our previous 
LeViT-UNet [7] that improves both the encoding and decoding processes for efficient 
medical image segmentation. The main contributions of this study are as follows: 
(1) We introduce a Haar Wavelet Multi-scale Downsampling module (HWMD) that 
combines wavelet-based information preservation with parallel depthwise convolutions 
at multiple scales. HWMD retains complementary structural information during spatial 
downsampling while providing multi-scale representations with limited computational 
overhead for the encoder. 
(2) We propose a Depthwise-based Local and Global feature fusion and learning 
decoder (DLGD) that efficiently integrates local spatial features from the convolutional 
encoder with global contextual representations from the Transformer. By leveraging 
lightweight depthwise convolutional blocks for progressive feature fusion and refinement, 
DLGD reduces decoder computational overhead while effectively integrating 
complementary local and global information. 
(3) We develop LeViT-UNet++, a convolution – Transformer hybrid encoder –
decoder framework that integrates HWMD and DLGD to jointly preserve fine-grained 
structural information, capture global contextual representations, and improve 
computational efficiency. 
(4) We conduct extensive experiments on four challenging medical image 
segmentation benchmarks covering both 2D and 3D segmentation scenarios. The results 
demonstrate that LeViT-UNet++ achieves a competitive balance between segmentation 
performance and computational efficiency compared with representative state-of-theart methods.

Sumeet Vadhavkar, Xiajun Jiang, Yubo Ye, Maryam Toloubidokhti, Linwei
Wang
Computational Biomedicine Lab Rochester Institute of Technology Rochester New York
USA
Abstract
A digital twin (DT) of a patient-specific heart offers significant potential in
personalized medicine. However, its rapid and dynamic adaptation to an
individual’s live data and its predictive capability after adaptation remains
a central challenge. We examine this challenge from its two building blocks:
DT formulation where mechanistic and data-driven models show competing
merits and limitations, and DT optimization strategies that are largely driven
by a reconstruction objective leading to un-identifiable models. We address
both bottlenecks via HAPI — an AI framework for building hybrid, adaptive,
and predictive DTs with three key enablers. First, HAPI constructs a physicsintegrated gray-box model in which an interpretable mechanistic backbone is
augmented by a neural component that models its residual to the observed
data. Second, rather than attempting to pre-encode all possible variations
in a static hybrid model, HAPI enables rapid on-the-fly adaptation of the
hybrid model to few-shot live data, achieved by feedforward meta-learners
realizing amortized inference of both mechanistic and neural parameters of
the hybrid model trained with predictive objectives. Finally, we show that
this adaptivity corresponds to the construction of a conditional generative
model (i.e., the hybrid DT) that endows it with theoretical identifiability and
thus strong performance in predictive scenarios. We demonstrate the proofof-concept of HAPI in cardiac electrophysiology using a hybrid monodomain
model with mechanistic reaction kinetics and neural graph diffusion. Across
synthetic and real-data studies, we show that HAPI’s mechanistic-neural

1. Introduction
Personalized in-silico heart models, such as those describing its electrophysiology (EP), have shown promises in improving personalized cardiac care
such as risk stratification, diagnosis, and treatment planning [39, 18, 11]. Towards their utility as a digital twin (DT) of the heart, there are two longstanding challenges. First, a DT needs to be dynamically and rapidly updated to
the live data of an individual, especially in their functional parameters. Second, once updated to the available data, the DT not only needs to be able
to explain the observed data but, more crucially, to support decision making
by predicting in scenarios beyond what are observed. Significant challenges
exist towards these two goals, which we summarize below from the lens of
DT formulation and DT optimization strategies.
In terms of DT formulation, earlier works have focused on physics-based
mechanistic models which, with their encoded principle of biophysics,
are adept at extrapolation in predictive scenarios [14, 6, 38, 17, 44, 32, 2,
53]. However, their computational cost raises challenges for rapid adaptation/personalization [40, 48]; furthermore, due to simplifications and imperfect knowledge, mechanistic models are often associated with a myriad of
assumptions that cannot be resolved by optimizing model parameters alone,
leaving significant challenges for uncertainty quantification [30, 26]. Alternatively, machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) offer computationallyefficient data-driven surrogates to approximate the input-output relationship in mechanistic models directly from data [20, 28, 54, 25]: due to the unavailability of in-vivo measurements of the quantities of interest, e.g., tissue
properties or spatiotemporal electrical activity of the heart [11, 5, 19], there
has been increasing efforts in learning these surrogates from data generated
from in-silico mechanistic models. While these data-driven surrogates are
much faster to deploy, they face significant challenges of generalizability and
interpretability: this includes both the simulation-to-reality gap they inherit
from the in-silico models used to train them, and their inherent struggle
to generalize and extrapolate due to bypassing the underlying biophysics.

4.3 Digital Twin-Guided Personalized Medicine 
The ultimate validation of organ digital twin technology lies in its capacity to improve clinical decision-making 
and patient outcomes. While widespread adoption is still emergent, several pioneering applications 
demonstrate the translational potential of this paradigm (Fig. 6). These successes typically involve a closedloop workﬂow: integration of multimodal patient data to personalize a biophysical model, execution of insilico trials to predict treatment response, and translation of the virtual insights into a clinical action. The most 
mature examples are found in cardiology and neurology, where model personalization is supported by rich 
functional imaging and electrophysiological data. In cardiovascular medicine, cardiac digital twins have 
advanced from research to clinical decision support, particularly in complex arrhythmia management133,155,156. 
The most notable clinical application is the planning of catheter ablation for atrial ﬁbrillation (AF) using patientspeciﬁc electrophysiological models. The optimal ablation strategy is determined through an iterative 
computational process: the digital twin simulates AF to locate initial ablation sites, perform virtual ablation, 
and then test the AF inducibility. This virtual ablation-and-test cycle repeats until AF can no longer be 
sustained, deﬁning a ﬁnal, personalized lesion set. In a proof-of-concept study with ten AF patients, this 
model-guided approach signiﬁcantly improved procedural success rates and reduced operative time 
compared to standard strategies156. A second, rapidly advancing application is in transcatheter aortic valve 
implantation, where biomechanical twins of the aortic root derived from CT are used to simulate device 
deployment, predict paravalvular leak risk, and optimize valve sizing and positioning preoperatively157.

evidence_passages.text:
PocketTSLM
Deployment settings for health time-series inference. Most time-series-to-language and wearablehealth language models are developed and evaluated in server-side or offline research settings
[10, 11, 19, 29], so privacy, latency, and per-query cost remain deployment constraints rather than
solved properties of the model. On-device LLM inference is an emerging direction, but it is tightly
constrained by memory and efficiency, including for clinical models [14, 15]. For privacy, federated
learning decentralizes training rather than inference [30], and fog execution keeps inference within
a trusted local network [31]. On-device, ODCSIS [32] runs a small language model on a phone
for human activity recognition, but injects sensors by serializing statistical features into text rather
than encoding the raw time-series data. PocketTSLM therefore targets a remaining deployment
constraint: soft-prompt TSLMs require embedding-level input and enough context headroom for raw
time-series windows, whereas text serialization preserves an unchanged token-level generation path
at the cost measured in §4. Prior work therefore covers time-series-to-language modeling, wearable
and physiological language systems, privacy-preserving inference, and on-device language models,
but not soft-prompt physiological TSLM inference fully on a consumer smartphone.
3 Methods
Reference model and migration strategy. PocketTSLM ports OpenTSLM-SP, the soft-prompt variant
of OpenTSLM, from PyTorch into an iOS/MLX-Swift runtime. The PyTorch reference does not run
in the target environment without reimplementation, as the model depends on framework-specific
modules and a generation path that accepts projected input embeddings. We migrate the model in
two stages: first from PyTorch to Python MLX, then from Python MLX to Swift MLX. This staging
separates framework-level parity from Swift runtime parity and provides a Python MLX reference for
the final port.
Soft-prompt architecture. The architecture receives channel- or lead-wise physiological time-series
windows, including the single-channel EEG (Sleep-EDF sleep staging) and 12-lead ECG (ECG-QA)
inputs evaluated in §4. A raw physiological time series is split by temporal position into fixed-length
patches and fed to a time-series encoder: a CNN patch encoder followed by a Transformer that produces
one embedding per patch (Fig. 1). Patch length, stride, z-normalization, and lead ordering follow the
OpenTSLM reference without modification.
A learned multilayer perceptron (MLP) projector maps the encoder outputs into the input space of a
frozen pre-trained LLM, Llama-3.2-1B in our deployment. The projected embeddings are interleaved
with the embedded text prompt as soft-prompt tokens, meaning continuous vectors are injected directly
into the model’s embedding sequence rather than vocabulary tokens. [11] Different LoRA adapters [33],
each roughly 1% of the model’s parameters, adapt the frozen backbone to the ECG and EEG tasks. The
selected adapter determines the modality-specific mapping used at inference. This representation-level
pathway reduces prompt length, as each time-series patch becomes one embedding, but it requires
the decoder forward pass to accept precomputed embeddings rather than only token identifiers.
Migration implementation. The first migration stage reimplements three OpenTSLM-SP components
in Python MLX: the TransformerCNNEncoder, the MLPProjector, and the interleave logic that inserts
projected time-series embeddings between text-token embeddings before the LLM forward pass. The

We present PocketTSLM, an on-device port of OpenTSLM-SP to MLX-Swift that evaluates whether
the soft-prompt pathway can run on a consumer smartphone without changing the reference model’s
greedy-decoding behavior. The port preserves the encoder-projector-LLM architecture while modifying
the on-device generation path to accept projected time-series embeddings. PocketTSLM is scoped as a
deployment and evaluation of on-device soft-prompt physiological time-series reasoning, not clinical
validation, autonomous medical action, or behavior-change efficacy. We contribute: (1) a method
for migrating soft-prompt TSLMs to MLX-Swift; (2) a numerical parity protocol that compares the
on-device implementation against the reference under greedy decoding; (3) an on-device contexteconomics benchmark comparing soft-prompt encoding with a text-serialized baseline on the same
backbone; and (4) a HealthKit-enabled iPhone demo that runs ECG and EEG reasoning locally without
sending health data off-device.
2 Related Work
Time-series interfaces for language models. Integrating time-series data into LLMs is an active
research area [17], with approaches spanning text serialization, model reprogramming, soft prompting,
and cross-attention fusion [18]. Text serialization preserves the ordinary token interface and has been
used for forecasting and wearable-health prediction [16, 19], but language models often struggle to
reason over numbers presented this way [20]. Since every serialized sample consumes vocabulary
tokens, long time-series windows can spend the same context window needed for instructions and
generated text. Reprogramming methods keep the language-model backbone frozen while aligning
time-series patches or text prototypes to the model input space [21, 22]. These methods show that
representation choice matters, but they primarily target prediction, classification, or forecasting rather
than natural-language rationales grounded in raw time-series data [16, 19, 21, 22]. Representationlevel fusion instead learns a time-series encoder whose embeddings are injected into the model as soft
prompts or cross-attention inputs, preserving free-form generation [23, 24]. OpenTSLM [11] uses this
approach for chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning [25], coupling a time-series encoder to a frozen LLM
through soft prompts and generating rationales for clinical time-series tasks. We port its soft-prompt
variant fully onto a smartphone and quantify the token, memory, and latency cost of soft prompts
against text serialization on the same backbone (§4).
Wearable and physiological time-series language systems. In personal-health and wearable sensing,
recent LLM systems often reason over derived variables, contextual summaries, or tool-generated
features rather than raw physiological time-series windows [10, 19]. SensorLLM and LLaSA align
inertial measurements with language outputs for human activity recognition and sensor question
answering, but they focus on motion sensing rather than physiological ECG or EEG interpretation [26,
27]. ECG-QA provides a benchmark for ECG question answering, and ECG-Chat trains an ECG-language
model for report generation and dialogue [28, 29]. These systems expand time-series language
modeling for health and wearables, but they do not establish whether a soft-prompt physiological
TSLM can run fully on a consumer smartphone.

evidence_passages.heading: 1 Introduction
evidence_passages.text:
PocketTSLM
1 Introduction
Consumer devices now collect physiological time-series data that were previously limited to clinical or
research environments [1, 2]. Smartwatch irregular-pulse notifications have been evaluated for atrial
fibrillation screening in large cohorts [3], phone-connected systems make electroencephalography
(EEG) acquisition more accessible [4], and passive wearable streams such as heart rate, sleep, and
activity have been used for infectious-disease surveillance, COVID-19 detection, and prospective
health-risk assessment [5–7]. In each case, measurements are captured close to the patient, but the
interpretation delivered to a patient or downstream system is often a label, score, or study endpoint.
Digital biomarker pipelines make this pattern explicit: continuous measurements are translated
into digital endpoints or biomarkers for evaluation and decision support [8]. Those outputs support
screening, monitoring, and study endpoints, but they do not explain the source time-series window itself.
Recent personal-health large language model (LLM) systems interpret wearable-derived sleep, activity,
and fitness data through natural-language coaching or insight generation [9, 10]. Therefore, patientfacing assistants, clinician review tools, and supervised health agents need descriptions grounded in
source time-series windows that can be retrieved, routed, summarized, or used to defer a response
when the evidence is insufficient.
Time-series language models (TSLMs) are designed for this time-series-to-language interface. They couple time-series encoders to language models and generate natural-language descriptions or rationales
from raw physiological time-series data such as electrocardiogram (ECG), EEG, and accelerometry [11, 12]. These outputs give software a text interface to sensor evidence while preserving the
temporal structure in the model input [11]. Time Series Language Models may enable systems that
reason over sensor windows rather than only aggregate features.
Personal-health LLM systems are important reference points, but they do not solve the deployment
problem addressed here: they reason over derived wearable data with large language models rather
than running a time-series-native model on the phone [9, 10]. When interpretation is served remotely,
personal physiological streams or derived sensor evidence must leave the device, making privacy and
secondary-use risks part of the inference pathway [13]. Server-side inference also adds a network
dependency and per-query compute cost. General on-device LLM work identifies limited device
memory as a central inference bottleneck [14]. Medical LLM benchmarks show the same tradeoff: local
inference improves the privacy and cost posture, while memory and efficiency become the limiting
constraints [15]. For physiological time-series data, moving inference onto the phone shifts the system
boundary: raw data can remain local, offline analysis becomes possible, and cloud storage is no longer
required for each query.
The main obstacle is representation rather than model size. Mobile LLM runtimes are built around
token-identifier input and do not expose a path for injecting precomputed embeddings, so a timeseries encoder’s output cannot be fed to the model directly. If the runtime cannot accept encoder
embeddings, the time-series data must be serialized as text. Text serialization reuses an unchanged
language-model interface and can cast time series as next-token prediction [16], but it expands
each sample into multiple vocabulary tokens, formats or rounds numeric values, and spends the
same limited context window needed for instructions and generated text. OpenTSLM soft-prompt
(OpenTSLM-SP) avoids that prompt-level bottleneck by using representation-level fusion: a time-series
encoder projects time-series windows into soft-prompt embeddings that are injected directly into the
LLM’s embedding sequence [11]. That design is better matched to physiological time-series data, but

(CDHI), University of St. Gallen, Switzerland
Correspondence mrosenbl@stanford.edu · Code github.com/SchmiedmayerLab/PocketTSLM · Code license MIT
Abstract
Consumer phones and wearables increasingly collect physiological time-series data, yet most mobile systems
treat these streams as summaries or text rather than as temporal evidence. This representation is poorly
matched to personal health systems that need to retrieve, route, or summarize sensor evidence while preserving
temporal structure. Cloud-hosted time-series language models avoid smartphone limits, but they repeatedly
move sensitive physiology off the device and add latency and per-query compute cost. Mobile model alternatives
that aggregate time-series data into statistical features or serialize raw samples as text either compress temporal
structure or exhaust the context and memory budgets of small on-device models. We present PocketTSLM, a
mobile-native deployment of OpenTSLM SoftPrompt, the soft-prompt variant of the OpenTSLM time-series
language model. PocketTSLM runs fully on a consumer smartphone by injecting encoded time-series windows
as embeddings instead of tokenizing time series as text. A numerical parity protocol verifies identical greedydecoded token sequences between the Swift port and a Python reference using Apple’s MLX machine-learning
framework. Answers also match the PyTorch reference, although rationale wording can differ. An on-device
context-economics benchmark compares the soft-prompt path with a text-serialized baseline on the same
backbone. In our benchmark format, soft-prompting uses approximately 12× fewer time-series tokens and
reduces prompt-prefill cost. PocketTSLM processes 30-second Sleep-EDF electroencephalography clips for sleep
staging and a 1,000-sample (10 s) 12-lead electrocardiogram clip from ECG-QA. In comparison, text-serialized
baselines exceed the phone’s context or memory budget at longer time-series windows. All inference runs
entirely on the device, with no health data transmitted during inference.
A version of this paper was accepted at the Workshop on Deploying AI in Healthcare (DAIH) at the Conference on
Language Modeling (COLM 2026).

5 Limitations and Future Evaluation
The present evaluation establishes implementation parity and on-device context economics. The
OpenTSLM study included clinician review of ECG rationales from its model family [11], and our
numerical parity protocol (§3) confirms identical greedy-decoded token sequences between the Swift
port and the Python MLX reference. Decoded answers also agree with the PyTorch reference, although
rationale wording can differ under bf16 arithmetic. This supports implementation equivalence for
the evaluated prompts, but it does not constitute new clinical validation. The benchmarks use fixed
Sleep-EDF sleep-staging samples [34, 35] and ECG-QA samples [28] rather than prospective HealthKit
data from patients. Consumer wearable time-series data may include sensor noise, lower or variable
resolution, missing data, device-specific preprocessing, and population shift not captured by these
samples. Prospective studies with real-world wearable time-series data, clinical review, institutional
review board (IRB) approval, and predefined safety boundaries are needed before patient-facing or
clinical use.
On-device deployment remains bounded by measured memory and effective prompt budget. We use
Llama-3.2-1B, as it fits the target device while supporting the adapted OpenTSLM-SP pipeline. Larger
backbones were not evaluated and may exceed the memory budget of current smartphones in this
architecture. Quantization and future hardware may increase feasible model and input size, but the
present claim is limited to the 1B backbone, the evaluated device class, and the soft-prompt path
tested here. Tablets such as the iPad Pro may relax the thermal and memory constraints observed on
the phone. The evaluation also covers only the soft-prompt fusion pathway. Cross-attention fusion,
as in Flamingo [18] and OpenTSLM-Flamingo [11], is an alternative embedding-level interface, but
it modifies the decoder’s internal attention layers rather than only the input-embedding sequence
adapted here; porting and benchmarking it on device is left to future work.
Local inference reduces exposure from routine cloud inference, but it does not remove governance
obligations. In the current demo, inference runs on the device and HealthKit data are not transmitted
during inference. Whether Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), General Data
Protection Regulation (GDPR), or other privacy requirements apply depends on the deployment context,
data controller or covered-entity role, consent model, logging, export behavior, and downstream data
flows. The local design also changes monitoring trade-offs. If deployed without central telemetry,
performance surveillance and drift detection would require privacy-preserving reporting, local audit
mechanisms, or supervised clinical review rather than server-side logs. Pre-deployment parity testing
can confirm that the port preserves reference behavior before evaluation, but it is not a substitute for
real-world monitoring.

evidence_passages.text:
Operation-aware Multimodal Clinical Decision Support System
for ICU Discharge Risk Assessment
Guoqing Zhang,1 Rafik Hadfi,1 Takayuki Ito1
1Graduate School of Informatics, Kyoto University, Kyoto, Japan
zhang.guoqing.27t@st.kyoto-u.ac.jp, rafik.hadfi@i.kyoto-u.ac.jp, ito@i.kyoto-u.ac.jp
Abstract
Unplanned 30-day intensive care unit (ICU) readmission following hospital discharge is a major benchmark for evaluating healthcare quality and patient safety in modern critical
care medicine. Most existing predictive approaches assume
that readmission risk is determined solely by a patient’s individual pathophysiological state, ignoring the institution’s
resource capacity and operational context (Hospital Operational Context). In clinical practice, discharge decisions are
frequently dynamic trade-offs made by intensivists balancing patient medical stability against ward bed turnover pressures. To address this gap, we design an Operation-aware
Multimodal Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS) for
ICU discharge risk assessment. On the one hand, the system unites multi-agent collaborative extraction with selfevolving retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to eliminate
formatting-template noise across lengthy progress notes. On
the other hand, it constructs departmental workload indicators (icu_speedup_los) alongside admission flow characteristics, unifying continuous vital signs, hierarchical sparse
medical codes (ICD/DRG), and discharge summary semantics. Addressing the extreme class imbalance (∼10.5% readmission incidence) and the challenge of alarm fatigue, the
system implements data normalization, class reweighting optimization, and an F1 decision-threshold calibration pipeline.
In 20 independent multi-seed runs conducted on a cohort of
20,000 ICU stays from MIMIC-III, empirical findings show
that: a single-modality baseline depending exclusively on vital
signs possesses limited predictive capacity under real-world
class imbalance (PR-AUC of only 0.1387 ± 0.0086); directly concatenating raw text embeddings causes performance
degradation in decision tree models (XGBoost and LightGBM PR-AUC drop to 0.3893 and 0.4030, respectively);
whereas an end-to-end multimodal fine-tuning architecture
(Transformer E2E FineTune) utilizing layer-wise parameter
freezing and differential learning rates successfully reverses
text negative transfer, achieving the overall highest AUROC
of 0.8288±0.0110, PR-AUC of 0.4373±0.0310, and a competitive F1-Score of 0.4757±0.0196. Mechanistic attribution
analyses also confirm that operational indicators supply independent risk signals, establishing an engineering foundation
for deploying high-utility clinical decision support tools in
bedside hospital wards.

S1
Introduction
In intensive care clinical decision-making, identifying vulnerable patients at risk of latent deterioration and avoiding
premature step-down to general wards are core imperatives of
critical care medicine. Patients experiencing unplanned ICU
readmission within 30 days of discharge undergo substantially prolonged hospital stays and face elevated in-hospital
mortality (Klinge et al. 2020; Barbieri et al. 2020; Sheetrit,
Brief, and Elisha 2023). While recent multicenter investigations confirm the promise of machine learning for postdischarge surveillance (Lim et al. 2025), existing clinical
early warning systems commonly encounter barriers during
ward deployment due to alarm fatigue: in low-prevalence
locales where readmissions occur in only ∼10% of cases,
typical models optimized for high AUROC tend to trigger
substantial false-positive alarms, prompting clinicians to turn
off the alert systems. To construct an actionable Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS), one must preserve screening
sensitivity while substantially improving precision, thereby
driving PR-AUC and F1 scores toward clinically acceptable
operating points.
Although electronic health record (EHR) repositories such
as MIMIC-III (Johnson et al. 2016) have advanced machine learning in critical care—spanning deep temporal focus (Madinei, Keyvanpour, and Shojaedini 2024), graphical
EHR representations (Choi et al. 2020), and recent readmission benchmarks (Fathy, Emeriaud, and Cheriet 2025)—
state-of-the-art predictive models still encounter two fundamental deployment bottlenecks. First, they exhibit a neglect
of hospital operational context. Standard models conceptualize patients as closed physiological entities, presuming that
deterioration following transfer stems entirely from built-in
disease progression. In clinical practice, however, ICU discharge is fundamentally a resource deployment and scheduling process carried out under institutional bed constraints
(Kim et al. 2015; Wagner et al. 2013; Long and Mathews
2018). Intensivists must routinely weigh incomplete physiological recovery against acute bed demands driven by emergency department (ED) boarding or post-operative transfers.
Patient transfer frequency before ICU admission, ED boarding durations, and ward acceleration driven by bed saturation
directly mirror operational workflow strain and care coordination friction; yet, customary doctrines remain entirely
agnostic to this systemic background. Second, models suffer

icu_speedup_los (early turnover) significantly correlates with higher readmission risk (20.1% continuous IG attribution). This refutes indication confounding and confirms
that the metric captures external operational bed-turnover
pressure and premature discharge before complete physiological stabilization.
Third, hierarchically decoupled sparse medical codes
(xcode
i
) capture hierarchical EHR coding structures (Choi
et al. 2020). Primary ICD diagnoses and primary DRG codes
select the Top-128 categories, mapped into categorical indices feeding a learnable continuous embedding layer (128
dimensions). Secondary diagnoses (Top-32), surgical procedures (Top-64), and prescribed medications (Top-64) are
encoded into multi-hot sparse vectors, projected through embedding weight matrices, mean-pooled across active entries,
and concatenated into compact representations.
Fourth, unformatted clinical progress representations
(xtext
i
) incorporate free-text clinical progress notes. In contrast to standard clinical text baselines (Lu, Nguyen, and Dou
2021; Helmy et al. 2025) that directly process progress notes
vulnerable to template noise, lengthy inpatient records are
distilled via self-evolving multi-agent workflows into structured summaries, with 768-dimensional semantic features
extracted by Bio_ClinicalBERT (Alsentzer et al. 2019).
S3
Operation-aware CDSS Architecture
S3.1
Unstructured Text Mining: Multi-Agent
Self-Evolving RAG Mechanism
Orchestrated multi-agent architectures sustain diagnostic fidelity under complex clinical workloads compared to monolithic models (Klang et al. 2026). To overcome verbosity
and repetitive administrative boilerplate in clinical progress
notes, the system establishes a self-evolving multi-agent distillation pipeline across five coordinated stages: (i) Hierarchical Specialist Collaboration: Clinical text is segmented
across 7 specialized clinical domains (Nursing, Radiology,
ICU Care, ECG, Attending Physician, Discharge Summary,
and Echocardiography), where independent domain agents
extract acute warning signals. (ii) Meta-Agent Synthesis: A
supervisory Meta-Agent aggregates domain summaries, synthesizing a structured JSON report containing a prioritized
vital factor roster and composite risk score. (iii) Reflective Evolution Loop: When predictions diverge from clinical ground truth during training, a Reflection Agent audits causal failure points, extracting physician-vetted heuristic rules into a knowledge base (3,085 rules); correctly
classified trajectories are cataloged as gold-standard exemplars (1,899 cases). (iv) Lightweight RAG Retrieval: Guided
by all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings and a FAISS index, the pipeline dynamically retrieves the Top-5 relevant heuristic rules and Top-1 exemplar case per admission as few-shot in-context demonstrations. (v) Feature Embedding & Projection: Distilled summaries are encoded
by Bio_ClinicalBERT into 768-dimensional contextual
vectors and projected to a d-dimensional embedding Enote
aligned with temporal representations.
S3.2
Cross-Modal Network Architecture and
Deep Fusion Schemes
The framework investigates three architectural paradigms.
First, we evaluate tree-based baselines: XGBoost (Chen and
Guestrin 2016) and LightGBM (Ke et al. 2017) fitted on
physically concatenated vectors combining temporal statistical aggregations, static covariates, multi-hot codes, and 768dimensional text embeddings (Chen et al. 2025). Second,
we construct sequential late fusion (LSTM Late Fusion):
a 4-layer bi-directional LSTM with self-attentive temporal
pooling encodes physiological sequences, concatenated at
the classification tier with static, code, and text representations projected via independent MLP branches. Third, we
formulate parallel multi-branch extraction and late fusion.
Dynamic physiological sequences are encoded via a deep
Transformer encoder (Vaswani et al. 2017) into Zcls; static
operational indicators and medical codes are mapped via independent MLPs into dense vectors Eops and Ecode. These
representations are concatenated with text embedding Enote
to form Zfused = [Zcls ∥Eops ∥Ecode ∥Enote] ∈R2d+64,
feeding a 2-layer MLP head for joint risk estimation. To prevent representational collapse during end-to-end training, the
initial 8 layers of Bio_ClinicalBERT are frozen, leaving deeper layers (Layers 9–12) active; BERT parameters
receive a 0.1× scaled learning rate (lr * 0.1) with gradient checkpointing enabled.
S3.3
Training Optimization and Leak-Free
Validation Protocols
To ensure leak-free evaluation under severe class imbalance (∼10.5% prevalence) and achieve stable multimodal convergence, we institute four disciplined methodological
safeguards:
(i)
Zero-Leakage
Normalization:
StandardScaler parameters are fitted strictly on training splits; validation and testing cohorts inherit these statistics without re-estimation, precluding distribution leakage.
(ii) Dynamic Cost-Sensitive Loss: To counter minority-class
sparsity, a weighted binary cross-entropy loss deploys dynamic inverse class ratio weighting derived strictly from
the training split: wpos = Nneg/Npos ≈8.97. (iii) Cosine
Scheduling & Rollback: A CosineAnnealingLR schedule regulates learning rate decay, paired with early stopping (patience=15) on validation loss; upon termination,
model parameters rollback to the checkpoint achieving the
minimal validation loss. (iv) Decision Threshold Calibration: On validation splits, exhaustive grid search (step size
0.01) determines the optimal decision cutoff t∗maximizing
the F1-Score, replacing the uncalibrated default 0.5 threshold
for final test evaluation.
S4
Experimental Evaluation and Validation
S4.1
Evaluation Protocol and Cohort Setup
Experiments are run across 20,000 ICU stay records from
the MIMIC-III database. The cohort is partitioned into training (14,000 stays), validation (2,000 stays), and test splits
(4,000 stays) in a 7:1:2 ratio, with positive readmission prevalence ranging from 10.5% to 11.4%. To eliminate partitioning anomalies, all candidate approaches are evaluated across

evidence_passages.text:
from data disparity and text template noise. Intensive care
records span high-frequency temporal streams, sparse diagnostic codes, and lengthy unstructured progress notes. While
recent studies explore medical text via knowledge graphs
(Lu, Nguyen, and Dou 2021) or multimodal architectures
for readmission prediction (Helmy et al. 2025; Datta et al.
2025), clinical free-text is often lengthy, laden with jargon,
and burdened by copy-pasted administrative templates. Directly feeding unadapted high-dimensional text embeddings
fails to yield meaningful gains and instead introduces severe
feature interference (negative transfer) with strong baselines
such as gradient-boosted decision trees.
To resolve these problems, we reframe ICU discharge
evaluation as an operationally aware multimodal decisionsupport task and develop a CDSS architecture that encompasses self-evolving textual distillation and deep cross-modal
correlation. The core contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:
• Operation-aware Decision Framework: Overcoming randomized timestamp offsets in MIMIC-III, we introduce unit-benchmarked turnover deviation indicators
(icu_speedup_los) and care flow complexity features, eliminating the subjective assumption that outcomes depend solely on physiological status.
• Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Text Distillation: We formulate a 7-domain specialist agent collaborative division
of labor paired with a reflective evolutionary experience
repository, accumulating 3,085 rules across 5,000 patient samples. Combined with FAISS vector retrieval for
structured information distillation, we propose a layerwise, frozen, end-to-end fine-tuning scheme that systematically mitigates interference from template noise in clinical notes.
• Thorough Testing under Low-Prevalence Conditions:
Across a cohort of 20,000 ICU stays, we conduct 20 independent randomized multi-seed runs (Seeds 42–61),
exposing the weakness of single-modality physiological
prediction (PR-AUC of only 0.1387) and verifying the
robustness of the end-to-end fine-tuning architecture in
achieving global optimality (AUROC 0.8288, PR-AUC
0.4373, F1 0.4757).
• Interpretability & Clinical Utility Analysis: Through integrated gradients (Sundararajan, Taly, and Yan 2017),
we systematically explain the mechanistic contributions
of separate physiological channels, pivotal time-based attention windows, and operational flow variables in 30-day
readmission forecasting.
S2
Clinical Workflow and Problem
Formulation
S2.1
Clinical Prediction Task and Endpoint
Definition
The prediction target is unplanned ICU readmission within
30 days following discharge (30-Day Readmission). In light
of complex intra-hospital patient trajectories, endpoint labels
yi ∈{0, 1} follow strict clinical mutually exclusive criteria:
• Cross-admission readmission: The patient undergoes a
separate hospital admission and enters an ICU within
30 days post-discharge (same SUBJECT_ID, distinct
HADM_ID).
• Within-admission readmission: During the same hospitalization episode, the patient is transferred out of the
ICU, deteriorates, and is subsequently readmitted back to
the ICU (multiple ICU stays under the same HADM_ID,
where the subsequent admission timestamp postdates
the preceding transfer timestamp, i.e., INTIMEk+1 >
OUTTIMEk).
• Mortality Mutual-Exclusion: Patients who suffer inhospital mortality (HOSPITAL_EXPIRE_FLAG = 1)
have their readmission risk strictly calibrated to 0, eliminating logical contradictions.
S2.2
Multimodal Clinical Data Streams and
Domain Alignment
For each ICU stay event i ∈{1, . . . , N} (experimental cohort N = 20, 000), the input is structured as a heterogeneous
quadruple:
Xi =

(S1)
First, for high-frequency dynamic physiological sequences
(Xseq
i
∈R48×8), the system captures 8 core physiological
signs during the initial 48 hours following ICU admission:
Heart Rate (HR), Respiratory Rate (RR), Oxygen Saturation (SpO2), Systolic Blood Pressure (SBP), Diastolic Blood
Pressure (DBP), Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP), Temperature (Temp), and Blood Glucose (Glucose). Blood pressure
measurements explicitly distinguish invasive arterial pressure from non-invasive cuff pressure; when both coexist, the
invasive arterial line—the gold standard in critical care—is
preferred. Time series are resampled into 1-hour regularized
bins, with missing steps forward-filled.
Second, structured demographic and operational indicators (xstat
i
∈R15) capture baseline patient context and care
delivery friction across three facets: (i) Baseline & Surgical
covariates include age, gender, marital status, ethnicity, insurance, admission source/type, first ICU unit, surgical procedure count, surgery binary indicator, and log-transformed
surgery-to-ICU entry gap ln(1 + ∆tsurg). (ii) Transfer Patterns track the number of ward transfers prior to ICU admission (pre_icu_transfers) along with log-transformed
emergency department wait time ln(1+tED). (iii) Ward Pressure & Turnover Deviation: addressing the obstacle where
randomized absolutetimestamps inMIMIC-III precludeconcurrent bed occupancy observation across patients, we formulate a stay deviation metric aligned with historical unit
benchmarks (e.g., MICU, SICU) along with stay duration

icu_speedup_los = LOSunit −LOSactual

computed at the exact moment of the step-down transfer
order, sharing the same temporal cross-section with discharge notes and precluding future information leakage. Crucially, contrary to the naive assumption that shorter stays

risk driver rather than exogenous noise. Fourth, threshold
calibration is indispensable against alarm fatigue: in lowprevalence settings (∼10%), default 0.5 thresholds collapse
precision; dynamic validation-set grid search for t∗is mandatory to avoid alert abandonment.
Two-Stage Deployment Roadmap: Real-world EHR systems
are optimized for legal archiving rather than machine learning, and critical care cannot tolerate trial-and-error on live patients. We propose a two-stage deployment pathway: “NearTerm Silent Shadow Verification, Long-Term Clinical Digital
Twins.” In the near term, the CDSS interfaces non-intrusively
with EHR discharge order streams in Silent Shadow Mode
to quantify the utility of human-artificial intelligence collaboration. In the long term, longitudinal EHR repositories
enable high-fidelity Clinical Digital Twins simulation sandboxes (Li et al. 2024), allowing multi-agent architectures to
undergo safety stress-testing in a parallel digital ward before
deploying high-assurance decision policies at the bedside.

Comprehensive Performance Comparison
and Paradigm Defense
Table S1 summarizes the evaluation measures across 15
model configurations evaluated at their optimal F1 decision
thresholds across 20 randomized runs. Three core empirical insights emerge. First, we observe text negative transfer in shallow concatenation. Directly appending unadapted
768-d text embeddings into decision trees (XGBoost/LightGBM) triggers notable performance decline. Inpatient notes
are saturated with administrative templates and boilerplate
shorthand; high-dimensional embeddings diffuse greedy tree
node splitting, diluting compact, high-SNR physiological
and operational signals. Second, results demonstrate the
strength of structured baselines and multimodal reframing.
Purely structured LSTM Base establishes a solid benchmark (F1 = 0.4798), demonstrating the fitting efficiency of
recurrent cells over 48-hour dynamics along with discrete
codes. The multimodal goal is therefore not to surpass structured models trivially, but to resolve a harder clinical challenge: safely incorporating high-value text semantics without
suffering negative transfer (as observed in Transformer EarlyFusion, which degrades under raw text noise). Third, we
achieve a reversal of negative transfer via end-to-end finetuning. With layer-wise parameter freezing (Layers 9–12 active) and differential learning rates, Transformer E2E
FineTune is the sole architecture reversing text negative
transfer into positive gains, securing global peaks in both
AUROC (0.8288) and PR-AUC (0.4373). Paired hypothesis tests across 20 matched random seeds confirm that the
AUROC gain of end-to-end fine-tuning over static early fusion is highly statistically significant (mean AUROC 0.8288
vs. 0.8177; Paired t-test t = 4.89, p < 0.001; Wilcoxon
p < 0.001). This provides strong empirical evidence that
end-to-end backpropagation prevents the text representation
from being overshadowed by dense temporal dynamics, enabling the language model to better align textual risk cues
with structured physiological trajectories.

From AI-Enabled Remote Patient Monitoring Toward 
Agentic Robotics: Embodiment, Governance, and 
Care Integration 
Ivana Ragusa,1,2 Lorenzo Guiducci,1 and Filippo Cavallo1,2 
1Department of Industrial Engineering, University of Florence, Florence, Italy; email: filippo.cavallo@unifi.it 
2CoAImed S.r.l., Sesto Fiorentino, Florence, Italy 
Keywords 
remote patient monitoring, RPM, artificial intelligence, agentic AI, embodied AI, healthcare 
robotics, AI governance, digital health 
Abstract 
AI-enabled remote patient monitoring is evolving beyond passive data collection toward agentic 
AI systems that interpret patient states, coordinate care, and initiate action across domestic and 
clinical settings. This structured scoping review finds that mature agentic care has not yet emerged: 
Most systems remain human led, while stronger decision–action coupling and embodied AI remain 
largely confined to prototypes and pilots. Healthcare robotics makes the transition from monitoring 
to action especially visible by translating AI-generated recommendations and decisions into 
speech, movement, prompting, physical assistance, escalation, and care coordination, making 
embodiment, clinical integration, human oversight, and governance fundamental design 
requirements. Further progress requires safe and interoperable care architectures in which 
intelligent components operate through clinically validated and accountable workflows. We 
propose agentic robotics as a future direction for supervised systems embedded in the care 
ecosystem, connecting AI agents and robots with clinicians, caregivers, and patients through 
auditable workflows that can be interrupted and remain subject to human oversight and explicit AI 
governance.

3
systems must implement a full perception–inference–decision–action loop under strict safety and 
reliability requirements. Remote care is one of the most demanding instantiations of this problem 
because it addresses adverse events such as falls, nonadherence medication, dementia and 
cognitive decline, chronic disease progression, mental health crisis, and social isolation. These 
situations unfold in homes where sensory and contextual information is often incomplete and 
responsibility is distributed across patients, caregivers, clinicians, and devices. 
With the maturation of IoT and AI, the focus progressively shifted toward more complex care 
architectures that integrate data through interoperable and standardized systems, enabling context 
awareness and decision support. More recently, advances in robotic technologies have introduced 
the Internet of Robotic Things (IoRT) paradigm (6), which connects robots with distributed sensing 
and AI-enabled infrastructures allowing monitoring to lead to situated interaction and action (7). 
This evolution is further reinforced by emerging agentic AI approaches, which increase the 
potential for autonomous planning, adaptation, and coordination across home care services (8). 
From this perspective, robotics becomes a key enabling technology when AI-enabled remote 
healthcare must move beyond digital inference to act directly in the physical environment. Robots 
provide AI with an embodied presence, enabling sensing and reasoning to guide situated acting in 
domestic environments. This embodiment creates technical, architectural and governance 
challenges for remote setting, since safe and meaningful deployment depends on interoperable and 
accountable systems that are clinically relevant, and acceptable to users, caregivers, and healthcare 
organizations. This article therefore examines how robotic embodiment is incorporated into AIenabled remote patient monitoring (RPM), ambient assisted living (AAL) and remote or 
distributed care architectures, with particular attention to how architecture and governance shape 
the transition from monitoring to real-world care action. 
Robotic prototypes were included in the core corpus only when embedded in, or explicitly 
specified as part of, an architecture connecting sensing and inference with monitoring, decision 
support, actuation, escalation, or governance. Accordingly, the observed prevalence of 
embodiment refers in particular to architecturally integrated robotics within AI-enabled 
RPM/AAL corpus and should not be generalized to healthcare robotics as a whole. Complete core 
and background corpus registries, including the embodied robotic subset, are provided in 
Supplemental Tables 19–21. 
Addressing the growing interest in agentic AI for healthcare , this structured scoping review, 
treating agency as a system-level property of the care architecture, maps how sensing, inference,

supports monitoring, prediction, alerting, or decision support while humans retain responsibility 
for clinical action. Findings from the small embodied subset require cautious interpretation, 
physical embodiment is neither a prerequisite for higher decision–action coupling nor sufficient to 
make a system deployable. More specifically, the evidence shows that embodied systems are 
disproportionately associated with higher decision–action coupling. Unlike a dashboard, a robot 
can turn AI output into situated physical or social behavior through speech, movement, prompting, 
navigation, manipulation, and interaction with patients or caregivers. Embodiment therefore 
makes the transition from monitoring to action visible while raising the burden of safety, oversight, 
validation, and accountability. 
The temporal trend supports this interpretation. Earlier RPM/AAL systems made care more 
visible through cloud monitoring, dashboards, and rule-based alerts. Edge–hybrid architectures 
then moved inference closer to patients and homes, while predictive machine learning improved 
detection without necessarily changing authority. More recent systems have explored distributed 
and decision-capable ecosystems in which AI models, sensors, devices, robots, clinicians, 
caregivers, and users coordinate bounded care action. The field is therefore redistributing 
intelligence across a care ecosystem rather than progressing linearly from rules to machine learning 
and autonomous control. 
The evidence map supports the governed, ecosystem-embedded care robot as a prospective 
design horizon. We use the term “agentic robotics” to describe this prospective horizon beyond 
the maturity levels observed across the corpus. Agentic robotics refers to a multiagent care 
architecture in which artificial agents, robotic embodiments, clinicians, caregivers, and patients 
share perception, decision support, action, and accountability across a supervised care loop. Within 
this architecture, robots operate through clinically validated action policies appropriate to their 
intended use and level of risk, with explicit human authority over clinically consequential 
decisions. Their agency derives from participation in a context that makes action informed, 
constrained, traceable, and accountable. By integrating patient and environmental sensing, 
distributed inference, clinical and caregiver knowledge, local interaction, and governance, such 
architectures could strengthen perception and adaptation in unstructured home environments. In 
this model, embodiment provides AI with a situated interface to daily life, while ecosystem 
integration prevents situated action from becoming isolated, opaque, or unsafe. 
This design horizon extends beyond the maturity demonstrated by the reviewed systems. Those 
with the strongest decision–action coupling remain below sustained deployment, while

while remaining far from deployable in real care settings. Associations between embodiment and 
higher decision–action coupling were explored using a two-sided Fisher’s exact test, comparing 
A0–A1 with A2–A3 systems. Odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals were reported. 
Together, SIDAG, A levels, and M levels allowed us to apply the same analytical question 
across dashboards, AAL platforms, telecare systems, IoRT configurations, and embodied robots: 
Where does the system stop along the sensing-to-action chain, and what happens when inferred 
patient state is translated into care-relevant action? Robotic embodiment was therefore treated not 
as a topic separate from RPM but rather as a particularly demanding case of agentic remote care, 
because physical or social action requires architectural integration, human oversight, safety 
constraints, auditability, and accountability. 
Bibliographic and conceptual information was extracted from all 113 included records using a 
61-field extraction form covering bibliographic metadata, screening decisions, study 
characteristics, technology details, governance, limitations, gaps, and provenance. System-level 
SIDAG, A-level, M-level, embodiment, architecture, and governance coding was applied to the 
93 core system papers used for corpus-level synthesis. AI-assisted extraction was introduced only 
after human consensus had finalized eligibility decisions and preliminary classifications and was 
limited to the postconsensus enrichment of empty or incomplete extraction fields. Human-entered 
values were preserved as authoritative, and all AI-generated fields were flagged for human 
verification before analysis. 
3. EVIDENCE MAP: EMBODIMENT IN THE TRANSITION FROM MONITORING TO 
CARE ACTION 
3.1. The Remote Patient Monitoring Baseline: Monitoring Matures Before Agency 
The broader RPM/AAL corpus establishes the baseline against which the robotic signal becomes 
meaningful. Across 93 core systems, decision–action coupling was concentrated at A1. 67 papers 
(72.0%) described systems that analyze, alert, or recommend while humans retain authority over 
care action. Only 22 systems (23.7%) reached A2 or A3, where the system proposes, coordinates, 
prepares, triggers, or executes care-relevant action. Validation maturity shows a parallel 
concentration before deployment. 52 systems (55.9%) remained at prototype or laboratory level 
(M1), 30 (32.3%) reached pilot or real-user validation (M2), and only 4 (4.3%) reached sustained 
real-world deployment (M3).

prepared to participate in health monitoring and self-management following discharge. During the post-discharge 
phase, the pathway incorporates structured follow-up through RPM, scheduled check-ins, and proactive responses 
to system-generated alerts. Municipal healthcare services play a central role in monitoring incoming data, responding 
to deviations from expected health parameters, and maintaining regular contact with patients. By enabling earlier 
identification of potential deterioration, the redesigned pathway supports timely intervention and may contribute to 
reducing the risk of hospital readmission. 
 
Figure 9: Norway redesigned care pathway matrix 
The redesigned matrix for Romania (Figure 10) provides a structured overview of the patient pathway, from the onset 
of symptoms and initial assessment through hospital admission, discharge, and return home. The redesigned 
pathway highlights the integration of remote patient monitoring (RPM) into post-discharge care, with the aim of 
strengthening continuity of care and supporting coordination between patients and healthcare professionals 
following the transition from hospital to home. Patients are recruited during hospitalization once they are considered 
clinically ready for discharge. At this stage, patients and their families receive training in the use of home-monitoring 
devices and the transmission of clinical data, enabling them to actively participate in post-discharge monitoring and 
follow-up. A key feature of the redesigned pathway is the maintenance of continuous communication between 
patients and the clinical team after discharge. Patients transmit daily health data collected at home, which are 
reviewed by healthcare professionals. When clinically appropriate and feasible, treatment plans may be adjusted 
remotely based on the information received. This approach supports the early identification of changes in a patient's 
clinical status and promotes timely intervention when required. Overall, the redesigned pathway aims to reduce 
fragmentation of care by establishing a more continuous and coordinated follow-up process after discharge, thereby 
strengthening continuity of care and supporting safer transitions from hospital to home.
